This move aligns the bank’s operations with circular economy principles, providing customers with a way to support environmental sustainability through their everyday financial choices. Commenting on the launch, Managing Director/CEO Senarath Bandara said: “This sustainability initiative is a continuation of the bank’s Corporate Sustainability Goals (CSG), reflecting a deep-seated commitment to reducing the environmental footprint of traditional banking operations. The successful realisation of this eco-friendly product was made possible through the technical and production expertise of Lake House Printers and Publishers PLC, alongside the global payment technology leadership of Mastercard. Together, these partners have ensured that the Ocean Plastic card meets the highest international standards of durability and security while remaining an emblem of environmental responsibility.” Chief Manager - Cards Services Shihan Pathiraja added: “From an operational standpoint, transitioning to ocean-bound plastic was a meticulous process to ensure that sustainability did not compromise functional excellence. We have integrated this eco-friendly material into our existing debit card infrastructure seamlessly, ensuring that our customers enjoy the same high-speed transaction capabilities and global acceptance they expect from Cargills Bank. This product allows our cardholders to carry a piece of our conservation mission in their pockets, turning every point-of-sale interaction into a statement of environmental advocacy.” To further drive awareness and community engagement, Cargills Bank will be providing extensive visibility for this initiative across its social media channels, inviting customers to become active participants in the bank’s journey toward a greener future. This launch underscores the bank’s belief that modern financial services must not only be innovative but also ethically aligned with the preservation of the planet for future generations.

audit.headline: Corrugated carton industry under growing cost pressure
audit.summary: Sri Lanka’s corrugated carton industry is facing mounting financial pressure as the cost of paper and other essential inputs continues to rise. For many manufacturers, the challenge is no longer simply maintaining profitability; it is ensuring the industry’s sustainability. While several packaging sectors have adjusted their prices in response to rising costs, corrugated carton manufacturers initially took a more cautious approach. Many held prices steady, expecting global supply-chain disruptions, geopolitical tensions and commodity-price increases to ease. That relief has yet to arrive. Instead, the prices of key paper grades used in carton production, including Kraft Liner, White Liner, Test Liner and Medium, have continued to climb by 30-50% across different paper grades.
audit.body: Sri Lanka’s corrugated carton industry is facing mounting financial pressure as the cost of paper and other essential inputs continues to rise. For many manufacturers, the challenge is no longer simply maintaining profitability; it is ensuring the industry’s sustainability. While several packaging sectors have adjusted their prices in response to rising costs, corrugated carton manufacturers initially took a more cautious approach. Many held prices steady, expecting global supply-chain disruptions, geopolitical tensions and commodity-price increases to ease. That relief has yet to arrive. Instead, the prices of key paper grades used in carton production, including Kraft Liner, White Liner, Test Liner and Medium, have continued to climb by 30-50% across different paper grades. Manufacturers are also contending with higher costs for energy, transport, chemicals, starch, inks, labour, maintenance and other operating needs in line with growing inflation and global market realities. Together, these increases are placing the sector under severe strain. Manufacturers have worked to absorb as much of the additional cost as possible while continuing to serve customers at competitive prices. They have reduced waste, improved machine efficiency, managed energy use, optimized transport and strengthened production productivity. These efforts have helped, but they cannot offset rising costs indefinitely. Paper accounts for a substantial share of the cost of producing corrugated cartons. Even a modest increase in paper prices can significantly affect the final cost of a carton; when prices rise across all major grades, the cumulative impact is considerable. This leaves manufacturers caught between escalating costs and intense competition. Customers need affordable packaging, while producers must recover enough to maintain quality, invest in machinery, retain skilled employees and deliver reliably. The consequences could extend well beyond the carton industry. Corrugated cartons are an essential part of Sri Lanka’s manufacturing and export supply chain. Food and beverage producers, tea exporters, agricultural businesses, apparel manufacturers, pharmaceutical companies and many others depend on a reliable supply of quality cartons. If carton manufacturers face growing financial difficulties, the effects may spread across these industries. Higher packaging costs could also weaken Sri Lanka’s export competitiveness, particularly when local exporters are already competing with producers that may have better access to raw materials or lower production costs. The sector is therefore calling for a realistic understanding of the pressures it faces. Manufacturers did not rush to raise prices when costs first began to rise. They waited, hoping conditions would improve and paper prices would return to more sustainable levels. Instead, the pressures have persisted. A responsible adjustment to carton prices may now be necessary, not simply to improve margins, but to help ensure that manufacturers can continue operating sustainably. The challenge is to balance customers’ need to manage costs with the need for carton manufacturers to remain financially viable. The industry is not asking for an easy solution; it is asking for recognition of the realities facing the sector. A sustainable corrugated carton industry is essential to Sri Lanka’s manufacturing and export sectors. Preserving it will require cooperation among paper suppliers, manufacturers, customers, exporters and policymakers. Without appropriate market adjustments, continued cost pressures could have consequences far beyond the carton industry itself.

audit.headline: Fitch assigns ‘A-(EXP)(lka)’ rating to Asia Asset Finance’s proposed debentures
audit.summary: Fitch Ratings yesterday assigned Asia Asset Finance PLC’s (AAF) proposed Sri Lankan rupee-denominated subordinated listed debentures of up to Rs. 3 billion an expected National Long-Term Rating of ‘A-(EXP)(lka)’. AAF is rated ‘A+(lka)’ with a Stable Outlook. The debentures are likely to have a five-year maturity and will be listed on the Colombo Stock Exchange (CSE). AAF plans to use the proceeds to strengthen its Tier 2 capital base, the secondary layer of regulatory capital, and to support loan-book expansion. The final rating is subject to Fitch receiving final documentation that conforms to information already received. The proposed debentures are rated two notches below AAF’s National Long-Term Rating. Fitch said it applied its Bank Rating Criteria in rating the instrument, as it believes the prudential capital framework for Sri Lankan finance companies is closer to that for banks.
audit.body: Fitch Ratings yesterday assigned Asia Asset Finance PLC’s (AAF) proposed Sri Lankan rupee-denominated subordinated listed debentures of up to Rs. 3 billion an expected National Long-Term Rating of ‘A-(EXP)(lka)’. AAF is rated ‘A+(lka)’ with a Stable Outlook. The debentures are likely to have a five-year maturity and will be listed on the Colombo Stock Exchange (CSE). AAF plans to use the proceeds to strengthen its Tier 2 capital base, the secondary layer of regulatory capital, and to support loan-book expansion. The final rating is subject to Fitch receiving final documentation that conforms to information already received. The proposed debentures are rated two notches below AAF’s National Long-Term Rating. Fitch said it applied its Bank Rating Criteria in rating the instrument, as it believes the prudential capital framework for Sri Lankan finance companies is closer to that for banks. The expected rating reflects Fitch’s baseline notching for loss severity for this debt class and its expectation of poor recoveries in the event of default. Fitch applied no additional notching for non-performance risk, as the debentures do not contain going-concern loss-absorption features, meaning they cannot be written down or converted to equity while the company continues to operate. AAF’s own National Long-Term Rating reflects Fitch’s expectation that its majority shareholder, India-based Muthoot Finance Ltd (MFL), rated ‘BB+’ with a Stable Outlook, would provide extraordinary support to AAF if needed. Fitch based this view on MFL’s 78.4% shareholding, its record of ordinary equity support, and the strategic and operational alignment between parent and subsidiary in their core product, gold-backed loans. Even so, the agency assesses AAF’s strategic importance to MFL as limited, given the subsidiary’s small size, modest role and contribution, limited brand sharing and operations in a different jurisdiction. AAF’s standalone credit profile does not drive the rating, and Fitch assesses it as significantly weaker than the support-driven rating. As the subordinated debt rating is linked to AAF’s National Long-Term Rating, which is in turn driven by expected support from MFL, Fitch said any upgrade or downgrade of AAF’s National Long-Term Rating would lead to a corresponding upgrade or downgrade of the expected subordinated debt rating.

audit.headline: How can public sector become more customer-centric?
audit.summary: - Transforming public service into a culture of responsiveness, accountability and trust Putting the citizen at the centre of governance The public sector is one of the most influential institutions in the daily lives of Sri Lankan citizens. From obtaining a birth certificate, national identity card, passport or driving licence to registering a business, securing a building permit, receiving healthcare, accessing education or obtaining social welfare benefits, citizens depend on public institutions at almost every stage of their lives. Yet, for many people, dealing with a government institution can be an exhausting experience. Long queues, multiple visits, complex procedures, excessive documentation, unclear requirements, delayed decisions and the absence of reliable information can turn what should be a straightforward public service into a frustrating ordeal.
audit.body: - Transforming public service into a culture of responsiveness, accountability and trust Putting the citizen at the centre of governance The public sector is one of the most influential institutions in the daily lives of Sri Lankan citizens. From obtaining a birth certificate, national identity card, passport or driving licence to registering a business, securing a building permit, receiving healthcare, accessing education or obtaining social welfare benefits, citizens depend on public institutions at almost every stage of their lives. Yet, for many people, dealing with a government institution can be an exhausting experience. Long queues, multiple visits, complex procedures, excessive documentation, unclear requirements, delayed decisions and the absence of reliable information can turn what should be a straightforward public service into a frustrating ordeal. In some instances, citizens may feel that they must adjust to the convenience of the institution rather than expect the institution to respond to their needs. This raises an important question: How can the public sector in Sri Lanka become more customer-centric? Customer-centricity is the practice of designing and delivering services around the needs, expectations and legitimate interests of the people who use them. In the public sector, the term customer does not mean that citizens are merely consumers purchasing a product or a service. Citizens are rights-holders, taxpayers, stakeholders and, ultimately, the owners of the democratic institutions that serve them. Consequently, public-sector customer-centricity must go beyond courtesy at service counters. It must become a fundamental principle of public administration, policymaking, service delivery and institutional accountability. Sri Lanka needs a public service that does not merely administer rules but helps citizens navigate them; that does not simply process applications but resolves people›s problems; and that does not measure success by the number of files completed but by the value created for the public. Achieving this transformation requires a change in institutional culture, leadership, employee competencies, operating procedures, technology, performance measurement and public accountability. Above all, it requires a fundamental shift in mindset: ‘from government serving itself to government serving the people’. Customer-centricity must be driven from the top and embedded throughout the management system Redefining the purpose of the public service The first step towards customer-centricity is to redefine the purpose of public service. Traditionally, many public institutions have operated around administrative structures, departmental responsibilities, established procedures and hierarchical authority. These are important elements of governance, particularly where legality, financial discipline and procedural fairness are concerned. However, they can become obstacles when compliance with internal procedures takes precedence over the legitimate needs of citizens. A customer-centric public service begins by asking a different set of questions: nWhat does the citizen need to achieve? nWhy is the service necessary, and can the process be simplified? nHow much time, money and effort must the citizen expend? nCan the service be delivered more quickly without compromising legality or fairness? nHow can the institution make the experience more accessible, transparent and predictable? nHow can the service be provided in an efficient and transparent manner? Consider a citizen applying for a government certificate. A process-oriented institution may focus on whether the correct form has been completed and submitted to the relevant officer. A customer-centric institution will examine the entire experience, from explaining the requirements and accepting the application to communicating progress and delivering the certificate. The distinction is significant. The first approach concentrates on the institution›s responsibilities; the second considers the outcome experienced by the citizen. Sri Lanka should therefore establish customer-centricity as a core public-service value, alongside integrity, impartiality, professionalism, efficiency and accountability. Every Ministry, department, provincial council, local authority and public agency should understand how its work contributes to the public good and how citizens experience its services. Professionals of the ‘Lanka Reformist Forum’ stand ready to volunteer support to Government Institutions to enhance efficiencies toward customer centricity. This principle must also apply to services delivered by state-owned enterprises and public utilities. Whether a person is dealing with a government hospital, a local authority, a public transport service or an electricity provider, the expectation of fair and respectful treatment should remain consistent. Changing the mindset: From administrative authority to service responsibility A customer-centric public service requires a fundamental change in the relationship between public officials and citizens. Public officials exercise authority on behalf of the state. That authority is necessary to enforce laws, collect revenue, protect public resources and ensure public safety. However, authority must never become an excuse for indifference, discourtesy or unnecessary bureaucratic control. The public servant’s role should be understood as one of responsible service. An officer must apply the law correctly while helping the citizen understand the process and complete the required transaction. For example, when an application is incomplete, the officer should explain precisely what is missing and how the applicant can correct it. Simply rejecting the application, without adequate explanation, may satisfy a narrow procedural requirement but does little to create a positive service experience. Similarly, a person seeking assistance from a public institution should not be passed from one department to another without guidance. Where another agency must act, the responsible officer should explain the next steps and, where practicable, facilitate the referral. This change in mindset must be driven by senior leadership. Ministers, ministry secretaries, department heads and institutional leaders must demonstrate through their decisions and behaviour that service quality matters. Employees will not take customer-centricity seriously if their leaders reward procedural compliance alone while ignoring delays, complaints and poor treatment of citizens. Public service is not about exercising power over the public. It is about exercising public authority responsibly, fairly and in the public interest. Every public institution should appoint a senior officer accountable for service improvement, supported by a cross-functional team representing operations, human resources, information technology, finance and frontline service delivery Simplifying bureaucratic procedures and reducing red tape One of the most immediate ways to improve public-sector customer-centricity in Sri Lanka is to simplify administrative procedures. Over time, institutions often accumulate forms, approvals, signatures, supporting documents and internal checks. Some are essential for legal compliance and the prevention of fraud. Others may have survived simply because they have always been part of the process. The government should conduct a systematic review of high-volume public services to identify unnecessary steps, duplicated documentation, excessive approval levels and avoidable delays. Every procedure should be examined against three questions: 1.Is this requirement legally necessary? 2.Does it serve a clear public-interest or risk-management purpose? 3.Can the same purpose be achieved through a simpler, faster and less costly method? 4.Can this purpose be achieved with lesser resources and in less time? Where information is already held by a government agency, citizens should not routinely be required to submit the same information again, subject to appropriate legal authority, privacy safeguards and data accuracy. Inter-agency information sharing should reduce the burden on citizens rather than transfer the administrative burden from one public office to another. The objective should be to make the simplest lawful route the normal route. Process simplification must not, however, become an excuse to weaken financial controls, bypass procurement rules or disregard due process. A good system eliminates unnecessary bureaucracy while retaining the controls needed to protect the public interest. The result should be a public service that is easier to navigate, less expensive to operate and better able to deliver timely decisions. Establishing clear service standards and citizens› charters Citizens should not have to guess how long a public service will take, what documents are required or whom they should contact when a problem arises. Every public institution should publish a practical Service Charter that sets out its principal services and the standards citizens can reasonably expect. nA useful charter should specify: nThe services provided and the eligibility requirements. nThe documents and fees, if any, required for each service. nThe expected processing time and the conditions that may affect it. nThe officer or unit responsible for handling the request. nThe available methods of accessing the service. nThe complaint and escalation procedures. nThe institution’s commitments concerning respectful treatment, confidentiality and accessibility. These commitments must be realistic, measurable and visible. Publishing a charter is not sufficient; institutions must monitor their performance against it. For example, if an agency commits to processing a complete application within ten working days, it should record the submission date, monitor the progress of the application and identify the reasons for any delay. If a deadline cannot be met, the applicant should receive an explanation and an updated expected completion date. Service standards should distinguish between the time an application is under the institution›s control and time genuinely required from an applicant or another agency. This prevents institutions from improving reported performance simply by excluding difficult cases. They should be displayed at service centres and published online in accessible formats. A Service Charter is more than an information document. It is a public commitment that makes service expectations visible and creates a basis for accountability. Building a digitally enabled, integrated public service Digital transformation offers Sri Lanka a significant opportunity to improve customer experience while reducing administrative costs. Citizens should increasingly be able to obtain information, submit applications, make authorised payments, track progress, receive notifications and obtain documents through secure digital channels without repeatedly visiting government offices. However, digitalisation must not merely reproduce existing bureaucracy on a computer screen. If a citizen must upload the same documents to several disconnected systems, print an online application and take it to an office for a manual signature, little meaningful improvement has occurred. Since a citizen-centric government should therefore pursue end-to-end digital service delivery, supported by interoperable systems and redesigned business processes, the current Government has taken a step forward to initiate the groundwork for a Trade National Single-Window System. This TNSWS is long-overdue and Kudos to the Government for taking the bold step to initiate it. The NTSWS will digitally enabled public service to incorporate the following features: A single point of access: Citizens will be able to find reliable information about relevant government services through a well-organised digital portal, even when several institutions are involved. This system will render a paperless and cashless trading platform. Public institutions must also protect whistleblowers and people who report improper conduct, in accordance with applicable law. Employees should feel able to raise concerns about dysfunctional processes, unethical practices and risks to public resources without fear of retaliation. It is unfortunate, however, that whistle-blowers do not have protection under the Companies Act No.7 of 2007 The benefits to our people will include Single submission of information: Where legally permitted, information provided once will be reusable by authorised public agencies, reducing repetitive documentation. Application tracking: Applicants will be able to determine whether their applications have been received, are being processed, require additional information or have been completed. Secure electronic transactions: Appropriate services will support digital payments, electronic acknowledgements and authenticated delivery of documents. Proactive communication: Citizens will receive timely notifications about appointments, missing information, decisions and expected completion dates. Interoperability: Government systems will exchange authorised information through secure, governed arrangements instead of forcing citizens to act as couriers between agencies. Sri Lanka’s Trade National Single Window initiative provides a useful context for this principle. Where traders must interact with multiple regulatory agencies, an integrated digital service can reduce duplicated submissions, improve visibility and make trade-related procedures more predictable. The same underlying philosophy can inform other public services. Nevertheless, technology must serve citizens rather than exclude them. Older people, persons with disabilities, residents of rural areas and those without reliable internet access or digital skills may need assisted digital services or traditional service channels. Digital transformation should offer citizens more choices, not create new barriers. The ultimate objective is a government that is digitally capable but remains human-centered. Developing a service-oriented public-sector workforce No public-sector reform can succeed without the commitment and competence of the people responsible for implementing it. Public servants work under different conditions, and many demonstrate considerable dedication despite limited resources, outdated systems and heavy workloads. Therefore, customer-centric reform should not assume that every service failure results from an unwillingness to serve. Some problems arise from inadequate training, unclear responsibilities, poor work design, staffing shortages or systems that make efficient service difficult. The government must address these issues through a comprehensive human resource development strategy. First, customer service competencies should be developed across the public service. Training should cover communication, active listening, problem-solving, conflict management, empathy, ethical conduct and the ability to explain procedures in plain language. Second, managers should be trained to facilitate service delivery. Their responsibility is not simply to supervise attendance, maintain files and enforce rules. They must remove operational obstacles, allocate resources, coach employees, monitor performance and encourage continuous improvement. Third, performance appraisal should recognise service quality. Employees should be assessed not only on their technical responsibilities but also on timeliness, accuracy, teamwork, respectful treatment and their contribution to improving services. Fourth, exemplary service should be recognised. Public institutions can introduce credible recognition schemes for employees and teams that demonstrate initiative, integrity and measurable improvements in citizen satisfaction. Recognition should be based on evidence and transparent criteria rather than personal connections or favouritism. Training alone, however, will not transform the culture. Employees must also be given the authority, information, tools and support required to perform their duties effectively. A frontline officer cannot be expected to resolve a citizen›s problem if every minor decision requires several levels of approval. Within clearly defined legal and financial boundaries, appropriate decision-making authority should be delegated to the people closest to the service user. The desired outcome is a workforce that understands both what it must do and why its work matters to the public. Strengthening leadership, accountability and ethical governance Customer-centricity must be driven from the top and embedded throughout the management system. Institutional leaders establish priorities through the objectives they set, the behaviour they model and the performance they reward. If senior management focuses exclusively on expenditure, staffing and procedural compliance, employees will naturally concentrate on those measures. If leaders also examine service delays, unresolved complaints, citizen feedback and the accessibility of services, customer-centricity becomes a genuine management priority. Every public institution should appoint a senior officer accountable for service improvement, supported by a cross-functional team representing operations, human resources, information technology, finance and frontline service delivery. These teams should regularly examine performance, identify recurring problems and agree on corrective action. Their discussions must lead to decisions with named owners, deadlines and measurable outcomes. Accountability must also be supported by integrity and impartiality. Citizens should receive services according to the law and objective eligibility criteria, not political connections, personal influence, social status or the ability to offer unofficial payments. Reducing unnecessary face-to-face transactions, publishing requirements and fees, introducing traceable digital payments and recording decisions can reduce opportunities for arbitrary treatment and corruption. Yet digitalisation alone cannot eliminate misconduct. Effective internal controls, independent oversight, protected complaint mechanisms and credible disciplinary procedures remain essential. Public institutions must also protect whistleblowers and people who report improper conduct, in accordance with applicable law. Employees should feel able to raise concerns about dysfunctional processes, unethical practices and risks to public resources without fear of retaliation. It is unfortunate, however, that whistle-blowers do not have protection under the Companies Act No.7 of 2007. Equally important is the need to separate legitimate accountability from a culture of fear. If public officers are punished indiscriminately for every mistake, they may avoid making decisions even when action is necessary and lawful. A mature accountability framework distinguishes deliberate wrongdoing, negligence and repeated poor performance from reasonable decisions made in good faith under difficult circumstances. The objective is a public service in which integrity is protected, performance is visible and responsibility cannot be avoided. Lanka Reformist Forum (LRF) A new Civil Society has been formed under the nomenclature of Lanka Reformist Forum. As I understand, this forum consists of professionals, business leaders and entrepreneurs who have decided to support a governance that has genuine love for the country and therefore act in its best interest. This group established the LRF in 2024 supporting the incoming NPP Government and are offering their professional services free of fees/costs for the love of our country. It is now up to the Government to harness their support to steer Sri Lanka in a righteous path where integrity, transparency and respect for the law take pride of place. I believe that the LRF is gaining strength from membership escalations and their undying commitment to bring Sri Lanka to a first world country corruption-free and where discipline and integrity must be established among school children from primary education through secondary and University levels. When your grandchildren/great grandchildren ask you, “Seeya (grandfather)/Athamma (grandmother), what have you contributed toward establishing Sri Lanka as a safe and economically developed, righteous and disciplined nation?” What will be your answer to them? Pause to think! (The author is a sought-after management consultant, coach and corporate management trainer. He has held Regional Director positions in multinational and Fortune 500 companies for East Africa and for the Southeast Asia and India regions. He has carried out consulting assignments for the CEB, SLTMobitel, Airport and Aviation Services, SriLankan Airlines, Sri Lanka Tourism Promotion Bureau, CRIB, World Bank, the ADB and the UNDP)

audit.headline: Is tourism gentrification a useful lens to understand impacts of tourism on cities?
audit.summary: The Galle Fort Small fishing village Kalametiya Kompangna Veediya “A good city is like a good party – people stay longer than really necessary because they are enjoying themselves,” said Jan Gehl, the Danish architect and urban planner. When tourism arrivals hit record levels in tourist hot spots, it doesn’t necessarily mean that tourists spend their money on the goods and services that host countries would like them to or spend time in the zones that need tourism most. Tourism gentrification refers to bespoke gentrification -- areas of cities undergo transformation specifically to make the area attractive to tourists, while gentrification in general is the process by which disadvantaged areas of a city undergo an influx of people who renovate, rebuild and regenerate an area, increasing property values.
audit.body: The Galle Fort Small fishing village Kalametiya Kompangna Veediya “A good city is like a good party – people stay longer than really necessary because they are enjoying themselves,” said Jan Gehl, the Danish architect and urban planner. When tourism arrivals hit record levels in tourist hot spots, it doesn’t necessarily mean that tourists spend their money on the goods and services that host countries would like them to or spend time in the zones that need tourism most. Tourism gentrification refers to bespoke gentrification -- areas of cities undergo transformation specifically to make the area attractive to tourists, while gentrification in general is the process by which disadvantaged areas of a city undergo an influx of people who renovate, rebuild and regenerate an area, increasing property values. The collateral damage of gentrification is the displacement of the relatively less well-off inhabitants who leave due to the rapid inflation of prices that occurs due to gentrification. Ruth Glass originally coined the word gentrification in reference to London[1]. The city grew along the banks of the River Thames, and as people migrated to the capital in search of work in the 1800s, the areas closest to the river became working-class neighbourhoods. Two centuries later, young professionals moved into these areas, forever changing their social character. Neil Smith argues that capital, more flexible than people, moves in a way to exploit gaps in rents[2]. Neighbourhoods change as gaps widen between lower-middle-class areas and middle-class areas next to them, capital moves in to gentrify it and rents it at higher values. If we imagine that the planet is one (very) large neighbourhood, we see this is true for tourism too. When neighbourhoods undergo tourism gentrification, this necessarily involves the local population. Tourism gentrification is a useful lens because it highlights the complex relationship that investors, tourists and local residents have with each other. Also, like tourism, tourism gentrification requires a high-risk investment in infrastructure that is dependent on factors that are sometimes beyond anyone’s control. Centuries-old neighbourhoods Growing up in Sri Lanka has given me a unique view of both tourism and tourism gentrification. I have witnessed the ebb and flow of the tourist tide and seen what happens in the times when the tide abruptly recedes. This has enabled me to observe the temporary and permanent impacts of tourism gentrification from the perspective of a relatively small player in the global tourist industry, Sri Lanka, where tourism (or the lack of it) can make a dramatic difference to the economy. I use the examples of three distinct areas, namely the UNESCO heritage site Galle Fort, Kalametiya, a fishing village in southern Sri Lanka and the distinct neighbourhood of Kompangna Veediya (Company Street), Colombo, which houses long-term residents with strong identities and connections to their neighbourhood that are centuries-old[3]. I have viewed each example through the analysis suggested by political scientist Margaret Kohn and look first at the displacement of local communities, the transformation of the existing space, and finally the polarisation that results[4]. I illustrate the paradox of homogenisation that occurs with over-tourism, defined as the excessive growth of visitors leading to overcrowding in areas where residents suffer the consequences of temporary and seasonal tourism peaks, which have caused permanent changes to their lifestyles, denied access to amenities and damaged their general well-being[5]. Understanding the impacts of tourism on cities involves a wide variety of factors, and a deep dive into tourism gentrification is a useful lens through which to examine these impacts. The Galle Fort The Galle Fort, on Sri Lanka’s southwest coast, dates from 1588. The Portuguese colonists established an outpost here, but it was soon taken by the Dutch, who turned it into a 52-hectare granite fortress with fourteen bastions from which they ran the Dutch East India trading company. The British conquerors added a lighthouse, and the picture-perfect Fort with its labyrinth of quaint, cobblestoned lanes was complete. Containing homes, businesses, libraries and schools that mix Dutch architectural style with traditional Moorish interiors, Galle Fort is presently regarded as the best-preserved “living fort” in Asia. The descendants of the Arab traders who frequented Galle, the Sri Lankan Muslim Moors, are the longest-term inhabitants of the Galle Fort, having lived for centuries in old homes with common verandas and roofs inside a walled community that has a magical appeal. 1988’s UNESCO designation of the Fort as a World Heritage Site marked a sea change in the life of the Galle Fort[6]. Investors raced into rent, restore and change Galle Fort homes, property prices skyrocketed from $50 to over $300 per square foot, and the global flow of capital began to move in, creating incredible changes. Verandas connecting homes that created a sense of community, are now boutique shops, restored homes boast interiors of efficient Scandinavian design and linked roof tops that were playgrounds for kite fliers are now walled off. Local property owners, dazzled by high prices, sold up and moved away. Tourism gentrification was encouraged with a revamped sewage system and an Army camp to guarantee tourists’ safety. On the positive, tourists can expect a safe and exotic stay in Asia’s oldest living Fort with the bonus of being able to sip matcha lattes and eat thin-crust pizzas while they ‘do’ Galle. On the negative, there are very few original residents left due to tourism gentrification – they are now a minority, like a curiosity in a zoo. The majority of Galle Fort’s population are now tourists, who ironically came in search of the life lived by the earlier majority. Tourists are encouraged to learn how to make and eat traditional kidu rice while taking tours of family homes to see where ‘real people’ once lived. Sharon Zukin, four decades ago, predicted the “Instagrammability” of gentrification[7]. The romanticising of traditional spaces and the objectification of history exclude its people. Coffee shops, fashion boutiques, swimwear retailers and jazz bars now line Galle Fort streets, creating familiarity for tourists who had originally come to view another world, but are happy to spend their dollars regardless. Although the global tourist claims to be in a perennial search for unique experiences, gentrification creates homogeneity. Sharon Zukin further talks about how the tourist needs points of reference through creature comforts, particularly in alien environments[8]. Paradoxically, this creates a homogeneity in all “hot spots” for global travel. The same spas, boutiques, trinkets, multinational branded drinks, coffees and fast food create a zone of exclusion for the local inhabitants – almost a no-go zone. The economic benefit of tourism is very valuable to Sri Lanka, but tourism gentrification has meant that many tourists never see the ‘real’ Galle. It begs the question, what, in 2026, is the ‘real’ Galle? Is it still Sri Lanka’s ninth-largest city in terms of population? Do Sri Lankans choose to purchase property, find work and settle in Galle? No, as they are unable to afford the inflated costs of renting or owning in Galle? Do Sri Lankans feel ‹ at home’ in Galle Fort, where they need to pay over the odds for a plate of rice and curry? No, tourism has rendered Galle Fort inaccessible for visiting locals. Tourist gentrification has meant longer-term conversions of old Galle Fort homes into boutique hotels, sparking tensions between tourists and residents in a myriad of ways. Noise pollution and relative cultural impropriety take their toll on this relationship. When quiet streets filled with the rustle of long dresses of the Galle Muslim women are suddenly taken over by happily loud surfers in swimwear, undercurrents of difference simmer below the surface. This must be addressed if tourism gentrification is to continue. Small fishing village Kalametiya Kalametiya, a small fishing village on Sri Lanka’s southern coast, attracts tourists who want an ‘off-the-beaten-track’ experience. Professor Oscar Amarasinghe argues that the south coast is one of the poorest regions in the country, and although dependent on fishing and farming, it is now facing a twin challenge – the corporatisation of fishing through trawlers and the opening of the beaches to large-scale construction of hotels and private villas that now line the pristine coast[9]. A new expressway halved the journey time to Kalametiya, and it is now a regular stop for tourists on their way to the national wildlife parks. Kalametiya now runs bird-watching tours in the mangroves, and the fisher families have sold their boats, as fishing is no longer profitable. Kalametiya is becoming increasingly dependent on tourism for survival. A particular problem is garbage disposal – with the rapid increase in ecological footprint, State garbage collection cannot keep pace. Large open dump sites have been created inland, which seep into groundwater supplies. Tourism gentrification has left a mixed legacy here – multiple new opportunities for the youth of Kalametiya to move away from the uncertain life of a family reliant on fishing for all income, but possibly the pace of tourism gentrification and failure of the Government to keep up with it has now made this hidden gem, a once self-sustaining village, a social and environmental time bomb. Sri Lanka will continue to prioritise tourism with its irresistible domino effect. Although we need a long-term strategy to protect the economy from the vagaries of tourism, approximately 50% of income from tourists goes into the unofficial sector – directly to guides, drivers, beach cafes and smaller hotel owners, which is why the impact of an increase or decrease in tourism on incomes and livelihoods is immediate and crucial. To make this impact more sustainable, tourism gentrification must not focus only on the end-product tourism, but on holistic inclusion, making certain that all impacted are on board. The priority must be to attract top-dollar tourists while ensuring that the smallest participants in the tourist industry are treated fairly by extending small loans and prioritising eco-tourism, to ensure the sustainability of natural assets. Isolation and exclusion invariably lead to friction Kompangna Veediya 2009 marked the end of Sri Lanka’s civil war, and successive governments have been aware of the crucial importance of tourism for the country’s GDP, leading to State-enforced tourism gentrification. 2011’s transfer of control of Colombo’s Urban Development Authority (UDA) to the Ministry of Defence (MOD) lead to the launch of the Urban Regeneration Program (URP) to create a “world-class city” by “liberating high value land” to create an attractive destination for global travelers. Legally, military force could be used to spark urban regeneration and achieve tourism gentrification. According to the Centre for Policy Alternatives (CPA), with an aim to create a slum free Colombo, the Government began forced evictions between 2011 and 2014[10] Notably, land was cleared for an Integrated Casino Resort, resulting in 20,000 families being relocated to purpose-built high-rise developments. Those displaced were not slum dwellers, but proud residents of Kompangna Veediya, a tightly knit neighbourhood that has existed next to the Fort (Colombo’s financial district) since the 17th century. Dr. Asha Abeyasekara, a sociologist, reveals how gendered and inequitable the impact of the URP has been. Replacement properties were registered in the name of the male resulting in women losing their social network, protection and neighbourhood day care system. Abeysekara calls this “intimate evictability” describing how the State creates “unwanted citizens”[11]. Multi-generational families, bonded together by emotion, memory and common purpose, describe Kompangna Veediya as their birthplace[12]. Following the first wave of evictions, Firi Rahman co-founded “We Are From Here” – a collective with fellow artists that highlights the experiences of a deeply interconnected community who continue to map in creative ways the impact of gentrification driven by State and corporate interests that threaten the existence of their neighbourhood by painting hyper-realistic portraits of the Java Lane Team, (Colombo’s oldest football club), on the alley walls to recreate life as it once was [13]. Off the coast of Colombo, close to Kompangna Veediya, is the new 269-hectare Port City, built through Chinese investment on reclaimed land, the biggest strategic infrastructure development since the civil war ended. Port City is billed to be the new face of modern Colombo; bespoke tourism with amusement parks, yachts and resort-quality golf courses. Tourism gentrification in Port City and Kompangna Veediya will have a positive impact on job creation in the neighbourhood. Unfortunately, apart from the small percentage of staff from the area being hired to work in the new casinos, resort hotels and restaurants, there will be little or no trickle-down effect to regenerate the neighbourhood’s own economy. The tourists will come, eat at the restaurants, gamble in the casinos and stay at the hotels, and then leave. There has been no provision made for holistic tourism to be a beneficiary of tourism gentrification; the money that comes in is unlikely to reach the original inhabitants of Kompangna Veediya. If tourists are given the unique opportunity to explore a living Colombo neighbourhood, perhaps they will stroll the streets of Kompangna Veediya, joining the locals to play a game of football. If not, Port City may become ‘just another casino city. Indeed, today, the Collective for Historical Dialogue and Memory (CHDM) conducts $20 Memory Walks where tourists explore the by lanes of Kompangna Veediya with a guide, but it remains to be seen whether tourists will choose to come and spend their dollars at Port City instead of Singapore’s Sentosa Island. Perhaps Port City need not become another generic theme park town. Instead, if Kompangna Veediya’s old corner shops, bars, and train station platforms are restored, and given a new lease of life, tourists and locals alike will celebrate the neighbourhood --currently trending is the Kampong, Colombo’s newest speakeasy restaurant, where all menu items pay homage to Kompangna Veediya’s historic past – including a preparation of spicy sardines – a nod to the workers from Madagascar that were brought over during Portuguese colonial times. Tourism gentrification is a useful lens to understand the impact of tourism on cities better – residents see the appeal or lack thereof to those who visit and then learn how to live with change themselves. The four years of recent challenges that we went through as a country meant far fewer tourists and belt-tightening all round. We ‘locals’ became tourists – travelling the island to occupy empty hotel rooms virtually free of charge. It was a difficult time, but it gave me a glimpse of how strong societal bonds are, and how neighbourhood must rely on each other in times of crisis. With adversity came true community spirit as shortages of vegetables sparked barter exchanges with neighbours. Now, free of bankruptcy, under an International Monetary Fund (IMF) reform, Sri Lanka is back trending on the global tourist map. Sadly, businesses built around tourism have gone bankrupt, and brain drain has taken its toll. Prioritising tourism Sri Lanka will continue to prioritise tourism with its irresistible domino effect. Although we need a long-term strategy to protect the economy from the vagaries of tourism, approximately 50% of income from tourists goes into the unofficial sector – directly to guides, drivers, beach cafes and smaller hotel owners, which is why the impact of an increase or decrease in tourism on incomes and livelihoods is immediate and crucial. To make this impact more sustainable, tourism gentrification must not focus only on the end-product tourism, but on holistic inclusion, making certain that all impacted are on board. The priority must be to attract top-dollar tourists while ensuring that the smallest participants in the tourist industry are treated fairly by extending small loans and prioritising eco-tourism, to ensure the sustainability of natural assets. Isolation and exclusion invariably lead to friction. This, coupled with the lack of a long-term strategy, means that the prosperity of tourist hotspots may be short-lived. Once tourists leave, who remains to keep the neighbourhood alive? The residents. It is wise to use tourism gentrification as a lens through which to look at the impacts of tourism, as it shows us the complexities of relationships between residents and tourists and helps us to understand better how to help all parties to co-exist in the long run. End Notes: [1] Ruth Glass London: Aspects of Change, 1964 [2] Neil Smith Towards a theory of gentrification, 1979 [3] UNESCO is the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation [4] Margaret Kohn What is Wrong With Gentrification, 2013 [5] C.Milano, J.M. Cheer & M. Novelli Overtourism: excesses, discontents and measures in travel and tourism, 2019 [6] Nethra Samarawickrama Remaking of the Fort, 2012 [7] Sharon Zekin Loft Living, 1982 [8] Sharon Zekin Culture of Cities, 1995 [9] Amarasinghe, Baavnik Building Resilience: Fisheries Cooperatives in Southern Sri Lanka, 2011 [10] Centre for Policy Alternatives (CPA), Forced Evictions in Colombo, the high cost of beautification, 2014 [11] Asha Abeysekera, The Hidden Cost of Urban Renewal in Colombo, 2025 [12] Basu, I and Hettiarachchi, R, Agentive Minorities: place-memory, identity and ontological security in post-war Sri Lanka, 2025 [13] Firi Rahman (fifth generation resident of Kompangna Veediya) founded the Artists Collective

audit.headline: Mercy, robes and the rule of law in Sri Lanka
audit.summary: Ven. Gnanasara Thero, Father Mathew Peiris, Ven. Somarama Thero Presidential pardons and the disrobing of imprisoned Buddhist monks may appear to belong to distinct legal domains. Yet both bring into focus a fundamental question of constitutional governance: how should public power be exercised when it intersects with criminal accountability, religious authority and public trust? Two controversies, one constitutional question The relationship between religion and the State in Sri Lanka is frequently examined through the constitutional recognition accorded to Buddhism under Article 9 and the general guarantee of religious freedom under Article 14. These provisions raise enduring questions about the relationship between the State’s special constitutional obligations towards Buddhism and the protection of religious freedom.
audit.body: Ven. Gnanasara Thero, Father Mathew Peiris, Ven. Somarama Thero Presidential pardons and the disrobing of imprisoned Buddhist monks may appear to belong to distinct legal domains. Yet both bring into focus a fundamental question of constitutional governance: how should public power be exercised when it intersects with criminal accountability, religious authority and public trust? Two controversies, one constitutional question The relationship between religion and the State in Sri Lanka is frequently examined through the constitutional recognition accorded to Buddhism under Article 9 and the general guarantee of religious freedom under Article 14. These provisions raise enduring questions about the relationship between the State’s special constitutional obligations towards Buddhism and the protection of religious freedom. These questions have recently assumed renewed public significance, with a large gathering reported around Viharamahadevi Park in protest against State decisions concerning Buddhism. Against this backdrop, two developments invite closer constitutional scrutiny: the Supreme Court’s decision invalidating former President Maithripala Sirisena’s 2019 pardon of Ven. Galagoda Aththe Gnanasara Thero, and the introduction of new prison regulations governing the removal of the robes of imprisoned Buddhist monks. Although the two controversies concern different exercises of State authority, they converge on a common constitutional question: what limits should govern the exercise of public power when it intersects with criminal accountability, religious status and the rule of law? The two developments are legally distinct. Article 34 of the Constitution confers a power of presidential clemency, whereas the removal of monastic robes engages prison administration and the rules governing religious discipline. Nevertheless, both reveal the importance of distinguishing the existence of a power from the legitimacy of its exercise. A constitutional power may be broad without being arbitrary. Equally, respect for religious self-governance does not require the State to surrender its responsibility to administer criminal justice. The central challenge is to determine how these forms of authority can coexist without undermining the rule of law. The significance of these controversies becomes clearer when considered against the historical development of the pardon power, the political role of Buddhist clergy in Sri Lanka, and the symbolic and institutional significance of the monastic robe. The prerogative of mercy: historical origins and constitutional tensions The power to pardon has historically served as an exceptional mechanism for tempering the rigidity of criminal law in the interests of justice, equity and public welfare. It may provide a remedy for miscarriages of justice, mitigate disproportionate sentences, recognise rehabilitation, or respond to compelling humanitarian circumstances. Although wrongful convictions are ordinarily addressed through appellate remedies, clemency retains significance where judicial remedies are inadequate and in capital cases, where mitigating circumstances may warrant the commutation of a death sentence or longer prison sentences. Nevertheless, its exceptional nature demands that the power be exercised consistently with the rule of law. In England, the royal prerogative of mercy became concentrated in the Crown and was subsequently inherited, in modified constitutional forms, by several jurisdictions influenced by English common law. The historical association between clemency and sovereign authority explains its unusual constitutional character. Whereas courts determine criminal liability and impose sentences according to law, the power of mercy permits the executive to intervene after conviction. This intervention may serve legitimate humanitarian purposes, but it also creates the possibility of political favouritism and arbitrary interference with the administration of justice. The United States Constitution provides a useful comparison. Article II, Section 2 empowers the President to grant reprieves and pardons for federal offences, except in cases of impeachment. Although clemency may correct injustice or mitigate excessive punishment, its exercise has raised concerns about impartiality and accountability, particularly where beneficiaries have personal or political connections to the President, as illustrated by President Joe Biden’s controversial pardon of his son, Hunter Biden, in December 2024. However, American history also reveals a striking counterpoint: in United States v. Wilson (1833), George Wilson refused to accept a pardon granted by President Andrew Jackson for mail robbery. The case established that a pardon must be accepted to take effect, illustrating that even the extraordinary power of presidential mercy cannot necessarily be imposed upon its intended beneficiary. These examples expose an enduring dilemma. The pardon power may operate as an instrument of compassion, reconciliation and correction, but its exceptional breadth can also make it vulnerable to political manipulation. The appropriate response is not necessarily to abolish executive discretion. It is to identify the constitutional and institutional safeguards that distinguish legitimate mercy from arbitrary favour. Presidential clemency under Article 34: discretion as a constitutional trust Article 34(1) of the Sri Lankan 1978 Constitution authorises the President, in the case of an offender convicted of an offence by a court within Sri Lanka, to grant a free or conditional pardon, grant a respite, substitute a less severe punishment, or remit all or part of a punishment or penalty. The provision confers substantial discretion. However, the breadth of the language does not resolve the question of how that discretion should be exercised. In a constitutional democracy, the powers of public institutions derive their legitimacy from the Constitution and must be exercised consistently with its governing principles. The distinction between a constitutional power and a personal prerogative is therefore fundamental. A pardon is not a private act of generosity by the officeholder. It is an exercise of public authority capable of affecting the administration of justice, the interests of victims and the public’s confidence in the legal system. The constitutional position also requires a distinction between a pardon and the judicial determination of guilt. Clemency may relieve an offender from the execution of a sentence to the extent authorised by the pardon, but it does not empower the President to set aside the judicial determination itself. Otherwise, the executive would effectively assume a judicial function and disturb the constitutional allocation of powers. Although a pardon may lawfully affect the punishment imposed, an unexplained or arbitrary exercise of clemency in such circumstances may raise serious concerns about judicial independence and the authority of the courts. The question is therefore not simply whether the President possesses the power to pardon. It is whether the particular decision represents a lawful exercise of that power. Padron for Gnanasara Thero: judicial review and executive accountability These issues came into sharp focus in Centre for Policy Alternatives and Dr. Paikiasothy Saravanamuttu v. Maithripala Sirisena and Others, SCFR 256/2019, considered together with Sandhya Ekneligoda v. Attorney General and Others, SCFR 257/2019. In its judgment of 10 September 2026, the Supreme Court invalidated the pardon granted to Ven. Galagoda Aththe Gnanasara Thero in May 2019. Gnanasara Thero had been convicted by the Court of Appeal in 2016 on counts of contempt of court arising from his conduct at the Homagama Magistrate’s Court. The convictions concerned conduct that interfered with the authority and proceedings of the court. President Sirisena subsequently granted him a full pardon under Article 34(1). The petitioners challenged the pardon on constitutional grounds, arguing that it undermined the rule of law, judicial independence and the separation of powers and violated the guarantee of equality under Article 12(1). The Supreme Court’s decision is significant for reasons extending beyond the identity of the beneficiary. It affirmed that the exercise of presidential clemency is capable of judicial scrutiny under the fundamental rights jurisdiction of the Court. The constitutional discretion conferred by Article 34 does not place a presidential decision beyond review where the applicable constitutional requirements for such review are satisfied. A particularly important aspect of the judgment concerned the absence of a contemporaneous record adequately explaining the decision. The Court also examined the circumstances in which the pardon was processed, the treatment of requests both supporting and opposing clemency, and the apparent reliance on a recommendation prepared by the Additional Secretary (Legal), without a documented independent assessment by the President of the relevant considerations. The Court concluded that the decision was arbitrary and invalid. It declared the pardon, as recorded in the presidential minute dated 21 May 2019, null and void and of no force or avail in law. At the same time, it clarified that the decision did not permanently prevent a future pardon, provided that any subsequent decision was made lawfully and after proper consideration of the relevant material. The judgment thus drew a distinction between the existence of the pardon power and the legality of its exercise. The President retained the constitutional authority to grant mercy, but that authority could not be exercised in disregard of the constitutional framework. Presidential immunity and the possibility of judicial review and accountability in the exercise of clemency Presidential immunity under Article 35 of the Constitution is a qualified protection against personal civil and criminal proceedings, rather than an absolute exemption from constitutional accountability. It rests on the need to protect the functioning of the highest executive office, premised on the expectation that presidential powers will be exercised in the interests of the State and its people, and not to their detriment. The question of prison attire in previous cases does not appear to have provoked the same controversy as it has in the case of Ven. Gnanasara Thero. Neither Father Mathew Peiris’s case nor that of Ven. Somarama Thero appears to have raised any contestation over the clothing worn following conviction. The approach appeared to have upheld equality among prisoners and at the same time never intended to diminish their religious faith or prevent personal religious observance. Indeed, Peiris was reportedly seen wearing a cross bearing a figure of the crucified Christ even within prison premises The proviso to Article 35(1) preserves the right to institute fundamental rights proceedings under Article 126 against the Attorney-General in respect of acts or omissions of the President in the exercise of official functions. Significantly, the Nineteenth Amendment strengthened this safeguard by permitting such proceedings even while the President remains in office. Accordingly, proceedings challenging the legality of a former President’s official acts reinforce the principle that the exercise of executive power remains subject to constitutional scrutiny and that the rule of law does not cease to operate at the highest levels of government. The possibility of judicial scrutiny, in turn, raises the question of how the exercise of presidential clemency can be meaningfully assessed. Recording reasons for a pardon can help establish whether the decision was based on relevant considerations and exercised for a proper purpose, rather than for arbitrary or improper reasons. Such considerations may include the gravity and circumstances of the offence, the sentence imposed, the offender’s conduct and rehabilitation, the interests of victims, and the wider public interest. Their relative significance will depend on the circumstances of each case. The objective is not to replace presidential discretion with a rigid checklist, but to ensure that the exercise of this exceptional power remains reasoned, defensible and consistent with the rule of law. The monastic robe: religious status, prison administration and institutional competence The second controversy concerns a different form of authority. On 24 October 2026, an Extraordinary Gazette notification amended the Department of Prisons’ Standing Orders to establish procedures governing the removal of robes worn by Buddhist monks when they are imprisoned. Under the newly inserted Standing Order 356A, the Commissioner of Prisons is required to consult the Department of Buddhist Affairs concerning the removal of a monk’s robes. The Department must inform the relevant Nikaya or chapter and communicate its position on the proposed action within ten days. The amendments also address the clothing that a monk may wear when taken outside prison, including circumstances in which the relevant Nikaya or chapter has not permitted the wearing of robes. The significance of these provisions lies in the institutional distinction they recognise. Imprisonment is a matter for the State’s criminal justice and prison administration systems. The question of whether a monk should be disrobed, however, may also concern the disciplinary authority of the Buddhist monastic order to which the monk belongs. The robe is not merely an item of clothing. It signifies membership of the Sangha, a symbol of religious vocation and an institutional identity governed by religious traditions and disciplinary rules. Its removal can therefore have implications beyond the practical administration of imprisonment. The new procedures establish a formal channel between prison authorities, the Department of Buddhist Affairs and the relevant monastic institution. They recognise the relevance of ecclesiastical authority without displacing the State’s responsibility to enforce lawful sentences and maintain prison administration. This does not mean that the robe provides immunity from criminal law. A monk remains subject to investigation, prosecution, conviction and imprisonment in accordance with the law. Nor does imprisonment automatically establish that the monk has been formally disrobed. These are distinct questions requiring attention to their respective legal and institutional frameworks. The underlying issue is one of institutional competence: which authority is entitled to make which decision, and within what limits? The State must not surrender its responsibility for criminal justice, but it should also distinguish the administration of a prison sentence from the determination of religious status where the governing rules allocate a role to the relevant religious institution. Nevertheless, the involvement of religious authorities should not be confused with an exemption from criminal law. A monk remains subject to the law of the State. The robe cannot confer immunity from arrest, prosecution, conviction or imprisonment. The amendment is therefore best understood as an attempt to regulate the point of intersection between State authority and monastic discipline, rather than as a transfer of criminal jurisdiction to religious authorities. These principles extends to the clergy of other faiths, with appropriate regard for their respective religious traditions and institutional practices. Somarama Thero: the robe and criminal accountability The relationship between Buddhist monastic identity and political power has a long history in Sri Lanka. The assassination of Prime Minister S.W.R.D. Bandaranaike in 1959 provides a particularly revealing example. The political mobilisation associated with Bandaranaike’s rise to power was popularly described through the phrase “Sanga, Veda and Guru” - the Buddhist clergy, medical practitioners and teachers. The phrase captured the political significance of these groups in the social and electoral transformation of the 1950s. The irony of the assassination was that Ven. Somarama Thero, a Buddhist monk who was also an Ayurvedic practitioner and associated with teaching at an Ayurvedic institution, became the central figure in the criminal proceedings arising from Bandaranaike’s death. The religious and professional identities that carried social and political authority did not place him beyond criminal accountability. The historical record also contains an episode directly related to the symbolism of religious attire - the question of robes. During his trial, Somarama stopped wearing his yellow robes when appearing in court. Justice T.S. Fernando reportedly observed that Somarama had “a streak of conscience” because he did not attend court in his saffron robes. The episode should not be mistaken for a legal determination that Ven. Somarama had been formally disrobed by his monastic institution. The robe may communicate a symbol of religious vocation and social authority, but it cannot determine criminal liability. Nor should the wearing or removal of robes become a substitute for examining the conduct of the individual concerned. The distinction matters: personal conduct, institutional discipline and State-imposed punishment are separate matters, even when they intersect. The historical example illustrates the political significance of religious identity and the limits of the authority it confers. A comparative perspective: religious office and the limits of State authority The distinction between criminal punishment and religious status extends beyond Buddhist monastic life. The case of Anglican priest Father Mathew Peiris offers a useful, albeit institutionally distinct, comparison. Following his conviction for the murders of his wife, Eunice Peiris, and Russel Ingram, Peiris spent approximately twelve years in prison before his release in October 1997 under a general amnesty. He was reportedly permitted to wear clerical attire during his initial court proceedings and remand custody but wore ordinary prison clothing following his conviction. Upon release, he was again seen in clerical attire and continued to be addressed as “Father”. Contemporary reporting, however, indicated that he no longer held his Bishop’s licence and could participate in church activities only in the capacity permitted to lay members. His case illustrates the distinction between religious identity, ordination and institutional authorisation to exercise the functions of a religious office, particularly when a person is outside prison. While the State determined his punishment through its criminal jurisdiction, it also implies his attire during imprisonment in accordance with the principle of equality before the law. Contrasting fates Significantly, the question of prison attire in previous cases does not appear to have provoked the same controversy as it has in the case of Ven. Gnanasara Thero. Neither Father Mathew Peiris’s case nor that of Ven. Somarama Thero appears to have raised any contestation over the clothing worn following conviction. The approach appeared to have upheld equality among prisoners and at the same time never intended to diminish their religious faith or prevent personal religious observance. Indeed, Peiris was reportedly seen wearing a cross bearing a figure of the crucified Christ even within prison premises. Also, it was Father Peiris who baptised Somarama Thero in Welikada Prison, giving him the name “Peter” just two days before he was hanged for the assassination of Prime Minister S.W.R.D. Bandaranaike. Father Peiris, by contrast, left Welikada Prison following his release under a general amnesty in October 1997. (The author is an Attorney-at-Law, and Senior Lecturer in Law, Asia Pacific Institute of Information Technology (APIIT), Sri Lanka)

audit.headline: Resus Energy becomes first Sri Lankan corporate to list Green Bonds on Luxembourg Stock Exchange
audit.summary: The Damana solar power project Resus Energy PLC has announced the dual listing of its Rs. 1 billion Green Bond on the Luxembourg Stock Exchange (LuxSE) and its display on the Luxembourg Green Exchange (LGX), effective 19 October 2026. With this milestone, Resus Energy becomes the first non-financial corporate issuer from Sri Lanka to be featured on LGX, the sustainable finance platform operated by LuxSE. The dual listing follows the issuance and listing of the Bond on the Colombo Stock Exchange (CSE) in July 2025 and marks Sri Lanka’s first-ever Green Bond issuance by a non-banking and finance company and the first by a local energy company, with NDB Investment Bank Limited acting as the Financial Advisor and Manager to the transaction. The listing is a significant step for the company and for Sri Lanka’s growing sustainable finance market.
audit.body: The Damana solar power project Resus Energy PLC has announced the dual listing of its Rs. 1 billion Green Bond on the Luxembourg Stock Exchange (LuxSE) and its display on the Luxembourg Green Exchange (LGX), effective 19 October 2026. With this milestone, Resus Energy becomes the first non-financial corporate issuer from Sri Lanka to be featured on LGX, the sustainable finance platform operated by LuxSE. The dual listing follows the issuance and listing of the Bond on the Colombo Stock Exchange (CSE) in July 2025 and marks Sri Lanka’s first-ever Green Bond issuance by a non-banking and finance company and the first by a local energy company, with NDB Investment Bank Limited acting as the Financial Advisor and Manager to the transaction. The listing is a significant step for the company and for Sri Lanka’s growing sustainable finance market. Launched by the Luxembourg Stock Exchange in 2016, LGX was the world’s first platform dedicated exclusively to green, social and sustainable securities. Being displayed on LGX increases the international visibility of Resus Energy PLC’s Green Bond among ESG-focused investors and demonstrates how a Sri Lankan renewable energy company can meet international expectations for green finance disclosure. Sri Lanka’s presence on LGX has grown steadily, led primarily by financial institutions. Resus Energy PLC’s listing marks the entry of a company directly involved in developing and operating renewable energy assets into this group, providing international investors with an opportunity to support capital investment in clean power generation. “Bringing our Green Bond to the Luxembourg Stock Exchange and the Luxembourg Green Exchange is a proud milestone for Resus Energy PLC and for Sri Lanka. It confirms that a Sri Lankan renewable energy company can meet the highest international standards of sustainable finance. It also connects the projects powering our national grid with investors around the world who want their capital to make a measurable climate impact,” saidManaging Director Kishan Nanayakkara. Managing Director Kishan Nanayakkara The listing comes as Sri Lanka works toward ambitious national targets. Under its updated Nationally Determined Contributions, the country has committed to generating 70% of its electricity from renewable sources by 2030 and to making electricity generation carbon neutral by 2050. The Green Bond issue comprised up to 10 Million Listed, Rated, Unsecured, Senior Redeemable Green Bonds of Rs. 100 each, in two tenors: Type A, four years at a fixed annual coupon of 11.55%; and Type B, five years at a fixed annual coupon of 11.75% Fitch Ratings Lanka Limited rated the bond A-(lka). The bond was structured in line with international sustainability standards, and all of its proceeds are committed to developing renewable energy projects. More than 55% of the proceeds are allocated to developing 8 MW of new solar capacity, expected to deliver approximately 15 GWh of clean electricity annually to the national grid and avoid approximately 10,000 tonnes of CO₂ emissions.

audit.headline: Baila scene this 31st Night!
audit.summary: Features Published on By Share Tweet Dear Mr. Alvis, Please publish this at your earliest convenience. This has reference to some of the articles you have published regarding the setup at a New Year’s Eve dance. Going by what is on social media, I believe the baila will be quite prominent on 31st Night as some of the bands that have been highlighted are more into the Sinhala music setup. I can’t see them bringing into their repertoire those nostalgic favourites, generally associated with a New Year’s Eve dance. What makes a New Year’s Eve dance extra special are those perennial favourites, especially during the lead up to the dawning of the New Year.
audit.body: Features Published on By Share Tweet Dear Mr. Alvis, Please publish this at your earliest convenience. This has reference to some of the articles you have published regarding the setup at a New Year’s Eve dance. Going by what is on social media, I believe the baila will be quite prominent on 31st Night as some of the bands that have been highlighted are more into the Sinhala music setup. I can’t see them bringing into their repertoire those nostalgic favourites, generally associated with a New Year’s Eve dance. What makes a New Year’s Eve dance extra special are those perennial favourites, especially during the lead up to the dawning of the New Year. As mentioned by you in your articles, I don’t think some of the bands advertised have ever heard of songs like ‘This Land Is Your Land,’ ‘You Are My Sunshine,’ ‘When The Saints Go Marching In,’ ‘Roll Out The Barrel,’ ‘Celebration,’ ‘She’ll Be Coming Round The Mountain,’ ‘Happy Days Are Here Again,’ ‘Auld Lang Syne,’ etc. A New Year’s Eve event, without those songs, would be just another dance, and we have such dances right throughout the year, with the baila dominating the scene at these dances. I have absolutely nothing against baila music and I love what Wally Bastianz created, M.S Fernando, Anton Jones, Nihal Nelson, and also Desmond De Silva and Sunil Perera. However, at every event in the country the baila is there in a big way, so let’s make New Year’s Eve an exception. Let the baila come into the scene, immediately after the dawning of the New Year, and then again for the final set. Thank you, Benny J.

audit.headline: Beyond recovery: Policy priorities to achieve durable growth in Sri Lanka
audit.summary: By Rashmi Anupama and Kalani Kiriveldeniya, Research Assistants, Institute of Policy Studies of Sri Lanka (IPS) Sustaining Sri Lanka’s post-crisis macroeconomic stability requires productivity-enhancing reforms to achieve durable and inclusive growth. Against this backdrop, the Institute of Policy Studies of Sri Lanka (IPS) hosted a roundtable discussion on 14 October 2026 on its flagship publication, Sri Lanka State of the Economy 2026, to discuss policy priorities to rebuild the country’s economic foundations amidst ongoing domestic and global uncertainties.
audit.body: By Rashmi Anupama and Kalani Kiriveldeniya, Research Assistants, Institute of Policy Studies of Sri Lanka (IPS) Sustaining Sri Lanka’s post-crisis macroeconomic stability requires productivity-enhancing reforms to achieve durable and inclusive growth. Against this backdrop, the Institute of Policy Studies of Sri Lanka (IPS) hosted a roundtable discussion on 14 October 2026 on its flagship publication, Sri Lanka State of the Economy 2026, to discuss policy priorities to rebuild the country’s economic foundations amidst ongoing domestic and global uncertainties. IPS Research Fellows Dr Asanka Wijesinghe and Dr Lakmini Fernando presented key findings, followed by interventions from Dr Yashodha Senadheera, Deputy Director of the Economic Research Department of the Central Bank of Sri Lanka (CBSL); Dr Liliya Aleksanyan, Senior Country Economist for Sri Lanka at the Asian Development Bank (ADB); Sanjaya Ariyawansa, Senior Economist at Sampath Bank; and other invited parties. Growth Has Returned, but Can Sri Lanka Sustain It? Dr Asanka Wijesinghe discussed Sri Lanka’s macroeconomic performance, external sector competitiveness, and policy priorities for durable growth.
