You see it all, read it all, do it all and only then face the final hurdle, the FRCS. When you pass, colleagues jokingly call you “007”. Licence to kill? Oh No, a mission to accomplish: Pristine health for the patients. Over the years, our old school dependence on physical diagnostic skills was supplemented and often surpassed by high tech investigations such as CT, MRI, PET, and more. Medicine evolved. Our training evolved. Our safeguards evolved. Lawyers, however, have no such one-to-one apprenticeship. After the law finals and a year’s apprenticeship, you are “good to go”. A few years later, one may be appointed a magistrate, and eventually climb to the Supreme Court. Training is on the job. Support systems are minimal. And yet these individuals or three of them together are entrusted with deciding someone’s fate, or the right and wrong of a 62 year old land dispute that has bounced between courts for decades. Can such a system guarantee justice? Clearly, no. The Problem Like many democracies, Sri Lanka’s legal system is a hierarchy of courts culminating in the Supreme Court. Under Dominion Ceylon, an aggrieved party could appeal beyond our shores to the Privy Council in England, and there are instances where Supreme Court judgments were reversed. This facility was abolished in 1972 when Ceylon became the Republic of Sri Lanka. To preserve the principle that justice must not only be done but be seen to be done , the alternative was introduced, appealing to the Chief Justice for a five- or seven judge bench. This certainly made justice appear more robust. But appearances are not necessarily the reality. Is it fair that a case entering its seventh decade is heard by a panel of three judges of whom only one may be fully awake and leading, while the other two may be slumbering and later sign, “I agree”? Indirectly, the people’s sovereign power appoints judges. The people elect the executive, and the executive appoints the judges. Yet the losing party must accept the verdict, even if the presiding judge does not go through all case notes and concentrates only on “whether the appellant defendants’ case for ownership through prescription has merit”. Cause of the Problem Political influence over Sri Lanka’s judiciary began after Independence (1948) through executive control over appointments, but became structurally entrenched following the introduction of the 1978 Constitution by President J. R. Jayewardene. The first clear instance appears immediately after Independence: Prime Minister D. S. Senanayake bypassed the most senior Supreme Court judge Felix Reginald Dias Bandaranaike, in 1948, instead appointing Arthur Wijewardene, then Attorney General. That was a political appointment. From the 1950s to the 1970s, governments continued appointing judges based on political loyalty. During Sirimavo Bandaranaike’s 1970-77 administration, partisan appointments were made, including individuals with SLFP backgrounds. Barnes Ratwatte, PM Sirimavo’s brother was elevated from a lower court to the Supreme Court by his nephew, Justice Minister Felix Dias Bandaranaike. These were episodic, personality driven interventions. I could list what happened under each and every government since but the story is the same. JRJ openly said he did not want judicial obstruction to deploying what people entrusted him to do. Others followed suit. The public perception is that judges handpicked by ruling party politicians often deliver judgments favourable to the government in power. Justice Neville Samarakoon, appointed by JRJ, was a rare exception. When he delivered a judgment unpalatable to the government, he faced political wrath and retired. Solution In criminal cases, especially murder trials, for example, a jury assists the judge. Why? Because the system recognises its major flaw, a single human being deciding whether a defendant walks free, receives a lesser sentence, or is convicted of premeditated murder. I propose that the Supreme Court, too, have additional layers of safety. Layer 1: Citizens’ Back-up Jury A well-educated, physically and mentally sound group of individuals, selected through a point-based system sits through cases, deliver their own verdict before the judges deliver theirs. Layer 2: Judicial AI Assistant (JAIA) An Artificial Intelligence system trained in Sri Lankan law, relevant precedents, and the Constitution of the Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka. JAIA listens to all arguments throughout the proceedings and produces its own judgment. Judges may access JAIA’s output only after they have independently reached their decision. These layers increase transparency, reduce bias, and strengthen public confidence. Analysis This combination minimises the chances of a wrong judgment by a human only court due to: 1. Human Fallibility “To err is human” is not a cliché, it is a reality. Judge fatigue is real, especially in cases that have aged into geriatric status within the court system. 2. Bias and Groupthink In any group, mountaineers, sailors or even cricketers, consensus often emerges before action. This can and may happen in three, five, or seven judge benches. 3. Committee Dynamics Strong voices steer committees. I sat on the Sri Lanka Medical Council for 15 years (1985–2000) as an elected member and was often the lone voice against audaciously insane arguments from senior members. 4. Human Cost A judicial system, shaped by decades of political influence and human limitations, cannot guarantee justice through human judgment alone. Additional layers a Citizens’ Back-up Jury and a Judicial AI Assistant are not luxuries. They are necessities. Justice must not only be done. It must be seen , felt , and trusted . And for that, the system must evolve. audit.headline: A Lankan powerhouse in music: Ashanthi De Alwis
audit.summary: 27 Oct 2026 | .By Stefania Perera and Kusali Rupasinghe In a male-dominated industry like the music business, breaking in requires tremendous effort. Ashanthi De Alwis, however, did just that. As a rapper, singer, and songwriter, she did not only break into the industry; rather, she established a significant and long-lasting presence for herself. Ashanthi is the only female Sri Lankan musician who has signed deals with not one, but two major record companies: Sony and Universal. One might underestimate how challenging her journey was after seeing her as the formidable figure we know her to be today, but Ashanthi remembers it well. This is illuminated when asked for an artefact, that is, any object which reminds her of her journey, she says, “for me more than a physical object, I think that it’s always been inner strength”.
audit.body: 27 Oct 2026 | .By Stefania Perera and Kusali Rupasinghe In a male-dominated industry like the music business, breaking in requires tremendous effort. Ashanthi De Alwis, however, did just that. As a rapper, singer, and songwriter, she did not only break into the industry; rather, she established a significant and long-lasting presence for herself. Ashanthi is the only female Sri Lankan musician who has signed deals with not one, but two major record companies: Sony and Universal. One might underestimate how challenging her journey was after seeing her as the formidable figure we know her to be today, but Ashanthi remembers it well. This is illuminated when asked for an artefact, that is, any object which reminds her of her journey, she says, “for me more than a physical object, I think that it’s always been inner strength”. She reiterated this by saying, “having a lot of inner strength and courage to take every single step towards the bigger picture has gotten me this far.” From a young age, Ashanthi was interested in music. Laughing, she recalls how she used to grab her elder sister’s Walkman from its hiding place and listen to music . “When we were kids, we didn’t have Google or YouTube. It was all a cassette tape and writing your own lyrics. No professional vocal coaches who taught you how to sing”, she says, illustrating how different it was back then and how she had to perfect the art by herself. She fondly recalls how the first cassette she found was a Mariah Carey tape which she used to listen to “on repeat”. When she flipped the said tape and saw the words “Sony Music” on it, nine-year-old Ashanthi thought to herself, “One day I am going to be signed to Sony Music”. Talk about manifestation! “I believe so strongly in manifestation. Because if you have a vision, clearly think about it, and don’t let go of your goals, make sure that your whole activities and your thoughts are aligned, you can really manifest what you want,” says Ashanthi. Elaborating on her journey, Ashanthi recalls her mother’s importance to it. Antoinette De Alwis too was a pioneering musician back in the 70s. Describing her mother as “the ground beneath [her] feet” and “[her] role model”, she recalls how her mother juggled a sick husband, a music career and two kids. Ashanthi owes her strength to her mother saying, “I think it made me stronger. Because when you see those things, you don’t take things for granted. You appreciate everything that you’ve been given. And you also tend to have your feet on the ground because you can see the reality of life.” Her grounded nature is evident as she doesn’t shy away from being vocal when the need arises, despite usually presenting herself publicly as apolitical. What matters to her is not politics, but the people. “I’m not supporting a party. I’m supporting the Sri Lankan people, freedom of speech, the freedom to have and exercise our fundamental rights as human beings,” says Ashanthi. When she saw the struggles of everyday Sri Lankans, she knew she had to use her platform and speak up. She states with conviction, ”As an influencer or an artist if you don’t do that for your people, there is no point in being an influence in the country at all. So, it’s a job we have been given to take responsibility for on behalf of ourselves and others who don’t have a voice. If we don’t use our voice, what’s the point?” This is not the first time however that Ashanthi has raised her voice for important social causes. Instead of focusing on solely creating commercial music, she focused on using music as a medium to talk about causes that she is passionate about such as depression, suicide prevention and bringing awareness to gender-based violence. Two of her famous tracks addressing these issues are Hitha Danna Mithuranne and Rajiniye, which went on to win some international awards. Ashanthi reflects, “Our culture is such a closed culture. We don’t talk about anything; everything is on the surface. How are you feeling? I’m good, you will never even think twice before answering a question like that.” Ashanthi herself is no stranger to such treatment, especially within the music industry. In her own words it took her “double the strength, double the courage, double the energy and double everything” to be in this industry. “We have to fight twice as hard. Because we have to prove, hey, yes, I’m a woman but I also can do this,” she says. As a rapper, singer, and songwriter, one might think Ashanthi has more than enough on her resume, but nothing brings her more joy than teaching at her music academy, Ashanthi School of Music. She founded the academy in 2009 to teach everything she knew about pop music. “When I come into a classroom to teach, I’m at complete ease” , says she. She mentions a few of her students who are now producing their own music and, her school and her students with pride, love, and fondness. She’s particularly excited about teaching Sri Lankan kids in foreign countries, she says, “It's keeping Sri Lankan kids close to their culture in terms of teaching an experience, and it’s connecting Sri Lankans who are connected in music across the globe with each other.” Despite all her impressive feats, Ashanthi strives to be humble and approachable. She attributes this nature to her mother whom she speaks of with pride. Ashanthi recalls, “Seeing my mom as a celebrity and on a stage, I learnt so much from that to be humble and have humility. Because I saw that character onstage and offstage, who was my mom who did everything that she is supposed to as a mom for me.” She wishes that people saw celebrities in the same light as they do a doctor or a lawyer, as just another person with a job. Nevertheless, one thing she’s very proud of is that her music with a cause has become a conversation starter on difficult and under-discussed matters. With pride, she says, “You can read the YouTube comments on the videos, and I have literally seen people saying ‘this song saved my life’… it’s a huge victory.” The primary source of happiness for Ashanthi is her work. “My whole day is filled with music. And I cannot even imagine, every day, how much joy and happiness that brings to me without even knowing… I’m blessed to be able to have my passion as my job”, she explains. If somebody asked someone to tell what they would say to their younger self, many would say something along the lines of “Do this instead of that”, but not Ashanthi. She muses and firmly states, “If I’m to go back and tell my nine-year-old self, what to do, I’d say, do exactly the same thing that you did, without knowing. Because that is what got you here.” (Stefania Perera is the Finance and Operations Manager for Everystory Sri Lanka. She is an ardent believer in the need for both Equity and Equality for all girls/women in Sri Lanka and her interests revolve around social democracy and anti-corruption. She holds an LLB (Hons) from the Staffordshire University and is an Attorney-at-Law) (Kusali Rupasinghe is a Workplace Experience candidate at Everystory Sri Lanka. She is a passionate young feminist and has been running an Instagram film account, @cinemaismonamour, since April 2022, where she shares her passion for cinema. Kusali is a first-year student at the University of Colombo’s Faculty of Arts) This article has been commissioned by the feminist collective Everystory Sri Lanka as part of their Stories of Sri Lankan Women (SOSLW) programme, a digital collection of the lives of women who have shaped and been shaped by Sri Lanka’s social, political, and cultural contexts. This interview was conducted in 2021. audit.headline: A new milestone for Sri Lankan Tennis
audit.summary: For years, the Sri Lanka Tennis Association (SLTA) has aspired to develop international-standard court facilities to provide young players with the best possible environment to train and compete. However, financial constraints have held back these ambitions for many years. This year, with the support of the Sri Lanka Tennis Premier League (SLTPL), which helped secure sponsors for the court renovation project, this long-standing vision finally began to take shape. With the guidance of the SLTA President and the assistance of the SLTA Committees, the project progressed. Anupa Maththamagoda, Head of Tennis Development at the SLTA was appointed as the Court Development Project Manager, his dedication played a key role in bringing phase one to completion.
audit.body: For years, the Sri Lanka Tennis Association (SLTA) has aspired to develop international-standard court facilities to provide young players with the best possible environment to train and compete. However, financial constraints have held back these ambitions for many years. This year, with the support of the Sri Lanka Tennis Premier League (SLTPL), which helped secure sponsors for the court renovation project, this long-standing vision finally began to take shape. With the guidance of the SLTA President and the assistance of the SLTA Committees, the project progressed. Anupa Maththamagoda, Head of Tennis Development at the SLTA was appointed as the Court Development Project Manager, his dedication played a key role in bringing phase one to completion. Out of a six court renovation project, this three newly renovated courts feature an Australian Open-standard playing surface, alongside modern lighting facilities, providing consistent playing conditions and greater opportunities for training and competition. This development marks a significant investment in the future of Sri Lankan tennis, strengthening the nation’s ability to nurture young talent, host international tournaments, and elevate the standard of the sport in the country. The ceremonial opening was held on 22 October in the presence of Presidential Secretariat Director General Legal Senior Attorney-at-Law J M Wijebandara and Western Province Governor Hanif Yusoof, alongside other distinguished guests. Also present were Sri Lanka Tennis Association (SLTA) President Iqbal Bin Isaac, General Secretary Pradeep Goonesekara and Vice-President Rukmal Cooray, together with members of the SLTPL Steering Committee, sponsors and the project team. With phase two of the court renovation project underway, a further three courts are also set to be opened, continuing this important investment in Sri Lanka's tennis infrastructure.

audit.headline: All schools closed today
audit.summary: All schools across the country will remain closed today (27) as a precautionary measure in view of the prevailing adverse weather conditions, the Ministry of Education said. The Ministry said the decision had been taken to ensure the safety of students and school staff amid the current weather situation. The practical exams for the GCE O/L Aesthetic Subjects will be conducted as scheduled. The island-wide closure follows an earlier move to empower Provincial Directors and Provincial Secretaries of Education to decide on the opening or closure of schools in their respective areas in response to the prevailing weather. The Ministry has reportedly issued the relevant instructions to provincial education authorities.
audit.body: All schools across the country will remain closed today (27) as a precautionary measure in view of the prevailing adverse weather conditions, the Ministry of Education said. The Ministry said the decision had been taken to ensure the safety of students and school staff amid the current weather situation. The practical exams for the GCE O/L Aesthetic Subjects will be conducted as scheduled. The island-wide closure follows an earlier move to empower Provincial Directors and Provincial Secretaries of Education to decide on the opening or closure of schools in their respective areas in response to the prevailing weather. The Ministry has reportedly issued the relevant instructions to provincial education authorities. Accordingly, Central Province Governor Dr Harsha Suranga Fernando said that the operations of 26 schools in several educational zones in the Kandy and Nuwara Eliya Districts had been suspended. The closure comes as Cyclone Arnab intensifies over the Bay of Bengal ahead of its expected landfall on India’s Andhra Pradesh coast tomorrow (28). Although the storm is not expected to directly affect Sri Lanka, officials have warned of rainfall of 100-150 millimetres in some areas over the coming days, along with strong winds of 40-50 kilometres per hour at times in several provinces.

audit.headline: As Pakistan reach tri-series final: Shadab ton stuns England
audit.summary: Shadab Khan's maiden century rescued Pakistan from a dire situation and took them to a stunning one-wicket victory over England in the one-day international in Lahore on Sunday, booking the hosts' spot in the final of the tri-series. Defending a modest 242-run target, England were on the cusp of victory with the home team reduced to 154-9, but Shadab's unbeaten 113 condemned Harry Brook's side to a third defeat in five days in the series, which also involves Sri Lanka. England, who failed to defend a 430-run target against Sri Lanka on Thursday, were left stunned as number 11 Haris Rauf cracked the winning boundary with 17 balls to spare, sparking huge celebrations in the Pakistan dug-out. Haris, who scored an unbeaten seven, ably played his part in a match-winning 89-run partnership with Shadab for the last wicket.
audit.body: Shadab Khan's maiden century rescued Pakistan from a dire situation and took them to a stunning one-wicket victory over England in the one-day international in Lahore on Sunday, booking the hosts' spot in the final of the tri-series. Defending a modest 242-run target, England were on the cusp of victory with the home team reduced to 154-9, but Shadab's unbeaten 113 condemned Harry Brook's side to a third defeat in five days in the series, which also involves Sri Lanka. England, who failed to defend a 430-run target against Sri Lanka on Thursday, were left stunned as number 11 Haris Rauf cracked the winning boundary with 17 balls to spare, sparking huge celebrations in the Pakistan dug-out. Haris, who scored an unbeaten seven, ably played his part in a match-winning 89-run partnership with Shadab for the last wicket. Shadab, who cracked five sixes and 13 boundaries, was lucky to survive a leg-before decision off Gus Atkinson with 20 needed. But while trudging off distraught, he took a review which overturned the decision. Restored to the crease, the 28-year-old guided Pakistan to victory and a spot in next Saturday's final – his score now is the highest batting at number eight in all ODIs. It was a stunning tournaround which left pakistan skipper Shaheen Shah Afridi struggling for words, "I can't say much, Shadab and Haris, the way they finished the game, 89-runs partnership is amazing," said Shaheen. "I've never seen that in my life. Really happy as captain, the team effort was top drawer." Brook refused to blame his bowlers in spite of their inability to close out the game, just days after their nightmare against Sri Lanka. "I don't think we went wrong with the ball, to be honest," said Brook. "I thought we did an exceptional job but maybe didn't quite get enough runs on the board." Pakistan lost opener Fakhar Zaman and Babar Azam for 10 each and Saim Ayub for six in a poor start before Saad Baig (32) and Salman Agha (26) briefly revived the innings. Match-winner Shadab then entered the fray in the 24th over with Pakistan on 103-6. Defeat means England's chances of reaching a place in the 31 October final hang in the balance as they need Pakistan to beat Sri Lanka on Tuesday and then win against the island nation on Thursday. Earlier, England's 241 all out was aided by a century by opener Ben Duckett, who anchored the innings with 105. Duckett's knock and Sam Curran's 42 during a 93-run fifth-wicket stand revived England from a precarious position of 19-3. Atkinson contributed an unbeaten 36 at the bottom of the order. For Pakistan, Shaheen claimed 4-46, while Razaullah took 2-38 on his ODI debut as England were bowled out in 46.4 overs. Duckett hit 10 fours and two sixes before falling to spinner Arafat Minhas, who finished with 2-26. Opting to bowl first, Pakistan skipper Shaheen removed Tom Banton for four in the opening over – his 150th ODI wicket. The lanky left-armer is the 13th bowler from Pakistan to take 150 or more wickets. In his next over, Shaheen got the prized wicket of Joe Root for five, caught cutting a short delivery. England plunged into further trouble when Harry Brook – who scored the fastest-ever ODI double century in his team's shock defeat to Sri Lanka – was run out for one. Duckett's fifth ODI hundred and Curran's resolute batting briefly steadied England before Shaheen took two more wickets to end the innings.

audit.headline: Attacks on Saudi: Monitoring is not a plan
audit.summary: When the United States ordered its own diplomats and their families out of a country, it was acting on intelligence the rest of the world did not see. Last week, Washington ordered non-emergency government staff and their families to leave Saudi Arabia, citing Houthi attacks on civilian airports and critical infrastructure. Meanwhile, India is working to bring home some 3,000 Umrah pilgrims. Sri Lanka’s response, however, as we reported on Sunday, is simply that no Sri Lankan has been reported affected. That is, of course, welcome news. Yet it is also beside the point. The question is not whether any of our citizens have been hurt so far. Instead, the question is what the Government intends to do if, or when, they are. Indeed, the facts are sobering. Since early October, the Houthis have struck Saudi airports again and again.
audit.body: When the United States ordered its own diplomats and their families out of a country, it was acting on intelligence the rest of the world did not see. Last week, Washington ordered non-emergency government staff and their families to leave Saudi Arabia, citing Houthi attacks on civilian airports and critical infrastructure. Meanwhile, India is working to bring home some 3,000 Umrah pilgrims. Sri Lanka’s response, however, as we reported on Sunday, is simply that no Sri Lankan has been reported affected. That is, of course, welcome news. Yet it is also beside the point. The question is not whether any of our citizens have been hurt so far. Instead, the question is what the Government intends to do if, or when, they are. Indeed, the facts are sobering. Since early October, the Houthis have struck Saudi airports again and again. By mid-month, the Saudi-led coalition put the toll from those attacks alone at 19 dead and more than 360 injured, with Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport targeted some 20 times in under a fortnight. Then, on 21 October, the attacks reportedly reached King Fahd International Airport in Dammam and Aramco’s Shaybah oil field. As a result, government agencies in Riyadh have told staff to work from home. Moreover, even the holy cities have not been spared: an attack on a power station in Madinah drew condemnation from Pakistan earlier this month. Clearly, this is no longer a skirmish on a distant border. It has reached the capital, the oil-rich east and the very places our pilgrims go to pray. Against that backdrop, consider what our authorities have offered. To begin with, SriLankan Airlines has suspended flights to Riyadh and Dammam until 1 November. In addition, the Consulate General in Jeddah issued a notice on 16 October about possible flight disruptions, while the Department of Muslim Religious and Cultural Affairs asked tour operators to take precautions. What is more, no one knows how many Sri Lankans are performing Umrah right now. The Hajj and Umrah Committee Chairman conceded as much. Unlike Hajj, Umrah is arranged privately, throughout the year, on individual visas, and pilgrims are free to travel well beyond Mecca. In other words, the State cannot say how many of its citizens are inside a country under missile attack, let alone where they are. Likewise, the suggestion that the Rs 2 million licence fees paid by operators could fund a repatriation is not a plan. On the contrary, it is a hope that the private sector will do the Government’s job. Nevertheless, pilgrims are the smaller part of the story. Saudi Arabia is one of the largest destinations for Sri Lankan migrant labour. Many are housemaids and low-wage workers whose passports may sit with their sponsors, and whose employers decide whether they can move at all. Consequently, in a crisis they are the last to be evacuated and the first to be forgotten. After all, their remittances helped carry this country through the worst economic collapse in living memory. Surely, we owe them more than a press line. Therefore, what is needed is preparation. First, an urgent registration drive for every Sri Lankan in the Kingdom, pilgrims and workers alike, through the embassy, the consulate, the Foreign Employment Bureau and licensed tour operators. Second, a clear advisory urging citizen to defer non-essential travel, including Umrah, until the situation stabilises. Third, a contingency evacuation plan, with airlift arrangements through Jeddah, overland routes identified in advance, and understandings with India and other partners to share capacity. Fourth, a dedicated emergency fund that does not depend on operators’ deposits. Finally, a round-the-clock hotline and regular public briefings, so that families at home are not left to rumour and WhatsApp forwards. Furthermore, Saudi Arabia is not our only exposure. The wider confrontation involving Iran has already seen Gulf states targeted this year, and that is precisely where the bulk of our expatriate workforce lives. Accordingly, a full-blown regional war would bring an oil shock, a collapse in remittances and the sudden return of tens of thousands of workers to a labour market that cannot absorb them. Is there a plan for that? If there is, the public has yet to see it.

audit.headline: Bilateral talks: SL, Türkiye to sign air transport protocol amendment
audit.summary: A Memorandum of Understanding on Agricultural Cooperation between Sri Lanka and Türkiye, as well as a protocol amending the Air Transport Agreement between the two countries, will be signed during the ongoing visit of Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Employment Arun Hemachandra in Türkiye, according to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Foreign Employment, and Tourism. audit.headline: Bringing light to every corner of the island
audit.summary: 27 Oct 2026 | BY ASWIDA BASURU MADIHAGE Why does the world pause every October to look after its eyes, and how the College of Ophthalmologists of SL is helping a Nation see? audit.body: 27 Oct 2026 | BY ASWIDA BASURU MADIHAGE Why does the world pause every October to look after its eyes, and how the College of Ophthalmologists of SL is helping a Nation see? In the year 2000, the world’s eye-health community came together around one simple message: prevent avoidable blindness and protect the gift of sight. That message has not changed in more than two decades. The World Sight Day is observed on the second Thursday of October, and this year (2026) it fell on 8 October. It reminds the public, decision-makers and health-service providers that eyesight is a foundation of a good life. Sight is how a child learns, how a farmer reads the sky, how a grandmother recognises her grandchildren, and how a worker earns a living. It is also easy to take for granted until it begins to fade. The scale of what is at stake is large. The WHO estimates that 2.2 billion people worldwide live with some form of near or distance vision impairment, and nearly 30 per cent of them live in the WHO South-East Asia Region, which includes Sri Lanka. At least one billion of these cases could have been prevented or have yet to be addressed. The remedies are largely known, and many are as simple as a pair of spectacles or a surgery lasting a few minutes, yet, millions still live with impaired vision because that help has not reached them. The WHO’s latest estimates break the picture down. Cataract accounts for about 94 million cases contributing to distance vision impairment or blindness, and uncorrected refractive error for 88.4 million. Glaucoma, which damages the optic nerve and often gives no warning until the damage is permanent, accounts for 7.7 million, and diabetic retinopathy for 3.9 million. About 826 million more live with unaddressed near-vision impairment from presbyopia, the age-related loss of close focus. The WHO projects that by 2030, the world will have 2.1 billion people with presbyopia and 3.36 billion with myopia, or short-sightedness. The statistics that matter the most are about access. In low-income countries, two out of every three people who need glasses do not have them, and globally, one in two people who need cataract surgery cannot get it. Behind each number is a person who stopped working, a child who fell behind in class, or an older relative who stopped walking outside after a fall. Vision loss falls most heavily on low-income families, women and older people, the groups least able to pay for an eye examination or a pair of spectacles. The said Region has taken stock of how far it has to go. Its World Sight Day statement this year noted that cataract, uncorrected refractive error and diabetic retinopathy together account for more than 90% of the Region’s blind and visually impaired population. In 2021, the World Health Assembly endorsed two global eye-care targets for 2030, and the Region has committed to both: a 40-percentage-point increase in effective refractive error coverage and a 30-percentage-point increase in effective cataract surgical coverage. The starting points are modest, at about 27% and 26%, respectively. The Regional action plan adds a commitment to screen 80% of people with diabetes for retinopathy and to treat 80% of those found with sight-threatening disease. The Region has eliminated trachoma There is good news as well. The Region has eliminated trachoma as a public health problem, following the validation of Timor-Leste last month (September). Sri Lanka and seven other countries have begun rolling out the WHO’s SPECS 2030 initiative to widen access to spectacles, and Sri Lanka, together with Bhutan and the Maldives, is developing a national eye health strategy built on those principles. The WHO has also published a free app – WHOeyes - that lets people check their visual acuity at home. It does not replace an examination by an eye-care professional, it helps people notice a problem early and act on it. The Ophthalmological Society of Ceylon In Sri Lanka, much of this work is carried out by one professional body - the College of Ophthalmologists of Sri Lanka (COSL). Its roots go back to 1 December 1957, when clinicians met at the Victoria Memorial Eye Hospital in Colombo to form the Ophthalmological Society of Ceylon, the second-oldest specialist association in the country, with Dr W H D Ferdinands as its founding President. The COSL was formally established in 1991 as its direct continuation. It is the only professional body of Ophthalmologists in the country, with its office at the National Eye Hospital in Colombo, the main training centre for ophthalmic postgraduate trainees, technologists and nurses. Working alongside the Health Ministry, it carries out the functions of Vision 2020 in Sri Lanka, the global initiative to eliminate avoidable blindness. Much of the College’s work happens out of public view. It advises the Ministry, takes part in national and regional policy decisions, and sees itself as the collective voice of the profession. It trains specialists, holds an annual congress and publishes a peer-reviewed journal. Its subcommittees include the Glaucoma Interest Group and Retina Sri Lanka, and its partners range from the Ministry and the WHO to the National Eye Bank. At a recent congress, research was presented on a teleophthalmology model designed so that a patient in a remote village has the same chance of early diagnosis as one living near a major hospital. Today, the College is led by its President for 2026, Dr K R Dayawansa. That work has led to the College’s best-known initiative. Sri Lanka has skilled eye surgeons; the difficulty is getting the care to everyone who needs it. The idea behind the Gift of Vision was born in March of last year (2025), when Dr Kusum Ratnayake was the President of the College, and he is the initiator of the project. At the time, there was growing public concern about long waiting lists for cataract surgery. The country was not short of surgeons. The delays came from the system around them: limited operating-theatre time, insufficient equipment, and logistical and administrative hurdles. Instead of accepting those limits, the COSL decided to work around them, using careful planning, coordination and support to let a very large number of operations be done in a short time, especially where the need was most urgent. 1.7% of the population is blind because of cataract Dr Ratnayake, now the immediate Past President, has explained why the effort matters. Cataract remains one of the leading causes of blindness worldwide, and Sri Lanka is no exception. National data suggest that around 1.7% of the population is blind because of cataract, and many more live with impairment that limits their ability to work, move freely and manage everyday tasks. The barriers to treatment are many: costs, doubts about whether the surgery is safe, social obstacles to travelling alone, chronic conditions such as diabetes and hypertension that need attention first, and, in rural areas, long distances and limited transport. The Gift of Vision was built to address these obstacles directly. Its structure sets it apart. The programme is not run from a single central point. Regional eye surgeons plan and carry out surgical camps in their own areas, where they know the hospitals, the patients and the local constraints. Hospitals are chosen on the basis of need, and patients are identified, screened and prioritised beforehand so that urgent cases are seen first. The effort rests on a wide network of volunteers, including consultant eye surgeons, medical officers, nurses, optometrists and technical staff, many of whom travel long distances, often arranging their own transport and rearranging their personal lives. This collective generosity has allowed the initiative to run at a scale that would have been very hard to reach otherwise. The first camp took place at the Teaching Hospital in Anuradhapura, where 316 surgeries were carried out. The programme then moved across the country, reaching Nuwara Eliya, Dikoya, Matara, Kahawatta, Polonnaruwa, Mahiyanganaya, Trincomalee, Badulla and Gampola. Each location brought its own difficulties, but the method stayed the same: identify the need, mobilise resources and deliver care within a defined time. Then came two days in March 2026 that the COSL describes as golden in its history. On 21 and 22 March, at the National Eye Hospital, surgical teams completed 1,129 cataract surgeries in just two days. The work continues in all parts of the country, and the total now stands at 6,500 cataract surgeries. Cataract is the most visible of the College’s concerns, but not the only one. Its thinking follows the WHO’s: find problems early, because the conditions that cause the most irreversible damage often give the least warning. Glaucoma, the leading cause of irreversible blindness in the world, affects an estimated 80 million people, a number expected to reach 120 million by 2040. Known as the silent thief of sight, it is generally painless, and by the time a person notices that their side vision going, much of the damage is done. The Glaucoma Interest Group therefore runs screening camps in underserved areas, always in collaboration with the local eye surgeon so that patients receive continued follow-up. During the World Glaucoma Week, from 8 to 14 March 2026, it organised awareness programmes and free screening camps, aimed especially at people over 40, people with diabetes and those with a family history of glaucoma. Awareness is part of the treatment, since many people believe that cataracts are unavoidable or do not know that glaucoma can harm the eyes without warning. The COSL plans to continue the Gift of Vision regularly across the country. The lessons are practical: anyone over 40 should have regular eye examinations, people with diabetes should have their eyes checked every year, and children who squint or struggle to read the board should have their sight tested. The WHO’s invitation this year is simple: check your vision, care for your eyes and encourage others to do the same. The lesson is the one that the world first heard in 2000: much of blindness can be prevented, and protecting sight is work that every one of us can help with. The writer holds a Bachelor of Science (Honours) in Biotechnology degree from the Nilai University, Malaysia The views and opinions expressed in this column are those of the writer, and do not necessarily reflect those of this publication

audit.body: 27 Oct 2026 | By Sindy Fernando The Central Bank of Sri Lanka (CBSL) has stressed that public trust must remain central to the adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) as the technology increasingly influences institutional decision-making, CBSL Governor Dr P Nandalal Weerasinghe said at its 76th Anniversary Oration on Friday (23). Speaking at the event, held under the theme The Intelligent Central Bank: Building Trust in the Age of AI , Dr Weerasinghe said: “As we embrace emerging technologies, we must ensure that innovation strengthens rather than diminishes trust. AI is rapidly transforming the way institutions generate insights, make decisions, deliver services, and manage risk.” “The Central Bank’s trust has always been our most valuable asset. Public confidence in our institutions underpins the effectiveness of monetary policy, the stability of the financial system and the integrity of our nation’s financial infrastructure,” he said. Dr Weerasinghe added: “Across the world, central banks and financial institutions are exploring how AI can improve operational efficiency, strengthen data-driven policymaking and create more responsible institutions.” “At the same time, we must support innovation not only within our own organisations but also across the broader financial ecosystem, enabling technology to strengthen economic performance, financial inclusion, and institutional effectiveness without compromising stability or public confidence,” he said. Dr Weerasinghe further said: “However, the AI revolution is not merely a question of technology at its core. It’s a question of trust. While AI presents immense opportunities, it also introduces new challenges as systems can operate at unprecedented speed and scale, influence decision-making, generate highly convincing content, and create new avenues for cyber threats and misuse.” The risks associated with AI-generated content have also emerged in Sri Lanka. According to the Ministry of Mass Media, the Sri Lanka Computer Emergency Readiness Team (CERT) reported numerous complaints in June this year involving fraudulent videos that used AI to impersonate prominent public figures and promote investment scams. Such incidents highlight the potential for AI-generated content to mislead the public and expose individuals to financial fraud. Dr Weerasinghe added: “Throughout these decades, the Central Bank has adapted to changing economic, financial, and technological landscapes, while remaining steadfast in its commitment to deliver the mandate through maintaining price stability and financial system stability.”

audit.body: 27 Oct 2026 | BY Dhanushka Dharmapriya Rights group seeks special custody for cellmate eyewitness The Officer-in-Charge (OIC) of the Crimes Division and two Sub-Inspectors (SIs) attached to the Homagama Police were yesterday (26) interdicted over alleged administrative lapses following the death of a suspect in Police custody. Meanwhile, a prisoners’ rights group claims the only eyewitness to the incident is being threatened by the Police. The deceased, Ishara Harsha Kumara, a 29-year-old father of two from Kiriwaththuduwa, died on 25 October after being arrested and detained by the Homagama Police in connection with a drug-related investigation. He allegedly died following an assault at the Homagama Police Station. The Committee for Protecting the Rights of Prisoners (CPRP) has requested that the eyewitness, who shared a cell with Kumara, be placed in special custody for his safety. The group claims the Police are threatening him with charges of possessing more than 10g of crystal methamphetamine Ice. According to the CPRP, the witness has also been denied access to family members and lawyers. When contacted, CPRP President Attorney-at-Law Senaka Perera said the cellmate had witnessed what happened to Kumara. “He has seen the entire incident, but the Police aren’t allowing anyone to speak to him. We have information from reliable sources that the Police are going to file a case against him for possessing more than 10 g of Ice, and that he is being blackmailed to prevent him from revealing what happened,” he alleged. According to Perera, Kumara was questioned by the Crimes Division of the Homagama Police following his arrest, and was allegedly tortured during this inquiry, which subsequently led to his death. Kumara’s wife and brother had reportedly seen him alive and in good condition approximately one and a half hours before his death. However, he was later brought back to the cell with assistance, bleeding and unable to walk, Perera said. Kumara’s wife and relatives have accused the Homagama Police of torturing him and failing to provide him with medical care, which they claim led to his death. According to the CPRP, the post-mortem examination has been ordered to be conducted at the Colombo South Teaching Hospital instead of the Homagama Hospital, to safeguard the transparency of the process. According to the Police Media Division (PMD), the suspect was arrested by Homagama Police officers at Pitipana Junction, within the Homagama Police Division, on Sunday (25). He was a resident of Moonamalewatta, Kiriwaththuduwa. The PMD said the suspect suddenly fell ill after being brought to the police station and was subsequently admitted to the Homagama Base Hospital for treatment, where he later died. Following notification of the death to the Homagama Magistrate’s Court, the Acting Magistrate visited the hospital, inspected the scene and conducted a magisterial inquiry into the incident, the PMD said. A post-mortem examination is scheduled to be held at the Kalubowila Hospital today (27). The PMD further stated that the Superintendent of Police in charge of the Homagama District (I) had suspended three officers with effect from yesterday, pending investigations into the circumstances surrounding the suspect’s death. The suspended officers include two Sub-Inspectors of Police who served as Officers-in-Charge of the Crimes Division and the Anti-Corruption/Raids Unit at the Homagama Police Station, respectively, and a Police Constable assigned to support duties. The PMD further said investigations were being conducted under the direct supervision of the Senior Superintendent of Police in charge of the Homagama Division, with the Assistant Superintendent of Police in charge of the Homagama District (II) overseeing the inquiry. Meanwhile, acting on the orders and instructions of the Inspector General of Police, the Western Province South Divisional Crimes Division and the Police Special Investigation Unit had also launched investigations into the incident.

audit.body: 27 Oct 2026 | BY Dhanushka Dharmapriya Up to 150 mm of rain forecast Rivers rise and spill gates open Red warning for deep-sea fishermen 278 persons moved to relief camps Sri Lanka is bracing for several days of heavy rain, strong winds and possible flooding as Cyclone ‘Arnab’ continues to intensify over the Bay of Bengal, even though the storm itself is not expected to directly affect the island, officials said yesterday (26). The cyclonic storm, which formed over the east-central and adjoining south-east Bay of Bengal yesterday, approximately 1,100 km north-east of Kankesanthurai, after moving westwards, the Department of Meteorology said. It was expected to move west-north-westwards and intensify into a severe cyclonic storm over the west-central Bay by 5:30 p.m. yesterday, before strengthening further into a very severe cyclonic storm today (27). Although the cyclone will not make landfall here, wind flows associated with it are expected to increase rainfall over the south-western parts of the island in the coming days. Deputy Minister of Defence Aruna Jayasekara said that with ‘Arnab’ intensifying into a very strong cyclone by today, rainfall of 100-150 millimetres (mm) was expected in some areas of the Northern, Western, Sabaragamuwa, Central and North-Central Provinces. Showers or thunderstorms are expected at times in the Northern, Western, Sabaragamuwa, Southern, North-Western, Central and North-Central Provinces and in the Trincomalee District, with fairly heavy falls above 75 mm likely at some locations. Showers may occur in other parts of the country after 1 p.m. Strong winds of 40-50 kilometres per hour (kmph) are expected at times over the western slopes of the Central Hills, the Northern, North-Central and North-Western Provinces, and the Trincomalee and Hambantota Districts. The Department also issued an Amber advisory for heavy rain covering the Northern, Western, Sabaragamuwa, North-Western, Central and Southern Provinces and the Anuradhapura District. The advisory, issued at 3 a.m. yesterday, remained in force until 5:30 a.m. today, with rainy conditions expected to continue over the next few days. In the past 24 hours, Karandipowal in the Puttalam District recorded the highest rainfall at 195.7 mm, followed by Kuliyapitiya (193 mm) and Illuppaikkadavai (187.5 mm). Irrigation Department Director of Hydrology and Disaster Management L S Sooriyabandara said a minor flood situation had developed in the Kalu Ganga at Ratnapura and in its downstream areas, while rising water levels in the Kelani Ganga and the Attanagalu Oya posed a risk to residents of low-lying areas. With water also being released from the Deduru Oya, Rajanganaya, Tabbowa and Inginimitiya reservoirs, people living in low-lying areas downstream have been urged to remain vigilant. Jayasekara said 278 individuals from 72 families in the Ampara, Colombo, Gampaha, Matara and Ratnapura Districts were being directed to relief camps in their respective areas by the National Disaster Relief Services Centre. He added that the tri-forces, the Police, the Civil Security Department and the Coast Guard Department had been readied to respond to any emergency. The Department has issued a red warning for strong winds and rough seas for multi-day fishing vessels operating in the deep and shallow sea areas of the Bay of Bengal, where wind speeds may increase to 80-100 kmph at times and waves may reach three to four metres. Naval and fishing communities have been advised not to venture into the sea areas bounded by latitudes 10°N to 20°N and longitudes 80°E to 95°E until further notice, while those already in these areas have been told to move away. The public has also been urged to take precautions against damage caused by temporary, localised strong winds and lightning, and to closely follow official warnings. The warnings come less than a year after Cyclone Ditwah struck the island on 28 November 2025, in what became Sri Lanka’s worst natural disaster in two decades.

audit.body: 27 Oct 2026 | BY Buddhika Samaraweera Cite increased rains, hydropower generation In the wake of the National System Operator (NSO) Private Limited seeking a 2.88 per cent increase in electricity tariffs for the fourth quarter (October-December) of this year (2026), electricity tariffs could instead be reduced by at least 10% due to the increased hydropower generation amid heavy rainfall and rapidly rising reservoir levels, the ECA stated. Speaking to The Daily Morning , Electricity Consumers' Association (ECA) General Secretary Sanjeewa Dhammika said that the Public Utilities Commission of Sri Lanka (PUCSL) had conducted a preliminary review of the NSO’s proposal and found that a smaller increase could be considered. “The PUCSL has observed that the proposed increase could be limited to around 1.46%. However, when we look at the data, we can say that electricity tariffs could be reduced by at least 10%." He further said that the country is receiving heavy rainfall, with water levels in reservoirs rising rapidly and several reservoirs spilling over. He said that this could allow the electricity companies to increase hydropower generation and reduce the reliance on more expensive sources of electricity, creating room for a tariff reduction. “Reservoirs are filling rapidly these days, and many are spilling over. This must also be taken into consideration when implementing the tariff revision.” Energy Minister Anura Karunathilaka was unavailable for comment. The NSO has reportedly requested PUCSL approval for a 2.88% tariff increase for the October to December quarter. The PUCSL has published its fourth-quarter tariff review on its official website, and PUCSL Director-General Damitha Kumarasinghe has confirmed that the proposal is undergoing review and that public consultations have commenced. The PUCSL’s preliminary assessment has indicated that the proposed increase could be reduced to approximately 1.46%, according to the published review.

The three-match ODI series will be played at the Rangiri Dambulla International Cricket Stadium (RDICS) in Dambulla. The first ODI is scheduled for 4 March, followed by the second on 6 March and the third two days later.

audit.headline: External sector: Export earnings surpass $ 13.6 b in 9M 2026
audit.summary: Sri Lanka’s total exports have reached $ 13.61 billion during the first nine months of 2026, recording a year-on-year growth of 5.04% compared with $ 12.96 billion in the corresponding period of 2025, according to the latest export performance figures released by Sri Lanka Customs, together with the EDB’s estimates. In the category of gems and jewellery and petroleum products, merchandise exports grew by 5.35% to $ 10.76 billion during January–September, compared with $ 10.22 billion recorded in the corresponding period of 2025. Meanwhile, services exports grew by 3.88% to $ 2.85 billion, up from $ 2.74 billion in the corresponding period of the previous year. The performance of both segments highlights the importance of strengthening Sri Lanka’s export competitiveness while diversifying its sources of export earnings.
audit.body: Sri Lanka’s total exports have reached $ 13.61 billion during the first nine months of 2026, recording a year-on-year growth of 5.04% compared with $ 12.96 billion in the corresponding period of 2025, according to the latest export performance figures released by Sri Lanka Customs, together with the EDB’s estimates. In the category of gems and jewellery and petroleum products, merchandise exports grew by 5.35% to $ 10.76 billion during January–September, compared with $ 10.22 billion recorded in the corresponding period of 2025. Meanwhile, services exports grew by 3.88% to $ 2.85 billion, up from $ 2.74 billion in the corresponding period of the previous year. The performance of both segments highlights the importance of strengthening Sri Lanka’s export competitiveness while diversifying its sources of export earnings. Sri Lanka recorded a particularly strong performance in September this year, with total exports reaching $ 1.69 billion, an impressive year-on-year increase of 17.23% compared with $ 1.44 billion in September 2025. Merchandise exports were the main driver of this monthly growth, increasing by 21.66% to $ 1.39 billion, compared with $ 1.14 billion in September 2025. Services exports also recorded a positive performance, rising by 0.67% to $ 306.17 million from $ 304.14 million in the corresponding month last year. The strong growth in merchandise exports during September contributed significantly to the overall improvement in export earnings, reinforcing the positive trajectory of Sri Lanka’s export sector. Commenting on the export performance in September this year, Sri Lanka Export Development Board (EDB) Chairperson and Chief Executive Officer Mangala Wijesinghe stated: “Sri Lanka’s total exports reaching $ 13.61 billion during the first nine months of 2026, representing a growth of 5.04% compared with the corresponding period of 2025, reflects the continued resilience and progress of our export sector.” “Particularly encouraging is the strong performance recorded in September, when total exports increased by 17.23% year-on-year to $ 1.69 billion, driven by a significant 21.66% growth in merchandise exports. This performance demonstrates the potential of Sri Lankan exporters to strengthen their presence in international markets despite an increasingly competitive global trading environment,” he added.

audit.headline: From Lanka to the Culinary Olympics: The Sweet Mastery of Chef Dilip
audit.summary: 27 Oct 2026 | BY MUAARD RAZICK In the precise and demanding world of international pastry, few Sri Lankan names command as much respect as Chef Dilip Rajapaksha. What began as a young trainee's curiosity at NAITA and in the kitchens of the iconic Mahaweli Reach Hotel in Kandy has blossomed into a glittering global career that spans over two decades and several continents. Chef Dilip is not just a pastry chef; he is an artist, an engineer of sugar and chocolate, and a proven champion on the world's toughest culinary stage. Having honed his craft with luxury hospitality giants including Radisson Blu, Golden Tulip, and Hilton across the UAE and Oman, he has mastered everything from delicate sugar flower artistry and towering chocolate showpieces to intricate pastillage work. His excellence is internationally certified.
audit.body: 27 Oct 2026 | BY MUAARD RAZICK In the precise and demanding world of international pastry, few Sri Lankan names command as much respect as Chef Dilip Rajapaksha. What began as a young trainee's curiosity at NAITA and in the kitchens of the iconic Mahaweli Reach Hotel in Kandy has blossomed into a glittering global career that spans over two decades and several continents. Chef Dilip is not just a pastry chef; he is an artist, an engineer of sugar and chocolate, and a proven champion on the world's toughest culinary stage. Having honed his craft with luxury hospitality giants including Radisson Blu, Golden Tulip, and Hilton across the UAE and Oman, he has mastered everything from delicate sugar flower artistry and towering chocolate showpieces to intricate pastillage work. His excellence is internationally certified. He is a multi-medalist at the culinary world's most prestigious competitions, winning Gold and Silver at the IKA / Culinary Olympics in Germany 2024 and Gold and Bronze at the Culinary World Cup in Luxembourg 2022, and was part of the Guinness World Record-setting team for 2,586 varieties of desserts with the Emirates Culinary Guild in 2019. Today, he also serves as a qualified international culinary judge, shaping the next generation of global standards. Now, he has brought that Olympic-grade expertise back home. As the co-founder of Ceylon Hospitality Academy (Pvt) Ltd in Kandy, his mission is to transform Sri Lankan hospitality education and prove that world-class pastry can be taught, perfected, and pioneered from the hill capital itself. Following are excerpts from the interview: Chef Dilip, let's start at the beginning. From your training at NAITA and your early days at Mahaweli Reach Hotel in Kandy, what inspired you to choose pastry and bakery as your specialty? During my training at NAITA and my early work at the Mahaweli Reach Hotel, global culinary trends were changing drastically. The waves of that modern culinary shift were just beginning to reach Sri Lanka. At the time, our local industry was hungry for new knowledge, technique, and international standards. I quickly noticed that the pastry and bakery section was the most versatile, precise, and creative discipline in the kitchen, it was truly an art form. That realisation inspired me to fully commit my career to the art of pastry and bakery. You have worked with world-renowned brands like Radisson Blu, Golden Tulip, and Hilton in the UAE and Oman. What was the biggest challenge you faced when you first moved abroad, and how did you adapt? Coming from Sri Lanka at that time, we were still developing in terms of modern culinary standards, specialised techniques, and premium ingredients. When I first stepped into international kitchens, almost everything was completely new to me. To overcome this, I worked around the clock, literally absorbing knowledge from global experts across different nationalities. I was immensely driven, and that passion allowed me to adapt quickly and refine my skills to meet international expectations. You won Gold and Silver medals at the IKA / Culinary Olympics in Germany 2024 and Gold & Bronze at the Culinary World Cup in Luxembourg 2022. How does it feel to win at the highest level of world culinary competition? Standing on the podium at the Culinary Olympics and the Culinary World Cup—competing against the best master chefs on the planet—is validation of years of relentless practice, sleepless nights, and uncompromising discipline. It proves that Sri Lankan talent can not only compete on the global stage, but actually lead and define world-class standards. Your expertise includes chocolate showpieces, sugar flower artistry and pastillage work. Can you explain to our readers how much time and precision goes into creating one of these artistic pieces? Artistic pastry work is where culinary skill meets engineering and fine art. A single showpiece can take anywhere from tens to hundreds of hours of painstaking preparation, from initial conceptual sketches and structural blueprints to climate-controlled assembly. Working with materials like pulled sugar or chocolate requires absolute temperature precision and extreme patience; a fraction of a degree or a minor mistake can destroy weeks of work in a second. It demands total focus, delicate handcrafting, and a deep understanding of physics and aesthetics. In 2019, you were part of the team that set a Guinness World Record for 2,586 varieties of desserts with Emirates Culinary Guild. What was that experience like behind the scenes? It was absolute operational mastery and intense teamwork. Creating thousands of distinct, high-quality dessert varieties within a strict timeframe required flawless organisation, logistical precision, and endless energy. Behind the scenes, hundreds of chefs worked seamlessly in high-pressure shifts. The atmosphere was electrifying, and breaking that world record showed what can be achieved when top-tier culinary minds collaborate with a shared vision. Now you are also a qualified international culinary competition judge. How is judging different from competing, and what do you look for when you evaluate a dish? When you compete, to be honest, your main goal is to win and show your maximum technique. But when you sit on the judging panel, your focus shifts toward evaluation and mentorship. You look at the immense effort, thought process, and creativity the chef has poured into their creation. Beyond technical perfection and taste, I specifically evaluate what the dish contributes to the evolving culinary world in terms of innovation and learning. You are also known for health-conscious wellness dessert concepts. How do you balance taste, presentation and health in modern pastry? Modern gastronomy is evolving, and diners are far more conscious of what they consume. Balancing health with luxury means rethinking fundamental ingredients without sacrificing flavor or texture. I focus on natural sweeteners, alternative plant-based textures, nutrient-dense superfoods, and clean presentation. A great wellness dessert should feel indulgent and visually stunning, while leaving the guest feeling nourished rather than heavy. You co-founded Ceylon Hospitality Academy (Pvt) Ltd in Kandy. What was your vision behind starting a dedicated pastry and bakery school in Sri Lanka? Human civilisation changed for the better when we learned to cook and share meals, and Sri Lankans are naturally a deeply hospitable nation. My vision was to establish a benchmark center to educate our youth according to global modern culinary standards, producing world-class, passionate pastry and bakery chefs who can contribute meaningfully to the global industry. That is why our motto is "Passion to Perfection." How is the training you offer at Ceylon Hospitality Academy different from traditional hotel school education, and how are you bringing Olympic-grade standards to Kandy? Traditionally, a student completes a basic course and then spends years navigating an unmethodical, trial-and-error path across various hotel kitchens just to acquire practical knowledge. It is a time-consuming and uncertain journey, which often discourages young talent. At Ceylon Hospitality Academy, we have built a true five-star commercial kitchen environment with global hygiene standards, state-of-the-art machinery, and modern equipment. Training with us for six months is equivalent to working methodically in a top-tier hotel kitchen in Dubai or Europe. When our students graduate, they step directly into the industry fully prepared, confident, and skilled at an international standard. For a young Sri Lankan who dreams of becoming an international pastry chef like you, what are the three most important qualities or habits they need to develop? First, you must have a clear vision of where you want to go. Second, you must maintain the right attitude—stay humble, remain eager to learn, and respect the discipline of the kitchen. Third, you need immense patience. Mastering culinary arts is a marathon, not a sprint; consistency and dedication will always carry you to the top. The views and opinions expressed in this column are those of the interviewee, and do not necessarily reflect those of this publication

audit.headline: Getting spooky this Halloween
audit.summary: 27 Oct 2026 | By Apsara Rodrigo Halloween, celebrated on 31 October, is known for its costumes, carved pumpkins, haunted houses and children going from door to door asking for sweets. Although the festival has its roots in Western traditions, it has gradually found a place in Sri Lanka, particularly among young people, families and businesses looking for new ways to celebrate. In Colombo and its surrounding areas, Halloween has become an opportunity for people to dress up, attend themed parties and enjoy a night of spooky entertainment. Restaurants, hotels, shopping malls and event organisers have also embraced the occasion, offering themed menus, decorations, costume competitions and special events. For some, it is an excuse to gather with friends and enjoy a night out. For others, it is a chance to get creative with costumes, make-up and decorations.
audit.body: 27 Oct 2026 | By Apsara Rodrigo Halloween, celebrated on 31 October, is known for its costumes, carved pumpkins, haunted houses and children going from door to door asking for sweets. Although the festival has its roots in Western traditions, it has gradually found a place in Sri Lanka, particularly among young people, families and businesses looking for new ways to celebrate. In Colombo and its surrounding areas, Halloween has become an opportunity for people to dress up, attend themed parties and enjoy a night of spooky entertainment. Restaurants, hotels, shopping malls and event organisers have also embraced the occasion, offering themed menus, decorations, costume competitions and special events. For some, it is an excuse to gather with friends and enjoy a night out. For others, it is a chance to get creative with costumes, make-up and decorations. However, Halloween in Sri Lanka looks different from the celebrations seen in countries such as the United States. The tradition of trick-or-treating is not widespread, and the festival is largely celebrated through organised events rather than neighbourhood activities. Its growing popularity also raises questions about how international celebrations become part of local culture. While Halloween is not a traditional Sri Lankan festival, its appeal lies in its playful nature. It offers people an opportunity to step away from their everyday routines, experiment with different identities and take part in a celebration built around imagination, creativity and a little fright. Halloween has a long history, with its origins commonly linked to Samhain, an ancient Celtic festival marking the end of the harvest season and the beginning of winter. Over time, later traditions and later popular culture helped shape the celebration into the event known today. In countries where Halloween is widely celebrated, children often wear costumes and visit neighbouring homes to collect sweets. Adults participate in costume parties, haunted attractions and other themed activities. Pumpkins, ghosts, witches and skeletons have become familiar symbols of the occasion. In Sri Lanka, Halloween has developed along a different path. Rather than being centred on neighbourhood trick-or-treating, celebrations tend to take place at hotels, restaurants, clubs, shopping centres and private gatherings. These events allow people to experience the festival without requiring it to become part of everyday community life. “I love getting dressed up and going to Halloween parties,” Nethara De Silva ,18, said. “My school always does something like a carnival or a haunted house.” International films, television shows and social media have also helped introduce Halloween to Sri Lankan audiences. Images of elaborate costumes, pumpkin decorations and themed parties have made the celebration familiar to people who may never have experienced it abroad. For many people, one of the biggest attractions of Halloween is the opportunity to dress up. Costumes can range from classic witches, vampires and ghosts to characters from popular films, television series and books. Unlike everyday fashion, Halloween encourages people to experiment with their appearance. Dramatic make-up, unusual accessories and imaginative outfits become part of the fun. In Sri Lanka, where the tropical climate can make heavy costumes uncomfortable, lightweight clothing and creative make-up can be practical alternatives. People can also put together costumes using clothes and accessories they already own instead of spending large amounts of money on a single occasion. “I’ve always wanted to recreate Cady Heron’s costume from Mean Girls,” Amaya De Silva,27, said. “I know it’s a lot of work but I’m looking forward to it.” Social media has added another dimension to this aspect of the celebration. Costume photographs, make-up tutorials and themed videos allow people to share their creations with friends and wider audiences. For those who enjoy fashion, beauty and photography, Halloween provides an opportunity to explore a more theatrical style without taking themselves too seriously. Social media has made it easier for people in Sri Lanka to discover celebrations taking place around the world. Photographs and videos from countries where Halloween is a major event can inspire local parties, decorations and costume ideas. Younger audiences may also encounter Halloween through international entertainment, online communities and friendships with people living overseas. For some, taking part in the celebration is a way to connect with global popular culture. “I see a lot of people on TikTok talking about rewatching horror movies and rereading horror stories,” Shalini K, 28, said. “Honestly, I’m happy to just get out some of my spooky reads. I’m starting with Carrie.” At the same time, its growing visibility does not necessarily mean that Halloween is celebrated by most Sri Lankans. Many people may be familiar with the occasion without participating in it, while others may prefer to celebrate through small gatherings rather than organised events. There are also practical considerations. Costumes and decorations can be expensive, and the absence of an established trick-or-treating tradition means that families may have fewer opportunities to celebrate in the same way as those in North America or parts of Europe. Nevertheless, Halloween does not need to follow one fixed format. A themed dinner, a film night, a costume party or a simple gathering with friends can all provide ways to mark the occasion. Halloween may not have originated in Sri Lanka, but it offers people another reason to celebrate, socialise and express themselves creatively. “I think Sri Lankan culture can play a part in the celebration,” Sheruni Alwis,32, said. “We have our own traditions and ghost stories and I think channeling your inner Amanda Jayathissa character can still be true to the spirit of Halloween and Sri Lankan culture.” Its local appeal reflects the way traditions can travel across borders and take on new forms. While some celebrations are rooted in religion, history or national identity, others grow through entertainment, fashion and shared experiences. For Sri Lankans who enjoy dressing up, decorating their homes or attending themed events, Halloween provides a chance to try something different. It can be as elaborate as a costume party or as simple as watching a spooky film with friends.

audit.headline: Global uncertainty: SL adopts three-month rolling forecasts
audit.summary: 27 Oct 2026 | By Nethmi Rajawasam The Government is adopting a three-month-ahead forecasting approach to respond to ongoing global uncertainty and energy price shocks, with the aim of maintaining its growth trajectory and export orientation, Deputy Minister of Industry and Entrepreneurship Development Chathuranga Abeysinghe said in a video interview with Indian broadcaster NDTV . “Basically we will have to keep a watch. audit.body: 27 Oct 2026 | By Nethmi Rajawasam The Government is adopting a three-month-ahead forecasting approach to respond to ongoing global uncertainty and energy price shocks, with the aim of maintaining its growth trajectory and export orientation, Deputy Minister of Industry and Entrepreneurship Development Chathuranga Abeysinghe said in a video interview with Indian broadcaster NDTV . “Basically we will have to keep a watch. So now as a Government what we are doing is forecasting three months ahead and trying to ensure that we won’t drop our ball on the growth trajectory that we are in and also our export orientation,” Abeysinghe said. “We are also an energy-dependent country, so basically everything adjusts based on the energy prices. Within this year, energy prices have escalated three times, and it has impacted us with higher inflation and also pushed our cost of manufacturing up. So what we are doing now is, given the fiscal consolidation we have, the Government is continuing to maintain a fiscal buffer. So we were able to adjust to a certain level.” Abeysinghe said the global crisis had led to a short-term slow down in Sri Lanka’s growth trajectory. Sri Lanka’s real GDP grew by 4.2% in Q2 2026, marking a slowdown from the 5.1% growth recorded in Q1. He also revealed the timeframe for 18 industrial zones to be established within one to two years, under the purview of the Ministry of Industry and the Board of Investment (BOI) of Sri Lanka. “It’ll take about another one or two years to get these economic zones built. My ministry is doing 11 and BOI is doing seven. So altogether there will be 18 new industrial zones,” he said. Abeysinghe further noted that the Government expects to see collaboration between Sri Lankan and Indian corporates in the interim. “Until that, I expect those large or midsize corporates which we spoke to look at possible partnerships with Sri Lankan entities because those Sri Lankan entities already have access to Europe, already have access to the US, and already in the global market, and to see how they can partner with technology or investment or market access.”

audit.headline: Med imports compensation case: SC releases Keheliya, others on bonds
audit.summary: The Supreme Court (SC) yesterday (26) ordered the release on bonds of former Minister Keheliya Rambukwella and three other respondents who failed to pay in full the compensation the Court ordered in connection with the importation of substandard medicines. The Court has also prohibited them from leaving the country. In March, the Court ruled that fundamental human rights had been violated through the process of importing substandard medicines during the previous Government. It ordered five respondents, including Rambukwella, to pay compensation. Rambukwella was directed to pay Rs 75 million. However, his attorney informed the Court that he had paid only Rs 20 million of the stipulated amount.
