The Court has also prohibited them from leaving the country. In March, the Court ruled that fundamental human rights had been violated through the process of importing substandard medicines during the previous Government. It ordered five respondents, including Rambukwella, to pay compensation. Rambukwella was directed to pay Rs 75 million. However, his attorney informed the Court that he had paid only Rs 20 million of the stipulated amount. The latest order followed a motion filed by Transparency International Sri Lanka, which alleged that Rambukwella and the other respondents had committed contempt of Court by failing to pay the prescribed compensation in full. The order was delivered by a three-Judge bench headed by Chief Justice Preethi Padman Surasena.

audit.headline: NCE reviews export sector barriers, FX ops
audit.summary: The National Chamber of Exporters of Sri Lanka (NCE) reviewed sectoral issues, export-market requirements and overseas trade plans at its council meeting on 20 October. Held in partnership with Prime Group and Melwa at the Prime Marina Sales Suite in Port City, the meeting considered matters the chamber is taking up with authorities. The council reviewed issues being pursued with government institutions. Among the matters discussed was the delay in implementing the Madrid Protocol. WIPO’s Madrid System provides trademark holders with a one-stop solution to secure and manage brand protection and covers 117 members representing 133 countries and over 80% of global trade, with more than 1.7 million registered trademarks. According to NIPO, the final draft is now to be submitted to Parliament for approval.
audit.body: The National Chamber of Exporters of Sri Lanka (NCE) reviewed sectoral issues, export-market requirements and overseas trade plans at its council meeting on 20 October. Held in partnership with Prime Group and Melwa at the Prime Marina Sales Suite in Port City, the meeting considered matters the chamber is taking up with authorities. The council reviewed issues being pursued with government institutions. Among the matters discussed was the delay in implementing the Madrid Protocol. WIPO’s Madrid System provides trademark holders with a one-stop solution to secure and manage brand protection and covers 117 members representing 133 countries and over 80% of global trade, with more than 1.7 million registered trademarks. According to NIPO, the final draft is now to be submitted to Parliament for approval. The council also discussed restrictions affecting the forest sector, and difficulties faced by electrical and electronic product exporters. During January–August, Sri Lanka’s Electrical and Electronic Components (EEC) exports grew exceptionally, by 57.49% YoY to $ 440.31 million. For August alone, sector earnings reached $ 62.4 million, supported by a 30.83% rise in Insulated Wires and Cables. Overall, this performance highlights the industry’s expanding competitiveness and export potential. The NCE has been following up with the relevant authorities on these issues, including seeking a documented action plan from the Ministry of Environment. The chamber has also requested further support from the Sri Lankan Commercial Officer in India in addressing trade difficulties arising from India’s BIS-QCOs, and discussions with the Inland Revenue Department on VAT refunds are also being pursued. Changes to import procedures and new European Union regulations were mentioned in the meeting’s review of trade-related concerns. Following Customs’ shift to digital processing of import documentation on 1 October, the NCE is surveying exporters to identify difficulties with importing raw materials, machinery, packaging materials, and other inputs. Meanwhile, the chamber and other stakeholders are seeking technical assistance and training for exporters preparing to help Sri Lankan exporters comply with regulations, including EU’s new limits on mineral oil contaminants (MOAH) in food and agricultural products, due to take effect in January 2027. The EU’s Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation was also discussed, given its implications for exporters supplying that market. At the next sectoral discussions, members will address mineral-based products, chemicals, engineering, and electrical and electronic products. Topics include supply-chain bottlenecks, tariff barriers under bilateral free trade agreements, standardisation and raw-material costs. Conducting a presentation on Export and Beyond, KIK Group of Companies Founder and Chairperson, entrepreneur, Chartered Engineer and inventor Lalith Kahatapitiya called for new foreign-exchange channels beyond existing sources. He emphasised the importance of several measures for the economy, including re-exports, local suppliers serving exporters, and the need for a new National Business Facilitation Centre. The chamber’s overseas programmes are also taking shape, a visit to Italy and Sweden is planned for March 2027, with a trade show in Milan and business meetings in Stockholm. The council also discussed several upcoming plans, such as the upcoming NCE Budget Forum on 19 November and the 34th NCE Export Awards on 11 December.

audit.headline: Oil slips from near six-months highs
audit.summary: Oil prices fell on Monday after surging to near six-month highs late last week, although ongoing attacks on Saudi Arabia kept supply concerns in focus. US crude futures were down $ 1.60, or 1.55%, at $ 101.67 per barrel by 0018 GMT. Brent crude futures were down $ 1.56 or 1.34% at $ 115.16. Prices had settled nearly $ 3 higher on Friday after Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia stoked energy supply concerns. Brent finished the week up 6% and WTI ended 2.3% higher. Attacks continued over the weekend with Houthis saying they had attacked the Saudi airport and oil facilities on Saturday. Saudi Arabia said on Sunday it had intercepted more missiles and drones. The top oil exporter restarted partial operations at its main airport on Sunday after damage in a previous round of Houthi attacks even as the militant group vowed to keep targeting the facility.

audit.headline: Over 10,000 people affected by adverse weather across 12 districts in Sri Lanka
audit.summary: 27 Oct 2026 | By Staff Writer More than 10,000 individuals have been affected by the prevailing rainy weather conditions across the country. The Disaster Management Centre (DMC) stated that 10,545 people belonging to 2,736 families across 57 Divisional Secretariat divisions in 12 districts have been affected. DMC Director Pradeep Kodippili said that 182 affected individuals are currently being accommodated at four safety centers. “Considering the districts, 10,545 people have been reported affected by the rainy conditions that began on October 23 in Ampara, Colombo, Gampaha, Jaffna, Kalutara, Kandy, Kurunegala, Matara, Puttalam, Ratnapura, Mannar and Trincomalee. “There is one safety center in the Colombo District, where 27 people are being accommodated.
audit.body: 27 Oct 2026 | By Staff Writer More than 10,000 individuals have been affected by the prevailing rainy weather conditions across the country. The Disaster Management Centre (DMC) stated that 10,545 people belonging to 2,736 families across 57 Divisional Secretariat divisions in 12 districts have been affected. DMC Director Pradeep Kodippili said that 182 affected individuals are currently being accommodated at four safety centers. “Considering the districts, 10,545 people have been reported affected by the rainy conditions that began on October 23 in Ampara, Colombo, Gampaha, Jaffna, Kalutara, Kandy, Kurunegala, Matara, Puttalam, Ratnapura, Mannar and Trincomalee. “There is one safety center in the Colombo District, where 27 people are being accommodated. A further 33 people are staying at two safety centers in the Ratnapura District, while 122 people are being accommodated at a safety center in the Mannar District. Accordingly, a total of 182 people are temporarily staying at these centers. He further stated that 215 houses had been partially damaged, while a 56-year-old person had died in a drowning incident in the Puttalam area. He added that rainfall exceeding 100 millimeters had been recorded in the Kilinochchi, Mannar, Jaffna, Mullaitivu and Kalutara districts during the preceding 24 hours. Meanwhile, the Department of Irrigation stated that 17 major reservoirs and 13 medium-sized reservoirs under its management are currently spilling. Director of Water Management at the Department of Irrigation, Engineer L.S. Sooriyabandara, said that minor flooding could occur in low-lying areas surrounding the Gin, Nilwala, Kalu and Kelani rivers, as well as the Attanagalu Oya and Maha Oya. Meanwhile, the National Building Research Organisation (NBRO) has issued red landslide warnings for 11 Divisional Secretariat divisions across three districts. Accordingly, the warnings have been issued for Ratnapura, Ayagama, Pelmadulla, Kuruwita, Elapatha and Opanayaka in the Ratnapura District, Bulathsinhala and Dodangoda in the Kalutara District; and Ambagamuwa Korale and Norwood in the Nuwara Eliya District. DMC Director Pradeep Kodippili further stated that Level 1 and Level 2 landslide warning notices have been issued for several districts. Meanwhile, the Department of Meteorology stated that Cyclone ‘Arnab’ has intensified into a very severe cyclonic storm. Meteorologist Nadeeka Ranaweera said that heavy rainfall exceeding 75 millimeters could occur in several parts of the island today.

audit.headline: Research and innovation: Dialog Axiata partners with IITM Pravartak
audit.summary: Dialog Axiata PLC, Sri Lankan connectivity provider, has entered into a strategic partnership with Indian Institute of Technology Madras (IITM) Pravartak Technologies Foundation, India, through the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) aimed at advancing applied research and technology development in Sri Lanka. The agreement brings together international expertise, and industry stakeholders to develop practical solutions to national and societal challenges. It also seeks to strengthen Sri Lanka’s research capabilities and create opportunities to translate new ideas into real-world applications. Under the agreement, Dialog will serve as the collaboration anchor and technology enabler, connecting IITM Pravartak’s research networks with Sri Lankan industry stakeholders.
audit.body: Dialog Axiata PLC, Sri Lankan connectivity provider, has entered into a strategic partnership with Indian Institute of Technology Madras (IITM) Pravartak Technologies Foundation, India, through the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) aimed at advancing applied research and technology development in Sri Lanka. The agreement brings together international expertise, and industry stakeholders to develop practical solutions to national and societal challenges. It also seeks to strengthen Sri Lanka’s research capabilities and create opportunities to translate new ideas into real-world applications. Under the agreement, Dialog will serve as the collaboration anchor and technology enabler, connecting IITM Pravartak’s research networks with Sri Lankan industry stakeholders. The partnership will explore five key areas: innovation and incubation, applied research and university laboratories, artificial intelligence and human-centric solutions, industry skills and talent development, and international knowledge-sharing. Potential areas for initial collaboration include Sinhala and Tamil conversational AI, technology-driven dengue prevention and response, and solutions to address human-elephant conflict. These will be explored through focused research initiatives and pilot projects, with opportunities for further development based on their outcomes. Commenting on the significance of the partnership, High Commissioner of India to Sri Lanka Santosh Jha said: “India and Sri Lanka share a longstanding and multifaceted relationship, underpinned by strong historical ties and a shared commitment to progress. As our bilateral partnership continues to evolve, cooperation in technology and research presents significant opportunities to deepen engagement between our institutions and people. I welcome this initiative as another meaningful contribution to the growing partnership between our two countries.” IITM Pravartak Technologies Foundation Chief Executive Officer Shankar Jayaraman said: “This collaboration creates an opportunity to strengthen the connection between academic research and practical application. By working closely with Dialog, Sri Lankan universities and local stakeholders, we hope to foster an environment where researchers and students can exchange knowledge, build technical capabilities and develop solutions that respond to real-world needs. We look forward to a productive partnership that creates value for both the research community and industry.”

audit.headline: Resus Energy lists Green Bond on the LuxSE
audit.summary: Resus Energy PLC announced the dual listing of its Rs 1 billion Green Bond on the Luxembourg Stock Exchange (LuxSE) and its display on the Luxembourg Green Exchange (LGX), effective last week (19), becoming the first non-financial corporate issuer from Sri Lanka to be featured on LGX, the sustainable finance platform operated by LuxSE. The dual listing follows the issuance and listing of the Bond on the Colombo Stock Exchange (CSE) in July 2025 and marks Sri Lanka’s first-ever Green Bond issuance by a non-banking and finance company and the first by a local energy company, with NDB Investment Bank Limited acting as the Financial Advisor and Manager to the transaction. Launched by the Luxembourg Stock Exchange in 2016, LGX was the world’s first platform dedicated exclusively to green, social, and sustainable securities.
audit.body: Resus Energy PLC announced the dual listing of its Rs 1 billion Green Bond on the Luxembourg Stock Exchange (LuxSE) and its display on the Luxembourg Green Exchange (LGX), effective last week (19), becoming the first non-financial corporate issuer from Sri Lanka to be featured on LGX, the sustainable finance platform operated by LuxSE. The dual listing follows the issuance and listing of the Bond on the Colombo Stock Exchange (CSE) in July 2025 and marks Sri Lanka’s first-ever Green Bond issuance by a non-banking and finance company and the first by a local energy company, with NDB Investment Bank Limited acting as the Financial Advisor and Manager to the transaction. Launched by the Luxembourg Stock Exchange in 2016, LGX was the world’s first platform dedicated exclusively to green, social, and sustainable securities. Being displayed on LGX increases the international visibility of Resus Energy PLC’s Green Bond among ESG-focused investors, and demonstrates how a Sri Lankan renewable energy company can meet international expectations for green finance disclosure. “Bringing our Green Bond to the Luxembourg Stock Exchange and the Luxembourg Green Exchange is a proud milestone for Resus Energy PLC and for Sri Lanka. It confirms that a Sri Lankan renewable energy company can meet the highest international standards of sustainable finance. It also connects the projects powering our national grid with investors around the world who want their capital to make a measurable climate impact,” said Resus Energy PLC Managing Director Kishan Nanayakkara. The listing comes as Sri Lanka works toward ambitious national targets. Under its updated Nationally Determined Contributions, the country has committed to generating 70% of its electricity from renewable sources by 2030 and to making electricity generation carbon neutral by 2050. The issue comprised up to 10 million Listed, Rated, Unsecured, Senior Redeemable Green Bonds of Rs 100 each, in two tenors: Type A: four years at a fixed annual coupon of 11.55%; and Type B: five years at a fixed annual coupon of 11.75%. Fitch Ratings Lanka Limited rated the bond A-(lka). The bond was structured in line with international sustainability standards, and all of its proceeds are committed to developing renewable energy projects. More than 55% of the proceeds are allocated to developing 8 MW of new solar capacity, expected to deliver approximately 15 GWh of clean electricity annually to the national grid and avoid approximately 10,000 tonnes of CO₂ emissions.

audit.headline: Review: The Social Reckoning
audit.summary: 27 Oct 2026 | By Apsara Rodrigo What happens when profit comes before people Social media has changed the way we communicate, access information, and understand the world around us. Platforms such as Facebook and Instagram promise to bring people together, giving everyone a space to share their opinions and connect with others. However, behind this promise lies a troubling question: what happens when the companies controlling these platforms put profit before the people using them? Directed by Aaron Sorkin, The Social Reckoning (2026) explores this question through the story of Frances Haugen, a former Facebook employee who becomes a whistleblower after discovering evidence of the platform’s harmful effects. Working with Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz, she attempts to expose what the company knows about the dangers of its technology.
audit.body: 27 Oct 2026 | By Apsara Rodrigo What happens when profit comes before people Social media has changed the way we communicate, access information, and understand the world around us. Platforms such as Facebook and Instagram promise to bring people together, giving everyone a space to share their opinions and connect with others. However, behind this promise lies a troubling question: what happens when the companies controlling these platforms put profit before the people using them? Directed by Aaron Sorkin, The Social Reckoning (2026) explores this question through the story of Frances Haugen, a former Facebook employee who becomes a whistleblower after discovering evidence of the platform’s harmful effects. Working with Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz, she attempts to expose what the company knows about the dangers of its technology. The film follows their investigation into Facebook’s role in spreading misinformation, encouraging extremist views, and contributing to wider social problems. A follow-up in spirit to The Social Network (2010), the film moves away from the story of Facebook’s creation to examine the consequences of its growth. Rather than focusing on the ambitions of young entrepreneurs, it asks whether powerful technology companies should be held responsible for the damage their products cause. With strong performances and a subject that remains relevant, The Social Reckoning offers a serious look at the relationship between technology, business, and public responsibility. However, its message is sometimes more powerful than its storytelling. One of the film’s greatest strengths is its examination of how social media algorithms influence what people see online. These systems are designed to recommend content that keeps users engaged. However, content that creates anger, fear, or outrage can attract attention more easily than balanced information. The film shows how Facebook’s recommendation systems can direct users towards extremist groups and harmful content. Its central argument is that these problems are not simply the result of individual users making poor choices. They are also connected to the design of the platforms themselves. This makes the story particularly unsettling. Social media companies often present themselves as neutral spaces where people can communicate freely. Yet the content users encounter is shaped by decisions made by companies with financial interests. By focusing on the gap between Facebook’s public promises and its internal knowledge, the film raises important questions about corporate accountability. Its message is clear: when a company understands the risks associated with its product, ignorance can no longer serve as an excuse. The film benefits from Mikey Madison’s performance as Frances Haugen. She presents Haugen as an intelligent and determined woman who gradually becomes unwilling to remain silent about what she has discovered. Her decision to become a whistleblower is not presented as an easy choice. Challenging a powerful employer can bring professional, personal, and legal risks. Jeremy Allen White plays Jeff Horwitz, the journalist who works with Haugen to bring the information to the public. Their relationship provides the film with much of its momentum. Haugen has access to the company’s internal information, while Horwitz understands how to investigate, verify, and report it. Their partnership also highlights the importance of investigative journalism. Information alone does not always lead to change. It must be carefully examined, supported by evidence, and communicated to the public. Jeremy Strong plays Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg, portraying him as a distant executive whose business priorities appear to outweigh concerns about the platform’s wider effects. His performance reinforces the film’s criticism of corporate leadership, although the character sometimes feels more like a symbol of corporate greed than a fully developed person. Comparisons with The Social Network are inevitable. The earlier film, directed by David Fincher, examined Facebook’s beginnings and the ambition, competition, and personal conflicts surrounding its creation. Its sharp dialogue and tense atmosphere made the story of a technology company feel like a gripping drama. The Social Reckoning takes a more direct approach. Sorkin, who wrote both films, focuses on the consequences of Facebook’s success rather than the excitement of building something new. The result is a film that feels closer to an investigative journalism drama than a corporate thriller. Although the subject is important, the film occasionally struggles to match its predecessor’s energy. Its dialogue is sharp, but its arguments can feel overly direct. At times, characters seem to exist mainly to explain the film’s message rather than develop naturally within the story. Perhaps the film’s greatest weakness is also its most important question: what does accountability look like when powerful companies face little pressure to change? The film draws on the events surrounding Haugen’s disclosures and the 2021 Facebook Files investigation. It examines how the company’s internal research raised concerns about the effects of its platforms, even as its public image depended on presenting them as beneficial to society. Yet exposing wrongdoing does not necessarily solve it. Public attention, congressional hearings, and investigative reporting can reveal serious problems, but meaningful reform requires companies and governments to act. This leaves the film with an uncomfortable sense of incompleteness. Its investigation may produce important revelations, but the larger systems that allow these problems to continue remain in place. In a world where social media continues to shape political debate and public opinion, the story feels relevant, even if some of its events already belong to the recent past. The Social Reckoning is a thought-provoking film that asks important questions about the responsibilities of technology companies. Its strongest moments come from Frances Haugen’s determination to expose what she believes the public deserves to know, as well as its examination of the relationship between profit and public welfare. However, the film is less successful as a piece of storytelling. Its straightforward approach, heavy dialogue, and tendency to explain its message leave it short of the tension and complexity that made The Social Network so memorable. Ultimately, The Social Reckoning is worth watching for its subject matter and performances. It reminds audiences that social media platforms are not simply tools for communication. They are businesses whose decisions can influence individuals, communities, and entire societies. The film’s most troubling implication is that knowing about a problem and doing something about it are two very different things. It may not offer a satisfying solution, but it leaves viewers with an important question: if technology companies understand the harm their platforms can cause, who should be held responsible when they choose not to act?

audit.headline: SLPA report flags CECT shortcomings: $ 200 m annual revenue potential remains untapped
audit.summary: 27 Oct 2026 | BY SULOCHANA RAMIAH MOHAN With Colombo’s container volumes rising and regional competition intensifying, the unfinished operational transition at the Colombo East Container Terminal (CECT) raises questions about procurement delays, management decisions, and the port’s ability to retain future shipping business. The Sri Lanka Ports Authority’s (SLPA) ‘CECT Operational Plan and Transformation Progress Update Report’ of August 2026 warns that Colombo risks losing cargo to regional hubs such as Dubai and Singapore, projecting that port throughput could fall about 3.2 million Twenty-foot Equivalent Units (TEUs) short of regional demand by 2035 even if CECT reaches its full planned capacity.
audit.body: 27 Oct 2026 | BY SULOCHANA RAMIAH MOHAN With Colombo’s container volumes rising and regional competition intensifying, the unfinished operational transition at the Colombo East Container Terminal (CECT) raises questions about procurement delays, management decisions, and the port’s ability to retain future shipping business. The Sri Lanka Ports Authority’s (SLPA) ‘CECT Operational Plan and Transformation Progress Update Report’ of August 2026 warns that Colombo risks losing cargo to regional hubs such as Dubai and Singapore, projecting that port throughput could fall about 3.2 million Twenty-foot Equivalent Units (TEUs) short of regional demand by 2035 even if CECT reaches its full planned capacity. The controversy surrounding the East Container Terminal (ECT), now known as CECT, is a telling example of how nationalism and the fight to protect national interests can prevail politically but do not necessarily translate into results on the ground. In 2019, Sri Lanka signed a tripartite Memorandum of Cooperation with India and Japan to develop and operate the terminal, with the foreign partners expected to hold a 49% stake. However, following sustained protests by Colombo Port trade unions and wider opposition to foreign involvement in a strategic national asset, the Government abandoned the arrangement in February 2021, deciding that the terminal would remain fully under SLPA ownership and operation. Yet, more than five years later, the CECT is still not fully operational as a complete, autonomous facility, despite having commenced partial operations. In November 2025, Parliament’s Committee on Public Enterprises highlighted a 548-day construction delay at the CECT and a contractor’s compensation claim of Rs 4.227 billion. The latest SLPA document identifies further delays linked to outstanding procurement, infrastructure, systems, and staffing requirements. The CECT is transitioning towards a semi-automated operating model, but several equipment, infrastructure, systems, and human resources requirements remain outstanding. The document outlines the terminal’s operational background, equipment programme, market forecasts, financial potential, and measures proposed to complete commissioning. It also sets out a four-phase commissioning and testing programme covering August 2026 to June 2027, alongside a nine-point action programme for consideration by SLPA management and the board. The CECT began container operations on 29 October 2020. It moved towards a semi-automated operating model on 13 May 2024, with manpower arrangements initially outsourced. Supporting operational, human resources, and marketing plans were subsequently prepared to facilitate the transition. Five areas require further progress: productivity, infrastructure, terminal operating system implementation, human resources recruitment, and equipment deliveries. Located within the Port of Colombo alongside existing container operations, the CECT also has an identified 800-metre expansion pathway associated with the proposed North Port development. A Cabinet decision in February 2021 provided for the CECT to be developed and operated wholly by the SLPA. The latest document recommends formally reaffirming this arrangement at board level as part of implementing the terminal’s proposed operating model. Twelve Ship-To-Shore (STS) cranes and 40 Automated Rail-Mounted Gantry (ARMG) cranes have been delivered under an equipment programme valued at $ 282 million. The Navis N4 Terminal Operating System and ABB automation platform have also been deployed. The terminal’s design includes automated gates, an automated container yard, remote operations, and a command centre. It provides for 12 STS cranes, with space for two additional cranes, and 40 ARMGs, with provision for a further 12. The planned yard includes 12,700 ground slots, with provision for another 3,800, and 1,042 reefer slots, including capacity associated with integration of the Rubber-Tyred Gantry (RTG) yard. A target of 32 or more container moves per hour at the optimum operating stage has been set. Achieving this target depends on equipment testing, process validation, operational dry runs, and continuous optimisation under the Master Testing Plan. However, procurement of straddle carriers remains a key outstanding requirement. These vehicles form part of the planned equipment arrangement for transferring containers between the quay and the yard. The workshop and accommodation buildings, gate works, equipment repair and maintenance arrangements, and additional supporting systems are also outstanding. The proposed action programme calls for accelerated procurement and construction decisions on these items. Further work is required on the Electronic Container System (ECS), repair and maintenance services, and other supporting systems. The document recommends beginning the relevant tenders while progressively integrating these systems with the Navis N4 and ABB platforms already deployed. The Master Testing Plan is divided into four phases. The first covers preparation of test teams and testing of individual events across six functional groups, including data entry, vessel planning, yard operations, equipment control, transfer operations, and gates and billing. The second phase involves end-to-end testing of core operational processes, including loading, discharging, receiving, and delivery. The third covers full operational dry runs, billing and reporting validation, issue resolution, and retesting. The fourth phase involves live equipment testing and operational review, with completion scheduled for June 2027. The plan also allows for live operations in a possible interim configuration before the straddle carriers arrive. This is intended to enable suitable terminal activities to commence while the remaining equipment is delivered, subject to operational configuration and testing requirements. Human resources and supporting services Completing the human resources framework is another requirement for the CECT’s operational transition. Outstanding approvals include the organisational structure, human resources policy, Scheme of Recruitment, and salary structures. The proposed actions also include standardising arrangements involving manpower companies and restarting recruitment and training within the current quarter identified in the action programme. Although implementation of the HR plan was delayed following a change in project direction, much of the preparatory work remains relevant and can be updated rather than developed from scratch. Recruitment cannot begin until the required approvals are secured. These are also necessary to schedule training in line with the commissioning phases and formally release experienced staff from the Jaya Container Terminal (JCT) to the CECT. Pending work includes finalising cadre numbers by grade and cluster in line with the CECT operating model, aligning recruitment phases with the commissioning schedule, and establishing intake numbers for four training channels: JCT on-the-job training, Mahapola Ports and Maritime Academy, Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM) training, and simulator training. Supporting services, including lashing, food court, and janitorial services, are also included in the recommended administrative actions. Recruitment, training, and selection of service providers are expected to proceed alongside equipment procurement and systems testing. Revenue potential and financial information The CECT could generate approximately $ 180 million in annual revenue when fully operational, according to one estimate in the document. Its executive summary and financial assessment also refer to annual revenue potential of approximately $ 200 million. These are projections for full operation rather than reported earnings to date. The CECT’s throughput is listed at approximately 560,000 TEUs in 2025. No consolidated cumulative figure is provided for the terminal’s revenue or net profit since container operations began in October 2020. The financial assessment compares the contributions of the SLPA-operated JCT with receipts from privately operated terminals. The JCT’s contribution over 2021–2025 is stated as Rs 63.2 billion, compared with a combined Rs 62.5 billion from South Asia Gateway Terminals (SAGT) and Colombo International Container Terminals (CICT) over the same period. It also records corporate tax payments of Rs 14.6 billion by the JCT during 2019–2025, compared with Rs 1.4 billion for CICT. These figures relate to the terminals named and are not the CECT’s own earnings. Financial reporting and funding arrangements are among the matters to be addressed as the CECT moves towards full commercial operation. A separate account of the terminal’s actual income, operating costs, capital expenditure, and remaining completion costs would be needed to establish its cumulative financial performance. Colombo’s container volumes and demand forecasts The Port of Colombo handled approximately 8.3 million TEUs in 2025, an increase of 6.4% over 2024. Throughput is projected to exceed 10 million TEUs in 2027. The document also refers to the development of the Colombo West International Terminal (CWIT), which began operations in April 2025. The CWIT handled more than 1 million TEUs during its first year and is expected to continue expanding towards its planned capacity. The CECT’s projected throughput is expected to rise from approximately 0.56 million TEUs in 2025 to its design capacity of 3.5 million TEUs by 2035. Existing terminals, including the JCT, SAGT, and CICT, are expected to operate close to their practical capacity levels over the forecast period, while the CWIT completes its planned ramp-up by 2030. Regional potential demand is estimated at 17.13 million TEUs by 2035, compared with projected Colombo throughput of 13.95 million TEUs, even with the CECT operating at its planned capacity. This leaves a potential difference of approximately 3.2 million TEUs between regional demand and the volume Colombo could handle. The document warns that this shortfall could result in cargo being diverted to competing regional hubs, including Singapore and Dubai. The figure is a long-term forecast of potential unmet demand; it does not establish that this volume has already been diverted from Colombo. Marketing and shipping line engagement A marketing plan was prepared following the CECT’s transition towards the semi-automated model in May 2024. The proposed actions call for its reactivation and structured engagement with shipping lines and alliances before full commissioning. The planned engagement includes discussions on berth windows, tariffs, commercial operating terms, and value-added services. These include empty container pooling, Delay-in-Transit (DIT) container handling, and container reworking. Integration of the manual RTG yard with the CECT Terminal Operating System is also identified as a way to support these services and provide access to additional reefer capacity. The document recommends communicating accurate commissioning timelines to shipping lines and maintaining regular dialogue on terminal readiness and planned services. The nine-point action programme recommends that the SLPA Board reaffirm full SLPA ownership and operation of the CECT, consistent with the Cabinet mandate described in the document. It calls for an accelerated timetable for straddle carrier procurement and decisions to move the workshop, accommodation building, and gate works towards award and construction. It also recommends beginning tenders for the ECS, repair and maintenance services, and other supporting systems. The remaining actions cover approval of the consolidated human resources package, adoption of the Master Testing Plan, establishment of commissioning governance, reactivation of the marketing plan, completion of supporting service selections, and monthly progress reporting to the chairman. The proposed governance arrangements include a terminal commissioning steering committee chaired at chairman level, a single accountable commissioning head, and weekly operational reviews involving operations, engineering, finance, information technology, and human resources. A monthly dashboard would track testing, equipment availability, procurement milestones, staffing mobilisation, and productivity indicators. The commissioning window covered by the Master Testing Plan runs from August 2026 to June 2027. The proposed measures are intended to coordinate the outstanding procurement, infrastructure, systems, staffing, and commercial activities within that period. Full reaffirmation of SLPA ownership and operation of CECT by SLPA Board, consistent with Cabinet mandate An accelerated timetable for straddle carrier procurement and decisions to move workshop, accommodation building, and gate works towards award and construction Beginning tenders for Electronic Container System, repair and maintenance services, and other supporting systems Approval of consolidated human resources package Adoption of Master Testing Plan Completion of supporting service selections Monthly progress reporting to chairman SLPA staff officers and engineers raise concerns The Joint Executives’ Alliance of the Sri Lanka Ports Authority (SLPA), comprising the Staff Officers’ Association and the Engineers’ Association, has raised concerns over the development, operational arrangements, and future capacity of the Colombo East Container Terminal (CECT), urging President Anura Kumara Dissanayake to address issues affecting the terminal and the country’s maritime interests. In a letter dated 20 October, the associations outlined concerns relating to the terminal’s development, infrastructure, equipment requirements, operational capacity, and management arrangements. They also examined the CECT in relation to other container terminals at the Colombo Port, including Colombo International Container Terminals (CICT) and South Asia Gateway Terminals (SAGT). The letter highlights the importance of ensuring that the CECT’s development supports the SLPA’s operational interests and Sri Lanka’s position as a regional maritime and transshipment hub. It also refers to container handling performance at existing terminals and sets out projections for the CECT’s future growth. A chart included in the document, titled ‘CECT Volume Ramp-Up – Capacity Build-Out Drives Growth (2025–2035),’ projects container volumes reaching approximately 3.5 million TEUs by 2035. The chart identifies 1.5 million TEUs as the first-stage capacity and 3.5 million TEUs as the full design capacity. The associations also discuss equipment and infrastructure requirements, including straddle carriers, and raise questions about the operational arrangements needed to support the terminal’s planned capacity. The letter further addresses private sector participation and public-private partnership arrangements in port development. The representations to the President call for attention to the issues surrounding the CECT’s development and operation, with emphasis on protecting the SLPA’s interests and ensuring that port development serves Sri Lanka’s long-term maritime objectives.

audit.headline: SLUSABC re-elects President at 10th AGM
audit.summary: The Sri Lanka-USA Business Council (SLUSABC) of the Ceylon Chamber of Commerce marked a decade of service at its 10th Annual General Meeting, held on 14 October at Hilton Colombo Residences, with the new US Ambassador to Sri Lanka, Eric Meyer, as the Chief Guest. Members re-elected Tilak Gunawardana of MAC Holdings (Pvt) Ltd as President for a second term. The AGM was among Ambassador Meyer’s first engagements with Sri Lanka’s private sector. Welcoming him, Gunawardana also thanked former Ambassador Julie Chung, Chargé d’Affaires Jayne Howell and the Embassy team for their support through the transition. Ambassador Meyer commended the council’s work in building a stronger business environment and advancing intellectual property (IP) protection, which he noted are important to attracting US investment and growing bilateral trade.
audit.body: The Sri Lanka-USA Business Council (SLUSABC) of the Ceylon Chamber of Commerce marked a decade of service at its 10th Annual General Meeting, held on 14 October at Hilton Colombo Residences, with the new US Ambassador to Sri Lanka, Eric Meyer, as the Chief Guest. Members re-elected Tilak Gunawardana of MAC Holdings (Pvt) Ltd as President for a second term. The AGM was among Ambassador Meyer’s first engagements with Sri Lanka’s private sector. Welcoming him, Gunawardana also thanked former Ambassador Julie Chung, Chargé d’Affaires Jayne Howell and the Embassy team for their support through the transition. Ambassador Meyer commended the council’s work in building a stronger business environment and advancing intellectual property (IP) protection, which he noted are important to attracting US investment and growing bilateral trade. He highlighted opportunities to deepen commercial cooperation in technology, energy, infrastructure, and logistics. He encouraged Sri Lankan businesses to consider investing in the United States, including through the upcoming SelectUSA Investment Summit, and underscored that transparent, predictable regulation, strong IP rights and fair competition are the foundations of investor confidence. Reviewing his first term, Gunawardana said the council’s work rested on three pillars: trade and market access, emerging sectors, and institutional partnerships. As US tariff changes put exporters under pressure, the council worked with the Chamber, the Export Development Board (EDB), the US Embassy in Colombo and the Sri Lanka Embassy in Washington to keep members informed and bring the private sector’s voice into the national position. He said the current 10% tariff rate, the lowest bracket available, reflected a collective national effort, and paid tribute to former Ambassador in Washington, Mahinda Samarasinghe, who attended the AGM. Highlights of the year included: SelectUSA: member awareness sessions and participation in the Summit in Washington, DC, alongside a strong Sri Lankan business delegation; IP Trade Corridor forum: bringing enforcement agencies, Customs, industry and the legal profession together on IP protection as a precondition for quality investment; Youth and startups: supporting youth and startup initiatives in Jaffna; and Partnerships: closer engagement with the Embassy’s Economic Section, the EDB and the Board of Investment (BOI), and a refreshed website and social media presence. Gunawardana said the council would now move “from responding to events to shaping opportunities,” with priorities including: a stable, durable bilateral trade framework; helping members meet market-access standards, from supply-chain traceability to rules of origin; championing two-way investment, building on SelectUSA; working with the US International Development Finance Corporation (DFC) and the BOI to bring US capital into energy, ports and logistics, and the digital economy; opening opportunities for members in technology and services, maritime, renewable energy and education; and widening membership to more SMEs and young entrepreneurs. Noting that the United States is Sri Lanka’s largest export market and stood by the country through its recovery and after Cyclone Ditwah , he said the business community must now turn that goodwill into trade, investment, and jobs. Office-bearers for 2026/2027 includes President Tilak Gunawardana of MAC Holdings (Pvt) Ltd; Senior Vice President Randeewa Malalasooriya of CBL Natural Foods (Pvt) Ltd; Vice President Tuan Farhath Armith of Fanam International (Pvt) Ltd; and Treasurer Halin Hettigoda of Sampath Bank PLC. In closing, Gunawardana thanked the Executive Committee, the Chamber Secretariat, sponsors and members. “Ten years ago, this council was founded on the belief that business can be a bridge between nations,” he said, adding that with a new Ambassador, a recovering economy and a deepening partnership, that belief “has never been more relevant.”

audit.headline: Three spill gates of Upper Kotmale Reservoir opened following heavy rainfall
audit.summary: 27 Oct 2026 | By Staff Writer Three spill gates of the Upper Kotmale Reservoir have been opened since yesterday afternoon (26) following heavy rainfall in the reservoir’s catchment areas, reservoir engineers said. The engineers have urged residents living along both banks of the Kotmale Oya downstream of the reservoir dam to remain vigilant, warning that the remaining spill gates will open automatically if further rainfall is recorded in the catchment areas.

audit.headline: Transformation Committees formed: Gamage suspends cycling and badminton bodies
audit.summary: Minister of Youth Affairs and Sports Sunil Kumara Gamage has issued two Extraordinary Gazette notifications temporarily suspending the registrations of the Cycling Federation of Sri Lanka and Sri Lanka Badminton. The Gazette notifications, dated 20 October were issued under Sections 32 and 33 of the Sports Law, No. 25 of 1973, as amended. The Minister has appointed separate transformation Committees to oversee the administration and restructuring of the two sporting bodies. According to the Gazettes, the Committees have been tasked with probing fraud, corruption and other irregularities, introducing new constitutions, registering eligible members and conducting Special General Meetings and Annual General Meetings. The Cycling Transformation Committee will be chaired by Anura Mahaarachchi, while the Sri Lanka Badminton Transformation Committee will be headed by M H S S Kusum Kumara.

The Gazette notifications, dated 20 October were issued under Sections 32 and 33 of the Sports Law, No. 25 of 1973, as amended. The Minister has appointed separate transformation Committees to oversee the administration and restructuring of the two sporting bodies. According to the Gazettes, the Committees have been tasked with probing fraud, corruption and other irregularities, introducing new constitutions, registering eligible members and conducting Special General Meetings and Annual General Meetings. The Cycling Transformation Committee will be chaired by Anura Mahaarachchi, while the Sri Lanka Badminton Transformation Committee will be headed by M H S S Kusum Kumara. Both Committees have been empowered to manage the respective organisations until new office bearers are elected. The Gazettes require elections to be held within 90 days of the registration of the new constitutions.

audit.headline: Public servants briefed on next steps of Prajashakthi Movement
audit.summary: A programme to brief District Secretaries, Divisional Secretaries and District Planning Directors on the next steps of the Prajashakthi National Movement was held at Temple Trees recently under the leadership of the President’s Secretary Dr Nandika Kumanayake. Kumanayake emphasised to those who were present that proper coordination among officials was essential to carry out all development activities, including those under the Prajashakthi programme. He also stressed that any issues obstructing development should be resolved systematically. He pointed out that public officials should cultivate certain qualities and that development work could be facilitated by working efficiently and as a team. He also explained the importance of developing personally as an official who acts without corruption.
audit.body: A programme to brief District Secretaries, Divisional Secretaries and District Planning Directors on the next steps of the Prajashakthi National Movement was held at Temple Trees recently under the leadership of the President’s Secretary Dr Nandika Kumanayake. Kumanayake emphasised to those who were present that proper coordination among officials was essential to carry out all development activities, including those under the Prajashakthi programme. He also stressed that any issues obstructing development should be resolved systematically. He pointed out that public officials should cultivate certain qualities and that development work could be facilitated by working efficiently and as a team. He also explained the importance of developing personally as an official who acts without corruption. Speaking further Kumanayake said one of the key demands that emerged during the ‘aragalaya’ was that corrupt politicians should be removed. ‘The issue of public servants also being responsible emerged alongside that demand. At the last election, the people had an opportunity to send corrupt politicians home and bring a new force to power. However, they cannot transfer public officials or send them home. There is no mechanism for that. When people visit a Government institution to obtain a service and experience irregularities, injustice or wrongdoing, there must be a place where they can report it. That is why we established Internal Affairs Units in Government institutions’. ‘What is corruption’? asked Kumanayake. ‘Even among public servants, there is no clear understanding of this. If an official uses the authority entrusted to them to perform their duties in any way for their personal benefit that is corruption. If such practices are not addressed at the outset, and if they are followed by those at the top, they become the normal way of doing things. That was the system that existed in our country. Why should we reject such practices? Ultimately, they can lead to an economic crisis. Investors will be reluctant to come to the country. Essential projects were not implemented, while unnecessary projects were undertaken. As a result, the country accumulated debt and eventually reached a point where it did not have sufficient foreign exchange to import fuel. Taxes were imposed at levels the public could not bear, and poverty increased. Corruption was the reason for this. These practices also destroy human relationships and lead to an increase in crime. They have now spread even to the private sector. As a result, our country fell to one of the lowest positions in the world in terms of preventing corruption’’. Kumanayake pointed out how people had no place to report these matters. ‘They were concerned about what would happen to their safety if they spoke out. Therefore, no one revealed what they knew. Eventually, these issues erupt somewhere, and the ‘aragalaya’ was one such result. We have to encourage people to come forward and report these matters. Through this, we expect to strengthen integrity among public servants. Internal Affairs Units were established in Government institutions for this purpose. Report any wrongdoing or injustice you experience to these units. We will intervene,’ he said. The President’s Senior Additional Secretary Kapila Janaka Bandara briefed the gathering on five areas: the rural road development database planned for 2027, the introduction of an Innovation Hub, the preparation of a strategic plan, the collection of data for an online information system relating to tanks and the Ellanga cascade irrigation system, as well as the introduction of an entrepreneurship development database.

audit.headline: Any Police officer in uniform can enforce traffic rules, spokesman says
audit.summary: Police Spokesman ASP F. U. Wootler stated that any single Police officer who is on duty, wearing the official uniform, is authorised to make a traffic detection and take legal action against traffic rule offenders. He said that according to the Motor Traffic Act, any Police officer who is in official uniform is a member of the Police force and that there is no need for him to be a traffic Police officer to detect any motor traffic violations and take legal action. He further clarified that under Section 134 of the Evidence Ordinance, that one traffic Police officer can make a traffic detection and take legal action against a traffic offender, and that no particular number of witnesses is required to prove the truth of any fact in any court case.
audit.body: Police Spokesman ASP F. U. Wootler stated that any single Police officer who is on duty, wearing the official uniform, is authorised to make a traffic detection and take legal action against traffic rule offenders. He said that according to the Motor Traffic Act, any Police officer who is in official uniform is a member of the Police force and that there is no need for him to be a traffic Police officer to detect any motor traffic violations and take legal action. He further clarified that under Section 134 of the Evidence Ordinance, that one traffic Police officer can make a traffic detection and take legal action against a traffic offender, and that no particular number of witnesses is required to prove the truth of any fact in any court case. Addressing the media yesterday (26), the Police Spokesman said that the authority to take action over traffic violations is not limited to officers attached to the Traffic Police and explained that any Police officer in official uniform can initiate legal action over traffic offences, even when carrying out duties alone. Clearing the misguided perceptions about the Police traffic officers and at times when motorists not wanting to stop their vehicles when one Police officer would stop the vehicle, he requested all motorists to abide by the traffic rules, laws and regulations of the country and ensure that they assist the Police officers on duty by following their instructions even if one Police officer on duty would instruct to stop a vehicle. Responding to concerns about Police officers hiding to catch traffic offenders, Wootler said that the IGP has informed all Police officers in the country that it is not necessary to conceal themselves when detecting traffic violations. The Police Spokesman made these clarifications in response to questions circulating on social media regarding the authority of Police officers to enforce traffic laws.

audit.headline: Temple elephant kills man
audit.summary: A 34-year-old unmarried tour guide, Piyasantha Jayalath, residing in Middaramulla, Ahungalla, was killed yesterday (26) after he was attacked by an elephant at the Kande Viharaya in Aluthgama. The incident occurred when the man had gone to visit the Kande Viharaya in a van with tourists and attempted to offer a fruit basket to the temple elephant. The elephant had struck him with its trunk and trampled him. Hospital doctors said the man was already dead on admission to the Balapitiya Hospital. His body is currently at the Balapitiya Hospital mortuary pending further investigations.

audit.headline: A preventable threat
audit.summary: T he continuous rainfall is affecting most parts of Sri Lanka, with severe weather warnings expected to remain in force until at least the end of this week. The current weather system is being driven by the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ), combined with a low-pressure area over the Bay of Bengal. Dengue is an unwelcome visitor whenever rainfall increases in the country. According to statistics from the National Dengue Control Unit (NDCU), the country has recorded around 105,000 dengue cases, with approximately 80 dengue-related fatalities. The latest dengue outbreak remains heavily concentrated in urban areas characterised by dense populations and rapid construction. The Western Province is the worst affected, accounting for more than 52 per cent of all reported cases nationwide.
audit.body: T he continuous rainfall is affecting most parts of Sri Lanka, with severe weather warnings expected to remain in force until at least the end of this week. The current weather system is being driven by the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ), combined with a low-pressure area over the Bay of Bengal. Dengue is an unwelcome visitor whenever rainfall increases in the country. According to statistics from the National Dengue Control Unit (NDCU), the country has recorded around 105,000 dengue cases, with approximately 80 dengue-related fatalities. The latest dengue outbreak remains heavily concentrated in urban areas characterised by dense populations and rapid construction. The Western Province is the worst affected, accounting for more than 52 per cent of all reported cases nationwide. With the onset of the northeast monsoon, health officials continue to stress the importance of community involvement, urging residents to clean gutters, empty water containers weekly and seek immediate medical attention for high fevers that persist beyond two days. Yet, some people in continue to ignore fever, regardless of its severity or the underlying cause. It is sheer ignorance that has repeatedly landed Sri Lanka in difficult situations when it comes to dengue. This ignorance takes two forms. People remain woefully unaware of potential dengue mosquito breeding sites, while also neglecting their own health, particularly when they develop a fever. Some simply swallow a couple of tablets and carry on with their daily work. Others send their children to school despite their fever. Nearly a decade later, many still fail to understand that dengue can be fatal. There are four distinct serotypes of the dengue virus: DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3 and DENV-4. All four can be transmitted to humans by infected female Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes, which acquire the virus by biting infected people. Infection with one serotype generally provides lifelong immunity against that particular serotype, but not against the other three. A person can therefore contract dengue more than once. In fact, a subsequent infection with a different serotype can increase the risk of severe dengue. Infection with all four serotypes is not a safe or recommended way to acquire immunity; it can have serious consequences. If one member of a household contracts dengue, the other family members and their neighbours can be protected by taking measures to prevent mosquitoes from biting the infected person. Keeping the patient under a mosquito net throughout the day and night, particularly during the first week of illness, can help prevent mosquitoes from acquiring the virus and subsequently transmitting it to others. This is neither impractical nor impossible. Mosquito nets are used in healthcare settings for this very reason. When a mosquito bites an infected person, it can acquire the virus, which then multiplies inside the mosquito before the insect becomes capable of transmitting it to other people. Unfortunately, many Sri Lankans remain unaware of this important aspect of dengue prevention. Even in healthcare settings, the consistent use of mosquito nets for dengue patients deserves greater attention. Ensuring that patients are protected from mosquito bites is an important component of dengue control, alongside eliminating mosquito breeding sites and preventing mosquito bites in the wider community. Mosquito repellents are another important line of defence. However, the duration of protection varies according to the product’s active ingredient, concentration and formulation. Some repellents may need to be reapplied every few hours, while others provide protection for longer. Therefore, applying repellent once or twice a day may not be sufficient, particularly in areas where dengue transmission is high. People should follow the product label’s instructions and take additional precautions to avoid mosquito bites. There are several other crucial aspects of dengue prevention that many people remain unaware of. Fogging is one method used to control adult mosquitoes, but it is not the only way to eliminate them. Its effectiveness depends on factors such as the insecticide used, the method of application and whether mosquitoes are exposed to it. Mosquitoes that are not adequately exposed to the insecticide may survive. Moreover, fogging provides only temporary relief unless it is accompanied by measures to eliminate breeding sites and prevent mosquitoes from multiplying. Adult Aedes mosquitoes, the primary vectors of dengue, typically live for two to four weeks in nature, although their lifespan varies depending on environmental conditions. Dengue mosquitoes generally have a limited flight range, often remaining within a few hundred metres of their breeding sites. Although they can travel farther under certain circumstances, there is little justification for automatically blaming properties 500 metres or even a kilometre away without evidence. One of the most effective ways to protect ourselves is to thoroughly inspect and clean our own homes, gardens and surrounding areas, while working with our neighbours to eliminate potential breeding sites. Families must also pay close attention to the health of all their members, particularly those who may be vulnerable to severe dengue. Rather than assuming that one sex is necessarily at greater risk of dying from the disease, public health measures should ensure that women and men alike receive timely medical attention and appropriate care. Fathers, husbands, sons and brothers have an important role to play in protecting their daughters, wives, mothers, grandmothers and sisters, just as every family member should look out for the others.

audit.headline: Afghanistan-Pakistan trade declines sharply as border crossings remain closed
audit.summary: Trade between Afghanistan and Pakistan has declined sharply amid rising tensions between the neighbouring countries and the continued closure of border crossings. Mohammad Younus Mohmand, Vice President of the Afghan Chapter of the Pakistan-Afghanistan Joint Chamber of Commerce and Industry, said that the bilateral trade has fallen by about 95 percent. “We no longer have trade with Pakistan. Our transit via Pakistan and Pakistan’s transit via Afghanistan to Central Asia have come to a complete halt,” Mohmand said. Pakistani newspaper Dawn reported on Monday that the figures released by the Trade Development Authority of Pakistan in August showed that bilateral trade between the two neighbouring countries fell 95 percent in 2026-27 compared with the previous year.
audit.body: Trade between Afghanistan and Pakistan has declined sharply amid rising tensions between the neighbouring countries and the continued closure of border crossings. Mohammad Younus Mohmand, Vice President of the Afghan Chapter of the Pakistan-Afghanistan Joint Chamber of Commerce and Industry, said that the bilateral trade has fallen by about 95 percent. “We no longer have trade with Pakistan. Our transit via Pakistan and Pakistan’s transit via Afghanistan to Central Asia have come to a complete halt,” Mohmand said. Pakistani newspaper Dawn reported on Monday that the figures released by the Trade Development Authority of Pakistan in August showed that bilateral trade between the two neighbouring countries fell 95 percent in 2026-27 compared with the previous year. The TDAP also reported that bilateral trade fell to US$ 358 million in fiscal year 2025-26, down from US$ 1.3 billion in fiscal year 2024-25, a decrease of about 74 percent. Pakistan closed the main border crossings with Afghanistan on Oct. 12, 2025, after deadly clashes between the Pakistani Forces and the Afghan Taliban. In September, Pakistani Government said that it was ready to re-open the border crossings if the Taliban took measures against the militant groups operating from Afghanistan. Relations between Pakistan and the Taliban deteriorated as Pakistani authorities accused the Taliban of harbouring the militant group, Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan, or TTP, which has taken responsibility for attacks inside Pakistan. The Taliban publicly deny harbouring any militant group, but a U.N. report, released in August, said that the Taliban continue to support TTP.? The closure of the border crossings has hurt Pakistani industries, particularly pharmaceuticals, according to Government data. Pakistan’s Dawn newspaper, citing Pakistan’s Bureau of Statistics, said pharmaceutical exports declined 25.53 percent in the first quarter of 2026-27, which is primarily attributed to the disruption of trade with Afghanistan. (VOA)

audit.headline: Inflation pushes nearly 10 Mn people below poverty line in Bangladesh
audit.summary: Inflation has placed a heavy burden on low- and middle-income people in Bangladesh, with an estimated 8 to 10 million people falling below the poverty line, Prime Minister’s Adviser on Finance and Planning Rashed Al Mahmud Titumir has said. Citing a World Bank report, Titumir said the introduction of family cards and farmer cards had been recognised by the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank as a groundbreaking initiative expected to help reduce poverty and ease people’s hardship. He made the remarks while speaking to journalists at the Rajbari Municipality auditorium at a meeting organised by the Rajbari District Administration recently. Titumir said the country was going through a critical transition, with the current administration inheriting a fragile economy marked by high inflation, rising unemployment and weak private-sector investment.
audit.body: Inflation has placed a heavy burden on low- and middle-income people in Bangladesh, with an estimated 8 to 10 million people falling below the poverty line, Prime Minister’s Adviser on Finance and Planning Rashed Al Mahmud Titumir has said. Citing a World Bank report, Titumir said the introduction of family cards and farmer cards had been recognised by the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank as a groundbreaking initiative expected to help reduce poverty and ease people’s hardship. He made the remarks while speaking to journalists at the Rajbari Municipality auditorium at a meeting organised by the Rajbari District Administration recently. Titumir said the country was going through a critical transition, with the current administration inheriting a fragile economy marked by high inflation, rising unemployment and weak private-sector investment. He said many people had been forced to use up their savings or take on debt to cope with rising prices, while unemployment among young and educated citizens had also become a major concern. The Middle East crisis had further increased fuel prices, adding pressure on the economy, he said, adding that misleading information and distorted data on gross domestic product (GDP) were also circulating on social media. Titumir said the previous Government had failed to take necessary steps to expand solar energy, explore domestic gas resources and ensure sustainable energy security. He alleged that cronyism and patronage had weakened the economic system and that around US$ 40 billion would now be needed to repair the banking sector. (TBS)

audit.headline: All schools closed today
audit.summary: All schools countrywide will be closed today (27) as a precautionary safety measure due to the prevailing adverse weather experienced across the country. audit.headline: International Athletes backed by Carnage dominate on Global Stage
audit.summary: From a historic world championship achievement in para triathlon to Commonwealth powerlifting medals, athletes supported by the Carnage Athlete Foundation are making their mark across disciplines. Launched in June 2026 under the banner “Building the next generation of Champion Athletes,” the Carnage Athlete Foundation is working to create more opportunities for Sri Lankan athletes to develop their potential and compete internationally. With a focus on identifying and nurturing talent, the Foundation aims to provide sustained support for athletes at different stages of their sporting journeys. Rather than focusing on individual partnerships or one-off successes, the initiative is built around creating a long-term pathway for sporting development. It also builds on Carnage’s existing commitment to local sport as a Partner of the National Olympic Committee of Sri Lanka and Sri Lanka Rugby.
audit.body: From a historic world championship achievement in para triathlon to Commonwealth powerlifting medals, athletes supported by the Carnage Athlete Foundation are making their mark across disciplines. Launched in June 2026 under the banner “Building the next generation of Champion Athletes,” the Carnage Athlete Foundation is working to create more opportunities for Sri Lankan athletes to develop their potential and compete internationally. With a focus on identifying and nurturing talent, the Foundation aims to provide sustained support for athletes at different stages of their sporting journeys. Rather than focusing on individual partnerships or one-off successes, the initiative is built around creating a long-term pathway for sporting development. It also builds on Carnage’s existing commitment to local sport as a Partner of the National Olympic Committee of Sri Lanka and Sri Lanka Rugby. “Sri Lanka has no shortage of sporting talent, but athletes need the right support and opportunities to take their abilities to the next level. Through the Carnage Athlete Foundation, we want to build something that goes beyond individual achievements and creates a lasting impact on the sporting landscape. We are proud of what our athletes have accomplished so far, and we see these successes as the beginning of a much bigger journey,” said Joel Tillekeratne, Director / CEO of Carnage. Among the Foundation’s recent successes is Khalid Oshman, who made history as the first visually impaired Sri Lankan to compete at the IRONMAN 70.3 World Championship. Racing with his guide, Mithun Liyanage, Oshman secured first place in the Para Open Category, marking a significant milestone for Sri Lankan para sport. Powerlifters Uvindu Jayasinghe and Rashitha de Silva also delivered strong performances at the 2026 Commonwealth Powerlifting Championship. Jayasinghe claimed bronze after working his way up from 10th place to finish third, while de Silva secured the silver medal with a second-place finish. The Foundation’s athletes are also using their sporting pursuits to make a difference beyond competition. Ultra-runner Cathryn Smart covered more than 330km across Sri Lanka to raise funds for a local charity supporting communities in need, demonstrating the potential of sport to contribute to wider social causes. From international podium finishes to the development of emerging junior talent, these achievements reflect the Foundation’s commitment to supporting athletes across disciplines and building pathways for Sri Lankan sport to make its presence felt on the international stage.

audit.headline: HNB invests Rs. 3.2 Mn for vocational training at SOS Children’s Villages Sri Lanka
audit.summary: Hatton National Bank (HNB) has strengthened its long-standing partnership with SOS Children’s Villages Sri Lanka, committing LKR 3.2 million towards the vocational training and career development of 80 young people at the SOS Vocational Training Centres in Jaffna and Malpotha. Recognising the importance of vocational skills in helping local youth transition into employment opportunities and independent adulthood, SOS Children’s Villages Sri Lanka operates Vocational Training Centres that provide practical, job-oriented training, career development, and workplace readiness. Building on this commitment, the partnership with HNB will further strengthen these opportunities for young people, equipping them with the skills and confidence needed to pursue meaningful employment, achieve greater financial independence, and build sustainable livelihoods.
audit.body: Hatton National Bank (HNB) has strengthened its long-standing partnership with SOS Children’s Villages Sri Lanka, committing LKR 3.2 million towards the vocational training and career development of 80 young people at the SOS Vocational Training Centres in Jaffna and Malpotha. Recognising the importance of vocational skills in helping local youth transition into employment opportunities and independent adulthood, SOS Children’s Villages Sri Lanka operates Vocational Training Centres that provide practical, job-oriented training, career development, and workplace readiness. Building on this commitment, the partnership with HNB will further strengthen these opportunities for young people, equipping them with the skills and confidence needed to pursue meaningful employment, achieve greater financial independence, and build sustainable livelihoods. SOS Children’s Villages Sri Lanka, National Director Divakar Ratnadurai said; “Vocational training offers holistic avenues of growth for young people with more than technical skills. It gives them the confidence, workplace readiness, and practical capabilities needed to take meaningful steps towards employment and independent living. We value our long-standing partnership with HNB and its continued commitment to creating opportunities that enable young people to build stronger and more sustainable futures.” The initiative builds on the broader role of SOS Children’s Villages Sri Lanka in supporting young people as they develop the skills and capabilities required for independent adulthood. Since 1981, SOS Children’s Villages Sri Lanka has provided long-term, family-like care for children who have lost parental care, while also supporting children who are at risk of losing parental care through its Family Strengthening Programmes. Through this partnership, HNB and SOS Children’s Villages Sri Lanka are investing in skills development as a pathway to greater independence, employability, and sustainable livelihoods for young people, while building skills to break the cycle of poverty.

audit.headline: Sri Lanka’s First Agri-PV Pilot Demonstrator opens in Kandy
audit.summary: A new approach to combining renewable energy with agriculture was showcased in Kandy when the Agri-Solar Pilot Demonstrator for Training & Research opened at the National Seminary of Our Lady of Lanka, Ampitiya, on October 23. The project introduces agrivoltaics , or Agri-PV, an approach that integrates solar photovoltaic (PV) electricity generation with agricultural cultivation on the same land. By allowing farming to continue beneath elevated solar panels, Agri-PV offers an opportunity to make more effective use of land while exploring how renewable energy generation and agricultural production can complement one another. The initiative is supported by the German Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy (BMWE) under the Renewable Energy Solutions (RES) Programme of the German Energy Solutions Initiative, with support from the German Energy Agency (dena).
audit.body: A new approach to combining renewable energy with agriculture was showcased in Kandy when the Agri-Solar Pilot Demonstrator for Training & Research opened at the National Seminary of Our Lady of Lanka, Ampitiya, on October 23. The project introduces agrivoltaics , or Agri-PV, an approach that integrates solar photovoltaic (PV) electricity generation with agricultural cultivation on the same land. By allowing farming to continue beneath elevated solar panels, Agri-PV offers an opportunity to make more effective use of land while exploring how renewable energy generation and agricultural production can complement one another. The initiative is supported by the German Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy (BMWE) under the Renewable Energy Solutions (RES) Programme of the German Energy Solutions Initiative, with support from the German Energy Agency (dena). It brings German renewable-energy expertise to Sri Lanka while promoting technology transfer, practical training and applied research. SUNfarming International GmbH, Germany, contributes its Agri-PV technology and engineering expertise, while SUNfarming Lanka (Pvt) Ltd coordinates local implementation in collaboration with the National Seminary, which hosts the facility. The installation has a total solar PV capacity of 51.48 kWp, comprising elevated Agri-Solar structures and a separate modular installation designed for practical PV training. The elevated structures incorporate SUNfarming-branded bifacial glass-glass solar PV modules, allowing agricultural activities to continue beneath them. The system incorporates a specially designed panel arrangement intended to protect crops from heavy rainfall and intense sunlight, while potentially helping to reduce soil moisture loss and crop stress. The demonstrator provided a practical platform for researchers and agricultural specialists to investigate which crops and cultivation methods are best suited to Agri-PV under Sri Lankan conditions. It also enabled agricultural performance to be monitored and assessed over time, building evidence on crop suitability, growing conditions and the practical application of Agri-PV in Sri Lanka. Technical training is another central component. During installation, 26 trainees from the Ceylon German Technical Training Institute (CGTTI) gained hands-on experience alongside the German engineering team. The facility is intended to support further practical training, technology demonstration and applied learning in solar PV and Agri-PV. For Sri Lanka, the project provides a practical starting point for exploring innovation at the intersection of agriculture and renewable energy. By combining technology demonstration, skills development and local assessment, it could help strengthen technical capacity and generate knowledge to inform future Agri-PV initiatives. As a pilot demonstrator dedicated to training and research rather than commercial-scale development, its longer-term value will lie in the lessons learned and the evidence generated under local agricultural and climatic conditions.

audit.headline: Assistant Scout Commissioner Munasinghe passes away
audit.summary: Sashik Anushan Munasinghe, the Assistant National Headquarters Commissioner of the Sri Lanka Scout Association and the Assistant Director of Archaeology for the Batticaloa and Ampara regions has passed away. He was 34 years old at the time of his demise. Munasinghe joined the scouting movement in 2003 as a scout cub and became a member of the C.W.W. Kannangara Central College Scout Group, then known as the 12th Kalutara Christophians Scout Group. Continuing his active involvement as a scout from 2004, he reached a monumental milestone in his scouting journey in 2008 when he received the President’s Scout Award, the highest recognition for a scout in Sri Lanka. He was appointed Assistant National Headquarters Commissioner in 2022. A graduate in archaeology from the Kelaniya University, he was also an assistant lecturer for some time at the university.
