audit.headline: Sri Lanka–Romania expand co-operation on employment, trade and investment
audit.summary: Sri Lanka and Romania have taken further steps to strengthen bilateral cooperation in employment, trade and investment following a business forum held in Timisoara, Romania. The forum, on 24 October, was organised by the Chambers of Commerce of Timis and Arad and attended by Deputy Minister Arun Hemachandra and Sri Lanka’s Ambassador to Romania, Samantha Pathirana, and representatives of the Romanian business community. Discussions focused on expanding suitable employment opportunities for Sri Lankan workers, promoting ethical recruitment practices, strengthening worker protection, and identifying new avenues for bilateral trade and investment. More than 28,000 Sri Lankans are currently employed in Romania, contributing to various sectors of the country’s economy.
audit.body: Sri Lanka and Romania have taken further steps to strengthen bilateral cooperation in employment, trade and investment following a business forum held in Timisoara, Romania. The forum, on 24 October, was organised by the Chambers of Commerce of Timis and Arad and attended by Deputy Minister Arun Hemachandra and Sri Lanka’s Ambassador to Romania, Samantha Pathirana, and representatives of the Romanian business community. Discussions focused on expanding suitable employment opportunities for Sri Lankan workers, promoting ethical recruitment practices, strengthening worker protection, and identifying new avenues for bilateral trade and investment. More than 28,000 Sri Lankans are currently employed in Romania, contributing to various sectors of the country’s economy. During the discussions, Florica Chirita, the Timis Chamber of Commerce President, expressed satisfaction with the performance and commitment of Sri Lankan workers, highlighting their reliability, dedication and contribution to Romanian businesses. The contribution of Sri Lankan workers was also recognised as an important element of Romania’s workforce. A key proposal emerging from the discussions was an initiative by the Timis Chamber of Commerce to organise a business delegation visit to Sri Lanka in 2027. The proposed mission is expected to bring together Romanian entrepreneurs interested in recruitment, trade and investment opportunities, creating further avenues for cooperation between the two countries. The engagement marks another step towards developing stronger economic ties between Sri Lanka and Romania, with an emphasis on creating decent employment opportunities, ensuring fair and ethical recruitment, safeguarding the rights and welfare of Sri Lankan workers, and encouraging mutually beneficial trade and investment. Sri Lanka remains committed to strengthen international economic partnerships that deliver practical benefits to its people while fostering sustainable cooperation with partner countries.

audit.headline: Dialog Axiata and IITM Pravartak forge partnership to advance research and innovation in Sri Lanka
audit.summary: Dialog Axiata PLC., has entered into a strategic partnership with Indian Institute of Technology Madras (IITM) Pravartak Technologies Foundation, India, through the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) aimed at advancing applied research and technology development in Sri Lanka. The agreement marks an important milestone in India-Sri Lanka cooperation, bringing together international expertise and industry stakeholders to develop practical solutions to national and societal challenges. It also seeks to strengthen Sri Lanka’s research capabilities and create opportunities to translate new ideas into real-world applications. Under the agreement, Dialog will serve as the collaboration anchor and technology enabler, connecting IITM Pravartak’s research networks with Sri Lankan industry stakeholders.
audit.body: Dialog Axiata PLC., has entered into a strategic partnership with Indian Institute of Technology Madras (IITM) Pravartak Technologies Foundation, India, through the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) aimed at advancing applied research and technology development in Sri Lanka. The agreement marks an important milestone in India-Sri Lanka cooperation, bringing together international expertise and industry stakeholders to develop practical solutions to national and societal challenges. It also seeks to strengthen Sri Lanka’s research capabilities and create opportunities to translate new ideas into real-world applications. Under the agreement, Dialog will serve as the collaboration anchor and technology enabler, connecting IITM Pravartak’s research networks with Sri Lankan industry stakeholders. The partnership will explore five key areas: innovation and incubation, applied research and university laboratories, artificial intelligence and human-centric solutions, industry skills and talent development, and international knowledge sharing. Potential areas for initial collaboration include Sinhala and Tamil conversational AI, technology-driven dengue prevention and response, and solutions to address human-elephant conflict. High Commissioner of India to Sri Lanka Santosh Jha said; “India and Sri Lanka share a longstanding and multifaceted relationship, underpinned by strong historical ties and a shared commitment to progress. As our bilateral partnership continues to evolve, cooperation in technology and research presents significant opportunities to deepen engagement between our institutions and people.” IITM Pravartak Technologies Foundation Chief Executive Officer Dr. Shankar Jayaraman said; “This collaboration creates an opportunity to strengthen the connection between academic research and practical application. By working closely with Dialog, Sri Lankan universities and local stakeholders, we hope to foster an environment where researchers and students can exchange knowledge, build technical capabilities and develop solutions that respond to real-world needs.” Dialog Axiata PLC., Director/Group Chief Executive of Supun Weerasinghe said; “At Dialog, we believe the true value of technology lies in its ability to address real challenges and create meaningful opportunities for people and communities. Through this partnership, we aim to connect global expertise with Sri Lankan talent to develop solutions that can make a lasting difference.” PICTURED – Exchanging the MoU between Dr. M.J. Shankar Jayaraman Chief Executive Officer of IITM Pravartak Technologies Foundation and Supun Weerasinghe Group Chief Executive of Dialog Axiata, in the presence of Santosh Jha High Commissioner of India to Sri Lanka. Together with – Devika Lal Counsellor (Economic & Commercial) High Commission of India; Aravindan Soundararajan Deputy Manager IITM, Pravartak Technologies Foundation Dr. M.J. Shankar Jayaraman, Chief Executive Officer IITM Pravartak Technologies Foundation and Viranthi Attygalle, Group Company Secretary Dialog Axiata.

The championship decider showcased the quality, competitiveness and potential of Sri Lanka’s next generation of rugby players. In the Bronze final earlier in the evening, the Colombo Aces secured third place defeating the Kandy Tuskers 29–24. Reaffirming the commitment to nurture future generations of athletes, SLT-MOBITEL served as the Powered By Partner, at the inaugural Jetour Next XV Rugby League.

Ruchira Weerakoon, Chief Officer – SLT-MOBITEL PEOTV, presenting medals to the Colombo Aces team The groundbreaking three-week tournament concluded with 140 Under-19 school rugby players participating under an innovative franchise-based model for the very first time. SLT-MOBITEL acted as a key catalyst in providing a high-performance platform for young athletes to unlock their fullest potential. Organised by the Sri Lanka Rugby in partnership with Eventistry Sports, the league featured intense rivalries for four new privately owned franchises such as the Colombo Aces, Galle Lions, Kandy Tuskers, and Jaffna Bulls. The intense competitive action at the tournament functioned as a vital player-development pathway under the close oversight of Sri Lanka Rugby, ensuring a structured focus on discipline, professionalism, and future national selection. Supported by experienced coaching teams, the young players gained valuable exposure and showcased their abilities in front of national selectors. SLT-MOBITEL’s leadership joined Sri Lanka Rugby officials on final day, with Rohana Ellawala, Chief Marketing Officer, and Chethana Attanayake, Chief Business Officer, Consumer Business, greeting players during the team line-up, and Ruchira Weerakoon, Chief Officer, SLT-MOBITEL PEOTV, presenting the Bronze medals to the Colombo Aces. SLT-MOBITEL brought the action to fans island-wide, as the Official Broadcast Partner. The tournament also introduced a new franchise-based commercial and entertainment model to Sri Lankan rugby, combining private franchise ownership, corporate partnerships, professional broadcast coverage and an enhanced match-day experience for fans. Pavithra Fernando, President, Sri Lanka Rugby, commented: “The Next XV Rugby League has demonstrated the depth of talent we have in school rugby. What has been particularly encouraging is seeing these young players adapt to a new competitive environment, playing alongside teammates from different schools. This is an important platform for identifying and developing the next generation of players who will represent Sri Lanka, and the finals day provided the perfect opportunity to celebrate this milestone.” Karin Wijeratne, Co-Founder, Eventistry Sports, said: “When we set out to build The Next XV alongside Sri Lanka Rugby, the ambition was to create something that went beyond another rugby tournament. Three weeks in, we have seen competitive rugby, passionate franchise owners, committed partners and most importantly, 140 young players embracing a completely new opportunity. This is exactly the kind of platform we want to build for the Sri Lankan sport. The first season is only the beginning, and we are excited about what The Next XV can become.” With the successful completion of its inaugural season, The Next XV has established a new platform for Sri Lanka’s emerging rugby talent and demonstrated the potential of a franchise-based model in strengthening the country’s rugby development pathway. SLT-MOBITEL will continue to champion sporting excellence, creating opportunities for the country’s youth to grow and excel in sport.

audit.headline: Ocean Lanka honours long standing employee dedication
audit.summary: Ocean Lanka (Pvt) Ltd honoured 106 employees at its Sewa Abhiman Loyalty Awards 2026, celebrating their longstanding service and the contributions that have helped shape the company’s journey over three decades. The awards recognised 49 employees completing 10 years of service, 49 employees completing 20 years, and eight employees reaching the milestone of 30 years. Coinciding with Ocean Lanka’s 30th anniversary, this year’s ceremony held special significance as the company recognised 30 years of employee service for the first time. The eight employees celebrating three decades of service share a unique connection with Ocean Lanka’s history, having grown alongside the organisation from its early years. Their recognition was a tribute to the commitment, experience and enduring contribution of those who have been part of the company’s development throughout its journey.

audit.headline: International Diplomat Day celebrated in Colombo
audit.summary: The Diplomatic Corps accredited to Sri Lanka commemorated International Diplomat Day 2026 at the Indonesia’s Embassy in Colombo on Saturday (24). The event brought together more than 150 participants representing over 21 diplomatic missions, the United Nations, and Sri Lanka’s Foreign Affairs, Foreign Employment and Tourism Ministry, along with family members and other guests. The gathering reflected the diplomatic community’s shared commitment to fostering friendship, solidarity and international co-operation. The event was attended by ambassadors, high commissioners, heads of diplomatic missions, members of the diplomatic community, and representatives of the Government. Foreign Affairs, Foreign Employment and Tourism Minister Vijitha Herath was the Chief Guest.United Nations’ Representatives were also present.
audit.body: The Diplomatic Corps accredited to Sri Lanka commemorated International Diplomat Day 2026 at the Indonesia’s Embassy in Colombo on Saturday (24). The event brought together more than 150 participants representing over 21 diplomatic missions, the United Nations, and Sri Lanka’s Foreign Affairs, Foreign Employment and Tourism Ministry, along with family members and other guests. The gathering reflected the diplomatic community’s shared commitment to fostering friendship, solidarity and international co-operation. The event was attended by ambassadors, high commissioners, heads of diplomatic missions, members of the diplomatic community, and representatives of the Government. Foreign Affairs, Foreign Employment and Tourism Minister Vijitha Herath was the Chief Guest.United Nations’ Representatives were also present. In her remarks, Dean of the Diplomatic Corps and Indonesia’s Ambassador to Sri Lanka Dewi Gustina Tobing paid tribute to the dedication and sacrifices of diplomats, whose responsibilities often require them to work far from their home countries and families. She underscored the importance of international co-operation in addressing increasingly complex global challenges, including climate change, armed conflicts, inequality and rapid technological developments. She expressed her appreciation for the spirit of friendship, solidarity and mutual support within the diplomatic community in Sri Lanka, highlighting the importance of the United Nations as a platform for dialogue and collective action. As a tangible expression of goodwill, she announced a charitable initiative by the Diplomatic Corps to provide essential supplies to local communities in Sri Lanka. United Nations Resident Co-ordinator in Sri Lanka Marc-André Franche underscored the importance of the United Nations Charter, international law and a rules-based international order in maintaining global peace, security and co-operation. He highlighted that respect for international rules, and the sovereignty of nations is essential to preventing conflict, strengthening trust, and ensuring a more peaceful and just world. He emphasised that all countries share a responsibility to uphold these principles through international co-operation and solidarity. Minister Herath emphasised the importance of friendship, peace, co-operation and mutual understanding among nations. He highlighted the long-standing relationships between countries represented in Sri Lanka, built on shared values, cultural ties, and a commitment to constructive engagement, diversity, democracy, and the peaceful resolution of conflicts. He also acknowledged the contributions of ambassadors and their families in strengthening diplomatic relations and fostering closer ties among nations, expressing his hope that the gathering would create lasting memories and further strengthen bonds of friendship. The celebration featured various sporting competitions, including mini soccer, badminton, volleyball, tennis, table tennis, chess and dominoes, alongside traditional Sri Lankan games.

audit.headline: Foreign suspect arrested at BIA with narcotics worth Rs. 51 Mn
audit.summary: Customs Narcotics Control Division officers arrested a foreign passenger early in the morning yesterday while he was attempting to smuggle a stock of ‘Kush’, valued at Rs. 51 million, out of the Katunayake Airport via the ‘Green Channel’ (Nothing to Declare). The suspect is a 24-year-old Indian national who works as a mobile phone repairman in India. He arrived at Katunayake Airport aboard a flight from Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam. Upon arrival, Airport Customs Narcotics Control Division officers subjected his luggage to a scan test, which revealed 5 kilogrammes and 100 grammes of ‘Kush’ hidden among his clothing in seven carefully prepared packets. The Indian passenger along with the seized stock of ‘Kush’ have been handed over to the Katunayake Airport Police Narcotic Bureau for further investigations.

audit.headline: Policy priorities to achieve durable growth in Sri Lanka
audit.summary: S ustaining Sri Lanka’s post-crisis macroeconomic stability requires productivity-enhancing reforms to achieve durable and inclusive growth. Against this backdrop, the Institute of Policy Studies of Sri Lanka (IPS) hosted a roundtable discussion on 14 October 2026 on its flagship publication, Sri Lanka State of the Economy 2026, to discuss policy priorities to rebuild the country’s economic foundations amidst ongoing domestic and global uncertainties. IPS Research Fellows Dr Asanka Wijesinghe and Dr Lakmini Fernando presented key findings, followed by interventions from Dr Yashodha Senadheera, Deputy Director of the Economic Research Department of the Central Bank of Sri Lanka (CBSL); Dr Liliya Aleksanyan, Senior Country Economist for Sri Lanka at the Asian Development Bank (ADB); Mr. Sanjaya Ariyawansa, Senior Economist at Sampath Bank; and other invited parties.
audit.body: S ustaining Sri Lanka’s post-crisis macroeconomic stability requires productivity-enhancing reforms to achieve durable and inclusive growth. Against this backdrop, the Institute of Policy Studies of Sri Lanka (IPS) hosted a roundtable discussion on 14 October 2026 on its flagship publication, Sri Lanka State of the Economy 2026, to discuss policy priorities to rebuild the country’s economic foundations amidst ongoing domestic and global uncertainties. IPS Research Fellows Dr Asanka Wijesinghe and Dr Lakmini Fernando presented key findings, followed by interventions from Dr Yashodha Senadheera, Deputy Director of the Economic Research Department of the Central Bank of Sri Lanka (CBSL); Dr Liliya Aleksanyan, Senior Country Economist for Sri Lanka at the Asian Development Bank (ADB); Mr. Sanjaya Ariyawansa, Senior Economist at Sampath Bank; and other invited parties. Growth Has Returned, but Can Sri Lanka Sustain It? Dr Asanka Wijesinghe discussed Sri Lanka’s macroeconomic performance, external sector competitiveness, and policy priorities for durable growth. He highlighted that while the economy’s recovery has beensatisfactory, sustained annual growth of approximately 8.3% between 2026 and 2030 would be required to regain the pre-crisis growth trajectory. Against this background, Sri Lanka needs to accelerate reforms towards achieving stated medium-term growth target of 7% or above. Rising global fuel prices and the resulting external sector pressures pose an immediate challenge to Sri Lanka’s economic growth. Sri Lanka recorded a Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth of 4.2% in the second quarter of 2026, with increased contribution of investment to economic output. However, the increased import bill has been a drag on output growth. The merchandise trade deficit widened considerably during January–August 2026, when compared to 2025. Improvements in fiscalconsolidation and debt management have given Sri Lanka breathing space amidst a hostile external sector. Dr Wijesinghe stressed the need to maintain fiscal discipline, strengthen external competitiveness, and continue engagement with international financial institutions as the country rebuilds its resilience. Dr Wijesinghe emphasised that expansion of exports is essential for achieving 7% economic growth, as growth driven primarily by domestic demand has its limitations. Sri Lanka’s reliance on non-reciprocal preferential market accessfaces growing challenges as competing economies negotiate reciprocal trade agreements. For example, Indonesia’s preferential access to the European Union (EU) and India’s trade agreement with the United Kingdom (UK) could weaken Sri Lanka’s competitiveness. This challenge could be further compounded by the potential loss of existing preferential arrangements for Sri Lanka, including the Generalised Scheme of Preferences Plus(GSP+). Securing more predictable tariff regimes in major export markets is a necessary precondition, and it requiresaccelerating tariff reforms and simplifying the tariff structure. However, these reforms must be carefully sequenced, assudden reductions in tariff protection could adversely affect domestic industries, particularly Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs). He also recommended a dedicated fund to support trade adjustment. Reorienting Fiscal Policy Towards Long-Term Growth Building on these discussions, Dr Lakmini Fernando explained how fiscal policy could support durable growth beyond the current International Monetary Fund (IMF) programme. During the adjustment period, government capital expenditure declined to historically low levels, constraining the scope for public investment to support long-term growth and development. Achieving 7% economic growth could require gross fixed capital formation equivalent to approximately 30–42% of GDP, depending on investment efficiency. Mobilising such investment also requires a supportive environment for private investment alongside productive public expenditure. She also highlighted the need to prioritise education, healthcare, skills development, social protection, climate-resilient infrastructure, and green investment to meet evolving future demand. Improving public financial management, strengthening project implementation capacity, and ensuring transparent and competitive procurement were also identified as essential reforms. On debt sustainability, Dr Fernando stressed adhering to a medium-term debt management strategy, strengthening fiscal institutions, and exploring innovative financing. Continued engagement with international financial institutions could ease financing pressures. She also highlighted the importance of long-term planning and consistent implementation. Expert Perspectives: Monetary Stability, Economic Resilience and Emerging Shocks Dr Yashodha Senadheera elaborated on the Central Bank’s monetary policy response to external supply-side shocks. She explained that although monetary policy has limited capacity to directly address supply-driven inflation, intervention may become necessary when such shocks generate persistent inflationary pressures or threaten inflation expectations. Maintaining price stability while considering broader economic conditions therefore requires careful, data-driven policy decisions. Dr Liliya Aleksanyan highlighted the lasting effects of successive crises and global energy-price volatility, emphasising the need for greater energy security through renewable energy. She also encouraged Sri Lanka to explore Asian export markets like India, alongside traditional markets such as EU and the United States of America (USA). Additionally, she highlighted the importance ofpreparing for emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence Sanjaya Ariyawansa focused on revenue mobilisation and climate risks. He called for improvements in tax administration, integration of SMEs into the tax system, and independent fiscal oversight. He also urged closer assessment of how climate-related shocks could affect agriculture, energy, public expenditure, and banking sector stability to strengthen preparedness and resilience. From Policy Recommendations to Implementation The subsequent roundtable discussion further explored several themes raised during the presentations and expert interventions. Participants discussed the assumptions underlying growth projections, the investment required to achieve higher growth, and opportunities to strengthen revenue mobilisation. To overcome the persistent gap between budgetary allocations and actual expenditure, participants also focused on improving the efficiency and timely utilisation of public investment. The discussion also explored fiscal responses to energy price shocks, the importance of supporting industries affected by tariff reforms, and the potential contribution of innovative climate financing instruments. Participants underscored that strengthening institutional capacity and anticipating risks are equally important as designing appropriate policies. The growth trajectory demands complementary reforms across macroeconomic management, international trade, public investment, fiscal institutions, and climate resilience.Ultimately, Sri Lanka’s long-term economic prospects will depend both on identifying the right policy priorities and implementing them consistently. As emphasised throughout the discussion, durable growth requires a forward-looking development strategy that strengthens the country’s capacity to withstand future shocks while delivering sustained improvements in economic well-being.

audit.headline: Pakistan Under 17s sweep Limited Overs series 4-1 over Sri Lanka
audit.summary: Pakistan U-17 cricket team continued their all-round performance when they recorded a 27-run win in the fifth One-Day match against Sri Lanka U-17 to take the five-match 50-over series 4-1 at the Multan Cricket Stadium on Saturday. Pakistan’s Mohammad Yousaf continued his batting form in the series with his second century which propelled the hosts to 283-7 in 50 overs. In reply, Sri Lanka U-17 finished with 256-7 in their 50 overs after struggling at 141- for 6 wickets. Pakistan captain Azan Ahmed opted to bat first but Sri Lanka made early breakthrough removing opening batter Daud Tauqeer Rana for 13 and Hamza Abbas Baloch for 14. However Yousaf and skipper Azan then laid the platform for a healthy total with a 138-run stand between them to build up the innings.
audit.body: Pakistan U-17 cricket team continued their all-round performance when they recorded a 27-run win in the fifth One-Day match against Sri Lanka U-17 to take the five-match 50-over series 4-1 at the Multan Cricket Stadium on Saturday. Pakistan’s Mohammad Yousaf continued his batting form in the series with his second century which propelled the hosts to 283-7 in 50 overs. In reply, Sri Lanka U-17 finished with 256-7 in their 50 overs after struggling at 141- for 6 wickets. Pakistan captain Azan Ahmed opted to bat first but Sri Lanka made early breakthrough removing opening batter Daud Tauqeer Rana for 13 and Hamza Abbas Baloch for 14. However Yousaf and skipper Azan then laid the platform for a healthy total with a 138-run stand between them to build up the innings. Azan fell for 91 off 92 balls striking six fours and three sixes while Yousaf (105, 130b, 12x4s) went on to score the second ton of this series. Sri Lanka’s pursuit of the 284-run target got off to a strong start with opening batters Yenula Hewavitharana (46, 71b, 7x4s) and Methuka Gunaratne (23, 28b, 2x4s, 1×6) putting on 70 runs. Sri Lanka then faced a setback when they lost five for 36, slipping from 105-1 to 141-6. No.7 batter Sandaru Malshan (56, 55b, 4x4s) and no.8 Chenul Milnaka (40 not out, 56b, 3x4s) then tried to salvage the innings with a 99-run stand but it was in vain as Pakistan restricted the visitors to 256-7. Sandaru Malshan, the all-rounder hit his second fifty of the series came to the fore in this tournament. Sri Lanka grab solitary win in opener However Sri Lanka had to be satisfied with a solitary win in the series which was the opening one dayer at Multan. The opener Methuka Gunaratne was the match winner scoring 77 well supported by Yenula Hewavitharana (36) and Reshon Solomans (42) to build up the total to 239 for 6 wickets. Pakistan under 17s were all out for 140 in 39 overs and Sri Lanka recorded 99 runs victory over hosts. The off spinner Sandaru Malshan was the successful bowler taking 3 for 16. In the second one day game between the two teams, Pakistan came to the fore scoring 274 for 9 wickets with Mohammed Yousaf top scoring 117. Reshon Solomons took 3 for 39. However Sri Lanka were struggling at 123 at one stage and Chenuka Dodangoda was the successful batter scoring a fifty. The third one day game once again Sri Lanka couldn’t make a challenging total as they were bowled out for 159 in 44 overs. The opener Methuka Gunaratne hit 49 while Sandaru Malshan scored a fighting knock of 52 as the number seven batter. Pakistan chased their target in only 41.5 overs with 5 wickets in hand. In the fourth one day game Pakistan made a challenging total of 273 for 9 wickets with skipper Azan Ahmed top scored 82. Sri Lanka chasing their target, Reshon Solomons made a good knock of 64 with 5 fours but that was not enough to reach the target. Despite the loss of one day series 1-4, Sri Lanka young players got good exposure during this Pakistan series. They had a one three-day game which was prior to the one day five match series and that game ended in a draw. Chief scores of 5th One Day: Pakistan U17 283-7, 50 overs (Mohammad Yousaf 105, Azan Ahmed 91, Hamid Raza 30’ Raveen Sachintha 2-51, Kalindu Sachinthana 2-53) Sri Lanka U17 256-7, 50 overs (Sandaru Malshan 56, Yenula Hewavitharana 46, Chenul Milnaka 40 not out, Methuka Gunaratne 23, Chenuka Dondangoda 22; Mohammad Saim 2-30) Oct 9-11 – Three-day game – Drawn, Oct 15 – 1st One-Day – Sri Lanka won by 99 runs, Oct 17 – 2nd One-Day – Pakistan won by 151 runs, Oct 19 – 3rd One-Day – Pakistan won by five wickets, Oct 21 – 4th One-Day – Pakistan won by 93 runs, Oct 23 – 5th One-Day – Pakistan won by 27 runs.

audit.headline: Combating crime while safeguarding the right to democratic dissent
audit.summary: S ri Lanka has a law and order problem that cannot be ignored. The daily reports of drug busts, arrests of suspected criminals and killings involving firearms make clear that criminality has become a serious challenge to public safety. There is a need to deal with this problem firmly and effectively. Addressing parliament, Minister of Public Security Ananda Wijepala said shooting incidents linked to organised crime have declined to 18 so far in 2026, compared to 29 incidents recorded in 2025.The Minister attributed the increase in shooting incidents in previous years to conflicts between organised criminal gangs and drug trafficking networks.The reduction in figures suggest that the government’s campaign against crime may be yielding results.
audit.body: S ri Lanka has a law and order problem that cannot be ignored. The daily reports of drug busts, arrests of suspected criminals and killings involving firearms make clear that criminality has become a serious challenge to public safety. There is a need to deal with this problem firmly and effectively. Addressing parliament, Minister of Public Security Ananda Wijepala said shooting incidents linked to organised crime have declined to 18 so far in 2026, compared to 29 incidents recorded in 2025.The Minister attributed the increase in shooting incidents in previous years to conflicts between organised criminal gangs and drug trafficking networks.The reduction in figures suggest that the government’s campaign against crime may be yielding results. The National People’s Power (NPP) government’s pursuit of corruption, fraud and other crimes involving powerful figures from the past and present represents an important departure from the perception that political connections can provide protection from the law. Former ministers, politicians and senior state officials have faced investigations and legal proceedings. Recent revelations and investigations have drawn attention to the relationships that can develop between criminal networks and individuals within political and law enforcement circles. Allegations and evidence concerning political patronage, protection afforded to suspected offenders and failures to investigate serious crimes have contributed to the perception that criminality has sometimes been sustained by powerful connections. The NPP has adopted a single-minded approach to addressing the country’s problems. Its emphasis on law enforcement reflects a determination to deliver results and meet public expectations. This approach has considerable public support, particularly when people see criminal gangs operating with apparent impunity and public resources being misappropriated. From an executive perspective, the need for effective laws and powers to tackle these problems is understandable.However, governments can become so focused on their mission to deliver results that they see problems primarily from their own perspective. This is a risk for any government, including one that has come to power promising system change. The government’s determination to combat crime must therefore be accompanied by an equally strong commitment to protecting the democratic rights of citizens, especially the right to dissent. If not, there is a danger that the law, rather than serving as an impartial instrument of justice, can become a weapon through which the government seeks to get its way. The experience following the Aragalaya people’s uprising provides a reminder of this danger. The protests represented the people’s right to dissent against government failures and oppression and contributed to a major political transformation. The manner in which participants were subsequently subjected to arrests and legal proceedings raised concerns about the undemocratic treatment of dissent by the then government. The lesson is that peaceful protest, criticism of government and civil disobedience cannot automatically be treated as threats to the state. In the case of the Aragalaya protests, they saved the state from plunging headlong into disaster. The government that was overthrown by people’s power on the streets was one that had brought the country to economic disaster by mishandling foreign loans and which had imposed a 100 percent ban on non-organic fertilizer and use of chemical pesticides that wrought havoc to farmers and to the national economy. The distinction between criminal conduct and legitimate dissent is essential to democracy. A government that emerged from a people’s uprising has particular reason to appreciate the importance of preserving that distinction. That distinction is exactly what overbroad laws erase, which is why the government’s legislative agenda matters. The proposed Protection of the State from Terrorism Bill, the Prevention of Organised Crimes Bill and the NGO Registration and Supervision Bill have been presented as responses to genuine concerns. Preventing terrorism, dismantling criminal networks and ensuring transparency in organisations that receive public or foreign funds are legitimate responsibilities of the State. Sri Lanka also has international obligations on organised crime and the financing of terrorism. The question is whether the powers proposed in the three bills under consideration are necessary, proportionate and accompanied by adequate safeguards. Taken together, these draft laws raise fundamental questions about the direction of governance reform in Sri Lanka. The Human Rights Commission of Sri Lanka , which is a state institution, has criticised the terrorism bill’s broad definition of terrorism, its potential impact on legitimate protest and trade union action, prolonged detention and weak judicial oversight. The organised crimes bill has drawn criticism for its detention powers, the admissibility of confessions made to police and extensive surveillance provisions. The NGO bill raises the same question from another side. Oversight of funded organisations is legitimate, but supervisory powers must not become a way to pressure groups that criticise the government. These concerns should not be dismissed as opposition to law and order. A law’s effectiveness is measured by whether it brings genuine offenders to justice without exposing innocent people to arbitrary arrest, detention or prosecution. The government can address these concerns through transparent consultation, clearer definitions of offences and stronger judicial oversight. At the heart of this debate lies a basic principle of criminal justice: the law must protect the innocent from wrongful prosecution or conviction. That is the basis of the requirement that guilt be proved beyond reasonable doubt. The principle does not make law enforcement easier, but it is essential to the just exercise of state power. It is also why the admissibility of confessions made to police is not a technicality. It goes directly to the reliability of convictions. The courts bear particular responsibility here. They must ensure that evidence supports criminal charges, that the rights of the accused are respected and that investigators and the executive stay within the law. They are the linchpin of the checks and balances that prevent arbitrary power. Independent judicial scrutiny makes the outcome of investigations more credible and helps ensure that those convicted are guilty of the offences for which they are punished. Justice must be done and be seen to be done.Public confidence depends on this. A country in which criminal networks operate with impunity, corruption flourishes and political influence decides how the law is applied cannot build the trust needed for lasting economic progress. Neither can a country prosper if citizens fear that state power may be turned on them for expressing dissent or challenging official decisions. The campaign against crime could be one of the government’s most important contributions to national recovery, but only if it is seen to be fair and not used to suppress political dissent which is the stuff of democracy. The three Bills concentrate powers that could be abused if not now in the future. It is essential for the government to substantially revise the bills where their provisions fail to meet constitutional and international human rights standards. The ultimate test of system change is not simply whether the present government can bring powerful individuals to justice. It is whether it can build institutions and establish legal safeguards that prevent itself and any future government from abusing those powers. The NPP has an opportunity to demonstrate that a determined campaign against criminality and corruption can go hand in hand with respect for democratic freedoms and the independence of the judiciary.A strong state is one that can enforce the law effectively. A just state is one that also knows the limits of its power. Sri Lanka needs both.

audit.headline: Proposed laws threaten FR, Opposition reiterates
audit.summary: Opposition Leader Sajith Premadasa during a consultation with foreign diplomats and representatives of international organisations at his office in Colombo on Sunday raised serious concerns regarding Government’s newly proposed security legislation. The talks focused on the Protection of the State from Terrorism Bill and the Prevention of Organised Crimes Bill, with former MP M.A. Sumanthiran alongside current and former Parliamentarians joining Premadasa in warning that the proposed laws threaten fundamental rights, judicial independence, and the rule of law. Premadasa stressed that while tackling terrorism and organised crime is essential, decisive State action must be balanced with strict judicial oversight and respect for civil liberties.
audit.body: Opposition Leader Sajith Premadasa during a consultation with foreign diplomats and representatives of international organisations at his office in Colombo on Sunday raised serious concerns regarding Government’s newly proposed security legislation. The talks focused on the Protection of the State from Terrorism Bill and the Prevention of Organised Crimes Bill, with former MP M.A. Sumanthiran alongside current and former Parliamentarians joining Premadasa in warning that the proposed laws threaten fundamental rights, judicial independence, and the rule of law. Premadasa stressed that while tackling terrorism and organised crime is essential, decisive State action must be balanced with strict judicial oversight and respect for civil liberties. The Opposition highlighted recent critical assessments from key oversight bodies, including the Human Rights Commission of Sri Lanka (HRCSL), which declared the Prevention of Organised Crime Bill “wholly incompatible” with the Constitution’s fundamental rights’ safeguards and international obligations. Concurrently, the Bar Association of Sri Lanka (BASL) called for the withdrawal of the Organised Crime Bill and major amendments to the Anti-Terrorism Bill, demanding the public release of the underlying expert committee report and its recorded dissents. In response, Premadasa outlined the Opposition’s demands for transparent reform, including the publication of expert recommendations, proportionate definitions of offences, restored judicial discretion over bail, protection against coerced confessions, and mandatory consultations with legal bodies before proceeding. Reaffirming Sri Lanka’s national sovereignty, Premadasa noted that resolving domestic legal questions remains the primary responsibility of Parliament and national courts, while emphasising the value of constructive dialogue with international partners to safeguard constitutional democracy.

audit.headline: SC nullifies Ranil Wickremesinghe’s remission
audit.summary: The Supreme Court (SC) has invalidated the remission of the prison sentence granted to a man by former President Ranil Wickremesinghe under a General Amnesty in September 2024, ruling that the decision violated the Fundamental Right to equality and equal protection of the law. A three-judge bench comprising Justices Janak De Silva, Dr. Sobhitha Rajakaruna and Sampath Wijeratne held that the man had received preferential treatment compared to another person jailed for the same offence. The Court found that the difference in the wording of their warrants of commitment, one referring to default in payment of a “fine” and the other to default in maintenance payments did not constitute a valid ground for granting substantially different remissions.
audit.body: The Supreme Court (SC) has invalidated the remission of the prison sentence granted to a man by former President Ranil Wickremesinghe under a General Amnesty in September 2024, ruling that the decision violated the Fundamental Right to equality and equal protection of the law. A three-judge bench comprising Justices Janak De Silva, Dr. Sobhitha Rajakaruna and Sampath Wijeratne held that the man had received preferential treatment compared to another person jailed for the same offence. The Court found that the difference in the wording of their warrants of commitment, one referring to default in payment of a “fine” and the other to default in maintenance payments did not constitute a valid ground for granting substantially different remissions. The judgement was delivered on a fundamental rights petition filed by Ahamend Jaleel Farmilla Begum, whose former husband had been sentenced to 29 months’ imprisonment after failing to pay maintenance arrears amounting to Rs. 1.74 million. The petitioner had obtained a maintenance order from the Colombo East Quazi Court directing her former husband to pay maintenance totalling Rs. 60,000. Following his failure to comply with the order, the Magistrate’s Court of Negombo issued an enforcement certificate for the arrears, and he was subsequently imprisoned in July 2024. However, following a recommendation by the then Justice Minister to grant a General Amnesty to mark Prisoners’ Day, the remainder of his sentence was remitted, and he was released on September 12, 2024. Challenging the decision, the petitioner argued that the remission was arbitrary and had adversely affected her ability to recover the outstanding maintenance payments. She also pointed out that another person, Mohamed Faizal Mohamed Nawshad, who had been imprisoned for defaulting on maintenance payments, had not received a similar benefit. The Supreme Court observed that Nawshad had served approximately eight months of a 27-month prison sentence by the time the amnesty was granted but received only a one-week remission. In contrast, the petitioner’s former husband had served less than two months of his 29-month sentence before the remainder was remitted. The Court held that both men were, in substance, in the same position, as their imprisonment arose from defaults in meeting maintenance obligations. The difference in the terminology used in their respective warrants could not justify the unequal treatment. Accordingly, the Court declared that the former President, the Justice Ministry Secretary and the Commissioner General of Prisons had violated the petitioner’s fundamental right to equality and equal protection of the law guaranteed under Article 12(1) of the Constitution. The respondent parties had justified the difference on the basis that the former husband’s warrant recorded his sentence as being in default of payment of a fine, whereas Nawshad’s warrant referred to default in maintenance payments. Rejecting that justification, the Court explained that the relevant legal provisions permitted maintenance arrears to be recovered in the same manner as fines. The terminology used in a warrant could not therefore justify treating the two men differently. The judgement further stated that the exercise of executive power must be directed towards the public interest and cannot be based on arbitrary distinctions.

audit.headline: BOC opens largest ever Debenture Issue on November 3, 2026
audit.summary: Bank of Ceylon (BOC) is set to create another milestone in the country’s capital market with the launch of Sri Lanka’s largest-ever listed debenture issue, with a maximum issue size of LKR 30 billion. The Bank proposes to initially raise LKR 10 billion, with an option to increase the issue to LKR 20 billion in the event of an oversubscription of the initial tranche and a further option to increase the total issue size up to LKR 30 billion, making it the largest listed debenture issue undertaken in Sri Lanka. The proposed issue comprises Basel III compliant, Tier 2, Listed, Rated, Unsecured, Subordinated, Redeemable debentures with a non-viability write-down feature. The debentures carry an issue rating of AA (Stable) from Lanka Rating Agency, while BOC’s issuer rating stands at AA-(lka)/Stable from Fitch Ratings Lanka Ltd.
audit.body: Bank of Ceylon (BOC) is set to create another milestone in the country’s capital market with the launch of Sri Lanka’s largest-ever listed debenture issue, with a maximum issue size of LKR 30 billion. The Bank proposes to initially raise LKR 10 billion, with an option to increase the issue to LKR 20 billion in the event of an oversubscription of the initial tranche and a further option to increase the total issue size up to LKR 30 billion, making it the largest listed debenture issue undertaken in Sri Lanka. The proposed issue comprises Basel III compliant, Tier 2, Listed, Rated, Unsecured, Subordinated, Redeemable debentures with a non-viability write-down feature. The debentures carry an issue rating of AA (Stable) from Lanka Rating Agency, while BOC’s issuer rating stands at AA-(lka)/Stable from Fitch Ratings Lanka Ltd. The debentures will be offered with five-year and seven-year maturities, providing with medium to long-term fixed income investment opportunities. The issue is confined to qualified investors and the minimum subscription for qualified investors is LKR 10,000, while individual investors are required to apply for at least LKR 5 million. The debentures are offered in four different types to meet diverse requirements of qualified investors. The Fixed coupon rate of the five-year debenture will be 12.75 percent per annum while the floating coupon rate will be 1.50 percent above the applicable twelve-month Treasury Bill rate. The Fixed coupon rate of the seven-year debenture will be 13.00 percent per annum while the floating coupon rate will be 1.75 percent above the applicable twelve-month Treasury Bill rate. BOC is a Corporate Finance Advisor licensed by the Securities and Exchange Commission of Sri Lanka. This largest Basel III Debenture issuance was exclusively structured and managed by the Investment Banking team who possess a wealth of expertise in structuring innovative capital market instruments. The issue follows BOC’s pioneering Sustainability Bond issuance, another landmark transaction structured and managed by the Bank’s Investment Banking Division, reflecting BOC’s continued leadership in developing innovative capital-market solutions while advancing sustainable finance in Sri Lanka. The Legal Department of BOC acts as the lawyers to the issue, while the Corporate Branch of the Bank acts as the bankers to the issue. The Investment Banking Division will also continue to act as the Registrar to the proposed issue, while Hatton National Bank PLC will be the trustee to the issue. The Bank is opening the subscription list of the BASEL III Debenture Issue at 9.30 a.m. on 3 rd November 2026 and will remain open for 14 market days unless the Bank decides to close it earlier based on subscription levels. Applications for the debentures will be accepted from qualified investors in accordance with the terms and conditions set out in the Prospectus. The Prospectus and application forms can be downloaded from the web sites of the CSE; www.cse.lk and BOC; www.boc.lk.

audit.headline: SC imposes travel ban on Keheliya, four others
audit.summary: The Supreme Court (SC) yesterday imposed a travel ban on former Health Minister Keheliya Rambukwella and four others in contempt of court proceedings arising from their alleged failure to comply with payment orders issued by the Court in a judgement delivered on March 27, 2026. The Controller General of Immigration and Emigration was directed to implement the travel ban forthwith. A Supreme Court three-judge bench comprising Chief Justice Preethi Padman Surasena and Justices Achala Wengappuli and Gihan Kulatunga also granted the five respondents three months from yesterday to pay the respective sums ordered to be paid to the State. Four of the respondents, including Rambukwella, were ordered to be released on bail upon furnishing bonds of Rs. 50 million each, with two sureties.
audit.body: The Supreme Court (SC) yesterday imposed a travel ban on former Health Minister Keheliya Rambukwella and four others in contempt of court proceedings arising from their alleged failure to comply with payment orders issued by the Court in a judgement delivered on March 27, 2026. The Controller General of Immigration and Emigration was directed to implement the travel ban forthwith. A Supreme Court three-judge bench comprising Chief Justice Preethi Padman Surasena and Justices Achala Wengappuli and Gihan Kulatunga also granted the five respondents three months from yesterday to pay the respective sums ordered to be paid to the State. Four of the respondents, including Rambukwella, were ordered to be released on bail upon furnishing bonds of Rs. 50 million each, with two sureties. The contempt proceedings were initiated by Transparency International Sri Lanka (TISL) over the alleged failure of the respondents to comply with the Supreme Court’s directions in case No. SC/FR/65/2023. In that judgement, the Court had ordered Rambukwella to pay Rs. 75 million to the State, while the other four respondents, including former National Medicines Regulatory Authority (NMRA) Chairman S. J. S. Chandraguptha, former NMRA Chief Executive Officer Prof. S. D. Jayaratne and former Medical Supplies Division Director Dr. Vijith Gunasekara, were each directed to pay Rs. 50 million. Appearing for Rambukwella, President’s Counsel Eraj de Silva tendered a receipt confirming a cash deposit of Rs. 20 million and undertook to pay the balance within two weeks. The second respondent, Chandraguptha, undertook to pay Rs. 5 million within a week and settle the remaining amount within two months. Prof. Jayaratne tendered a receipt as proof of payment of Rs. 50 million and sought to have the proceedings against him discharged. However, the Court said it would consider the application on the next hearing date, as the relevant payment documents had not been filed in the case. Dr. Gunasekara informed Court that Rs. 20 million would be paid within two weeks. He also undertook to dispose of other properties and settle the balance within three months. Counsel for the fifth respondent, Dr. A. T. Sudharshana, informed Court that Rs. 2 million would be paid within a week, followed by steps to dispose of other assets within three months to settle the outstanding amount.

Playing more WTT tournaments will always be important for this young player to improve his world ranking.

audit.headline: Naufer Moulavi, co-accused sentenced to 12 Years’ RI
audit.summary: The Colombo High Court Trial-at-Bar yesterday sentenced two accused to 12 years’ rigorous imprisonment over a case filed against them involving the unlawful stockpiling of explosives and a firearm at Lactowatta in Wanathavilluwa, Puttalam in 2018, in collaboration with Muslim religious extremists, including Zahran Hashim. Accordingly, Mohamed Ibrahim Sadik Abdullah alias Abu Umar and Mohamed Naufer Moulavi were sentenced by the Colombo High Court Trial-at-Bar. The bench also ordered that the time the accused had spent in custody and remand prison be deducted from their sentences. The order was delivered by the Colombo High Court Trial-at-Bar bench comprising High Court Judges Lal Ranasinghe Bandara, Rashmi Singappuli, and Nayomi Wickramasekara.
audit.body: The Colombo High Court Trial-at-Bar yesterday sentenced two accused to 12 years’ rigorous imprisonment over a case filed against them involving the unlawful stockpiling of explosives and a firearm at Lactowatta in Wanathavilluwa, Puttalam in 2018, in collaboration with Muslim religious extremists, including Zahran Hashim. Accordingly, Mohamed Ibrahim Sadik Abdullah alias Abu Umar and Mohamed Naufer Moulavi were sentenced by the Colombo High Court Trial-at-Bar. The bench also ordered that the time the accused had spent in custody and remand prison be deducted from their sentences. The order was delivered by the Colombo High Court Trial-at-Bar bench comprising High Court Judges Lal Ranasinghe Bandara, Rashmi Singappuli, and Nayomi Wickramasekara. On January 16, 2019, the Criminal Investigation Department (CID) seized a stock of nitrates (classified as explosives), twelve live rounds of ammunition, a firearm, and quantities of nitric acid and urea, materials required for the manufacture of explosives, from Lactowatta in Wanathavilluwa, Puttalam. On April 28, 2021, the Attorney General had filed indictments under 14 counts against six accused in connection with this incident. The charges filed against the accused under the Prevention of Terrorism (Temporary Provisions) Act included conspiracy, maintaining a secret location for the manufacture of bombs, and the stockpiling of explosives in collaboration with Muslim religious extremists, including Zahran Hashim. Meanwhile, the court was also informed that the third accused in the case is prepared to plead guilty and his sentencing is scheduled for today. These accused are among those who were convicted and sentenced on September 22 in the main Easter Sunday attacks case. On a previous occasion, first accused Abu Hanifa Mohamed Musif, and second accused Amir Hamza Mohamed Hamaz, pleaded guilty to the charges. After considering their plea, both accused were sentenced to 12 years’ rigorous imprisonment by the Colombo High Court Trial-at-Bar on October 7. The Attorney General had filed this case under 14 indictments against six individuals, including four who are also convicted in the main Easter Sunday attacks case, namely Abu Hanifa Mohamed Musif, Amir Hamza Mohamed Hamaz, Mohamed Sarifu Adam Lebbe, Mohamed Ibrahim Sadik Abdullah, Mohamed Ibrahim Mohamed Naufer, and Mohamed Ramees Mohamed Sajid.

audit.headline: Sri Lanka’s exports top US$13.6 Bn in first nine months
audit.summary: Sri Lanka’s export earnings rose 5.04% year-on-year to US$13.61 billion in the first nine months of 2026, supported by growth in merchandise and services exports, with electrical and electronic components, spices and processed food among the strongest-performing sectors. Total exports during January–September increased from US$12.96 billion in the corresponding period last year, according to the latest figures released by the Sri Lanka Export Development Board (EDB). Merchandise exports grew 5.35% to US$10.76 billion, while services exports increased 3.88% to US$2.85 billion, reflecting continued expansion across both segments. September recorded particularly strong growth, with total exports rising 17.23% year-on-year to US$1.69 billion. Merchandise exports surged 21.66% to US$1.39 billion, while services exports edged up 0.67% to US$306.17 million.
audit.body: Sri Lanka’s export earnings rose 5.04% year-on-year to US$13.61 billion in the first nine months of 2026, supported by growth in merchandise and services exports, with electrical and electronic components, spices and processed food among the strongest-performing sectors. Total exports during January–September increased from US$12.96 billion in the corresponding period last year, according to the latest figures released by the Sri Lanka Export Development Board (EDB). Merchandise exports grew 5.35% to US$10.76 billion, while services exports increased 3.88% to US$2.85 billion, reflecting continued expansion across both segments. September recorded particularly strong growth, with total exports rising 17.23% year-on-year to US$1.69 billion. Merchandise exports surged 21.66% to US$1.39 billion, while services exports edged up 0.67% to US$306.17 million. Among the key sectors, electrical and electronic components recorded the strongest growth during the first nine months, with earnings increasing 61.05% to US$508.86 million. Exports of spices, essential oils and oleoresins rose 30.53% to US$430.53 million, while food and beverages grew 20.90% to US$526.31 million. Rubber and rubber-based products generated US$773.88 million, up 8.44%, while coconut-based products increased 3.68% to US$942.5 million. ICT and business process management exports also expanded 3.69% to an estimated US$1.24 billion. However, apparel and textile exports declined 5.68% to US$3.78 billion, while tea exports fell 6.83% to US$1.08 billion. Seafood exports recorded a 2.03% contraction during the period. The United States remained Sri Lanka’s largest merchandise export destination, accounting for approximately 20.3% of total merchandise exports. India overtook the United Kingdom to become the second-largest destination, with exports rising 12.3% to US$889.84 million. EDB Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Mangala Wijesinghe said sustaining growth would require greater competitiveness, value addition, innovation, technology adoption and market diversification. The National Export Development Plan 2026–2030 targets annual export earnings of US$36 billion by 2030, providing a framework to expand market access, promote investment and strengthen the country’s export sector.

audit.headline: Aleksandar Vucic, the Serbian leader brought down by students
audit.summary: Aleksandar Vucic, who has shaped Serbia’s political life for more than a decade, has lost snap Parliamentary Elections to a student-led movement that led protests against him for almost two years. After a heated race, Vucic conceded defeat to the Student List in Sunday’s elections, which saw voter turnout reach its highest level in more than 30 years. “It is clear that we have lost these elections,” the leader of the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) told supporters after a sample of votes showed his electoral list was expected to win 105 seats in Serbia’s 250-member Parliament, compared with 135 to 140 for the Student List. The student movement emerged after 16 people were killed when a train station canopy collapsed in the city of Novi Sad on November 1, 2024.
audit.body: Aleksandar Vucic, who has shaped Serbia’s political life for more than a decade, has lost snap Parliamentary Elections to a student-led movement that led protests against him for almost two years. After a heated race, Vucic conceded defeat to the Student List in Sunday’s elections, which saw voter turnout reach its highest level in more than 30 years. “It is clear that we have lost these elections,” the leader of the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) told supporters after a sample of votes showed his electoral list was expected to win 105 seats in Serbia’s 250-member Parliament, compared with 135 to 140 for the Student List. The student movement emerged after 16 people were killed when a train station canopy collapsed in the city of Novi Sad on November 1, 2024. The youth-led protests grew into a broader wave of social unrest and evolved into the Student List political platform, which promised to tackle corruption, depoliticise public institutions and restore citizens’ rights. During the election campaign, the movement was led by Ilija Srdanovic, a professor at the Faculty of Medicine in Novi Sad. Vucic referred to the demonstrators, who included university professors, doctors and workers, as “blockaders” and accused them of seeking to destabilise Serbia. A former ultranationalist, Vucic cultivated an image of a pragmatic leader who maintained ties with the European Union, Russia and China as well as, increasingly, with Israel in recent years. (Aljazeera)

audit.headline: Finalist Pakistan to block Lanka’s ‘safe passage’ to Final
audit.summary: After a successful run chase against England last week at Rawalpindi, Sri Lanka will meet Pakistan once again at Lahore Gaddafi Stadium today in the fifth match of the ODI Tri-Nation Series. Pakistan pulled off a stunning one-wicket win over England at the Gaddafi Stadium on Sunday to enter the final of the Tri-Nation ODI Series, with a match in hand. In the meantime Sri Lanka with a superb win over England after a memorable run chase of 430 looking to beat Pakistan today. The last Pakistan – England game turned out to be a thriller. Pakistan chasing a target of 242 were struggling at 154 for 9 wickets but last wicket pair Sadab Khan and Haris Rauf added fighting unbeaten 89 runs stand which brought them a thrilling one wicket win. Sadab’s maiden century paved the way for them to victory with 17 balls to spare.
audit.body: After a successful run chase against England last week at Rawalpindi, Sri Lanka will meet Pakistan once again at Lahore Gaddafi Stadium today in the fifth match of the ODI Tri-Nation Series. Pakistan pulled off a stunning one-wicket win over England at the Gaddafi Stadium on Sunday to enter the final of the Tri-Nation ODI Series, with a match in hand. In the meantime Sri Lanka with a superb win over England after a memorable run chase of 430 looking to beat Pakistan today. The last Pakistan – England game turned out to be a thriller. Pakistan chasing a target of 242 were struggling at 154 for 9 wickets but last wicket pair Sadab Khan and Haris Rauf added fighting unbeaten 89 runs stand which brought them a thrilling one wicket win. Sadab’s maiden century paved the way for them to victory with 17 balls to spare. Back to back wins over Sri Lanka and England will surely boost confidence in the host team and they will try out their best to beat Sri Lanka today. Sri Lankan team led by Kusal Mendis already proved their batting power and the team has good confidence after successful run chase against England. Kamindu Mendis, Avishka Fernando, Pavan Ratnayake, Dasun Shanaka and Janith Liyanage were among the runs to chase their record victory and Sri Lanka team is all out to maintain their momentum against Pakistan. The two teams, Pakistan and Sri Lanka met each other in the opening game earlier at Rawalpindi and Pakistan won the game by 37 runs. Pakistan made 305 and Sri Lankan were heading for the victory after Janith Liyanage and Pavan Ratnayaka made 119 runs fifth wicket stand but Pakistan bowlers fought back strongly to get last five wickets in quick session to gain victory. Poor shot selection was the main issue for Sri Lanka’s defeat in this game. Sri Lankan middle order is more stable now as Pavan, Janith and Dasun are in good form. Their consistent performances will play a key role in today’s match against hosts. Avishka Fernando is once again back in the side and he has scored 97 to make a good start in the last game. Kamindu Mendis, the experienced left hander is also capable of making a good start during the Power Play. The young right hander Pavan Ratanayake has shown his consistent performance with a superb knock of 130 in previous game while Dasun Shanaka has shown his power hitting ability. Janith Liyanage put the finishing touches as expected to make success and these are good positives in Sri Lankan team’s World Cup journey. However Sri Lanka frequently enters ODI matches with only four front line bowlers, covering the remaining 10-over quota with all-rounders and part-time options such as Dasun Shanka, Janith Liyanage and Kamindu Mendis. These three bowlers conceded 123 runs in their 10 overs and this is a major issue to cover the middle overs. Sri Lankan team management has more concern about this issue. The opening bowlers make decent job to build up pressure on top order batters but conceding more runs in middle overs always compel to lose the control towards final stage of the innings. The young leg spinner Dunith Wellalage so far did a decent job and he has the ability to get early wickets. Meanwhile Pakistan led by Saheen Afridi is looking to make few changes as they have already qualified for the final. This is a good opportunity to test their other players before the final game which will be played on October 31. Minhas did his best to take six wickets in their first England game while skipper Afridi had 4-wicket haul in previous England game. Pakistan have a strong bowling line up and expected to come up with a good attack once again. The leg spinner Abrar Ahamed still not get a chance to play a single game and likely to get his place today. Pakistan opener Saim Ayub has been released from their ODI squad during this ongoing Tri-Nation series while Sahibzada Farhan was named as his replacement. It was confirmed by PCB yesterday. The 24-year-old Ayub requested his release following Pakistan’s thrilling one wicket win over England on Sunday expressing his desire to return to domestic cricket and regain his batting form. Th left handed opener Ayub has endured a difficult campaign in this series managing just 21 runs across three matches. In addition left-arm wrist spinner Sufiyan Moqim has been released from the Pakistan ODI squad in view of the nature of the pitches in Lahore. According to the team management, the decision has been taken after assessing the conditions on offer at the Gaddafi Stadium, which are not expected to assist wrist spin in the upcoming matches. Left-handed batter Maaz Sadaqat has been added to the squad as cover for players carrying minor niggles, the PCB stated.

audit.headline: National purpose beyond the classroom
audit.summary: S ri Lanka has a history of shifting governments but failing to reform the underlying systems that influence its long-term economic and social development. Among these systems, education is particularly critical, but it can be difficult to elevate the discourse on educational reforms, above the fray of daily politics. Postponing the implementation of the new Grade 6 Education reforms, which was planned for 2026, and is now scheduled for 2027, provides an opportunity to consider what kind of people Sri Lanka’s education system should create to foster over the next 5-10 years, and what kind of economy it should sustain? There is now a clearer timeline with the new government’s policy to review the curriculum for Grade 1 in 2026 and Grades 2 and 6 in 2027.
audit.body: S ri Lanka has a history of shifting governments but failing to reform the underlying systems that influence its long-term economic and social development. Among these systems, education is particularly critical, but it can be difficult to elevate the discourse on educational reforms, above the fray of daily politics. Postponing the implementation of the new Grade 6 Education reforms, which was planned for 2026, and is now scheduled for 2027, provides an opportunity to consider what kind of people Sri Lanka’s education system should create to foster over the next 5-10 years, and what kind of economy it should sustain? There is now a clearer timeline with the new government’s policy to review the curriculum for Grade 1 in 2026 and Grades 2 and 6 in 2027. But a timeline is not a strategy and the more important consideration is whether we can conduct a sustained meaningful discussion on the principles and values which should underpin the reforms. A debate beyond the classroom Discussions on education reform commonly focus on effects on students, teachers and parents. In fact, consequences of education reforms impact nearly all the households, businesses and organisations in a country. Consider the professionals, entrepreneurs, employees and managers in the private and public sectors who keep the economy of a country like Sri Lanka running. They may not always engage in public debates on the design of school curricula. However, the outcome surely impacts them. They hire and fire graduates, manage businesses and compete in the global marketplace. For them, education reform shapes the quality of employees, the cost of training and the capacity to innovate and improve the competitiveness of Sri Lankan businesses in the global marketplace. There is a recognised and growing need among professional and middle-class families to provide children with an education that gives the flexibility and practical skills to keep up with a changing world. Reform is not the preserve of the middle class. Rural communities and the economically disadvantaged also have a need for a high-quality education that helps children develop intellectually. Every child regardless of his/her socio-economic class, family income or living condition is deserving of potential development. The challenge is to channel these aspirations for a National Purpose. Preparing the workforce Sri Lanka needs Students will enter the job market, vocational training and higher education in Sri Lanka in the next 5-8 years. The skills they acquire will eventually shape Sri Lanka’s workforce during the country’s major economic transformation. The local economy cannot rely on low-productivity jobs for long and assume that students automatically become employable upon completion of their education. Businesses want a workforce with advanced communication and digital skills as well as the ability to quickly learn and adapt to new ways of working. The same is true for manufacturing, tourism and other related sectors and services. Continuous innovation and evolution in technology bring about major changes in industries. Automation and Artificial Intelligence have dramatically changed the way businesses operate. While there is a heightened emphasis in academic institutions to prepare students for a challenging, job-ready world, many teaching methods focus on memorising and regurgitating rather than encouraging critical thinking and understanding. Students must learn to think critically, be logically inferential and enthusiastically imaginative and creatively productive to develop ideas and solutions to problems. Learning outcomes must foster the ability to think and do things that remain valuable throughout one’s life and beyond. Genuine academic reforms must be able to assess the impact students have on improving their ability to enhance and enrich our society. Ultimately reforms must be gauged by how effectively students learn to achieve meaningful results that are valuable and relevant for the rest of their lives. Sri Lanka places importance on examinations as the pathway to opportunity. Many have strong feelings regarding the Grade 5 Scholarship Examination and G.C.E. Ordinary and Advanced Level Examinations. These feelings stem from the value people place on education and the significance of social mobility. While the functions of examinations are many, the key here is the identification of scholarly ability. Examinations should be part of a more comprehensive system that provides different avenues and identifies a broad array of skills. Students who are more skilled in fields such as technology, design, agriculture, engineering, the hospitality industry and trades should have alternative pathways to ensure their development as well as to promote those other paths, particularly in school. This is equally important for academically gifted students. They should likewise be encouraged to develop their communication skills, leadership and practical skills in problem solving. It is important that schools forge stronger partnerships with employers and universities and vocational education institutions. This is critical to serve the changing needs of the economy and societal expectations and provide the right breadth of skills. Vocational education and training should provide pathways to decent employment and entrepreneurship opportunities and further education and training. A country that promotes only a narrow range of academic achievements will fail to identify and harness a broad range of its human potential. Skilled migration as an economic opportunity Education requires urgent reforms due to its close links with global employment opportunities. Migrant workers in the Middle East make a major contribution to household incomes and foreign-exchange earnings in Sri Lanka. Their work should be recognized and valued. Meanwhile, Sri Lanka should also explore other avenues for its skilled and professional workers. Many Sri Lankans work as nurses, engineers and information technology specialists overseas. Employment in these fields abroad pays much better and can increase remittances. We must stop “exporting” young people at the expense of national employment. All Sri Lankans should be given the opportunity to pursue a decent and satisfying life and career in Sri Lanka or abroad. This is especially relevant for young people, who should be offered educational, technical and vocational training to build a strong foundation for a more advanced and relevant profession. The foundations of proficiency in a field take time and cannot be developed over a short period of time. The educational choices we make today will, in the long run, define the capacity of the Sri Lankan workforce to gain international employment, and the kinds of opportunities the workforce will have to compete and thrive in the world economy. Why the postponement should renew the debate The reforms for Grade 6 have been postponed over concerns about the English language learning module. Among other issues, an inappropriate web link was found. These demonstrate meaningful concerns on the quality of the materials, and where issues are raised, the teachers and parents, of course the children, deserve a reasonable preparation and communication. Let’s hope that real reforms will happen through an inclusive process with teachers, parents, and other stakeholders in education. The key, however, is to hold someone accountable, and perhaps the public will develop confidence in the process not because they were promised a flawless system, but because improvements and corrections were communicated. Reform must outlast political cycles Education reforms are susceptible to political discontinuity. There is often a disjuncture between the length of time required to create, implement and evaluate a new curriculum and the length of time a political administration is in power. The result is that the debate around education reform often lags with the political changes, and students become the unintended, but inevitable, casualties of political uncertainty. What Sri Lanka needs is a well-crafted national policy framework coupled with an inclusive, multi-sectoral, professional and evidence-based approach. Changes to policy should be undertaken on the basis of evidence and their consequences properly assessed. It is necessary to improve curriculum, teaching and learning, educational facilities, teaching and learning materials, and assessment systems and public awareness in tandem. Without adequately training teachers to update their knowledge and skills, the benefits of a reformed curriculum will not be realised. The same holds true for new methods of assessment. Ultimately, policies must facilitate the learning of students, and the question must be asked: Are students improving their ability to read and do mathematics? Are students becoming better and more confident communicators? Are disparities between schools narrowing? Are graduates better prepared for higher education, vocational training and employment? These questions should shape public reporting and future policy adjustments. This is the time to keep education in focus Of course, Sri Lankans are concerned with the economy, public finances, employment and cost of living. All in all, Education is the foundation of all these. Our education system must enable greater productivity and a larger pool of skilled employees. A failing education system will only exacerbate the divide and stagnate opportunities. We need a converhed effort from all stakeholders to make education reform a national priority. While educators have the primary responsibility for nurturing and developing young people, entrepreneurs and professionals must also play an active role in shaping their future. By working together to develop innovative, skilled and productive youth, we can strengthen Sri Lanka’s economy and create sustainable opportunities for the next generation. The Class 6 reforms have been pushed to 2027. That shouldn’t stop us from having the National debate. We need to expand the workforce that can build industries and create high-income jobs, improve public services and integrate breakthrough technologies. These require education reforms that are implemented consistently. Such reforms are usually only conducted during times of crisis. However, during recent discussions on the recovery and growth of Sri Lanka, reform of Education ought to have had a prime place. The real question is are we ready to build the next generation of Sri Lankans to improve productivity, prosperity and contribution of Sri Lanka on the world stage? This will be seen in course of time.

audit.headline: Cheap aluminium utensils among sources of lead poisoning in South Asia
audit.summary: T he International Lead Poisoning Prevention Week (ILPPW) is observed every year in the third week of October. The World Health Organisation (WHO) identifies lead as one of ten chemicals of major public health concern that require action by Member States to protect the health of workers, children, and women of reproductive age. WHO’s latest estimates indicate that nearly half of the two million lives lost to known chemical exposures in 2019 were due to lead poisoning. Lead exposure was also estimated to account for 21.7 million years lost to disability (disability-adjusted life years, or DALYs) worldwide that year. This included 30% of the global burden of idiopathic intellectual disability, 4.6% of the global burden of cardiovascular disease, and 3.0% of the global burden of chronic kidney disease.
audit.body: T he International Lead Poisoning Prevention Week (ILPPW) is observed every year in the third week of October. The World Health Organisation (WHO) identifies lead as one of ten chemicals of major public health concern that require action by Member States to protect the health of workers, children, and women of reproductive age.
