WHO’s latest estimates indicate that nearly half of the two million lives lost to known chemical exposures in 2019 were due to lead poisoning. Lead exposure was also estimated to account for 21.7 million years lost to disability (disability-adjusted life years, or DALYs) worldwide that year. This included 30% of the global burden of idiopathic intellectual disability, 4.6% of the global burden of cardiovascular disease, and 3.0% of the global burden of chronic kidney disease. WHO estimates that lead exposure contributed to more than 3.5 million deaths worldwide in 2023, largely through cardiovascular effects. Chronic lead exposure is a recognised cause of anaemia in children and contributes to delayed growth and stunting. Children experience far greater harm from lead than adults. They can absorb four to five times more lead and face higher exposure risk through age-related behaviours such as hand-to-mouth contact with contaminated objects, soil, or paint chips. Common pathways include toys, deteriorated paint in homes and playgrounds, and contaminated soil. There is no known safe level of lead. Once absorbed through the digestive tract, it is stored in teeth and bones and continuously released into the bloodstream. Blood concentrations as low as 3.5 µg/dL have been linked to decreased intelligence in children (WHO, 2021). A 2020 UNICEF assessment estimated that almost one in three children globally may have experienced blood lead levels of 5 µg/dL or higher at some point in their development. In 2020, UNICEF and the New York-based organisation “Pure Earth” estimated that around 800 million children worldwide had blood lead levels above 5 µg/dL. Nearly half of these children lived in South Asia. Of the 800 million, India accounted for an estimated 275.6 million children, Pakistan for 41.1 million, and Bangladesh for 35.5 million. A 2025 systematic review of 51 studies estimated a pooled mean blood lead level of 10.4 µg/dL among Indian children as a whole; even those without known high-risk exposure averaged 8.71 µg/dL. The neurological and behavioural effects of lead are considered irreversible. Long-term consequences include lower IQ, attention deficits, and reduced academic performance. MRI studies following children into adulthood have linked higher childhood lead levels to reduced grey matter. Some analyses have associated higher childhood exposure with elevated arrest rates, including for violent crime. A 2025 review of 43 human epidemiological studies and 37 animal studies concluded that the evidence indicates a “likely causal association” between lead exposure and antisocial behaviour. The Insidious Nature of Lead Lead does not announce its presence. It has no distinctive smell or visible warning. It cannot be detected simply by looking at a plate of rice, a child’s toy, or a shiny aluminium cooking pot. It can persist quietly in soil, dust, paint, spices, cookware, and cosmetics. It can travel home from a battery-recycling workshop on a worker’s clothes. Once inside a child’s body, it interferes with brain development. Since the phase-out of leaded petrol, food, spices, vegetables, rice, contaminated air, and consumer products have become the primary pathways of exposure. A comprehensive review published in 2025, covering Bangladesh, Nepal, Sri Lanka, India, and Pakistan, found that blood lead concentrations across South Asia frequently exceeded the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) reference value of 3.5 µg/dL. Bangladesh is estimated to have more than 1,100 informal or illegal used-lead-acid-battery recycling operations (UNEP assessment). Backyard smelting contaminates surrounding soil, dust, and air, and workers can carry lead home on their clothing. Some Bangladeshi turmeric processors have been found adding lead chromate, an industrial yellow pigment, to brighten inferior turmeric. A 2019 investigation detected the practice in seven of nine major turmeric-producing districts, with some samples exceeding the national lead limit by up to 500 times. Pure Earth’s Rapid Market Screening In 2021, the New York-based “Pure Earth” launched a project to analyse lead contamination in thousands of products and food samples from markets across 25 low- and middle-income countries. The Rapid Market Screening covered Armenia, Azerbaijan, Bangladesh, Bolivia, Colombia, Egypt, Georgia, Ghana, the Indian states of Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu and Uttar Pradesh, Indonesia, Kazakhstan, Kenya, Kyrgyzstan, Mexico, Nepal, Nigeria, Pakistan, Peru, the Philippines, Tajikistan, Tanzania, Tunisia, Türkiye, Uganda, and Vietnam. Items were tested on site for lead above 2 ppm using X-ray fluorescence analysers, with a subset verified in the United States by inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry. Results were compared against established regulatory thresholds. Across 5,007 samples, 18% exceeded relevant reference levels. The product categories that most frequently breached public-health or regulatory limits were metal utensils (51% exceeded 100 ppm), ceramics (45% exceeded 100 ppm), and paints (41% exceeded 90 ppm). Between April and June 2024, Pure Earth, working with local authorities and private educational institutions, conducted a pilot study in Tamil Nadu to assess lead in metal cookware used for school meals. Fifty-eight items from ten schools across six districts (Thiruvallur, Thoothukudi, Tenkasi, Virudhunagar, Thanjavur, and Kanyakumari) were tested with portable X-ray fluorescence technology. More than half (51.7%) were wide, open containers commonly used to cook large quantities of rice and curry. The average lead concentration across all items was 1,604 ppm; 98% exceeded the 500 ppm reference value. Although cooked food samples did not show detectable lead, the presence of lead in the cookware itself was a clear concern. Worn aluminium pots at one school in Virudhunagar had been in use for years and were likely leaching lead into meals. Contaminated aluminium cookware was subsequently replaced with SS304-grade stainless steel. Brochures explaining the risks and Pure Earth’s work were distributed, and some institutions received additional support to improve overall safety for students. A May 2025 government–UNICEF study of more than 2,100 toddlers in high-risk areas of seven cities found elevated lead exposure in roughly four out of ten children. In Hattar, Haripur, the figure reached 88%. UNICEF modelling suggests that as many as eight in ten Pakistani children could be affected—one of the highest proportions globally—though a nationally representative survey is still needed. The latest nationally representative data from Bangladesh are stark. The Bangladesh Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey 2025, conducted by the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics with UNICEF, tested around 11,000 children aged 12–59 months. It found that 38.4% had blood lead levels of at least 5 µg/dL (mean 5.21 µg/dL). Among pregnant women, 7.5% exceeded the same threshold. Lead has also been detected in paints, ceramics, toys, cosmetics, and recycled-metal cookware. A Pure Earth market survey in Bangladesh found it across nine categories of consumer products. Traditional eye cosmetics such as surma and kajal have shown extremely high readings in international investigations, and research confirms that recycled aluminium and brass cookware made in the region can leach lead. Sri Lanka, a Bright Spot Against this background, Sri Lanka is a bright spot. WHO notes that Sri Lanka has taken regulatory measures since 2013. Paint regulations limit lead to a maximum of 600 ppm (90 mg/kg for paints used on toys and children’s accessories). The national drinking-water standard for lead is 10 µg/L, aligned with the WHO provisional guideline. An environmental protection licensing system covers emissions and disposal of lead-containing waste such as batteries and electronic equipment. Lead remains a silent, pervasive threat. Addressing it requires continued vigilance across food systems, consumer products, informal recycling, and cookware—especially the aluminium vessels still widely used in institutional kitchens across South Asia.

audit.headline: Brazil’s Lula wins re-election with victory over Trump ally Bolsonaro
audit.summary: Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva was re-elected to a historic fourth term on Sunday, but his defeated rival and Trump ally Senator Flávio Bolsonaro said he would not accept the results and would mount a legal challenge. The 80-year-old leftist leader won more than 51% of votes, securing a runoff victory that bucks a broader rightward political shift across Latin America and comes after a campaign dominated by concerns over the Cost of Living, crime and corruption. Bolsonaro, who trailed Lula by about 4.4 million votes, said his team would challenge the result after the Supreme Court’s last-minute ruling to extend voting by two hours. “It is impossible to recognise the election result given how these events unfolded,” Bolsonaro told supporters in the capital Brasilia after Lula’s victory was declared. “We will take legal action.
audit.body: Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva was re-elected to a historic fourth term on Sunday, but his defeated rival and Trump ally Senator Flávio Bolsonaro said he would not accept the results and would mount a legal challenge. The 80-year-old leftist leader won more than 51% of votes, securing a runoff victory that bucks a broader rightward political shift across Latin America and comes after a campaign dominated by concerns over the Cost of Living, crime and corruption. Bolsonaro, who trailed Lula by about 4.4 million votes, said his team would challenge the result after the Supreme Court’s last-minute ruling to extend voting by two hours. “It is impossible to recognise the election result given how these events unfolded,” Bolsonaro told supporters in the capital Brasilia after Lula’s victory was declared. “We will take legal action. We will ask for this election to be annulled.” The vote marks the first time since the return of direct Presidential Elections in 1989 that a candidate has won the presidency after finishing second in the first round. “I can assure you that we are going to change the way we govern this country. We are going to give the people a greater role in our decisions,” Lula said after his re-election. Lula thanked the Brazilian people for their “generosity,” especially the country’s youth who “took to the streets to defend democracy.” In Rio de Janeiro, Lula’s supporters were seen hugging, beeping their car horns and raising the “L” sign. And in Belo Horizonte, capital of the key swing state Minas Gerais, supporters could be seen chanting and singing following Lula’s victory. Lula’s win is a major setback for the Bolsonaro political movement, with Flávio failing to accomplish what his father, imprisoned former President Jair Bolsonaro, also couldn’t to do in 2022: defeat Lula at the ballot box. But the results came after a turbulent election day, with voting being extended by two hours following last-minute pleas from both candidates to electoral authorities. (CNN)

audit.headline: A vision for SriLankan Airlines
audit.summary: SriLankan Airlines has spent far too long being treated as a national asset whose losses can be excused in the name of tourism, connectivity and national pride. That approach has failed taxpayers, drained public resources and allowed the airline to operate without the commercial discipline expected of a sustainable business. If the national carrier is to have a future, its first priority must be to become profitable. Everything else must follow from that objective. Recent reports that SriLankan Airlines is exploring opportunities to expand its network to Perth, China and Africa have once again raised questions about the airline’s strategic direction. The newly appointed CEO of the airline has argued that the airline must take the lead in developing routes that support Sri Lanka’s tourism industry, including destinations other airlines might initially consider commercially unattractive.
audit.body: SriLankan Airlines has spent far too long being treated as a national asset whose losses can be excused in the name of tourism, connectivity and national pride. That approach has failed taxpayers, drained public resources and allowed the airline to operate without the commercial discipline expected of a sustainable business. If the national carrier is to have a future, its first priority must be to become profitable. Everything else must follow from that objective. Recent reports that SriLankan Airlines is exploring opportunities to expand its network to Perth, China and Africa have once again raised questions about the airline’s strategic direction. The newly appointed CEO of the airline has argued that the airline must take the lead in developing routes that support Sri Lanka’s tourism industry, including destinations other airlines might initially consider commercially unattractive. The argument sounds attractive on the surface. More flights could bring more visitors, stimulate economic activity and strengthen Sri Lanka’s international connections. But it also reveals the fundamental confusion that has plagued the national carrier for years. Is SriLankan Airlines a commercial enterprise, or is it an instrument of government tourism policy? The distinction matters because SriLankan Airlines is not an independent business operating with unlimited capital. Its losses ultimately burden the Treasury, diverting public money from healthcare, education, infrastructure and other essential services. Every rupee used to sustain an unprofitable route is a rupee that must be justified to taxpayers. Tourism is undoubtedly vital to Sri Lanka’s economy. But developing tourism is not the airline’s primary responsibility. Its responsibility is to operate a viable airline, generate revenue, control costs and deliver a return on the capital invested in it. Tourism promotion can be a welcome secondary benefit, but it cannot serve as a permanent excuse for commercial failure. If the government believes that a particular route is essential to national tourism policy despite being commercially unviable, it should make that decision transparently and establish whether the wider economic benefits justify the cost. The airline should not be expected to conceal the price of public policy within its operating losses. The first task, therefore, is to establish a clear commercial strategy. SriLankan Airlines must determine what kind of carrier it can realistically become, given its finances, fleet, competitive position and access to markets. Can SriLankan be a smaller regional carrier connecting selected destinations? Can the airline profitably sustain a broader international network? Which routes generate adequate returns, and which merely consume scarce resources? These questions require evidence, not ambition. Expansion into Perth, China or Africa should proceed only where rigorous commercial assessments demonstrate a credible path to profitability. Opening a route simply because it might attract tourists is not a strategy. It is a gamble with public money. The airline must also examine its ancillary businesses. Ground handling, catering, cargo and aircraft engineering may offer opportunities to generate independent revenue and improve operational efficiency. These activities should have transparent accounts, measurable performance targets and clear management responsibilities. Where practical, their performance should be assessed separately so that profitable operations are not obscured by losses elsewhere. Any restructuring must, of course, account for shared costs and operational dependencies. Once SriLankan Airlines has demonstrated sustained operational improvement, the government should seriously consider strategic partnerships with credible international aviation companies. Such partnerships could bring capital, technical expertise, management discipline and access to wider commercial networks. But partners will be difficult to attract on favourable terms if the airline remains burdened by political interference and an unclear business model. Ultimately, SriLankan Airlines needs a strategic vision that survives changes of government. That vision must identify its core markets, define its competitive advantage, establish realistic financial targets and hold management accountable for results. National pride cannot be measured by the number of destinations on a route map. Nor can the value of a national carrier be judged by the flag painted on its aircraft. SriLankan Airlines deserves the opportunity to recover. But recovery requires an end to the comfortable assumption that taxpayers will always pay for its failures. The airline must learn to fly on its own wings and prove that it can do so profitably.

audit.headline: Minister highlights new investment opportunities ahead of SL EXPO 2027
audit.summary: Sri Lanka made a direct pitch to British investors at a special Business and Investment Forum in London, presenting the island as a stable, reform-driven economy ready for deeper partnership with the United Kingdom. Held under the patronage of Trade Minister Wasantha Samarasinghe, the forum drew business leaders, investors and industry representatives from both countries. Sri Lanka’s delegation included High Commissioner Nimal Senadheera, UK Trade Envoy Lord Hannett, Ministry of Industry and Entrepreneurship Development Secretary Thilaka Jayasundara, EDB Chairman/CEO Mangala Wijesinghe and Board of Investment (BOI) representatives.
audit.body: Sri Lanka made a direct pitch to British investors at a special Business and Investment Forum in London, presenting the island as a stable, reform-driven economy ready for deeper partnership with the United Kingdom. Held under the patronage of Trade Minister Wasantha Samarasinghe, the forum drew business leaders, investors and industry representatives from both countries. Sri Lanka’s delegation included High Commissioner Nimal Senadheera, UK Trade Envoy Lord Hannett, Ministry of Industry and Entrepreneurship Development Secretary Thilaka Jayasundara, EDB Chairman/CEO Mangala Wijesinghe and Board of Investment (BOI) representatives. Strong participation from British firms in IT, real estate, energy and food processing, the Minister said, “Clearly reflects their keen interest in expanding trade and investment cooperation with Sri Lanka,” He noted that the UK is among Sri Lanka’s most important trading partners and its third-largest export market. British investment reached US$1.73 billion by 2025, creating nearly 22,000 jobs. The UK is also Sri Lanka’s second-largest tourism source, sending more than 212,000 of the 2.3 million visitors in 2025. Samarasinghe credited a reform programme, implemented closely with the International Monetary Fund, with restoring macroeconomic stability, rebuilding foreign reserves and boosting confidence. The economy grew by 5% in both 2024 and 2025, while total goods and services export revenue climbed to US$17.3 billion in 2025. Investors were assured that a predictable, transparent business climate is a government priority. Regulations have been simplified, public service efficiency improved, and the BOI is providing necessary facilities to investors. “The government is ready to directly discuss the problems and needs of British businessmen,” the Minister said, openly inviting partnerships that would expand manufacturing capacity and create jobs. He expressed confidence that the relationships formed in London would “Develop into long-term partnerships for the common prosperity of both countries.” British investors were also formally invited to Sri Lanka EXPO 2027, the international exhibition to be held in Colombo in January 2027.

audit.headline: Mango Tree test of Arahat Mahinda
audit.summary: Before preaching Buddhism to King Devanampiya Tissa, Arahant Mahinda used a logical puzzle — often described as the world’s first recorded intelligence or wisdom test — based on a mango tree to check if the king had the intellectual capacity to understand the Dhamma - Modern daydream of an ancient envoy's return Age and a frail heart keep me confined to my home, yet an alert mind keeps me voraciously curious. Two private TV channels—both epitomising the vulgarity of free-market capitalism—keep me updated on the Sangha mischief in our public square. Pensive in my armchair, far removed from the calibrated, boorish ‘Bana’ at the Satyagraha sit-in at Viharamahadevi Park, my mind drifted into a desperate daydream. I closed my eyes and wondered: What if?
audit.body: Before preaching Buddhism to King Devanampiya Tissa, Arahant Mahinda used a logical puzzle — often described as the world’s first recorded intelligence or wisdom test — based on a mango tree to check if the king had the intellectual capacity to understand the Dhamma - Modern daydream of an ancient envoy's return Age and a frail heart keep me confined to my home, yet an alert mind keeps me voraciously curious. Two private TV channels—both epitomising the vulgarity of free-market capitalism—keep me updated on the Sangha mischief in our public square. Pensive in my armchair, far removed from the calibrated, boorish ‘Bana’ at the Satyagraha sit-in at Viharamahadevi Park, my mind drifted into a desperate daydream. I closed my eyes and wondered: What if? What if the time warp separating antiquity from today’s chaos were ripped open, and Arahat Mahinda Thero himself stepped out of the third century BC and onto the soil of twenty-first-century Sri Lanka? What if the legendary missionary son of Dharmasoka walked among us today, only to find that his pristine, liberating message of the Buddha had been weaponised, commodified, and reduced to pageantry and ritual, making the cry of ‹Sadhu’ an agitational refrains of hired hooligans? It was a mind-boggling possibility: the architect of Sinhala Buddhism surveying how a capricious, power-hungry priestly class had traded the profound logic of the Mihintale mango tree for luxury SUVs, political contracts, and televised circuses. In this mental theater, the ancient sage Arahat Mahinda had come to interrogate, wielding the sharp intellect that once founded a nation to utterly dismantle the pious fraud of its modern guardians. Arahat Mahinda Thero stood at the Satyagraha protest site. Under a canvas canopy, a group of saffron-clad figures sat in a single row, striking poses of deep, meditative exhaustion for a cluster of television cameras. This was the grand satyagraha, orchestrated at the behest of a defunct political dynasty whose members are currently adrift, desperate to reclaim their lost turf. Shrouded in simple, earth-toned robes, my imaginary Arahat Mahinda stepped straight out of the third century BC and into the chaotic theater of this modern political circus. He had no entourage, no media coordinator to assist him; he walked directly to the enclosure where the main architects of this spectacle sat. The test There sat Ulapane Sumangala, adjusting his microphone with practiced ease; Balangoda Kassapa, frantically checking his smartphone under the fold of his robe to see if his latest TikTok live-stream was trending; and Walanhanduwe Dharmaratna, the High Priest of Mihintale, looking noticeably uncomfortable so far from his mountain rock sanctuary and so close to actual public scrutiny. The trio blinked, squinting through the camera glare. There was something terrifyingly authentic, something fiercely primordial about the visitor that rendered their haughty air of entitlement suddenly very fragile. Hoping to capture a viral moment of monastic solidarity, Ulapane Sumangala cleared his throat, assumed a pose of pious pain, and bellowed into the microphone: “Welcome, Most Venerable Arahath Therun-wahanse, to our sacred struggle!” The transient political circuses built by greed are nothing more than passing shadows on the ever-changing landscape of time. They do not define our beautiful island, nor can they ever truly compromise the pristine core of the Dhamma. For twenty-three centuries, the true light brought by Arahat Mahinda has endured—not through golden fences, luxurious pageants, or the patronage of powerful politicians, but because the pristine Dhamma resides quietly and immovably within the hearts of ordinary, virtuous people Sumangala proclaimed, his voice booming through the speakers: “We sit here in noble sacrifice to save our nation, our heritage, and our Sasana from the treacherous hands of those who demand accountability and transparency!” The imaginary Arahat Mahinda looked at the elaborate sound system, the stock of bottled mineral water tucked behind the cushions on which the ‹Satyagrahis› sat, and the fleet of SUVs parked on the roadside behind the marquee. A faint, razor-sharp smile touched his lips. He did not recite a stanza, nor did he offer a conventional blessing. Instead, he pointed a calm, steady finger toward a large, leafy tree standing nearby.” “Monks,” Arahat Mahinda said, his voice carrying a thunderous, resonant clarity that dwarfed the loudspeakers. “What tree is that?” he intoned. Monk Walanhanduwe Dharmaratna, recognising the opening lines of the famous logic test that his own monastic perch had on our free-market economy, perked up. He saw an immediate opportunity to demonstrate his scriptural authority. “That, Most Venerable One, is a mango tree.” “Are there other mango trees besides this one?” Arahat Mahinda inquired, his demeanor glistening with sharp, deductive intensity. Age and a frail heart keep me confined to my home, yet an alert mind keeps me voraciously curious. “Yes, Most Venerable Arahath Therun-wahanse,” Balangoda Kassapa chimed in, eager to display his intellect to his digital followers. “There are many other mango trees in this park, and indeed, across the entire island.” “And are there trees here that are not mango trees?” asked Arahat, his voice tightening like a bowstring. “Of course, of course!” Ulapane Sumangala joined the fray, sensing a rhetorical victory. “There are Mara trees, Na trees, and many majestic banyans. There are countless trees that are not mango trees.” Arahat Mahinda paused. A sudden, dramatic silence overwhelmed the entire park. The wind ceased to blow. The birds stopped chirping. Then he leaned forward, his gaze flashing like lightning: “Apart from those other mango trees, and the trees that are not mango trees, does this specific mango tree itself remain?›” “Naturally, Venerable Sir!” Monk Walanhanduwe Dharmaratna answered confidently. “If you set aside all other mango trees and all non-mango trees, this solitary tree still stands right where it is. It is elementary!” responded the Mihintale custodian. Arahat Mahinda’s face hardened, shifting from calm inquisitor to Cosmic Arbiter. “An excellent grasp of basic botany. Now, let us apply this same rigorous line of reasoning to the political forest you have planted here today. Tell me, Sumangala, who are the people currently funding, supplying, and cheering for this noble satyagraha of yours?” Sumangala puffed out his chest, adopting a fiercely theatrical posture. “These are the righteous guardians of the old order, Sir! The visionary leaders who built great expressways, the generous patrons who gave us unchecked power, and the elite statesmen currently unjustly sidelined by the ungrateful masses!” “I see,” Arahat Mahinda, the Ashokan envoy, replied smoothly, his tone dripping with sarcasm. “And are there other corrupt, discredited politicians in this country besides the ones who paid for your tents, your cheer squads, and your ears today?” Kassapa shifted uneasily, his phone buzzing violently in his palm as the live comments started flying in. “Well... yes. History is full of them. There are many political opportunists across the land who have plundered the public purse.” “And are there people in this country who are not corrupt, discredited politicians?” Arahat pressed further, his voice rising to a crescendo. Portly Monk Walanhanduwe Dharmaratna coughed into his hand, looking nervously at the cameras that were now capturing his sudden panic. “Yes, technically. The vast majority of the citizenry are ordinary, hardworking people who simply wish to live in peace, feed their children, and see justice prevail.” The imaginary Arahat Mahinda of my daydream stepped onto the stage, his presence making the Satyagraha space feel suffocatingly small. ‘Then tell me, wise monks,’ Arahat Mahinda roared, his authoritative voice shaking the very poles of the makeshift tent. ‘If we set aside all those other corrupt politicians roaming elsewhere, and if we set aside the entire population of honest, hardworking citizens who want nothing to do with your theater... who is left sitting under this tent?!’” “An absolute, terrifying silence stilled the air. Television cameras zoomed in on the sweat breaking out on Sumangala’s brow. Arahat Mahinda’s deductive trap had snapped shut with the force of a steel jaw. By their own logic, the only entities remaining in the equation were the handful of compromised oligarchs pulling their strings, and the monks who consented to act as their spiritual human shields. ‘You see,’ Arahat Mahinda continued, his voice dropping to a devastatingly sharp whisper that cut deeper than a blade, “Twenty-three centuries ago, I used this very riddle to ensure that a king possessed the logical capacity to govern for the welfare of all living beings. I taught him that the land belongs to the people, and that the ruler is merely its temporary guardian. But you three have completely inverted Dhamma! You have become the vanguard of brazen rogues, using the sacred robes of the Enlightened One to protect the hordes of the greedy!›” “Venerable Sir!” Walanhanduwe protested, his face turning an angry shade of crimson as he clutched his relic casket for comfort. “We are protecting our traditional privileges! If the elite fall, who will sponsor our grand pageants? Who will build our golden fences? Who will pay for our luxury hybrid SUVs?!” “The Dhamma does not require a golden fence built with stolen public funds!” the resonant voice of the Arahat replied, firm as the Mihintale rock. “A true sanctuary is built on virtue, not on the patronage of a discredited court. Look at yourselves! You call this a satyagraha firm adherence to truth. Yet your truth is bought by the plateful, your fasting is a comedic illusion staged between television commercial breaks, and your devotion is a transactional lease signed with politicians currently adrift in the turbulent currents of their own bad karma!” Balangoda Kassapa quietly slipped his phone into his bag, suddenly very aware of how utterly ridiculous his live-stream looked to a nation laughing hysterically in the comments section. Ulapane Sumangala tried to rally his thoughts to launch a fierce counteroffensive about external conspiracies and threats to their heritage, but the words withered in his throat, completely vaporised under the cool, blinding light of the Arahat’s gaze. “The mango tree in Mihintale still bears fruit because its roots were planted in honest soil,” Arahat Mahinda said, turning his back on the stage with a dramatic sweep of his robes. “But this plastic garden of corruption you have built in the park will wither before the sun sets. Go back to your temples! Wash the political soot from your robes! And remember that the people of this island are no longer the naive subjects of a bygone era, they have passed the intelligence test, even if their supposed teachers have failed it miserably!” With that final, earth-shattering declaration, the imaginary Arahat stepped away from the soiled site of the fraudulent protest. Light that endures Vivid figures of my daydream faded back. I returned to the dull stillness of my quiet room. The heavy sorrow that had weighed so deeply on my eighty-four-year-old heart began to lift, replaced by a gentle, enduring conviction. The transient political circuses built by greed are nothing more than passing shadows on the ever-changing landscape of time. They do not define our beautiful island, nor can they ever truly compromise the pristine core of the Dhamma. For twenty-three centuries, the true light brought by Arahat Mahinda has endured—not through golden fences, luxurious pageants, or the patronage of powerful politicians, but because the pristine Dhamma resides quietly and immovably within the hearts of ordinary, virtuous people. As long as there are those who remember the simple, compassionate logic of that ancient mango tree—who seek truth, practice kindness, and guard their minds against hatred—the light of the Buddha remains undiminished. Governments rise and fall. Interim illusions invariably crumble into dust. The timeless path of virtue stands unshakeable, offering its eternal sanctuary of peace and ultimate hope to a waiting nation. As the Blessed One declared in the Dhammapada: ‘Selo yathā ekaghano vātena na samīrati, Evaṃ paṇḍitā nindāpasaṃsāsu na samiñjanti.’ “Just as a solid rock is not shaken by the storm, even so, the wise remain unmoved by praise or blame.”

audit.headline: Rains to pound most provinces today
audit.summary: Cyclonic Storm Arnab intensifies in Bay of Bengal No direct impact on SL Heavy rainfall between 100 mm and 150 mm is expected across most provinces today (27) and tomorrow (28) as Cyclonic Storm Arnab intensifies in the Bay of Bengal, Deputy Defence Minister Major General (Rtd.) Aruna Jayasekara stated yesterday (26). Addressing a press conference at the Disaster Management Centre (DMC), he said there is no direct impact on Sri Lanka, but the public should remain vigilant without being unnecessarily alarmed. Intermittent rain or thundershowers may occur in the Northern, Western, Sabaragamuwa, Southern, North Western, Central and North Central Provinces and around Trincomalee, with southwesterly winds of 30 to 40 kmph.
audit.body: Cyclonic Storm Arnab intensifies in Bay of Bengal No direct impact on SL Heavy rainfall between 100 mm and 150 mm is expected across most provinces today (27) and tomorrow (28) as Cyclonic Storm Arnab intensifies in the Bay of Bengal, Deputy Defence Minister Major General (Rtd.) Aruna Jayasekara stated yesterday (26). Addressing a press conference at the Disaster Management Centre (DMC), he said there is no direct impact on Sri Lanka, but the public should remain vigilant without being unnecessarily alarmed. Intermittent rain or thundershowers may occur in the Northern, Western, Sabaragamuwa, Southern, North Western, Central and North Central Provinces and around Trincomalee, with southwesterly winds of 30 to 40 kmph. The Deputy Minister said the DMC has informed all District and Divisional Secretaries and the District Disaster Management Committees, and its Emergency Operations Centre has been operating for the past few days. The ‘117’ unit is gathering information and passing it on to the public at district level. The Armed Forces have been placed on standby, and the Police, Civil Security Department (CSD) and Coast Guard are monitoring districts at risk. He urged the public to follow all risk advisories. Met Department Director General A.L.K. Wijemannage said the system was centered near Latitude 15.4°N and Longitude 88.5°E at 8.30 am yesterday, about 1,100 km northeast of Kankesanturai. It is expected to become a severe cyclonic storm over the west-central Bay of Bengal by 5.30 pm yesterday and a severe cyclonic storm today (27). It is forecast to make landfall on the Indian coast through Andhra Pradesh around 11.30 am tomorrow (28). Winds over the Bay of Bengal may reach 80 to 100 kmph, and up to 120 kmph in some areas. Rainfall is expected to intensify in the southwestern parts of the island and is expected to ease slightly after today. Winds of 40 to 50 kmph may occur at times in the Northern, North Central and North Western Provinces and the Trincomalee District. The Met Department’s forecast issued at 2.00 pm yesterday also mentioned the western slopes of the Central hills and the Hambantota District and said rainfall above 75 mm is likely in some places. The Met Department also said the El Niño phenomenon is developing and that it causes cyclones in the Bay of Bengal to intensify. It added that flash floods could occur in some places. DMC Director and Media Spokesperson Pradeep Kodippili said a person was injured when a tree fell in Ingiriya, Kalutara, and falling trees were reported in Galle, Matara and Ratnapura. The DMC and the State Timber Corporation have begun a programme to address hazardous trees. Irrigation Director L.S. Sooriyabandara said a minor flood is likely in low-lying areas of the Kalu Ganga floodplain within 24 hours. The areas at risk are the Pelmadulla, Nivitigala, Ratnapura, Kuruwita, Ayagama and Elapatha Divisional Secretariat Divisions in Ratnapura, and the Ingiriya, Horana, Dodangoda, Millaniya, Bulathsinhala, Madurawala and Palindanuwara Divisions in Kalutara. Water is being released from the Deduru Oya, Rajanganaya, Thabbowa and Inginimitiya reservoirs. Residents of low-lying areas along the Kala Oya and Mee Oya were also urged to be vigilant. Level 3 (Red) landslide warnings were issued for the Ratnapura, Ayagama, Pelmadulla, Kuruwita, Elapatha and Opanayake areas in the Ratnapura District. Several areas in the Galle, Gampaha, Kalutara, Kandy, Kegalle, Kurunegala and Nuwara Eliya Districts are under Level 1 or Level 2 warnings.

audit.headline: Digital VAT in Sri Lanka: Why platform liability and reverse charge are essential to avoid costing households and Treasury
audit.summary: Executive summary Sri Lanka’s VAT on cross-border digital services, in force since July 2026, is a necessary and overdue reform, but its design is incomplete. It relies only on registration by non-resident suppliers and fully carves out supplies to VAT-registered businesses. Without platform liability and a B2B reverse charge, it will likely under-collect and place the entire new burden on households. Key points Background: The reform was IMF-backed, with a modest expected yield (0.04-0.08% of GDP). Its stronger case is equal treatment of local and foreign suppliers. It was delayed twice before Act No. 14 of 2026 confirmed the July start. Weak enforcement: The Inland Revenue Department would have to chase foreign vendors with no local presence. Large brands may register, but smaller providers likely won’t.
audit.body: Executive summary Sri Lanka’s VAT on cross-border digital services, in force since July 2026, is a necessary and overdue reform, but its design is incomplete. It relies only on registration by non-resident suppliers and fully carves out supplies to VAT-registered businesses. Without platform liability and a B2B reverse charge, it will likely under-collect and place the entire new burden on households. Key points Background: The reform was IMF-backed, with a modest expected yield (0.04-0.08% of GDP). Its stronger case is equal treatment of local and foreign suppliers. It was delayed twice before Act No. 14 of 2026 confirmed the July start. Weak enforcement: The Inland Revenue Department would have to chase foreign vendors with no local presence. Large brands may register, but smaller providers likely won’t. B2B carve-out: (Supplies made to local VAT registrants): Reverse charge would raise real revenue from banks, financial institutions, life insurance companies and other VAT registered companies who are prevented from claiming full VAT input credit, which are exempt from invoice-credit VAT and therefore cannot claim input tax credits under that mechanism, while also creating an audit trail. The carve-out forgoes this, loses visibility, and leaves local providers at a disadvantage. Equity: Individuals pay digital VAT while businesses buying the same services pay nothing, which undercuts the aim of base broadening and any future cut to the 18% rate. Global practice: Simplified registration for B2C supplies and reverse charge for B2B supplies are widely used internationally. Platform liability is also increasingly adopted, including in the EU, UK, Australia, Canada and Singapore, but its scope varies. OECD guidance presents platform liability as an effective policy option. Recommendation: Keep simplified registration for B2C supplies, add platform liability for marketplaces, app stores, and replace the B2B carve-out with reverse charge. Support these with clear location-indicator guidance, proportionate penalties and data-sharing with financial institutions. Completing the framework with platform liability and reverse charge Sri Lanka’s decision to tax cross-border digital services represents a necessary and overdue modernisation of the Value Added Tax system. It responds to the reality that value is increasingly created and consumed online, often without any physical presence in the country of consumption. Local providers have long charged VAT on comparable services while many non-resident suppliers have not. The reform aims to correct that imbalance, broaden the tax base, and support the eventual possibility of reducing the high 18% standard rate. Yet the framework that has been enacted relies almost exclusively on vendor registration by non-resident suppliers and contains a complete carve-out for supplies to VAT-registered businesses. This design is incomplete. Without the addition of platform/marketplace liability and a reverse charge mechanism for business-to-business supplies, the regime risks delivering only a fraction of its potential revenue while placing the entire incremental tax burden on individuals and households. Policymakers still have the opportunity to strengthen the legislation and the accompanying administrative rules so that digital VAT becomes a genuine instrument of base broadening rather than a limited and largely symbolic measure. A record of ambition tempered by repeated delay The intellectual and policy origins of digital VAT in Sri Lanka are well documented. The International Monetary Fund’s June 2024 staff report identified the taxation of digital services as one element of a broader package intended to raise revenue and improve neutrality. The expected yield was modest, approximately 0.04% of GDP in the first full year, with some estimates ranging up to 0.08%. The stronger argument was never the absolute size of the revenue but the principle of equal treatment: a Sri Lankan consumer purchasing streaming, software or cloud services from a foreign provider should face the same VAT treatment as one purchasing from a local supplier. Legislative progress followed a familiar pattern of announcement, enactment and postponement, further prolonged by a Supreme Court challenge that delayed the regime’s finalisation and exacted a real opportunity cost in foregone revenue. The Value Added Tax (Amendment) Act No. 4 of 2025 was certified on 11 April 2025. Gazette Notification 2443/30 of 1 July 2025 set an original effective date of 1 October 2025. Cabinet subsequently deferred implementation to 1 April 2026. A further postponement moved the start to 1 July 2026. The Value Added Tax (Amendment) Act No. 14 of 2026, certified on 30 June and published in gazette on 3 July 2026, finally placed the regime on a firm statutory footing and confirmed the July 2026 commencement. Although Sri Lanka’s digital-services VAT provisions came into effect on 1 July 2026, with section 25L principally governing registration and section 25N providing that VAT is not charged where the recipient is VAT-registered, the regime remains non-operational in practice because the prescribed registration form has yet to be made available, preventing non-resident digital service providers from completing the registration process. The mechanics that emerged are conventional in outline but incomplete in substance. Non-resident suppliers of digital services through electronic platforms must register once their supplies to persons in Sri Lanka exceed Rs. 60 million in any twelve-month period or Rs. 15 million in a quarter. A recipient is treated as located in Sri Lanka if at least two of the following indicators are present: a billing or residential address in Sri Lanka, payment through a Sri Lankan bank or financial institution, a payment instrument issued in Sri Lanka, or a Sri Lankan IP address. Registration, return filing and payment are electronic; payment may be made in Rupees or an approved foreign currency, either directly or through a representative. Supplies to VAT-registered resident businesses are entirely carved out. No obligation is placed on platforms, marketplaces or app stores to collect or remit VAT on the underlying supplies they facilitate. Digital VAT: Real revenue, not a compliance checkbox This sequence of delays and the final design choices invite a sober assessment. Digital VAT should not be reduced to a compliance checkbox required by an external program. It should raise meaningful revenue, follow the proven architecture used by successful jurisdictions, and contribute to the larger project of base expansion that can eventually support a lower standard rate. Features that work elsewhere should not be discarded because of lobbying pressure, administrative convenience or incomplete understanding of implementation options. More than one hundred countries already collect VAT on non-resident digital services. The tax base belongs to the country of consumption. Sri Lanka is entitled to collect it fully. Introducing marketplace liability and reverse charge would convert a half-measure into a credible instrument of fiscal policy, one capable of raising revenue, promoting fairness between local and foreign suppliers, and supporting the longer-term objective of reducing the high standard VAT rate of 18% that currently weighs on consumers. The tools exist. International experience demonstrates that they work. The remaining question is whether Sri Lanka will choose to use them OECD recommendations and the global standard The OECD International VAT/GST Guidelines, together with subsequent practical toolkits, provide the clearest international consensus on how to tax cross-border supplies of services and intangibles. For business-to-consumer supplies the recommended approach is to require the non-resident supplier to register and account for the tax under a simplified regime. For business-to-business supplies the preferred mechanism is reverse charge: the local business customer accounts for the VAT as if it were the supplier. This arrangement relieves the foreign supplier of registration obligations on those particular supplies while ensuring that the tax is reported and, where the customer cannot claim full input credit, that revenue is actually collected. Where digital platforms facilitate the transactions, the OECD strongly encourages jurisdictions to impose liability on the platform itself—the “deemed supplier” or full platform liability model. Platforms already possess customer location data, control payment flows and can scale compliance far more efficiently than a tax administration attempting to locate and compel thousands of individual foreign vendors. International practice is not uniform. Simplified vendor registration for B2C supplies and reverse charge for B2B supplies are widely used across jurisdictions. Platform liability is also increasingly adopted, including in the European Union, the United Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand, Canada and Singapore, but its scope differs. OECD guidance identifies platform liability as an effective policy option. Australia’s extension of GST to imported digital services and the European Union’s progressive introduction of deemed-supplier rules illustrate the practical advantages of concentrating collection at the platform level. Enforcement becomes realistic, the long tail of smaller suppliers is captured, and revenue leakage is substantially reduced. Sri Lanka’s exclusive reliance on vendor registration, the absence of platform liability, and the substitution of a full B2B carve-out for reverse charge constitute the weakest available combination of collection methods. Large, reputation-conscious global brands may eventually register. The multitude of smaller software providers, freelance platforms, content creators and niche applications almost certainly will not. The Inland Revenue Department will be left to pursue entities that have no local presence, no local bank account and little commercial incentive to comply. When the same administration already faces well-documented challenges in securing full compliance from resident taxpayers, the expectation that it can effectively police non-residents who simply ignore registration or under-declare values is unrealistic. Platform liability reverses the burden of enforcement: a limited number of large, visible platforms become the collection points, using systems and data they already maintain. The revenue and equity cost of the B2B carve-out The decision to exempt supplies to VAT-registered businesses rather than apply reverse charge carries particularly serious consequences for both revenue and fairness. Under a reverse charge mechanism a local VAT-registered recipient self-assesses the tax. For a fully taxable business the net cash effect is neutral because the output tax is matched by an equal input credit. Banks, financial institutions, life insurance companies and other VAT registered companies who are prevented from claiming full VAT input credit are subject to the separate VAT on financial services but are exempt from invoice-credit VAT; accordingly, they cannot claim input tax credits under the invoice-credit mechanism. The same concern may arise for other businesses whose ability to recover input tax is restricted. Those sectors are significant purchasers of foreign cloud computing, software licenses, digital advertising, data analytics and related services. Reverse charge would therefore generate genuine additional revenue from a rapidly growing category of imports. It would also create a complete audit trail that allows the tax authority to monitor the volume and nature of cross-border digital purchases. Under the B2B carve-out, the foreign supplier does not charge VAT and the VAT-registered recipient does not self-assess it. However, the enacted framework may still require the foreign supplier to furnish prescribed information concerning such supplies to the Inland Revenue Department. The carve-out therefore does not necessarily leave these transactions entirely unreported, but it does not create the same recipient-level self-assessment and audit trail that a reverse charge would provide. This limits visibility and may make misclassification, for example, a private consumer presenting as a business is more difficult to detect. Local digital service providers continue to charge VAT while their foreign competitors do not on B2B sales, recreating the competitive distortion the reform was intended to eliminate. This outcome stands in direct contradiction to the stated policy objective of base broadening. Broadening the tax base cannot mean capturing only individuals, households and non VAT registrant businesses, while excluding businesses that are exempt from invoice-credit VAT, including banks, financial institutions, life insurance companies and other VAT registered companies who are prevented from claiming full VAT input credit, from the reverse-charge net. Yet that is the practical effect of the present design. Individuals, households and non VAT registrant businesses pay digital VAT on streaming subscriptions, applications, software and online services. Businesses purchasing comparable or identical services from non-resident suppliers face no corresponding liability. The entire additional burden of expanding the VAT base in the digital sphere therefore falls on ordinary consumers. Such an arrangement is inequitable. It is also fiscally short-sighted. Every Rupee of revenue left uncollected from B2B digital imports is a Rupee that cannot contribute to the fiscal space required for a future reduction in the standard 18% rate. Fairness, administrative capacity and the question of influence The present design raises uncomfortable questions of fairness. Domestic VAT registration thresholds have been subject to repeated adjustment; more local small and medium enterprises face compliance obligations and the associated costs. At the same time the largest global platforms face only a registration form that they may or may not complete, with no marketplace liability to enforce collection on the many underlying suppliers they host. Local providers charge VAT; foreign providers of B2B digital services do not. The competitive playing field remains tilted. It is legitimate to ask whether the abandonment of reverse charge and the omission of platform liability reflect purely technical judgment or the successful representation of interests that prefer the current, limited arrangement. Reverse charge, by its ordinary operation, would have brought businesses exempt from invoice-credit VAT, including banks, financial institutions, life insurance companies and other VAT registered companies who are prevented from claiming full VAT input credit, into the collection mechanism and produced revenue that the carve-out simply forgoes. Administrative convenience is not a sufficient justification for forgoing that revenue. Other countries with larger digital markets and more complex economies have implemented the fuller OECD package. Sri Lanka does not need to invent new systems. It can adapt existing models and begin with the largest platforms. The alternative, proceeding with vendor registration alone and a full B2B carve-out, almost guarantees modest receipts, persistent non-compliance among smaller foreign providers, zero contribution from the B2B segment, and, within a relatively short period, another round of legislative amendments to correct what could have been designed correctly from the outset. A practical and proven path forward A more robust framework is available and does not require radical innovation. It would retain simplified electronic vendor registration for business-to-consumer supplies, introduce platform liability for major marketplaces, app stores, and replace the B2B carve-out with a reverse charge mechanism. Supporting measures, clear guidance on the application of location indicators, proportionate penalties, and structured information exchange with financial institutions would complete the architecture. These are precisely the tools that have proven effective in other jurisdictions. They align with OECD recommendations, protect the competitive position of local providers, generate revenue from purchases by businesses exempt from invoice-credit VAT, including banks, financial institutions, life insurance companies and other VAT registered companies who are prevented from claiming full VAT input credit, and ensure that base expansion is not borne solely by households. Sri Lanka cannot afford a digital VAT regime that exists primarily to satisfy an external checklist. The digital economy is one of the few expanding tax bases available to the country. Confining collection to vendor registration while carving out the entire B2B segment is, in effect, planning for underperformance. Policymakers still possess the authority and the time to strengthen the regime before it settles into underwhelming practice. Introducing marketplace liability and reverse charge would convert a half-measure into a credible instrument of fiscal policy, one capable of raising revenue, promoting fairness between local and foreign suppliers, and supporting the longer-term objective of reducing the high standard VAT rate of 18% that currently weighs on consumers. The tools exist. International experience demonstrates that they work. The remaining question is whether Sri Lanka will choose to use them. (The author was awarded Tax Practice Leader of the Year 2024 (ASPAC) by International Tax Review (ITR) and was a top-four finalist for Tax Litigation and Disputes Practice Leader of the Year (ASPAC))

audit.headline: Bond market yields open steady to higher on selected tenors
audit.summary: By Wealth Trust Securities The secondary Bond market yesterday kicked off the fresh trading week with yields holding broadly steady across majority of the yield curve. However, selective selling pressure on the 2033 and 2034 tenors saw yields push higher. Market activity and transaction volumes remained at moderate levels, ahead of an auction packed week. The week will see back-to-back primary auctions, with a Rs. 100 billion Treasury Bill auction scheduled for tomorrow (28), followed by a Rs. 100 billion Treasury Bond auction on Thursday (29). The 15.02.28 maturity traded at the rate of 10.45%. The 01.08.30 and 15.10.30 maturities traded at the rates of 11.50% and 11.55%-11.54% respectively. The 01.12.31 maturity traded at the rate of 11.85%. The 15.12.32 maturity traded at the rate of 12.00%.

The 01.12.31 maturity traded at the rate of 11.85%. The 15.12.32 maturity traded at the rate of 12.00%.
