audit.headline: BASL to host inaugural Board Leader Ready Symposium on corporate governance and boardroom leadership
audit.summary: The Bar Association of Sri Lanka (BASL) will host its inaugural Board Leader Ready Symposium on Saturday, 7 November 2026, at the Courtyard by Marriott Colombo, bringing together distinguished legal professionals, corporate leaders, financial experts and governance specialists for a full-day program dedicated to preparing current and aspiring directors for the responsibilities of board leadership. The initiative recognises the growing importance of effective corporate governance and the need for directors to possess not only professional expertise but also a sound understanding of their legal obligations, financial oversight responsibilities and strategic role in guiding organisations towards sustainable growth. The keynote address will be delivered by the Securities and Exchange Commission of Sri Lanka (SEC) Chairman Senior Professor D.B.P.H. Dissabandara.
audit.body: The Bar Association of Sri Lanka (BASL) will host its inaugural Board Leader Ready Symposium on Saturday, 7 November 2026, at the Courtyard by Marriott Colombo, bringing together distinguished legal professionals, corporate leaders, financial experts and governance specialists for a full-day program dedicated to preparing current and aspiring directors for the responsibilities of board leadership. The initiative recognises the growing importance of effective corporate governance and the need for directors to possess not only professional expertise but also a sound understanding of their legal obligations, financial oversight responsibilities and strategic role in guiding organisations towards sustainable growth. The keynote address will be delivered by the Securities and Exchange Commission of Sri Lanka (SEC) Chairman Senior Professor D.B.P.H. Dissabandara. The symposium will feature four thematic sessions led by distinguished professionals from the legal, regulatory, financial and corporate sectors. The session on corporate governance titled ‘The Boardroom: Where Governance Begins’ will feature SEC Chairman Senior Professor D.B.P.H. Dissabandara; Central Bank of Sri Lanka (CBSL) Independent Director and Member of the Governing Board Nihal Fonseka; BASL President, CBSL former Governing Board Member and SEC former Commissioner Rajeev Amarasuriya; First Capital Holdings PLC Chairman Rajendra Theagarajah; and Independent Director Renuke Wijayawardhane. The session on directors’ Duties and Liabilities titled ‘Accountable at the Top: Duties, Liabilities and What Every Director Must Know’, will feature former Justice of the Supreme Court and Seylan Bank Chairman Justice Buwaneka Aluwihare, PC; President’s Counsel Dr. Harsha Cabral; Precedent Partner of Heritage Partners and SEC former Director General Dr. Arittha Wikramanayake; Nithya Partners Precedent Partner Naomal Goonewardena; and Sudath Perera Associates Partner Nipuni Samarasekara. The session on financially-savvy Board members titled ‘Financial Acumen for Board Directors: What Every Director Needs to Know’, will feature Union Bank Chairman and Sri Lanka Institute of Directors (SLID) Chairman Dinesh Weerakkody; Board Director and former Partner of EY, and CA Sri Lanka Past President Arjuna Herath; CA Sri Lanka President Tishan Subasinghe; David Pieris Holdings Ltd.., Group Finance Director and CA Sri Lanka Immediate Past President Heshana Kuruppu; Brandix Group General Manager – Strategy and Transformation and Director Mariam Omar; and Brandix Group Head of Group Legal and Company Secretarial and Inaugural Board Leader Ready Symposium Co-Chairperson Yanina Weerasinghe. The session on effective board committee governance titled ‘Beyond Compliance: The Director’s Role in Effective Board Committees’ will feature Boardroom Mastery (AICD Australia) and Guru Ltd., Director of Governance Dr. Suresh Marcandan; Colombo Stock Exchange Director Suren de Silva; B.R. De Silva and Co. Partner and CA Sri Lanka Past President Sanjaya Bandara; Non-Executive Independent Director Coralie Pietersz; and Maharaja Foods PLC Chairman Imran Furkan. BASL President Rajeev Amarasuriya said, the Inaugural Board Leader Ready Symposium presents an exciting opportunity for professionals to look beyond traditional career paths and explore the many possibilities that boardroom leadership offers. “For those in the legal profession, the opportunities extend beyond courtroom practice, with their knowledge and skills providing a valuable foundation for contributing to corporate strategy, governance and decision-making. The symposium is also an opportunity for the younger generation of professionals to gain the knowledge and confidence needed to aspire to board positions in the future. Equally, we hope to encourage more women to explore boardroom leadership and take their place in shaping the future of businesses in Sri Lanka. By opening up these possibilities and strengthening awareness of what it takes to be Board-ready, we hope to nurture a new generation of capable, diverse and responsible corporate leaders.” BASL Board Leader Ready Symposium Chairperson Renuke Wijayawardhane said: “I believe that investing in boardroom education and professional development is an important step towards strengthening corporate governance and building more resilient, responsible and sustainable organizations. Our aspiration is to create greater awareness of what it truly means to be Board-ready, while encouraging both current and future directors to approach their responsibilities with the requisite knowledge, integrity, independence and commitment. We hope this symposium will serve as a valuable platform for learning, knowledge-sharing and professional development, ultimately contributing to a stronger pool of corporate leaders who are well equipped to guide organizations towards long-term success.” The symposium is intended for existing board members, senior corporate executives and professionals aspiring to board positions. While executive experience provides a valuable foundation, effective board service demands a broader strategic perspective, the ability to question constructively and the independence of judgement necessary to oversee management and protect stakeholder interests. These competencies are particularly important in the context of listed companies, where governance standards, transparency and regulatory responsibilities are especially significant. Through this inaugural initiative, the BASL seeks to encourage greater awareness of what it means to be Board-ready and to support the development of capable, ethical and accountable corporate leadership. The symposium will be held from 8:15 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. on Saturday, 7 November 2026, at the Courtyard by Marriott Colombo. The registration fee is Rs. 17,500. For further details and registration, please contact the BASL Program Office on 077 588 8781 or email [email protected] The Daily FT is the official newspaper partner of the symposium, with Derana serving as the electronic media partner. BoardPAC and Brandix are the symposium’s strategic partners.

audit.headline: British Airways celebrates return to Sri Lanka with special fares
audit.summary: British Airways Captain Terry Smith and Hayleys Chairman and Chief Executive Mohan Pandithage cut a cake to celebrate the resumption of direct services on Saturday. British High Commissioner Andrew Patrick, British Airways General Manager – South Asia David Wright, Civil Aviation Authority Director General and CEO Capt. Daminda Rambukwella, British Airways Senior First Officer Pradeeb Vimalraj, IAG Cargo Regional Commercial Manager – Asia Pacific, India and Middle East Ankush Chawla and Hayleys Advantis Managing Director Ruwan Waidyaratne are among those who look on British Airways General Manager – South Asia David Wright The crew of the first British Airways flight - Reintroduces thrice-weekly direct services between Sri Lanka and UK for first time since 2015 - Says move to support tourism, trade and business travel on back of rebound in economic growth and tourism - Makes compelling...
audit.body: British Airways Captain Terry Smith and Hayleys Chairman and Chief Executive Mohan Pandithage cut a cake to celebrate the resumption of direct services on Saturday. British High Commissioner Andrew Patrick, British Airways General Manager – South Asia David Wright, Civil Aviation Authority Director General and CEO Capt. Daminda Rambukwella, British Airways Senior First Officer Pradeeb Vimalraj, IAG Cargo Regional Commercial Manager – Asia Pacific, India and Middle East Ankush Chawla and Hayleys Advantis Managing Director Ruwan Waidyaratne are among those who look on British Airways General Manager – South Asia David Wright The crew of the first British Airways flight - Reintroduces thrice-weekly direct services between Sri Lanka and UK for first time since 2015 - Says move to support tourism, trade and business travel on back of rebound in economic growth and tourism - Makes compelling offer of discounted World Traveller return fares with prices starting from Rs. 255,000 - Reveals searches on ba.com for flights from London to Colombo have increased by more than 10% in the past week - GSA Hayleys Advantis says BA’s resumption brings lasting value for travellers, tourism industry and Sri Lanka as a whole - Jaffna-born Senior First Officer Pradeeb Vimalraj operates inaugural flight; says proud to be part of new chapter connecting Sri Lanka and UK By Nisthar Cassim British Airways on Saturday marked a significant milestone with the arrival of its first flight into Colombo, reconnecting Sri Lanka with the UK for the first time in over 11 years. The inaugural flight, operated by Sri Lankan crew, was welcomed by traditional dancers and drummers on arrival to commemorate the occasion. The new route strengthens links between the two countries, supporting tourism, trade, and business travel. The thrice-weekly service will be operated by British Airways’ Boeing 777 fleet, featuring Club World (business class), World Traveller Plus (premium economy), and World Traveller (economy) cabins. To celebrate the launch, British Airways is offering special return fares with savings of up to 10% in World Traveller, starting from Rs. 255,000 for travel from Colombo to London Gatwick. British Airways Chief Planning and Strategy Officer Neil Chernoff in a statement said the resumption marks a special moment for British Airways, as it meant bringing Sri Lanka back to its global network and giving customers greater choice when planning their next getaway. “Sri Lanka is renowned for its warmth, rich culture, and hospitality, and we’re delighted to be flying there once again. To celebrate, we’re offering special fares and look forward to welcoming customers on board,” he added. Noting that Sri Lanka is one of the first re-entries in recent months, British Airways General Manager – South Asia David Wright during a media interaction post-first flight on Saturday stressed that Sri Lanka has always been a really important market for British Airways. “Between the UK and Sri Lanka, we have deep cultural and historic links, and so it is a market that we continue to keep an eye on. And obviously, over the last few years, we have seen that economic growth and tourism rebound post-COVID, and we continue to review our network, and we felt that the time was right to reintroduce our services from this winter,” he told journalists in Colombo. Wright said that a heart of a business case like this is very much tourism from the UK coming into the incredible island of Sri Lanka and everything it has to offer. “But we have also seen really positive demand across sectors: tourism going into the UK, but also across business sectors and also people visiting communities and friends and family as well.” He described the all-inclusive offers starting from Rs. 255,000 as “compelling.” The Boeing 777 has a capacity of over 300 seats and Wright noted that British Airways has been really pleased with the response. The special fares in World Traveller (economy) on return flights from Colombo to Gatwick, available for booking until 15 November 2026, for outbound travel between 20 October and 30 November 2026 and inbound travel between 26 October and 10 December 2026. British Airways General Sales Agents (GSA) Hayleys Advantis Ltd., Managing Director Ruwan Waidyaratne said: “The commencement of British Airways’ flight operations to Colombo marks a significant milestone in enhancing air connectivity between Sri Lanka and the UK. The service will offer customers greater travel options while supporting tourism and business travel between the two markets, and we look forward to continuing our partnership with British Airways.” He said Hayleys’ relationship with British Airways dates back to 1995, and it is delighted to welcome the airline back to Sri Lanka as this longstanding partnership enters a new chapter. Waidyaratne stressed that improved connectivity between Sri Lanka and the UK creates opportunities that extends beyond travel, supporting tourism, stimulating economic activities, and strengthening ties between the two countries. “We look forward to seeing this connection grow and deliver lasting value for travellers, the tourism industry, and Sri Lanka as a whole,” he added. Senior First Officer Pradeeb Vimalraj, who operated the airline’s inaugural flight in a statement said: “As a Sri Lankan, born and raised in Jaffna in my early years, bringing our first flight back home after more than a decade was particularly special. The warm welcome we received made it even more memorable, and I am so proud to be part of this new chapter connecting Sri Lanka and the UK.” British Airways also revealed that searches on ba.com for flights from London to Colombo have increased by more than 10% in the past week, reflecting continued interest in the destination. British Airways operates one of the largest and the most modern fleets of any airline in the world and is transforming the operations with a £ 7 billion investment plan. Departure from Gatwick is at 1640 hours on Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays and arrival in Colombo at 0935 hours the next day. Departure from Colombo is 1035 hours Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Saturdays with arrival at Gatwick at 1700 hours. British Airways said the new service gives customers travelling from the UK direct access to one of South Asia’s most captivating destinations. From golden beaches and ancient cultural sites to wildlife reserves, tea country and a thriving food scene, Sri Lanka offers a diverse range of experiences for travellers to discover.

audit.headline: Cabinet awards Rs. 562 m wastewater plant contract for Welipenna Expressway Service Area to Water Board
audit.summary: The Cabinet of Ministers has approved awarding the contract to construct two wastewater treatment plants for the Welipenna service area on the Southern Expressway to the National Water Supply and Drainage Board (NWSDB), at an estimated cost of Rs. 562.04 million. The service area is maintained by Canowin Hotels and Spas Ltd., a fully owned subsidiary of the Sri Lanka Insurance Corporation. It has been identified that the capacity of the existing wastewater treatment plants at the facility is insufficient. The NWSDB examined the prevailing conditions at the site and submitted a report recommending the construction of two new treatment plants, each with a capacity of 200 cubic metres per day. The proposal to this effect was submitted by President Anura Kumara Dissanayake in his capacity as the Finance, Planning and Economic Development Minister.

audit.headline: Cabinet clears drafting of Bill to amend Ayurveda Act
audit.summary: The Cabinet of Ministers has approved the formulation of a draft Bill to amend the Ayurveda Act, No. 31 of 1961, which governs the regulation, development, and control of Sri Lanka’s indigenous medical sector. The sector, which comprises Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani, and local therapies, is regulated under the Act. Although it has been amended from time to time as required, the need for further amendments has been identified. The proposed changes are aimed at enabling all activities in the local medical field to be managed more efficiently and productively, and at further formalising the regulation of the sector. They would also allow for the issuing of licences applicable to the export of local medicines, and support progress towards Sustainable Development Goals in the sector. The proposal to this effect was submitted by Health Minister Dr. Nalinda Jayatissa.

audit.headline: Cleaner, but not yet cheaper to invest in: Sri Lanka’s anti-corruption gains and investment question
audit.summary: - Perception scores have turned and prosecutions have risen. But investment has recovered only in step with the region, and nearly a decade of data shows corruption ratings alone do not drive it Sri Lanka has spent two years trying to convince the world that it is serious about corruption. There is progress to show on that front. There is less evidence that it has yet changed the country’s standing with foreign investors. A reversal in the ratings Transparency International’s Corruption Perceptions Index scores countries from 0 (highly corrupt) to 100 (very clean). Sri Lanka’s score fluctuated between 36 and 38 from 2013 to 2019 and stood at 37 in 2021. Then it began to slide: 36 in 2022, 34 in 2023, with a rank of 115, and 32 in 2024. The 2024 rank of 121 was the worst on record. In 2025 the trend reversed. The score rose to 35, and the rank improved to 107.
audit.body: - Perception scores have turned and prosecutions have risen. But investment has recovered only in step with the region, and nearly a decade of data shows corruption ratings alone do not drive it Sri Lanka has spent two years trying to convince the world that it is serious about corruption. There is progress to show on that front. There is less evidence that it has yet changed the country’s standing with foreign investors. A reversal in the ratings Transparency International’s Corruption Perceptions Index scores countries from 0 (highly corrupt) to 100 (very clean). Sri Lanka’s score fluctuated between 36 and 38 from 2013 to 2019 and stood at 37 in 2021. Then it began to slide: 36 in 2022, 34 in 2023, with a rank of 115, and 32 in 2024. The 2024 rank of 121 was the worst on record. In 2025 the trend reversed. The score rose to 35, and the rank improved to 107. Transparency International Sri Lanka cautioned against over-reading this. It said the 14-place jump overstates the improvement, since the underlying score rose by only three points. Perception indices also lag events, so the 2024 figure partly reflects the period before the change of Government. Enforcement is visibly different The sharpest change is in how the system treats powerful people. A retired High Court judge was appointed to head the Commission to Investigate Allegations of Bribery or Corruption in January 2025, and investigations and charges involving former ministers and senior officials followed. Parliament was told that 226 people were arrested between October 2024 and October 2026, including 55 politicians. The August 2025 arrest of former president Ranil Wickremasinghe was the first of a former head of state. Arrests are not convictions, and every case remains subject to due process. Institutional reform is also moving. A beneficial ownership register was launched on 31 March 2026. The legal groundwork came earlier: the 2023 Anti-Corruption Act created the pathway the current Government is using. Assessments of that period were cautious about enforcement. The International Crisis Group argued that the Government’s reliance on the largest party in Parliament inhibited investigations into the powerful. Questions remain on both sides. The Government’s opposition to a no-confidence motion against its energy minister damaged its reform credentials. Commentators have also warned that accountability for past wrongdoing must be matched by safeguards against abuse of state power. What the investment figures show Sri Lanka’s FDI figures are quoted on two different bases, which is why headlines differ. The international standard, used by the Central Bank, the World Bank, the IMF and UNCTAD, is net FDI on a balance-of-payments basis. It counts equity, reinvested earnings and inter-company debt, minus disinvestment. The Board of Investment instead reports gross inflows into its approved companies, including their foreign loans. This article uses the international measure. On that measure, UNCTAD’s World Investment Report 2026 puts inflows at $1.044 billion in 2025, up from $759 million in 2024, an increase of about 38%. The Board of Investment’s own basis showed a 72% rise, because its 2024 base was lower. Inflows then settled at close to $200 million a quarter in the first half of 2026, on preliminary Central Bank figures. That recovery is real but still below the pre-crisis peak. Net inflows reached about $1.6 billion in 2018, helped by one-off port deals, or about 1.7% of GDP. In 2025 they were about 1% of GDP. The inward FDI stock rose to $18.23 billion from $16.6 billion. The rebound also looks modest beside the region. FDI into South Asia as a whole rose from $34.1 billion to $46.1 billion, a gain of about 35%, so Sri Lanka roughly kept pace with its neighbours rather than outpacing them. Bangladesh’s inflows rose 45% to $1.78 billion, while Pakistan received $1.85 billion, down from $2.67 billion in 2024. India’s inflows rose 44% to $39 billion. Sri Lanka accounts for only about 2% of the regional total. On World Bank data for 2024, Sri Lanka ranked 139th among 182 countries on net FDI as a share of GDP, against a global average of 4.25%. What the data say about corruption and investment A first-pass statistical analysis of Transparency International scores and Central Bank net FDI for 2016–2024 found only a weak link. The correlation was about 0.28 and statistically insignificant. Using the previous year’s score gave a result near zero. The score explained under 8% of the variation in FDI. The explanation is visible in the series. The score moved by a few points over the decade, while FDI swung between about $430 million and $1.6 billion on its own schedule. The 2018 peak came from port-related deals. The 2019 fall followed the Easter attacks, and the 2020 low came with the pandemic. Inflows then recovered only partly after the 2022 sovereign default. The analysis cautions that nine annual observations make this indicative rather than a causal test. What investors say holds them back Investors’ stated concerns go beyond corruption. The US State Department’s 2025 Investment Climate Statement says FDI remains constrained, with most transactions in the $3 million to $5 million range. Despite the Government’s $5 billion FDI target for 2025, experienced investors say policy stability, regulatory reform and improved transparency must come first. The same assessment cites project reversals, regulatory shifts and slow decision-making. Adani Green’s February 2025 withdrawal from a $400 million wind project over contract renegotiation is often cited as an example. The analysis adds that approval authority is spread across several agencies, so the Board of Investment struggles to act as a true one-stop shop. The Ease of Doing Business rank improved from 113th in 2014 to 99th in 2019. That fell short of the Government’s target of 70th, and the World Bank has since discontinued the index. How the peers do it Sri Lanka’s score of 35 is below the Asia-Pacific average of 45, but above Pakistan (28) and Bangladesh (24). It is also above the Sub-Saharan African average of 32, though behind Ghana’s 43. Yet Bangladesh, with the weaker score, drew more FDI in 2025. The analysis attributes this to design rather than governance scores. Bangladesh runs export zones with ring-fenced customs and tax administration, and Vietnam courts investors through sector-targeted promotion and single-window licensing. Sri Lanka’s pitch, by contrast, has been generic and has shifted with each Government. What would make the difference The analysis proposes four steps. Each is a proposal, not a Government commitment. Give the Board of Investment binding approval authority, with statutory decision deadlines of perhaps 30 to 45 days and a public dashboard of pending approvals. Concentrate incentives and promotion on three or four sectors where the country has a real advantage, such as apparel, IT services, logistics and tourism-linked manufacturing. Publish enforcement results and procurement and land-allocation scorecards for large investment projects. Protect signed investment agreements in statute, so that a change of Government cannot reopen them. The verdict Sri Lanka has made real but early gains: a stronger law, visible enforcement, and a rebound in its score. Whether they are substantial will depend on court outcomes. The investment dividend has not yet arrived. FDI has recovered about as fast as the region’s, from a low base and still below its 2018 peak. The evidence suggests that faster approvals, targeted promotion and stable policy would matter at least as much as the score itself. audit.headline: Dialog and IITM ink MoU to advance research and innovation in Sri Lanka
audit.summary: IITM Pravartak Technologies Foundation CEO Dr. M.J. Shankar Jayaraman (third from left) and Dialog Axiata PLC Group Chief Executive Supun Weerasinghe (fifth from left) exchange the signed Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) in the presence of Indian High Commissioner Santosh Jha (fourth from left). From left: High Commission of India Counsellor (Economic and Commercial) Devika Lal, IITM Pravartak Technologies Foundation Deputy Manager Aravindan Soundararajan, IITM Pravartak Technologies Foundation CEO Dr. M.J.
audit.body: IITM Pravartak Technologies Foundation CEO Dr. M.J. Shankar Jayaraman (third from left) and Dialog Axiata PLC Group Chief Executive Supun Weerasinghe (fifth from left) exchange the signed Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) in the presence of Indian High Commissioner Santosh Jha (fourth from left). From left: High Commission of India Counsellor (Economic and Commercial) Devika Lal, IITM Pravartak Technologies Foundation Deputy Manager Aravindan Soundararajan, IITM Pravartak Technologies Foundation CEO Dr. M.J. Shankar Jayaraman, Indian High Commissioner Santosh Jha, Dialog Axiata PLC Group Chief Executive Supun Weerasinghe and Dialog Axiata PLC Group Company Secretary Viranthi Attygalle Dialog Axiata PLC said it has entered into a strategic partnership with Indian Institute of Technology Madras (IITM) Pravartak Technologies Foundation, India, through the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) aimed at advancing applied research and technology development in Sri Lanka. The agreement marks an important milestone in India-Sri Lanka cooperation, bringing together international expertise, and industry stakeholders to develop practical solutions to national and societal challenges. It also seeks to strengthen Sri Lanka’s research capabilities and create opportunities to translate new ideas into real-world applications. Under the agreement, Dialog will serve as the collaboration anchor and technology enabler, connecting IITM Pravartak’s research networks with Sri Lankan industry stakeholders. The partnership will explore five key areas: innovation and incubation, applied research and university laboratories, artificial intelligence and human-centric solutions, industry skills and talent development, and international knowledge sharing. Potential areas for initial collaboration include Sinhala and Tamil conversational AI, technology-driven dengue prevention and response, and solutions to address human-elephant conflict. These will be explored through focused research initiatives and pilot projects, with opportunities for further development based on their outcomes. Commenting on the significance of the partnership, Indian High Commissioner Santosh Jha said: “India and Sri Lanka share a longstanding and multifaceted relationship, underpinned by strong historical ties and a shared commitment to progress. As our bilateral partnership continues to evolve, cooperation in technology and research presents significant opportunities to deepen engagement between our institutions and people. I welcome this initiative as another meaningful contribution to the growing partnership between our two countries.” IITM Pravartak Technologies Foundation CEO Dr. Shankar Jayaraman said: “This collaboration creates an opportunity to strengthen the connection between academic research and practical application. By working closely with Dialog, Sri Lankan universities and local stakeholders, we hope to foster an environment where researchers and students can exchange knowledge, build technical capabilities and develop solutions that respond to real-world needs. We look forward to a productive partnership that creates value for both the research community and industry.” Dialog Axiata PLC Director/Group CEO Supun Weerasinghe said: “At Dialog, we believe the true value of technology lies in its ability to address real challenges and create meaningful opportunities for people and communities. Through this partnership, we aim to connect global expertise with Sri Lankan talent to develop solutions that can make a lasting difference. I would also like to express our sincere appreciation to His Excellency the High Commissioner and the team at the High Commission of India for their invaluable support in bringing this collaboration to fruition, as we continue our efforts to enrich and empower Sri Lankan lives and enterprises.” The partnership will adopt a phased approach, beginning with selected pilot projects to evaluate their potential before exploring opportunities to scale, ensuring that each initiative is guided by clearly defined objectives and measurable outcomes.

audit.headline: Digital deal can jump-start stalled ETCA: Wijesinha
audit.summary: - Standalone Digital Economy Agreement offers achievable ‘early harvest’ to revive India talks - ETCA dragged through 14 rounds; Govt. awaiting review of existing FTAs before new deals - Urges ASEAN DEFA-style interoperability over harmonising with Indian standards - Payments, paperless customs, e-commerce, e-signatures, cybersecurity, AI to be front-loaded - Talent mobility, cross-border data flows to be kept out given domestic sensitivities Sri Lanka can revive stalled negotiations on the Economic and Technology Cooperation Agreement (ETCA) with India by first concluding a standalone Digital Economy Agreement that builds on the momentum of recent bilateral digital cooperation, Centre for a Smart Future (CSF) Co-Founder and Economist Anushka Wijesinha said.
audit.body: - Standalone Digital Economy Agreement offers achievable ‘early harvest’ to revive India talks - ETCA dragged through 14 rounds; Govt. awaiting review of existing FTAs before new deals - Urges ASEAN DEFA-style interoperability over harmonising with Indian standards - Payments, paperless customs, e-commerce, e-signatures, cybersecurity, AI to be front-loaded - Talent mobility, cross-border data flows to be kept out given domestic sensitivities Sri Lanka can revive stalled negotiations on the Economic and Technology Cooperation Agreement (ETCA) with India by first concluding a standalone Digital Economy Agreement that builds on the momentum of recent bilateral digital cooperation, Centre for a Smart Future (CSF) Co-Founder and Economist Anushka Wijesinha said. Wijesinha noted that the ETCA negotiations had dragged through 14 rounds over many years and multiple governments, with momentum slowing significantly on the Sri Lankan side. The present Government is awaiting the completion of a unilateral review of existing free trade agreements (FTAs) before deciding how to proceed with any new ones, while the ETCA and its predecessor, Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA), carry political baggage as initiatives inherited from previous administrations. Against this backdrop, he said digital connectivity had been driving a new phase in bilateral relations. Initiatives around digital payments integration led by India’s Unified Payments Interface (UPI), collaboration on digital public infrastructure, especially the digital ID project, and the emergence of trade settlement in Indian and Sri Lankan rupees have characterised this phase, building on India’s 2022 crisis-era assistance and relief following Cyclone Ditwah. “Carving some of these initiatives out into an immediate, standalone Digital Economy Agreement can capture this momentum,” Wijesinha said. He argued that converting ad hoc, episodic initiatives into mutually negotiated commitments, with defined obligations and review mechanisms, would place digital cooperation within a firm institutional framework. “An achievable ‘early harvest’ win here would inject fresh enthusiasm into Indo-Lanka economic integration, while demonstrating tangible benefits to domestic stakeholders,” he said. Wijesinha pointed out that such a modular approach would not be unprecedented. India has already decided to unbundle investment chapters from comprehensive FTAs, expecting partners instead to sign Bilateral Investment Treaties (BITs) based on its Model BIT. This has been conveyed to Sri Lanka, and a new standalone BIT is expected to be signed rather than an investment chapter being included in the ETCA, as the Sri Lankan side had previously assumed. Applying the same precedent to the digital sphere, he said, would allow both nations to advance high-value integration without getting bogged down by traditional trade bottlenecks. For design, he suggested the two countries look to ASEAN’s Digital Economy Framework Agreement (DEFA), recently concluded and now awaiting ratification by Member States. The DEFA grew out of each member economy’s post-COVID push towards digitalisation, expanding into a pan-regional ambition from 2023. While acknowledging that sceptics might dismiss a 10-nation regional treaty as irrelevant to a bilateral relationship, Wijesinha said DEFA’s core value lay in how it navigated differences in scale and readiness among its members. Instead of demanding full regulatory harmonisation, which often triggers concerns over sovereignty and dominance, the framework relied on interoperability, tiering, sequencing, and flexible commitments. “Rather than requiring Sri Lanka to harmonise its laws and systems to Indian standards, a DEFA-inspired interoperability approach would allow divergent national systems to recognise and transact with each other without enforcing identical rules,” he said, adding that this could be backed by tiered and possibly sequenced commitments, with periodic reviews allowing ambition to grow over time. DEFA covers nine areas, ranging from payments and digital ID to cybersecurity, data flows, competition policy and talent mobility. However, Wijesinha said an India-Sri Lanka agreement need not cover all of these at once, and should focus on practical, non-controversial areas where collaboration is already underway or imminent. These include payment system interoperability, digital trade and paperless customs, treatment of cross-border e-commerce and digital goods, mutual legal recognition of e-signatures, cybersecurity cooperation, and cooperation on emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI). Sensitive areas that risk stalling negotiations could be excluded, he said. Talent mobility is politically sensitive in Sri Lanka, and DEFA’s provisions on the preferential movement of digital talent and entrepreneurs are possible in ASEAN partly because labour mobility is less politically charged among its members. In Sri Lanka, liberalising Mode 4 services, which covers professionals temporarily crossing borders to deliver services, attracts considerable domestic sensitivity, as earlier CEPA and ETCA rounds showed. Cross-border data flows are similarly difficult to model directly on DEFA’s default of free flow, he noted. India’s data protection regime leans towards retaining the ability to impose sector-specific data localisation requirements, while Sri Lanka is only just advancing its own data protection regime. Wijesinha stressed that negotiating a digital agreement first did not mean abandoning the broader ambition for a comprehensive deal such as the ETCA, but could instead serve as a stimulant to the stalled process. He recalled that when the CEPA was envisioned, the Joint Study Group showed bold ambition by mapping extensive cooperation areas beyond goods trade, just three years after the first bilateral agreement came into force. While such ambition and foresight appear to have dipped since, he said decoupling the digital agenda and forging a dedicated agreement could rekindle that forward-looking spirit, bring in new stakeholders and reflect contemporary aspirations on both sides. “India and Sri Lanka must not let legacy trade hurdles hurt optimism for new areas of economic integration,” Wijesinha said. He made these observations in an article for the Observer Research Foundation (https://www.orfonline.org/expert-speak/can-a-digital-economy-agreement-refresh-india-sri-lanka-economic-integration).

audit.headline: Economic transformation in Asian countries and lessons for Sri Lanka on new ways of earning
audit.summary: Whenever dollars run short, we borrow. We restrict imports. We restructure debt. We seek international help. These steps have saved us many times. Managing a shortage and ending it for good are two different jobs. We have done the first. We have hardly begun the second. So how does a nation end it for good? Some of our Asian neighbours found the answer. Their stories should give every Sri Lankan hope. Each of them lacked something the experts thought it needed. One was refused by the World Bank, others by the world’s biggest companies or by their own neighbours. None of them grew rich by doing more of what they already did. Each one found a new way to earn that nobody expected of it, and backed it with courage when others would not. Each one created an income that did not exist before.
audit.body: Whenever dollars run short, we borrow. We restrict imports. We restructure debt. We seek international help. These steps have saved us many times. Managing a shortage and ending it for good are two different jobs. We have done the first. We have hardly begun the second. So how does a nation end it for good? Some of our Asian neighbours found the answer. Their stories should give every Sri Lankan hope. Each of them lacked something the experts thought it needed. One was refused by the World Bank, others by the world’s biggest companies or by their own neighbours. None of them grew rich by doing more of what they already did. Each one found a new way to earn that nobody expected of it, and backed it with courage when others would not. Each one created an income that did not exist before. That is how their economic transformation started Most of us still remember the queues of 2022 for fuel, gas, medicine and food, and the long nights of waiting, never knowing whether anything would be left by the time we reached the front. Shelves were empty because the country had run out of dollars. We promised ourselves then that it would never happen again. Yet history gives us reason to worry Since 1965, Sri Lanka has entered into 17 lending arrangements with the IMF. Many brought reform, relief and recovery. Yet time and again, sooner or later, the shortage of foreign exchange returned. Before 2023, the last year Sri Lanka earned more from the world than it paid out to the world was 1977. That is nearly half a century of living beyond our dollar income. A country cannot keep its promise to its children with borrowed dollars. We have been managing shortages Whenever dollars run short, we borrow. We restrict imports. We restructure debt. We seek international help. These steps have saved us many times. Managing a shortage and ending it for good are two different jobs. We have done the first. We have hardly begun the second. So how does a nation end it for good? Some of our Asian neighbours found the answer. Their stories should give every Sri Lankan hope. Written off by the world, they rose anyway When Singapore left the Federation of Malaysia in 1965, few expected it to survive. It was a small island with no natural resources, no industry and limited land. It depended on the outside world even for its water, and unemployment was close to 9%. Three years later, Britain announced it would close its military bases on the island, which provided thousands of jobs. As much as a fifth of Singapore’s economy was put at risk. Singapore did not wait to be rescued. With no oil of its own, it built one of the three largest oil refining centres in the world. Its own Prime Minister later said the country had no natural advantage except that it had the idea and made it happen. South Korea wanted a steel mill but had little iron ore of its own. The World Bank turned down its loan request and judged the plan premature. A consortium of seven Western steelmakers, formed to raise the capital, failed and was dissolved. Korea refused to give up. It turned to Japan, which agreed to lend most of the money. The Pohang mill poured its first iron in 1973, and within little more than a decade it was the biggest single steel plant in the world. Korea’s leap into large shipbuilding followed the same path. Shipowners gave Korean builders a cold reception, and Japan refused to share its technology. Hyundai’s founder, Chung Ju-yung, travelled the world with a photograph of an empty beach in Ulsan and a 500 won banknote showing a turtle ship, a symbol of Korea’s shipbuilding past. A Greek shipowner took the risk and ordered two giant tankers. Hyundai broke ground in 1972. By 1983, it was the largest shipbuilder in the world. In the late 1960s, Penang had lost its free port status and was suffering severe unemployment, with no natural resources to fall back on. In 1972, Malaysia opened its first free trade zone there, and Intel came the same year. Within three years, that one plant was doing more than half of Intel’s assembly work. Penang grew into one of Asia’s great electronics centres. In the mid 1980s, Morris Chang set out to build a company that would make only chips designed by others, a business model the world had never seen. He asked Intel, Toshiba, Hitachi and Sony to invest. All of them said no. Only Philips came in from abroad, with Taiwan’s government as the largest shareholder. That company, TSMC, is now one of the most important manufacturers on earth. Around the same time, Gulf Air cut back its services to Dubai. Dubai answered by starting an airline of its own. Emirates flew its first flight in 1985 with a handful of aircraft and $10 million in start-up funding. The same year, Dubai opened the Jebel Ali Free Zone with just 19 companies. Today the zone hosts more than 11,000 businesses, Emirates is one of the world’s largest international airlines, and oil, once a third of Dubai’s economy, has shrunk to a tiny share of it. What they had in common Look closely, and a pattern appears. Each of them lacked something the experts thought it needed. One was refused by the World Bank, others by the world’s biggest companies or by their own neighbours. None of them grew rich by doing more of what they already did. Each one found a new way to earn that nobody expected of it, and backed it with courage when others would not. Each one created an income that did not exist before. That is how their economic transformation started. Why not Sri Lanka? Now think of what we start with. Sri Lanka has more land, more natural resources and more people than Singapore had in 1965. We sit beside one of the busiest east-west shipping routes in the world. Our people are educated and skilled, and hundreds of thousands of Sri Lankans work and build businesses across the globe. Our exporters have shown for decades that they can compete with the best. If Singapore could build a refining industry without a drop of oil, and Korea a steel industry with little iron ore, what could Sri Lanka build with everything it already has? The answer may already exist. It may be in the mind of an engineer in Colombo, a university student in Kandy, a teacher in Jaffna, an entrepreneur in Galle or a Sri Lankan professional in London. The next billion dollars may be sitting in an idea that no decision maker has heard yet. Sri Lanka has every reason to follow the Asian path, and no reason to be the exception. The clock is already running Hope alone will not do it. Neither will plans that stay on paper. New earnings take years to mature. Hyundai needed eleven years to go from an empty beach to the top of world shipbuilding. The dollars Sri Lanka will need in the 2030s must be planted now and nurtured. The signs of need are already here. 2025 gave us real reasons to feel proud: record remittances above $8 billion, tourism earnings of about $3.2 billion and a third year of current account surplus. The Government’s discipline deserves credit for this, and many began to feel the danger had passed. 2026 has reminded us how quickly the picture can change. With the conflict in the Middle East pushing up costs, the current account slipped back into a deficit of $291 million for January to August. The merchandise trade deficit widened to $7.2 billion, from $4.3 billion a year earlier. Tourist arrivals fell. By the end of September, the rupee had lost 6.3% against the dollar since the start of the year. There are quieter signals too. The dollars the Central Bank bought from the market fell from $1.76 billion in the first half of 2024 to $0.56 billion in the first half of 2026. And the IMF’s latest review assumes Sri Lanka will return to international bond markets for $3 billion in 2027 and 2028. The Government has rightly said these are the IMF’s assumptions, not its own projections. But the assumption tells us something important: unless new earnings grow fast enough, borrowing remains the default way to fill the gap. Our reserves of around $6.9 billion have been rebuilt with great care. But reserves are savings, not income, and our traditional earners each depend on things we do not control, from jobs in other countries to peace in the wider world. Hoping they will be enough is not a plan. Every new dollar we earn is a dollar we will not need to borrow. The door is already open On 22 September, the National Business Facilitation Centre, ViYASA, opened under the Presidential Secretariat, built on the President’s own concept. Its purpose is to clear the administrative and regulatory barriers that slow down investment and business. This is a far-sighted step, and it deserves the support of every Sri Lankan who wants this country to succeed. Here lies a rare opportunity. Most new earning ideas need several institutions to say yes. They belong to no single ministry, so for decades they have had nowhere to go. Many simply died on a desk. The Centre sits above those divisions. It can become the national home for new foreign exchange earning and saving pathways, alongside its work of removing bottlenecks. By now, the Centre may already have received proposals for new ways of earning foreign exchange. Some of those may be substantial foreign exchange inflow pathways holding the first seeds of Sri Lanka’s own transformation. Giving the Centre the role of evaluating these ideas and helping them through to activation could be set in motion in the fewest working days possible. The door the President has opened can become the door through which Sri Lanka walks out of its dollar trap for good. A call to the Chambers of Commerce and Industry and to every Sri Lankan Some of our most valuable ideas can come from people who have never sat in a planning meeting. To our chambers of commerce, trade associations and professional bodies: call your members together, hold brainstorming sessions, sift the ideas and bring the strongest ones to the Centre. One good idea, carried forward by a chamber with the weight of its members behind it, can open new dollar income paths that no single company could open alone. To our universities: which services could your faculties sell to the world? To Sri Lankans working overseas: which partners and markets could you bring home? To our industrialists: what could we make here that the world would buy, or that we now import without need? You do not need a detailed feasibility study to start. You need an idea, and the courage to put it forward. Start today: write your idea down, talk it over with your chamber or professional body, and have it ready to submit. Every Sri Lankan who brings a workable idea becomes part of building the country’s future. Facilitating business and removing bottlenecks is exactly the help most new foreign exchange earning paths will need, so in spirit they already belong within its work. But what is implied is easily overlooked; what is assigned gets done. What remains, then, is a small decision with a very large reach: to name the receiving and activating of new foreign exchange earnings and saving paths as a specific mandate of the Centre, assign it as a direct responsibility, and allow the whole nation to take part. This does not replace any existing policy. It adds to what is already being done. It does not cost the Treasury a fortune. It costs only attention, and the will to act before the next storm rather than during it. Each of the Asian transformations described here began with a bold decision, taken early and carried through with courage To the President and those who decide The hardest step, creating the Centre, has already been taken. Facilitating business and removing bottlenecks is exactly the help most new foreign exchange earning paths will need, so in spirit they already belong within its work. But what is implied is easily overlooked; what is assigned gets done. What remains, then, is a small decision with a very large reach: to name the receiving and activating of new foreign exchange earning and saving paths as a specific mandate of the Centre, assign it as a direct responsibility, and allow the whole nation to take part. This does not replace any existing policy. It adds to what is already being done. It does not cost the Treasury a fortune. It costs only attention, and the will to act before the next storm rather than during it. Each of the Asian transformations described here began with a bold decision, taken early and carried through with courage. Because new earnings take years to mature, every month we wait today becomes a month of shortage in the years ahead. The best answer to any bond assumption is a pipeline of new earnings strong enough to make it unnecessary. Imagine a Sri Lanka where anyone with an idea that could earn the country a dollar knows exactly where to take it. Imagine our children growing up never knowing what a fuel queue or fuel quota looks like. That is a legacy worth building. One day, other nations may tell Sri Lanka’s story the way we now tell Singapore’s and Korea’s. And it must begin now. Let us keep doing well what we already do. But let us also give the whole nation a reason, and a place, to discover what we have not yet begun to do. After decades of spending more than it earned, it is time Sri Lanka opened innovative new pathways for more dollars to flow in than the country needs for spending. (The author, CEng FIMechE FIET (UK) CEng FIE (SL), is Founder and Chairman of the KIK Group of Companies, an export-oriented engineering and switchgear assembly manufacturer and a Presidential Export Award winner, and serves on the Executive Committee of the Free Trade Zone Manufacturers’ Association of Sri Lanka. The views expressed are his own. He can be reached at [email protected].)

audit.headline: Experts outline Sri Lanka’s priorities in new world order
audit.summary: - ICC’s Maria Fernanda Garza names diversification, digital trade, rules-based cooperation as Sri Lanka’s key opportunities; warns over-dependence on few markets breeds vulnerability - Ex-envoy Mahinda Samarasinghe urges best of ties with US; says 45 countries won deals by conceding duty-free access, investment pledges Sri Lanka must diversify its markets, build trusted digital trade institutions, and balance between competing powers while keeping its ties with the US strong if it is to turn its post-crisis recovery into lasting prosperity in a fragmenting world order, three international experts said. International Chamber of Commerce (ICC) Global Honorary Chair Maria Fernanda Garza, Switzerland-based political consultant, campaign strategist, and political scientist Dr.
audit.body: - ICC’s Maria Fernanda Garza names diversification, digital trade, rules-based cooperation as Sri Lanka’s key opportunities; warns over-dependence on few markets breeds vulnerability - Ex-envoy Mahinda Samarasinghe urges best of ties with US; says 45 countries won deals by conceding duty-free access, investment pledges Sri Lanka must diversify its markets, build trusted digital trade institutions, and balance between competing powers while keeping its ties with the US strong if it is to turn its post-crisis recovery into lasting prosperity in a fragmenting world order, three international experts said. International Chamber of Commerce (ICC) Global Honorary Chair Maria Fernanda Garza, Switzerland-based political consultant, campaign strategist, and political scientist Dr. Louis Perron, and former Sri Lankan Ambassador to the US, Mexico and Trinidad and Tobago Mahinda Samarasinghe were speaking at the 50th webinar organised by the Daily FT, Association of Chartered Certified Accountants (ACCA), and the International Chamber of Commerce Sri Lanka, together with Women in Management (WIM), the Sri Lanka Institute of Directors, the MBA Alumni Association of the University of Colombo, and Pioneer Institute of Business and Technology, on Saturday. The webinar was titled “In an Emerging New World Order, What Are Sri Lanka’s Options?” Garza, who visited Colombo in 2023 amid the economic crisis, said stability had since improved, growth had returned, and reforms were underway, but the world had changed profoundly. “We are not witnessing the end of globalisation, we are witnessing its transformation,” she said. She identified three opportunities. The first was diversification and regional integration, as over-dependence on a few markets, suppliers, or partners created vulnerability. Sri Lanka’s Indian Ocean location, its ties with India, and its connections across Asia, Europe, and the US allowed it to deepen its role in regional value chains, logistics, services, and higher-value exports. “The objective should not be to choose between competing economic powers, but to build diversified relationships that preserve economic opportunity and strategic flexibility,” she said. The second was digital transformation underpinned by institutional trust. Welcoming progress towards paperless customs, Garza cautioned that technology could make procedures faster without making them better. “The countries that benefit most will not necessarily be those that adopt technology fastest, but those that develop the institutional capacity to use it effectively,” she said. The third was renewing international cooperation, as predictable rules were essential infrastructure for smaller economies, the most exposed when cooperation gave way to power-based negotiations, she said. Samarasinghe, Ambassador in Washington for five years, said the US remained the world’s largest economy and importer, which was why leaders scrambled to strike deals after the Donald Trump Administration’s reciprocal tariffs of April 2025. Some 45 countries had since signed agreements under what he termed a carrot and stick approach, with Washington pursuing geopolitical objectives through trade talks. The sticks included surcharges on buyers of cheap Russian oil, since rolled back but liable to return, and a 40% surcharge on Vietnam over transshipment. The US also insisted on bilateral terms, full or near-full duty-free access for its exports, and US standards for its agricultural exports, he said. The carrot was a locked-in tariff rate, such as 15%, 19%, or 20%, shielded from fresh probes including Section 301 investigations, plus zero rating for thousands of goods. In return, partners made large pledges: the EU a non-binding $ 600 billion in investment and $ 750 billion in oil, gas, and nuclear fuel purchases, Japan $ 550 billion, Taiwan $ 500 billion, South Korea $ 300 billion, and India $ 500 billion. While tariff pressure had expedited alternatives such as the India-EU free trade agreement (FTA) after 17 years of talks, the US would remain the predominant economic force, he said. He urged Sri Lanka to keep exercising “smart options,” citing its role in Operation Prosperity Guardian in the Red Sea under President Ranil Wickremesinghe and the present Government’s handling of the Iranian ship issue, which the White House and the State Department praised for keeping the US informed while maintaining neutrality. “It is in Sri Lanka’s interest to have the best of relations with the US,” he said. Dr. Perron said Donald Trump’s return marked the end of sole US dominance after the Cold War, giving way to competing superpowers. A likely Democrat House majority after the midterms would deepen gridlock, leaving the world’s largest economy able to pass a budget only under threat of a Government shutdown, he said. Regional and medium powers such as Turkey, Brazil, Saudi Arabia, and Indonesia would grow more assertive amid shifting alliances. “You get a better deal from the superpowers if you do a balancing act as a country,” he said, adding that Wickremesinghe had done an outstanding job of this for Sri Lanka. The new order would be unstable, with regional wars likely, forcing many countries to follow the Israeli and Polish model of heavy defence spending while international law, the UN, and the World Trade Organisation (WTO) were sidelined, Dr. Perron warned. Citing the diverging fortunes of Colombia and Venezuela, Poland and Ukraine, and South and North Korea, he said the difference lay in the choices of political leadership.

audit.headline: Finalise ETCA with India before other trade deals: Ranil
audit.summary: EX- President Ranil Wickremesinghe has called for Sri Lanka to finalise the Economic and Technology Cooperation Agreement (ETCA) with India as its first trade priority, ahead of free trade agreements (FTAs) with other Asian economies. “Our first one is that we have to do the agreement with India,” Wickremesinghe said, noting that the agreement was currently suspended. He was speaking at the 50th webinar organised by the Daily FT, Association of Chartered Certified Accountants (ACCA), and the International Chamber of Commerce Sri Lanka, together with Women in Management (WIM), the Sri Lanka Institute of Directors, the MBA Alumni Association of the University of Colombo, and Pioneer Institute of Business and Technology, on Saturday.
audit.body: EX- President Ranil Wickremesinghe has called for Sri Lanka to finalise the Economic and Technology Cooperation Agreement (ETCA) with India as its first trade priority, ahead of free trade agreements (FTAs) with other Asian economies. “Our first one is that we have to do the agreement with India,” Wickremesinghe said, noting that the agreement was currently suspended. He was speaking at the 50th webinar organised by the Daily FT, Association of Chartered Certified Accountants (ACCA), and the International Chamber of Commerce Sri Lanka, together with Women in Management (WIM), the Sri Lanka Institute of Directors, the MBA Alumni Association of the University of Colombo, and Pioneer Institute of Business and Technology, on Saturday. Asked whether India would change the global order, Wickremesinghe said that while the order currently appeared to rest on the US, China, and Russia, India could not be ignored. “It’s going to be the third-largest GDP in the world. It’s a military power and it is the dominant power in the Indian Ocean. So at some stage, India has to come in,” he said. The US, he noted, had also improved relations with Pakistan, and how it balanced these relationships would matter. On managing relations with India and China, he said Sri Lanka and India were close and should be closer, keeping the spirit of the exchange of letters between Rajiv Gandhi and J.R. Jayewardene that neither country would do anything to harm the security of the other. Relations had evolved since the time of Emperor Ashoka according to developments in the world, he said. “Now, it’s not a question of India or China, it’s how India and China manage their relationships,” he said. With China set to enter the Bay of Bengal, Myanmar and Bangladesh would become places of competing influence, he added, noting that India was strengthening its friendship with Myanmar and that both India and China, as BRICS members, would have to reach an understanding on how the region developed.

audit.headline: Gamani Corea Foundation Memorial Lecture on Sri Lanka’s foreign policy on 4 Nov.
audit.summary: The Gamani Corea Foundation will host the annual Dr. Gamani Corea Memorial Lecture 2026 on 4 November 2026 at the Bandaranaike Centre for International Studies (BCIS), Colombo 07. The lecture, titled “The Paradoxes of Sri Lanka’s Foreign Policy in the 21st Century,” will be delivered by Ambassador (Retd.) He also serves as a Board Member of the Gamani Corea Foundation, BCIS and MARGA. The program will commence at 4:30 p.m. Those interested in attending are encouraged to register on or before 29 October 2026.

audit.headline: Huawei and Qualcomm announce broad patent licence agreement
