audit.body: Huawei and Qualcomm has announced a multi-year, broad patent licence agreement that includes cross licences to the companies’ patent portfolios across a range of technology fields, including 5G, compute, AI, and networking, together with Qualcomm’s purchase of certain Huawei US patents in the areas of compute, AI, networking, and other technologies. This transaction will close following receipt of the necessary regulatory approvals. The agreement reflects the companies’ shared commitment to intellectual property rights and to licensing practices consistent with fair, reasonable and non-discriminatory (FRAND) principles. Huawei’s Chief Intellectual Property Officer Alan Fan said: “Huawei’s decades of sustained investment in fundamental R&D have driven innovation and progress in mobile communications and other technology fields. Huawei’s broad contributions to the 4G/5G standards, such as the near-physical-limit signal transmission technology using polar codes, have established Huawei’s leadership in the mobile communications industry, and continuously transformed the way people communicate and live.” “This agreement not only demonstrates the value of Huawei’s innovations, but also recognises Qualcomm’s foundational contributions to modern communication technologies,” Fan added. Qualcomm Technology Licensing Executive Vice President and General Manager John Han said: “Qualcomm has invested in foundational wireless technologies that have enabled successive generations of mobile innovation and earned broad recognition across the global wireless industry. This agreement reaffirms industry recognition of Qualcomm’s 5G technology leadership and the success of Qualcomm’s 5G SEP licensing program. This agreement likewise reflects Qualcomm’s recognition of Huawei’s continued innovation and intellectual property in 5G and other technology fields.”

audit.headline: Is saffron robe above the law?
audit.summary: Time has come to confront a dangerous and long-standing problem of the belief among certain Buddhist monks that wearing the saffron robe places them above the law. The ongoing campaign demanding a presidential pardon for the convicted monk Galabodaatte Gnanasara, accompanied by threats and ultimatums directed at President Anura Kumara Dissanayake, has exposed the arrogance of those who mistake religious robes for political immunity. The President and his Government must stand firm. No individual, regardless of their religious standing, should be permitted to intimidate the state or demand that justice be circumvented. During the protests calling for Gnanasara’s release, monk Balangoda Kassapa reportedly challenged President Dissanayake to either resign or grant the imprisoned monk a presidential pardon. The audacity is breathtaking.
audit.body: Time has come to confront a dangerous and long-standing problem of the belief among certain Buddhist monks that wearing the saffron robe places them above the law. The ongoing campaign demanding a presidential pardon for the convicted monk Galabodaatte Gnanasara, accompanied by threats and ultimatums directed at President Anura Kumara Dissanayake, has exposed the arrogance of those who mistake religious robes for political immunity. The President and his Government must stand firm. No individual, regardless of their religious standing, should be permitted to intimidate the state or demand that justice be circumvented. During the protests calling for Gnanasara’s release, monk Balangoda Kassapa reportedly challenged President Dissanayake to either resign or grant the imprisoned monk a presidential pardon. The audacity is breathtaking. By what authority does a religious figure presume to dictate terms to an elected head of state and on what grounds should a convicted criminal receive special treatment simply because he wears a robe? A presidential pardon is a constitutional power, not a bargaining chip to appease an angry religious faction. Its exercise must be guided by justice, principle and the public interest, not threats, political pressure or the fear of offending powerful religious institutions. If the law has been applied through due process, the mere fact that a convicted individual is a Buddhist monk cannot become grounds for demanding an exception. The spectacle becomes even more disturbing when one considers the conduct of those claiming to defend Buddhism. Last week, gathered monks reportedly resorted to chanting ‘vas kavi’ or curses directed at the President. These are supposedly men who have dedicated their lives to the teachings of the Buddha, whose Dhamma emphasises compassion, restraint, non-violence and the conquest of hatred. In the Kakacūpama Sutta, the Buddha instructs his disciples that even if bandits were to savagely sever their limbs with a two-handled saw, they should not allow their minds to become consumed by hatred. “Those who harbour ill will, he teaches, do not uphold my teachings” he says. Yet here we have individuals invoking Buddhism while publicly expressing hostility towards the country›s elected leader because he has not granted their demand. Of course, not all Buddhist monks behave this way, and many perform invaluable work in their communities. But respect for the genuine contribution of the Sangha must not become a shield for those who exploit religion for political influence, personal enrichment or protection from accountability. For far too long, sections of the clergy have enjoyed a status that discourages criticism and invites politicians to bend the knee. Successive Governments have often treated the demands of influential monks as political commands, fearful that challenging them might carry an electoral price. This culture of deference has allowed religious authority to be weaponised against democratic institutions and the rule of law. President Dissanayake›s Government has an opportunity and in fact an obligation to break with this tradition. It must make clear that the law applies equally to every citizen, whether they wear a suit, a uniform or a saffron robe. The police must enforce the law impartially, courts must operate without intimidation, and the Government must resist attempts to turn religious sentiment into a licence for coercion. This is not an attack on Buddhism. It is a defence of Buddhism against those who would hijack its moral authority for their own purposes. Nor is it an argument against the legitimate exercise of presidential clemency. It is an argument against demanding clemency as an entitlement. The saffron robe deserves respect when it represents the Dhamma. It deserves no immunity when it is used to intimidate, threaten or obstruct justice.

audit.headline: Lankan envoy in Bangladesh meets Dhaka Chamber of Commerce and Industry
audit.summary: The High Commissioner of Sri Lanka to Bangladesh, Dharmapala Weerakkody, met with the Dhaka Chamber of Commerce and Industry (DCCI) President Taskeen Ahmed, on 18 October 2026 at the DCCI office in Gulshan, Dhaka, to explore avenues for strengthening economic, trade and investment cooperation between Sri Lanka and Bangladesh. The DCCI is a prominent private-sector business organisation in Bangladesh that represents businesses and entrepreneurs, particularly in Dhaka, and promotes trade, investment and industrial development through policy advocacy, business networking and public-private sector collaboration. The discussions focused on enhancing bilateral trade and investment by creating opportunities for the business communities of both countries in pharmaceuticals, Information Technology (IT), renewable energy, logistics, tourism and other emerging sectors.
audit.body: The High Commissioner of Sri Lanka to Bangladesh, Dharmapala Weerakkody, met with the Dhaka Chamber of Commerce and Industry (DCCI) President Taskeen Ahmed, on 18 October 2026 at the DCCI office in Gulshan, Dhaka, to explore avenues for strengthening economic, trade and investment cooperation between Sri Lanka and Bangladesh. The DCCI is a prominent private-sector business organisation in Bangladesh that represents businesses and entrepreneurs, particularly in Dhaka, and promotes trade, investment and industrial development through policy advocacy, business networking and public-private sector collaboration. The discussions focused on enhancing bilateral trade and investment by creating opportunities for the business communities of both countries in pharmaceuticals, Information Technology (IT), renewable energy, logistics, tourism and other emerging sectors. During the meeting, High Commissioner Weerakkody briefed the DCCI President on Sri Lanka Expo 2027, Sri Lanka’s premier international trade exhibition, scheduled to be held from 14 to 17 January 2027 at the Bandaranaike Memorial International Conference Hall (BMICH) in Colombo. He invited the DCCI to facilitate the participation of a business delegation at the exhibition, which will provide a platform for businesses from both countries to explore trade, investment and commercial partnerships. The DCCI President welcomed the initiative and expressed a positive response to the proposed participation of a business delegation at Sri Lanka Expo 2027, highlighting the potential to strengthen business-to-business linkages and expand bilateral trade and investment. Highlighting advances in the artificial intelligence (AI) sector in both countries, the DCCI President invited Sri Lanka to participate in the “Bangladesh AI Business Summit 2026”, organised by the DCCI in partnership with the Ministry of Science and Technology (MoST) of Bangladesh. The Summit is scheduled to be held on 5 November 2026 at the Bangladesh-China Friendship Conference Center (BCFCC) in Sher-e-Bangla Nagar, Dhaka. The meeting also underscored the importance of strengthening direct engagement between the private sectors of Sri Lanka and Bangladesh and identifying new areas of collaboration to support sustained economic growth and closer bilateral relations. The Second Secretary of the High Commission of Sri Lanka in Dhaka, Gayanga Dias, the DCCI Vice President Salem Sulaiman, and other senior DCCI officials were also present at the meeting.

audit.headline: Lankan pharmaceutical manufacturers gain global exposure at CPHI Worldwide 2026 in Milan
audit.summary: The Sri Lanka Export Development Board (EDB), in collaboration with the Embassy of Sri Lanka in Rome and the Consulate General of Sri Lanka in Milan, facilitated an exposure visit for Sri Lankan pharmaceutical manufacturers to the 37th edition of CPHI Worldwide 2026, held from 6 to 8 October 2026 at Fiera Milano, Milan, Italy. The program also included dedicated business networking sessions in Milan for the pharmaceutical sector. A five-member business delegation representing five Sri Lankan companies participated in the exposure visit to explore opportunities to strengthen the international market presence of Sri Lankan manufacturers.
audit.body: The Sri Lanka Export Development Board (EDB), in collaboration with the Embassy of Sri Lanka in Rome and the Consulate General of Sri Lanka in Milan, facilitated an exposure visit for Sri Lankan pharmaceutical manufacturers to the 37th edition of CPHI Worldwide 2026, held from 6 to 8 October 2026 at Fiera Milano, Milan, Italy. The program also included dedicated business networking sessions in Milan for the pharmaceutical sector. A five-member business delegation representing five Sri Lankan companies participated in the exposure visit to explore opportunities to strengthen the international market presence of Sri Lankan manufacturers. The participating companies were State Pharmaceutical Manufacturing Corporation, Siddhalepa Exports Ltd., Lina Manufacturing Ltd., Vetpharma Biotechnology Ltd., and Aithra Pharmaceuticals Ltd,, representing the pharmaceutical, veterinary, cosmeceutical and natural products sectors. The program provided an opportunity to gain exposure to international markets, explore potential business partnerships and identify avenues for expanding Sri Lanka’s presence in global markets. CPHI Worldwide is a major international platform connecting stakeholders across the pharmaceutical value chain, including pharmaceutical manufacturers, active pharmaceutical ingredient (API) suppliers, contract development and manufacturing organisations (CDMOs), packaging providers, and specialist technical service companies. The event provides opportunities to explore emerging market trends, establish business relationships, and identify potential areas for commercial and technical cooperation. Participation in the event enabled the Sri Lankan delegation to gain exposure to international pharmaceutical industry developments, explore potential export markets, and identify opportunities for collaboration with international industry stakeholders. The pharmaceutical industry operates within a highly regulated environment, with manufacturers required to meet applicable product registration, quality, and regulatory requirements in both domestic and export markets. Obtaining market authorisation can be a lengthy and costly process, particularly in highly regulated markets where stringent manufacturing standards, including European Union Good Manufacturing Practice (EU-GMP) requirements, may apply. Despite these developments, the sector continues to face challenges in keeping pace with evolving international market requirements, emerging products and technologies, regulatory frameworks, marketing strategies, new molecules, advanced manufacturing systems, and global pharmaceutical supply chains. Addressing these knowledge gaps is important to support the transition towards higher-value production and improved access to more regulated export markets. Recognising these needs, the EDB facilitated the exposure visit to provide participating companies with opportunities to observe international industry developments, improve their understanding of global market expectations, and identify potential business and technology partnerships. In addition to the exhibition visit, the Consulate General of Sri Lanka in Milan organised business networking sessions for the Sri Lankan delegation. These sessions provided participants with opportunities to engage with potential buyers, distributors, and other pharmaceutical industry stakeholders, explore prospective export markets, and discuss possible business collaborations. The exposure visit to CPHI Worldwide 2026 enabled the Sri Lankan delegation to engage with international pharmaceutical companies and specialised service providers, including Barbados Pharmaceutical Inc. (Barbados), Orion GXP Consulting (Ireland), Gruppo Farmalpresa (Italy), Intertek (United Kingdom), Nanopharm (France) and NATAC (Spain), as well as representatives of the Ministry of Health of Tanzania. These engagements provided opportunities to explore potential business partnerships, technical cooperation, pharmaceutical product development, natural ingredients, regulatory requirements and international market development. The EDB said it will continue to work with industry stakeholders and Sri Lanka’s overseas missions to promote Sri Lankan pharmaceutical products, facilitate international business linkages, and support the long-term development and competitiveness of the country’s pharmaceutical export sector.

audit.headline: Monks pause protest seeking Gnanasara release
audit.summary: Protesting monks surrounded the Presidential Secretariat on 15 October before moving to Viharamahadevi Park where the protest was temporarily paused yesterday - Chief Prelates urge protesting monks to uphold discipline The satyagraha at Viharamahadevi Park in Colombo demanding the release of Bodu Bala Sena General Secretary Ven. Galagodaatte Gnanasara Thero has been temporarily suspended, Ven. Ulapane Sumangala Thero said yesterday. Addressing the media yesterday afternoon alongside the Buddhist monks taking part in the satyagraha, Ven. Sumangala Thero said the decision was taken following information that the Mahanayake Theros of the Three Nikayas were intervening to secure Ven. Gnanasara Thero’s release.
audit.body: Protesting monks surrounded the Presidential Secretariat on 15 October before moving to Viharamahadevi Park where the protest was temporarily paused yesterday - Chief Prelates urge protesting monks to uphold discipline The satyagraha at Viharamahadevi Park in Colombo demanding the release of Bodu Bala Sena General Secretary Ven. Galagodaatte Gnanasara Thero has been temporarily suspended, Ven. Ulapane Sumangala Thero said yesterday. Addressing the media yesterday afternoon alongside the Buddhist monks taking part in the satyagraha, Ven. Sumangala Thero said the decision was taken following information that the Mahanayake Theros of the Three Nikayas were intervening to secure Ven. Gnanasara Thero’s release. The Mahanayake Theros of the Three Nikayas yesterday called on Buddhist monks to uphold monastic discipline and harmony, warning that certain groups were exploiting ongoing protests demanding a presidential pardon for Ven. Galagodaatte Gnanasara Thero to damage the reputation of the Buddhist clergy locally and internationally. In a special statement, the senior prelates said they had already intervened and initiated discussions with the Government to resolve the matter through legal means and dialogue. The respect accorded to Buddhist monks in Sri Lanka’s religious and social context, they said, depended on the preservation of monastic discipline (Vinaya) and spiritual restraint. The prelates called on members of the Maha Sangha, the order of Buddhist monks, across all Nikayas to maintain unity and harmony within the clergy and to resolve disputes in accordance with the Dhamma and Vinaya, while acting in a manner that would strengthen public confidence and faith. The statement was issued by Siam Nikaya Malwathu Chapter Mahanayake Most Ven. Tibbatuwawe Sri Siddhartha Sumangala Thero, Siam Nikaya Asgiri Chapter Mahanayake Most Ven. Warakagoda Sri Pannananda Dhammasiddhi Thero, Sri Lanka Amarapura Nikaya Supreme Mahanayake Most Ven. Karagoda Uyangoda Maithree Moorthi Thero and Sri Lanka Ramanna Nikaya Mahanayake Most Ven. Makulawewa Sri Wimala Thero.

audit.headline: National QR payment adoption program ‘Lucky Draw’ debuts tomorrow
audit.summary: - Rs. 51 m in cash across over 6,000 winners - Weekly and monthly cash prizes up to Rs. 1 m per winner The national QR payment adoption program is set to soon launch its ‘Lucky Draw,’ with the first draws scheduled for 27 October 2026. This registration-free nationwide draw aims to encourage and reward the everyday use of LankaQR payments by both customers and merchants. All transactions made between 1 September 2026 – 28 February 2027 will be eligible, and every customer or merchant who has used LankaQR since 1 September 2026 is automatically considered, providing a hassle-free experience. Participants have the chance to win two types of cash prizes; a weekly draw prize of Rs. 5,000 (250 winners weekly) and a monthly grand draw prizes of Rs. 1,000,000 (two winners), Rs. 500,000 (two winners) and Rs. 250,000 (two winners).
audit.body: - Rs. 51 m in cash across over 6,000 winners - Weekly and monthly cash prizes up to Rs. 1 m per winner The national QR payment adoption program is set to soon launch its ‘Lucky Draw,’ with the first draws scheduled for 27 October 2026. This registration-free nationwide draw aims to encourage and reward the everyday use of LankaQR payments by both customers and merchants. All transactions made between 1 September 2026 – 28 February 2027 will be eligible, and every customer or merchant who has used LankaQR since 1 September 2026 is automatically considered, providing a hassle-free experience. Participants have the chance to win two types of cash prizes; a weekly draw prize of Rs. 5,000 (250 winners weekly) and a monthly grand draw prizes of Rs. 1,000,000 (two winners), Rs. 500,000 (two winners) and Rs. 250,000 (two winners). Weekly draws select 250 winners (125 merchants and 125 customers), whereas the monthly grand draws select six winners (three customers and three merchants). The total prize pool across the six months is estimated at Rs. 51,000,000. Each eligible LankaQR transaction (person to merchant transactions and person to person transactions are both eligible) enters both parties to both of these draws. All prizes will be credited directly to the winner’s bank account. For a given month, all four weekly draws and the monthly draw will be held in the following month. On 27 October, four weekly draws and one monthly grand draw will be conducted covering September. The draw is based on transaction data received from participating banks, and run by LankaPay and supported by GovTech. For transparency, a designated Draw Committee oversees every draw, comprising at least one representative from the Ministry of Digital Economy, the Ministry of Finance, Planning, and Economic Development, the Central Bank of Sri Lanka, and the Auditor General’s Department. To maintain transparency, winners will be announced within two weeks via each bank, and the prizepool distribution via the Ministry of Digital Economy and GovTech.

audit.headline: National forum to strengthen dialogue in public service
audit.summary: Public Administration, Provincial Councils and Local Government Ministry Secretary S. Alokabandara (left) hands over the Declaration on Social Dialogue in the Public Service to Secretary to the President Dr. Nandika Sanath Kumanayake at the launch of the National Public Service Forum - Public Administration, Provincial Councils and Local Government Ministry launches key initiative with support from International Labour Organisation, United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation and United Nations Population Fund The Public Administration, Provincial Councils and Local Government Ministry in partnership with the International Labour Organisation (ILO), last week launched the National Public Service Dialogue Forum.
audit.body: Public Administration, Provincial Councils and Local Government Ministry Secretary S. Alokabandara (left) hands over the Declaration on Social Dialogue in the Public Service to Secretary to the President Dr. Nandika Sanath Kumanayake at the launch of the National Public Service Forum - Public Administration, Provincial Councils and Local Government Ministry launches key initiative with support from International Labour Organisation, United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation and United Nations Population Fund The Public Administration, Provincial Councils and Local Government Ministry in partnership with the International Labour Organisation (ILO), last week launched the National Public Service Dialogue Forum. The Forum provides a formal and structured space for government administrators and public service employees across the country to discuss workplace issues and concerns. It allows workplace challenges and grievances to be addressed through dialogue and joint problem-solving. By improving workplace relations and strengthening accountability, the Forum aims to contribute to a public service that is more responsive and resilient. The framework operates at three levels—workplace, sectoral and national—so that issues can be addressed at the appropriate level. Workplace forums deal with issues within individual institutions. Issues that cannot be resolved there can be taken to sectoral forums. The National forum addresses issues that affect more than one sector or require action by central government authorities. Public Service handed over by Public Administration, Provincial Councils and Local Government Ministry Secretary S. Alokabandara said: “The National Public Service Dialogue Forum gives administrators and employees a permanent space to raise concerns early and resolve them together, so that services to citizens continue without interruption. It can also help ensure that reforms, including digitalization and training, take account of the experience of the people responsible for delivering public services.” Established workplace forums have already demonstrated how dialogue was used to address challenges ranging from promotion processes to workplace safety, while identifying ways to strengthen organizational performance and improve service delivery. Building on this experience, the national forum aims to contribute to peacebuilding, strengthen institutional resilience and social cohesion, and improve overall public service delivery. United Nations Resident Coordinator in Sri Lanka Marc-André Franche said: “Public services are where people experience government in their everyday lives. Strengthening those services also means strengthening trust between people and institutions. This Forum is a recognition that lasting peace must be built through dialogue, inclusion and social justice, not enforcement alone.” ILO Country Office for Sri Lanka and the Maldives Director Joni Simpson said: “Social dialogue helps build trust between public institutions and workers by providing a structured way to raise concerns, discuss solutions and manage change. This is essential to preventing disputes and supporting a public service that responds effectively to people’s needs.” The establishment of the National Forum is supported by the “Social Dialogue for Peace and Crisis Prevention in Sri Lanka” project, which promotes inclusive approaches to dispute resolution and strengthens cooperation across public institutions. This project is implemented by the International Labour Organisation (ILO), United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation (UNESCO) and the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA). The launch of the National Forum reflects a shift towards more proactive, collaborative governance, recognising that meaningful worker participation, responsive institutions and constructive engagement between government and employees can contribute to lasting peace and economic stability.

audit.headline: Nirosh De Silva elected JASTECA President for 2026/28
audit.summary: - New leadership to drive innovation, digital transformation and stronger Sri Lanka–Japan technical, business and cultural ties Nirosh De Silva has been elected President of the Japan Sri Lanka Technical and Cultural Association (JASTECA) for the 2026–2028 term at the Association’s 40th Annual General Meeting held recently. His election marks a new chapter for JASTECA, with a renewed focus on innovation, Japanese management excellence, professional development, youth engagement and stronger collaboration between Sri Lanka and Japan. Established in 1984, JASTECA plays an important role in strengthening bilateral relations by promoting Japanese management practices, technical knowledge, cultural understanding and business cooperation.
audit.body: - New leadership to drive innovation, digital transformation and stronger Sri Lanka–Japan technical, business and cultural ties Nirosh De Silva has been elected President of the Japan Sri Lanka Technical and Cultural Association (JASTECA) for the 2026–2028 term at the Association’s 40th Annual General Meeting held recently. His election marks a new chapter for JASTECA, with a renewed focus on innovation, Japanese management excellence, professional development, youth engagement and stronger collaboration between Sri Lanka and Japan. Established in 1984, JASTECA plays an important role in strengthening bilateral relations by promoting Japanese management practices, technical knowledge, cultural understanding and business cooperation. The Association also supports the development of Sri Lankan professionals through training opportunities facilitated by the Association for Overseas Technical Cooperation and Sustainable Partnerships (AOTS) in Japan. Under the new leadership, JASTECA aims to further expand its contribution to Sri Lanka’s industrial and economic development by promoting the principles of Kaizen (continuous improvement), 5S, Lean Management and operational excellence, alongside digitalisation, environmental, social and governance (ESG) practices, and sustainable business development. A key priority will be to connect traditional Japanese management philosophies with modern business innovation and emerging technologies, enabling Sri Lankan organisations to enhance productivity, quality, competitiveness and sustainability in an increasingly challenging global business environment. The new administration also intends to strengthen professional development opportunities for AOTS alumni, encourage greater participation by young professionals, and create stronger platforms for knowledge-sharing between industry leaders, academics, entrepreneurs and Japanese partners. Revitalising youth-focused initiatives and expanding corporate engagement are expected to be important elements of this effort. JASTECA’s National Awards program will continue to provide a platform for recognising organisations and professionals that demonstrate excellence in Japanese management practices, particularly in 5S, Kaizen, corporate social responsibility and ESG. These initiatives are intended to encourage a culture of continuous improvement and recognise practical innovations that contribute to organisational and national development. The Association will also seek to deepen its engagement with the Embassy of Japan in Sri Lanka, AOTS, the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA), the Japan External Trade Organisation (JETRO), Japan Sri Lanka business council and other institutional partners to create further opportunities for technical cooperation, professional exchange and bilateral trade. With a professional background spanning human resource development, and organisational development, De Silva brings extensive corporate experience to the presidency. His leadership is expected to place particular emphasis on strengthening institutional governance, enhancing member engagement and translating the Association’s objectives into practical, measurable outcomes. The 2026–2028 term will focus on building a more connected and future-oriented JASTECA, one that preserves the enduring values of Japanese management while embracing innovation, sustainability and digital transformation. Through closer cooperation between Sri Lankan and Japanese stakeholders, JASTECA aims to reinforce the longstanding friendship between the two countries and contribute to a more productive, innovative and globally competitive Sri Lankan economy.

audit.headline: PM tells CNN IMF priorities align with Govt.’s own
audit.summary: Prime Minister Dr. Harini Amarasuriya - Says IMF approachable, Govt. able to raise concerns on governance, corruption, fiscal discipline - Economic stability among immediate priorities after election Prime Minister Dr. Harini Amarasuriya has told CNN that several of the International Monetary Fund’s (IMF) priorities align with the Government’s own objectives, underpinning its decision to continue Sri Lanka’s IMF program despite her party’s earlier opposition. Dr. Amarasuriya said the Government had been able to discuss its concerns with the IMF, particularly on governance, corruption, and fiscal discipline.
audit.body: Prime Minister Dr. Harini Amarasuriya - Says IMF approachable, Govt. able to raise concerns on governance, corruption, fiscal discipline - Economic stability among immediate priorities after election Prime Minister Dr. Harini Amarasuriya has told CNN that several of the International Monetary Fund’s (IMF) priorities align with the Government’s own objectives, underpinning its decision to continue Sri Lanka’s IMF program despite her party’s earlier opposition. Dr. Amarasuriya said the Government had been able to discuss its concerns with the IMF, particularly on governance, corruption, and fiscal discipline. “When we came into power, the IMF agreement was already signed and we started working with them, and we found them approachable,” she told CNN’s Richard Quest of ‘Quest Means Business.’ Maintaining economic stability was among the administration’s immediate priorities following the election, she said, adding that the country had made considerable progress since the 2022 crisis. “We are doing remarkably well given what we’ve been through,” she said. The Prime Minister attributed the improvement primarily to fiscal management, financial discipline, efforts to address corruption and waste, and governance reforms. Two years into the administration, she said, the situation was ‘looking not too bad.’ Acknowledging that her party had opposed the IMF program due to Sri Lanka’s previous experiences with the institution, she said the Government had no choice but to continue it. We didn’t like it because we felt that our previous experiences with the IMF have not been great. This is not the first time we’ve entered an IMF program,” she said. She also acknowledged that the Government had faced pressure to demonstrate its ability to govern, saying many people had been waiting for it to fail. Dr. Amarasuriya also reaffirmed Sri Lanka’s commitment to geopolitical neutrality and non-alignment, saying conflicts such as the war in the Middle East ‘serve no one.’ Sri Lanka’s geographical position in the Indian Ocean made it important for the country to stay clear of geopolitical conflicts amid rising global tensions, she said. Avoiding entanglement in international power struggles was essential for its national interests and economic stability, she stressed, particularly as the country faces the impact of rising fuel prices and global energy costs. Acknowledging that maintaining balanced relations with major powers, including China, India, and the US, had historically been a key challenge for Sri Lanka’s foreign policy, she said aligning too closely with any single power had not worked to the country’s advantage. This, she said, underscored the importance of maintaining an independent foreign policy amid growing international tensions.

audit.headline: Ranil’s 10-point plan for Sri Lanka to survive new world order
audit.summary: Former President Ranil Wickremesinghe - Says rapid tech-led modernisation non-negotiable; without it Sri Lanka will ‘fade into insignificance like one of the small Pacific Isles’ - Urges BRICS membership, transactional geopolitics with US, China, Russia, Japan - Calls for maritime logistics hub, faster Colombo Security Conclave work, tech-advanced Navy built on small and medium ships - Flags Bay of Bengal as region not to be ignored; says China gaining second access to Indian Ocean through it - Warns $ 100 b economy too small to sell more to Europe, US; eyes FTAs with Indonesia, Malaysia, Vietnam FORMER President Ranil Wickremesinghe has set out a 10-point plan for Sri Lanka to secure a place in an emerging world order, with rapid technological modernisation, membership of BRICS, and a stronger maritime role at its core.
audit.body: Former President Ranil Wickremesinghe - Says rapid tech-led modernisation non-negotiable; without it Sri Lanka will ‘fade into insignificance like one of the small Pacific Isles’ - Urges BRICS membership, transactional geopolitics with US, China, Russia, Japan - Calls for maritime logistics hub, faster Colombo Security Conclave work, tech-advanced Navy built on small and medium ships - Flags Bay of Bengal as region not to be ignored; says China gaining second access to Indian Ocean through it - Warns $ 100 b economy too small to sell more to Europe, US; eyes FTAs with Indonesia, Malaysia, Vietnam FORMER President Ranil Wickremesinghe has set out a 10-point plan for Sri Lanka to secure a place in an emerging world order, with rapid technological modernisation, membership of BRICS, and a stronger maritime role at its core. “If we do not do this, we will have no place in the new world order,” Wickremesinghe said, delivering the keynote at the 50th webinar organised by the Daily FT, Association of Chartered Certified Accountants (ACCA), and the International Chamber of Commerce Sri Lanka, together with Women in Management (WIM), the Sri Lanka Institute of Directors, the MBA Alumni Association of the University of Colombo, and Pioneer Institute of Business and Technology, on Saturday. The webinar was titled “In an Emerging New World Order, What Are Sri Lanka’s Options?” Among the requirements he set out were rapid technological modernisation resulting in a strong, competitive economy, making Sri Lanka a maritime logistics centre, close economic cooperation with India, and stronger relations with Bay of Bengal and other Southeast Asian countries, leading finally to regional integration. He also urged Sri Lanka to join BRICS, strengthen relations with the US, China, and Russia, as well as Japan, engage in transactional geopolitics, accelerate the work of the Colombo Security Conclave, and build a technologically advanced Navy with small and medium naval ships. “If you want to survive in this new global order, where technology plays this role and trade will certainly have an importance, either we have to go along this way or fade into insignificance like one of the small Pacific Isles,” he said. Wickremesinghe framed his proposals around Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s address at the NDTV World Summit, which characterised the present as a world between orders, with one ending and another beginning. Modi had highlighted the weaponising of finance, trade, technology, and shipping as part of the new geopolitics, he noted, adding that post-World War II institutions were unable to intervene as they had not adapted to the changing order. Modi had also invoked Chanakya on the need to prevent Matsya Nyaya, where the strong swallow the weak. Citing a Goldman Sachs report, Wickremesinghe said Artificial Intelligence (AI) and data ownership, combined with dollar-dominated global financial markets, formed the basis of US dominance, while China, the other AI superpower, was seeking an alternative with BRICS members. “What we are witnessing today is a duopoly of AI and computing superpowers,” he said, adding that China and the US also led in space, ocean, and automation technologies, while India, the UK, France, Germany, Israel, Japan, and South Korea were developing their own. “We have to remember sovereignty today implies technology.” He said the decline of Western-led alliances was giving way to transactional geopolitics between the leading powers, and that Sri Lanka needed economic and social transformation based on technology-oriented modernisation, or it would be swallowed up. The Indian Ocean, he said, would be one of the centres of the new order alongside the emerging economies of Asia and Africa, strengthening its role as the main shipping artery between East and West, with immense undersea resources available for exploration. However, the US-Iran war had eroded the Indian Ocean’s status as a zone of peace and its freedom of navigation, he said, making it Sri Lanka’s interest to ensure that its two economic lifelines, the Suez Canal and the Gulf, remained fully operational. He urged policymakers not to ignore the Bay of Bengal as an economic region. Indonesia, projected to have the fourth or fifth largest GDP by 2050, would extend its influence, and Bangladesh would also emerge as an economic power, he said. Closer economic cooperation between Southeast Asia and Western China was producing the Chengdu-Chongqing corridor extending to Myanmar and Bangladesh, which he said would give China a second access to the Indian Ocean, this time through the Bay of Bengal. He also pointed to an economic region at Sri Lanka’s doorstep, a market of 600 million excluding India. Emerging technologies, including orbital maritime awareness satellites, hypersonic weapons, unmanned water vehicles, and drones, would play a major role in Indian Ocean security, he said, adding that protecting undersea cables in the region was a priority. On trade, Wickremesinghe, who said he had worked on agreements with Singapore and Thailand, named Indonesia, Malaysia, and Vietnam as the next targets. While Europe and the US remained important markets, Sri Lanka could not send more goods there and had to find markets elsewhere in Asia, “because that’s where the power is going to be.” “We are a hundred billion dollar GDP. We are so small. Most American corporations are bigger than that. So is Tata or Adani. We have to realise that and we must grow big,” he said. On the US midterm elections, he said foreign policy was unlikely to play a big role, and that both Vice President JD Vance and the Democrats appeared inclined to withdraw from global affairs, with the US relying instead on its financial and technological power. How the big powers and India drew their relations would determine “where and how we can play our pieces on the chessboard,” he said. “But to play the pieces on the chessboard, we have to become a strong economy. Otherwise, you are nowhere.” On AI, he warned of the emergence of trillion-dollar companies on both the US and Chinese sides, its impact on employment in India and Sri Lanka, and rising social tensions in the UK, France, and Germany if wealth concentrated among a handful of trillionaires. “We must know how to harness AI,” he said.

audit.headline: Reflections from IMF and World Bank Annuals in Bangkok
audit.summary: IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva (right) World Bank President Ajay Banga (second from right) Some global south governments, civil society, and think tanks, including Sri Lanka’s Institute of Political Economy, called for a different order of priorities, as many countries carry high debt-servicing obligations, poor public services, and lack access to adequate energy or water. They called for sufficient and predictable public finance to invest in health, education, energy, and food sovereignty. They raised the need for policy space to promote green industrial policies and to build the foundation for decent jobs for all The Thai hosts welcomed participants with remarkable hospitality and efficiency despite the conditions under which dissent was permitted.
audit.body: IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva (right) World Bank President Ajay Banga (second from right) Some global south governments, civil society, and think tanks, including Sri Lanka’s Institute of Political Economy, called for a different order of priorities, as many countries carry high debt-servicing obligations, poor public services, and lack access to adequate energy or water. They called for sufficient and predictable public finance to invest in health, education, energy, and food sovereignty. They raised the need for policy space to promote green industrial policies and to build the foundation for decent jobs for all The Thai hosts welcomed participants with remarkable hospitality and efficiency despite the conditions under which dissent was permitted. Hundreds of local demonstrators marched near the National Convention Centre, protesting land rights impacts, carbon pricing models, and policies perceived to u foreign capital over local livelihoods. Some made a strong case for a more fundamental reckoning: “Why Thailand Should Be Suing, Not Hosting the IMF.” The question was not rhetorical. It pointed to the land displacements, the conditionalities, and the structural adjustment legacies that have shaped Thailand’s own experience with the Bretton Woods institutions, and to the uncomfortable irony of a nation hosting the very architects of policies it has spent decades contesting. The local protests reflected the wishes of many participants who were keen to see meaningful reforms to the International Financial Institutions that would place the wellbeing of people and the environment over returns on wealth and capital. The status quo Whilst multiple global issues require urgent action, cooperation was lacking at the event and reflected the geopolitically fragmented world. As the US pushes back on climate financing, points fingers at the “distorted policies” of other countries, and fights a war of choice, it produces the energy crunch and negative consequences. IMF and the World Bank could and should have discussed the impact of these actions in a more insightful and meaningful manner. There was little self-reflection by the multilateral institutions on the policies and strategies that have contributed to the debt and economic crises facing many nations. The Debt Report 2026 (Broad Global South) published by Erlassjahr, a German think-tank, identified 44 countries in the Global South suffering from a “very high foreign debt burden,” with another 25 heavily burdened and 15 at latent risk. Artificial Intelligence (AI) was the answer to almost every question on growth posed to the Bretton Woods institutions, even as they sidestepped the structural failures such as debt, austerity, and the chronic underfunding of public goods, that define the actual constraints on growth in the Global South. More than a dozen official panel discussions addressed AI, including one titled “What would it take? Making Private Capital and AI Work for Countries”. Another panel featured Jack Clark, co-founder of Anthropic, as keynote speaker. This came in the same week that the Booker Prize–winning author Arundhati Roy published an essay titled “Apocalypse Now and Then”, on the dangers of AI driving inequality, in which she writes: “It feels a little like that moment before the tsunami in 2004. Remember how, in Thailand and Indonesia, the ocean drew back from the coastline? People ran out to marvel at the miles of pristine new beach that suddenly emerged, not realising that, far out at sea, a wall of water was building up and would come crashing over them. We’re in that moment now. A towering wall of stupidity is about to inundate us.” Benefits for the few Private capital took centre stage at the World Bank Group, which claimed $112 billion was mobilised during fiscal year 2026 while offering no evidence on the number or quality of jobs created. Warnings of record debt were met with more fiscal consolidation, tight monetary stances for price stability, supply-side and structural reforms, and inflation targeting through central bank policies from the IMF rather than replenishing its Poverty Reduction and Growth Trust, Resilience and Sustainability Trust, and Catastrophe Containment and Relief Trust to ramp up much-needed financing. It is disappointing that the international financial institutions have not been able to effectively replenish these specialised trust funds and financing vehicles managed by the IMF to support low-income and vulnerable economies. Help for the many Some global south governments, civil society, and think tanks, including Sri Lanka’s Institute of Political Economy, called for a different order of priorities, as many countries carry high debt-servicing obligations, poor public services, and lack access to adequate energy or water. They called for sufficient and predictable public finance to invest in health, education, energy, and food sovereignty. They raised the need for policy space to promote green industrial policies and to build the foundation for decent jobs for all. The most important conversations happened outside the official meetings. From the Borrowers’ Platform to coordinate on debt and financial architecture, the Xingu Talks for aligning global finance flows, the Southern Caucus on sovereign industrialisation, the Feminist Festival of Resistance and Alternatives making a compelling case for a gender-just economy, and the International Peoples Assembly mobilising for economic, social, and climate justice, Global South governments and movements were building their own alternatives. Their focus was policy sovereignty and a people-centred economy that values care and develops within planetary boundaries. These conversations reminded participants that alternatives are not only possible; they are already being imagined and built. There were calls for more grants and less debt, simple access, and faster disbursement. The serious issues facing Sri Lanka’s economy and its people as a result of the unjust global economic order echo what is being raised across the Global South. There is an urgent need for the Government and civil society organisations to show solidarity by uniting and joining forces with other nations and activists to drive reforms within the international financial institutions, through active participation in the UNCTAD Borrowers’ Platform and the UN Framework Convention on International Tax Cooperation, and by supporting the International Panel on Inequality, among other initiatives Where are the alternatives? Global debt and development campaigners such as Debt Justice UK, EuroDad, LatinDadd, Asia Peoples Movement for Debt and Development, AfroDad, Bretton Woods Project, MenaFem, IDEAs, Suramericana Vision, YukthiLk and numerous others, posed questions for finance policymakers. How can governments deal with the costs of today whilst protecting their ability to invest in tomorrow, at a time of limited fiscal space, high debt costs, energy and commodity price shocks, and the need to continue investing in health, education, climate resilience, and energy transition? How can debt governance incorporate external fiscal risks that affect debt sustainability but exist outside public borrowing? How can a new global standard on tax expenditure reporting, a vital step towards freeing up fiscal space, be introduced? And how can countries finance adaptation without worsening debt distress, external vulnerabilities, and pressures on essential public services? Local alternatives The serious issues facing Sri Lanka’s economy and its people as a result of the unjust global economic order echo what is being raised across the Global South. There is an urgent need for the Government and civil society organisations to show solidarity by uniting and joining forces with other nations and activists to drive reforms within the international financial institutions, through active participation in the UNCTAD Borrowers’ Platform and the UN Framework Convention on International Tax Cooperation, and by supporting the International Panel on Inequality, among other initiatives. The institutions that govern the global economy are structurally rigged against the South. Unilateral resistance is punished; collective action is shielded. Unity also means building alternatives, not merely demanding seats at a table that was never designed for them but sharing the vast resources of technical expertise, policy solutions and collective experience available to drive essential changes to a world that rewards capital controlled by a few, over the work of the many. (The author is a co-founder of the Institute of Political Economy (ipe-sl.org) and a former local councillor in London. He can be reached at [email protected].)

audit.headline: Sampath Bank’s Rs. 10 b debenture issue oversubscribed by 22.7%
audit.summary: Sampath Bank PLC’s debenture issue was oversubscribed and closed at its maximum of Rs. 10 billion, having drawn applications worth Rs. 12.27 billion, with a small number of large-value payments made through Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) transfers and Letters of Guarantee accounting for nearly the entire amount. According to the Registrars to the issue, Central Depository Systems Ltd., the bank received 31 applications for 122.66 million debentures as at 22 October, against a maximum of 100 million debentures on offer, oversubscribing the issue by 22.7%. Excess demand amounted to Rs. 2.27 billion, or 22.66 million debentures. The issue comprised up to 100 million Basel III-compliant Tier 2 listed, rated, unsecured, subordinated, redeemable debentures with five-year (2026/2031) and seven-year (2026/2033) tenures, at a par value of Rs. 100 each.
audit.body: Sampath Bank PLC’s debenture issue was oversubscribed and closed at its maximum of Rs. 10 billion, having drawn applications worth Rs. 12.27 billion, with a small number of large-value payments made through Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) transfers and Letters of Guarantee accounting for nearly the entire amount. According to the Registrars to the issue, Central Depository Systems Ltd., the bank received 31 applications for 122.66 million debentures as at 22 October, against a maximum of 100 million debentures on offer, oversubscribing the issue by 22.7%. Excess demand amounted to Rs. 2.27 billion, or 22.66 million debentures. The issue comprised up to 100 million Basel III-compliant Tier 2 listed, rated, unsecured, subordinated, redeemable debentures with five-year (2026/2031) and seven-year (2026/2033) tenures, at a par value of Rs. 100 each. It was structured as an initial 70 million debentures to raise Rs. 7 billion, with an option to issue a further 30 million to raise Rs. 3 billion at the bank’s discretion in the event of an oversubscription. Tier 2 debentures count towards a bank’s regulatory capital. Their non-viability conversion feature allows them to be converted into ordinary shares if the bank is deemed non-viable, meaning holders absorb losses ahead of depositors. RTGS transfers, the Central Bank of Sri Lanka (CBSL)-operated system for large-value interbank payments, were the dominant mode of payment. Eight applications paid via RTGS accounted for 80.5 million debentures worth Rs. 8.05 billion, or 65.6% of the total, an average of just over Rs. 1 billion per application. Payments by Letter of Guarantee came to Rs. 3.5 billion for 35 million debentures from three applications, or 28.5% of the total. In contrast, payments by bank drafts and cheques, which drew the highest number of applications at 20, amounted to Rs. 715.5 million for 7.16 million debentures, or 5.8% of the total value. By type, Type A debentures attracted 25 applications for 99.01 million debentures worth Rs. 9.9 billion. Of this, RTGS transfers accounted for Rs. 5.95 billion from six applications, Letters of Guarantee for Rs. 3.25 billion from two applications, and bank drafts and cheques for Rs. 700.5 million from 17 applications. Type B debentures drew six applications for 23.65 million debentures worth Rs. 2.37 billion. RTGS transfers accounted for Rs. 2.1 billion from two applications, a Letter of Guarantee for Rs. 250 million from one application, and bank drafts and cheques for Rs. 15 million from three applications.

audit.headline: Secondary Bond market yields see-saw; recover to close steady to higher
audit.summary: - Six- and 12-month Bill averages steady for second consecutive week - Foreign holdings in rupee Treasuries drops below Rs. 200 b - Rupee depreciates By Wealth Trust Securities The secondary Bond market initially commenced the trading week ending 23 October on a distinctly bearish footing, with aggressive selling interest driving yields sharply higher and extending the upward momentum from the previous week. However, the elevated yield levels attracted strong buying interest, which absorbed the selling pressure and provided firm support to the market. Traded volumes increased significantly as demand emerged at the higher levels. This paved the way for a recovery through the middle of the week, with yields reversing their initial increases and declining across medium to longer tenors amid sustained buying interest.
audit.body: - Six- and 12-month Bill averages steady for second consecutive week - Foreign holdings in rupee Treasuries drops below Rs. 200 b - Rupee depreciates By Wealth Trust Securities The secondary Bond market initially commenced the trading week ending 23 October on a distinctly bearish footing, with aggressive selling interest driving yields sharply higher and extending the upward momentum from the previous week. However, the elevated yield levels attracted strong buying interest, which absorbed the selling pressure and provided firm support to the market. Traded volumes increased significantly as demand emerged at the higher levels. This paved the way for a recovery through the middle of the week, with yields reversing their initial increases and declining across medium to longer tenors amid sustained buying interest. Activity and traded volumes remained healthy, reflecting improved demand at the recently elevated levels. Buying interest subsequently centred on the shorter 2028–2031 maturities, driving yields lower at the short end, while the remainder of the curve held broadly steady. Activity moderated towards the close of the week. Despite this recovery, two-way quotes closed slightly higher on the belly end of the curve after recovering from their intraweek highs while the short end remained steady, week on week. At the very short end of the curve, the 15.12.26 touched an intraweek high of 9.50% before trading down to a low of 9.42%, while the 15.01.27 traded at 9.50%. The 15.09.29 and 15.12.29 traded at 11.10% and 11.15% respectively. The 15.05.30 traded at 11.40%, while the 01.07.30 traded down from an intraweek high of 11.65% to a low of 11.50%. The 01.08.30 saw its yield ease off from 11.60%-11.50% while the 15.10.30 traded down the range of 11.65% to 11.55%. The 15.01.33 traded up to a high of 12.30% before easing to 12.17%, subsequent to hitting a weekly low of 12.10%. The 2031 and 2034 tenors exhibited the see-saw movement more profoundly, with the 01.02.31 and 01.12.31 increasing to weekly highs of 11.80% and 11.95% respectively from 11.65% and 11.80% opening lows before easing to 11.75% and 11.85% at the end of the week. All three 2034 tenors (15.06.34, 15.09.34 & 15.10.34) followed suit, increasing from an opening average low of 12.33% to highs of 12.55% and easing to close the week on 2-way quotes of 12.35%/12.45% across all the maturities. The 15.03.35 traded at 12.55%. At the weekly Treasury Bill auction conducted last Wednesday (21), weighted average yields were seen holding broadly steady for a second consecutive week with the rate on the 182-day and 364-day tenors remaining unchanged at 9.44% and 9.95% respectively for the second straight week. However, the 91-day tenor maturity saw its yield edge up marginally by 02 basis points to 9.32%. The Public Debt Management Office (PDMO) raised only Rs. 80.611 billion or 80.61% in total out of the Rs. 100 billion offered in total. The 91-day tenor recorded acceptance above its respective target allocation, while the 182-day and 364-day recorded acceptances below their respective offered amounts. Total bids received amounted to 1.86 times the overall offer. Meanwhile, the foreign holdings of rupee-denominated Government securities recorded a net outflow for the first time in four weeks, registering a decrease amounting 1.40% or Rs. 2.82 billion for the week ended 22 October. Accordingly, the total foreign holdings of rupee treasuries decreased to Rs. 199.54 billion. The Surplus liquidity in money markets was seen remaining elevated for the week ending 23 October 2026, at Rs. 384.90 billion albeit declining slightly as compared to its previous week’s closing level of Rs. 399.88 billion. The weighted average rates on Call Money and Repo closed last week at 9.00% and 9.06% as against 8.99% and 9.04% respectively the previous week. Furthermore, the rupee or the USD/LKR rate was seen depreciating, to close the week ending 23 October at Rs. 332.10/332.20 as against its previous week’s closing of Rs. 331.25/331.35. This was subsequent to trading within an intraweek high of Rs. 331.35 and a low of Rs. 332.26 intraweek. The average daily USD/LKR traded volume over the first four trading days of the week stood at $ 51.67 million. (References: Public Debt Management Office - Ministry of Finance, Central Bank of Sri Lanka, Bloomberg E-Bond Trading Platform, Money Broking Companies)

audit.headline: Sentiva’s Workforce Asia Summit on 4 Nov. to explore future of work in Colombo
audit.summary: First row from left: Dr. CJ Meadows, Anish Lalchandani, Yohan Liyanage, Zu Hui Yap, Kaushal Mendis, Azadeh Entezami. Second row from left: Ruwindhu Peiris, Chethana Liyanage, Ruwani Alwishewa, Suresh Muttiah, Rukshan Salgado Sentiva, an AI-native HR technology platform, will host Workforce Asia Summit 2026 on 4 November at The Forum, Cinnamon Life, Colombo. It brings together CHROs, HR practitioners and business leaders to examine how organisations can build the workforce of tomorrow. Workforce Asia Summit 2026 comes as organisations face shifting employee expectations, rapid advances in AI and fast-changing skill requirements. Its programme centres on talent management and skill-based organisations. It will cover workforce transformation, skills development, technology and leadership, with a focus on keeping people at the heart of progress.
audit.body: First row from left: Dr. CJ Meadows, Anish Lalchandani, Yohan Liyanage, Zu Hui Yap, Kaushal Mendis, Azadeh Entezami. Second row from left: Ruwindhu Peiris, Chethana Liyanage, Ruwani Alwishewa, Suresh Muttiah, Rukshan Salgado Sentiva, an AI-native HR technology platform, will host Workforce Asia Summit 2026 on 4 November at The Forum, Cinnamon Life, Colombo. It brings together CHROs, HR practitioners and business leaders to examine how organisations can build the workforce of tomorrow. Workforce Asia Summit 2026 comes as organisations face shifting employee expectations, rapid advances in AI and fast-changing skill requirements. Its programme centres on talent management and skill-based organisations. It will cover workforce transformation, skills development, technology and leadership, with a focus on keeping people at the heart of progress. Through keynote presentations, panel discussions and opportunities for professional engagement, participants will gain insights into the strategies and ideas influencing the future of organisations and their people. Overall, the summit will feature four Keynotes by local and global experts, each followed by an in-conversation session, two Interactive Sessions, a Leadership Panel where senior practitioners debate what great talent management looks like next, an Exhibitor Showcase with organisations bringing ideas, technology and innovation to the future of work together with networking opportunities throughout the day. Sentiva Founder and CEO Yohan Liyanage said: “People’s capabilities often extend far beyond their job titles. We created Workforce Asia Summit to challenge how organisations recognise and develop that potential - and ask honestly where AI can help, where it falls short and what leaders need to rethink. The summit will explore the changing workforce landscape, emerging skills, talent management, technology and leadership.” ARA Chief Executive Officer and MÕVA Managing Director Kaushal Mendis said: “I’m delighted to be back in the HR space at Workforce Asia Summit 2026, looking forward to thought-provoking conversations about how we recognise potential, develop skills, and create opportunities for people to thrive.” The keynote speakers at the summit include S P Jain School of Global Management- The Innovation and Entrepreneurship Centre Professor and Director Dr. CJ Meadows, A.P. Moller - Maersk Global Head of Talent Management and Author of ‘The Skills Advantage’ Anish Lalchandani, Sentiva Founder and CEO, Stanford GSB LEAD Distinguished Scholar and Forbes Technology Council Member Yohan Liyanage and Montfort Care Director, Strategy and Growth and Zu Hui Yap. The leadership panel will feature, Grant Thornton Stax Partner Ruwindhu Peiris; Capital Maharaja Group Chief Talent Officer Chethana Liyanage, Coach Masters Academy Director of Professional Developmen Azadeh Entezami and Great Place to Work Sri Lanka Chief Operating Officer Ruwani Alwishewa. The panel will be moderated by ARA Chief Executive Officer and MÕVA Managing Director Kaushal Mendis. The summit will also feature an Enterprise Case Study with Aitken Spence PLC Group Chief Human Resources Officer Suresh Muttiah and Sentiva Vice President – Head of Operations Rukshan Salgado. The session will offer a real-world perspective on using AI to manage talent acquisition at scale. With the future of work already reshaping how organisations attract, develop and retain talent, Workforce Asia Summit 2026 invites leaders to move beyond simply anticipating change and begin considering the actions needed to build stronger, more adaptable workplaces. Further information about the summit, its program and registration is available at www.workforceasiasummit.com.

audit.headline: Sri Lanka invites Georgian businesses to SL EXPO 2027
audit.summary: The Embassy of Sri Lanka in Ankara, concurrently accredited to Georgia, in collaboration with the Honorary Consuls of Sri Lanka in Tbilisi and Batumi, successfully organised the first-ever Sri Lanka-Georgia Business Forum in Tbilisi, on 16 October 2026. The Forum acted as a valuable platform to introduce Sri Lanka’s growing trade and investment potential to the Georgian business community and to encourage greater participation in Sri Lanka EXPO 2027 (SLEXPO 2027), Sri Lanka’s flagship trade and investment exhibition. The opening session featured remarks by the Ambassador of Sri Lanka to Georgia, resident in Ankara, Niluka Kadurugamuwa, Honorary Consul of Sri Lanka in Tbilisi Nino Makhviladze, and Honorary Consul of Sri Lanka in Batumi Misha Dzadzamia.
audit.body: The Embassy of Sri Lanka in Ankara, concurrently accredited to Georgia, in collaboration with the Honorary Consuls of Sri Lanka in Tbilisi and Batumi, successfully organised the first-ever Sri Lanka-Georgia Business Forum in Tbilisi, on 16 October 2026. The Forum acted as a valuable platform to introduce Sri Lanka’s growing trade and investment potential to the Georgian business community and to encourage greater participation in Sri Lanka EXPO 2027 (SLEXPO 2027), Sri Lanka’s flagship trade and investment exhibition. The opening session featured remarks by the Ambassador of Sri Lanka to Georgia, resident in Ankara, Niluka Kadurugamuwa, Honorary Consul of Sri Lanka in Tbilisi Nino Makhviladze, and Honorary Consul of Sri Lanka in Batumi Misha Dzadzamia. The speakers highlighted Sri Lanka’s potential as an emerging market and a promising investment destination, while underscoring the importance of strengthening business-to-business connections and expanding economic cooperation between Sri Lanka and Georgia. At the Forum, First Secretary (Commercial) of the Embassy of Sri Lanka in Ankara, Dilanga Hettiarachchi made a comprehensive presentation on Sri Lanka’s trade and investment opportunities. He also introduced SLEXPO 2027, highlighting the opportunities available for Georgian buyers, investors and business representatives to establish new partnerships, explore business prospects and strengthen commercial ties with Sri Lankan counterparts. The Forum brought together business representatives, traders, buyers and investors, facilitating networking, exchange of information and discussions on potential areas for enhanced bilateral trade and investment cooperation. The event received a wide media coverage in Georgia, including through its national television. Speaking to the media, the Ambassador invited the Georgian business community to explore Sri Lanka as a promising destination for trade, investment, and business partnerships, highlighting the opportunities available to strengthen economic cooperation between the two countries.

audit.headline: Sri Lanka, Romania hold sixth round of political consultations
audit.summary: The sixth round of Sri Lanka–Romania Political Consultations was successfully concluded on 22 October 2026 at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Romania, marking an important step in advancing bilateral relations. Established under a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) signed in 2013, the consultations serve as a platform for reviewing bilateral relations and exchanging views on regional and global developments. The consultations were Co-chaired by the Sri Lankan Foreign Affairs and Foreign Employment Deputy Minister Arun Hemachandra, and the Romanian State Secretary for Strategic Affairs Ana Cristina Tinca. Reviewing the progress made since the fifth round of consultations held in Colombo in June 2023, Deputy Minister Hemachandra briefed the Romanian delegation on Sri Lanka’s progress towards economic stabilisation and macroeconomic resilience.
audit.body: The sixth round of Sri Lanka–Romania Political Consultations was successfully concluded on 22 October 2026 at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Romania, marking an important step in advancing bilateral relations. Established under a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) signed in 2013, the consultations serve as a platform for reviewing bilateral relations and exchanging views on regional and global developments. The consultations were Co-chaired by the Sri Lankan Foreign Affairs and Foreign Employment Deputy Minister Arun Hemachandra, and the Romanian State Secretary for Strategic Affairs Ana Cristina Tinca. Reviewing the progress made since the fifth round of consultations held in Colombo in June 2023, Deputy Minister Hemachandra briefed the Romanian delegation on Sri Lanka’s progress towards economic stabilisation and macroeconomic resilience. He highlighted the governance reforms introduced since late 2024 following the election that gave the incumbent administration a two-thirds parliamentary majority, enabling the Government to address economic challenges and strengthen anti-corruption measures. Reaffirming Sri Lanka’s longstanding foreign policy of neutrality and universal friendship, Hemachandra emphasised that strengthening strategic, trade and diplomatic ties with Romania remained an important priority for Sri Lanka. State Secretary Tinca outlined Romania’s political landscape following the investiture of a new Government on 21 October 2026. She highlighted Romania’s strengths in high-value and high-growth sectors, including the chemical industry, green energy infrastructure and advanced cybersecurity, and invited further bilateral engagement in these areas. Human capital and labour cooperation featured prominently in the discussions, with Deputy Minister Hemachandra, noting that Romania had been a preferred destination for Sri Lankan professionals since 2016. Both delegations welcomed recent amendments to Romania’s foreign worker recruitment laws, which complemented the MoU on Labour Cooperation signed in March 2026. Emphasising the importance of safe, ethical and orderly labour mobility, the Co-Chairs acknowledged the untapped potential for commercial cooperation and agreed to expedite pending bilateral agreements and MoUs. The Co-Chairs also exchanged views on evolving multilateral developments and agreed to expand cooperation in key sectors, including academic exchanges, education, tourism, import and export, and social protection. Both delegations further agreed to strengthen institutional ties through Consular and Police cooperation to combat transnational organised crime. To mark the growing friendship between the two countries, both sides agreed to organise a series of commemorative events in 2027 to celebrate the 70th anniversary of diplomatic relations between Sri Lanka and Romania. Deputy Minister Hemachandra conveyed Sri Lanka’s interest in hosting the seventh round of Sri Lanka–Romania Political Consultations in Colombo in the latter part of 2027 to maintain the momentum of bilateral engagement. The Sri Lankan delegation included the Ambassador of Sri Lanka to Romania Samantha Pathirana; the Director General for Europe and North America of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Foreign Employment and Tourism Dilani Weerakoon, and the Counsellor of the Embassy Prarthana Kaushalya. The Romanian delegation included the Director Diana Tase, the Minister-Counsellor Albert Robu, the Second Secretary Theodora Drăgulescu, the Diplomatic Attaché of the Asia-Pacific and Latin America Division Vlad Popescu, and a representative of the National Visa Centre of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Romania Gabriela Ionescu.

audit.headline: Vas Kavi menace in world of screenagers and sodcasters
audit.summary: Such susceptibility to superstition is difficult to reconcile with Sri Lanka’s claim to have preserved the Theravada Buddhist tradition for more than two millennia. If the country’s Buddhists, who constitute roughly two-thirds of the population, genuinely followed the Buddha’s core teachings, they would be less vulnerable to the perceived menace of Vas Kavi. In the Kalama Sutta, the Buddha famously advised the Kalamas not to accept a claim merely because it came from a religious leader, priest, teacher, elder, or member of the social elite.
