audit.body: Such susceptibility to superstition is difficult to reconcile with Sri Lanka’s claim to have preserved the Theravada Buddhist tradition for more than two millennia. If the country’s Buddhists, who constitute roughly two-thirds of the population, genuinely followed the Buddha’s core teachings, they would be less vulnerable to the perceived menace of Vas Kavi. In the Kalama Sutta, the Buddha famously advised the Kalamas not to accept a claim merely because it came from a religious leader, priest, teacher, elder, or member of the social elite. Rather, they were urged to examine it rationally and embrace it only if they judged that it would promote genuine social well-being Vas Kavi culture Sri Lanka has recently seen a surge in antagonistic poetry composed by anonymous individuals and crafted to appeal to a broad public audience. Known locally as Vas Kavi, these verses purport to summon malevolent forces against the country’s current rulers. They have spread rapidly across social media and are replayed by citizens constantly absorbed in smartphones, tablets, and computers. The phenomenon reflects the rise of the “screenager”—a term in contemporary British English for a generation engrossed in digital screens. Those who broadcast such provocative audio loudly in public, whether alone or in groups, have also attracted the disparaging British label “sodcasters.” In Sri Lanka, the trend suggests that people are using these viral verses both for emotional gratification and to give voice to fears buried deep within their minds. The Vas Kaviya emerged alongside a Satyagraha campaign launched by a group of Buddhist monks demanding the release of a fellow monk sentenced to six years’ rigorous imprisonment for contempt of court. To rally public support for their cause, the participating monks walked the 115-kilometre Kandy–Colombo Road. When the march failed to produce the desired response, they gathered at Viharamahadevi Park, a public space intended for recreation and repose. There, they reportedly performed a ritual invoking Maha Sona, one of the fiercest demons in Sinhala folklore, to punish the rulers who refused to release the imprisoned monk unconditionally. A clay effigy of the ruler concerned was fashioned, and wooden nails were driven into it in Maha Sona’s name. Such acts are not Buddhist practices, but forms of primitive witchcraft passed down among the Sinhala people over millennia. Roots of superstition in a Buddhist society Such susceptibility to superstition is difficult to reconcile with Sri Lanka’s claim to have preserved the Theravada Buddhist tradition for more than two millennia. If the country’s Buddhists, who constitute roughly two-thirds of the population, genuinely followed the Buddha’s core teachings, they would be less vulnerable to the perceived menace of Vas Kavi. In the Kalama Sutta, the Buddha famously advised the Kalamas not to accept a claim merely because it came from a religious leader, priest, teacher, elder, or member of the social elite. Rather, they were urged to examine it rationally and embrace it only if they judged that it would promote genuine social well-being. Yet many contemporary Buddhists in Sri Lanka do not follow this rational standard. Professor Kotagama Vachissara Thero, who taught Buddhist civilisation in 1960s at the former Vidyodaya University—the predecessor of today’s University of Sri Jayewardenepura—offered an explanation for this divergence. He observed that when Arhat Mahinda introduced Buddhism to ancient Lanka, the indigenous population worshipped trees and rocks. Rather than confronting and uprooting these deeply embedded practices, Arhat Mahinda introduced the Dhamma without violently disrupting the community’s existing beliefs. The influence of these inherited beliefs remains visible today. Many Sri Lankans, when passing a large, spreading roadside tree, instinctively make an offering known as a panduru; others believe that a shrine built on a massive rock can confer divine favour. It is therefore unsurprising that Vas Kavi continues to inspire considerable fear among many Sri Lankans. I have seen older screenagers transfixed by their devices as they listen to these viral curses, uneasy smiles revealing a mixture of fear and fascination. Such reactions suggest how deeply this psychological vulnerability remains embedded in the nation’s cultural consciousness. Mythological warfare in the digital age The current Vas Kavi invokes a formidable demon king named Vajrapani to strike down a ruler accused of gaining power through falsehoods, although the intended target is deliberately left unnamed. Vajrapani is not a familiar figure in contemporary Sri Lankan folklore. The name combines vajra, the mythical diamond thunderbolt wielded by the deity Sakra, with pani, meaning the bearer or holder of that weapon. In Sri Lankan popular belief, whenever Buddhism faces an existential threat, Sakra is said to abandon his benevolent form and assume a terrifying demonic guise to destroy those who seek to undermine the faith. In the viral composition, this fearsome manifestation of Sakra is invoked to destroy rulers whom the composer accuses of plotting against Buddhism. Educated observers may dismiss the verse as mythology or superstition. Yet its influence should not be underestimated in a society where such esoteric narratives continue to shape the collective imagination. Epidemic of surface learning Why do Sri Lankans so readily turn to such destructive invocations? One explanation is the modern retreat from the rational inquiry encouraged by the Kalama Sutta, which has weakened the public’s capacity for critical thought. Increasingly, people acquire information through shortcuts—glancing at social-media posts or listening to brief, catchy songs designed to capture attention and lodge in the mind. This is surface learning, the opposite of the deep learning society should cultivate. Because surface learning is effortless and undemanding, it encourages people to skim headlines and absorb impressions rather than investigate the underlying truth. This intellectual complacency makes it easy for skilful manipulators to manufacture provocative headlines and circulate them widely. Nor is the drift towards surface learning confined to Sri Lanka; it has become a global concern. Educators in the Nordic countries and neighbouring Singapore have sought to counter it by renewing the emphasis on sustained reading and rigorous critical analysis—the foundations of deep learning. Sri Lanka is yet to announce the adoption of such a bold education reform. Instead, it worships AI and plans to introduce it as a facilitator of learning at schools. It is widely recognised that AI will stunt the development of human brain, though it can make it easy for teachers to assemble their teaching materials readily. In Sri Lanka, however, intense competition for admission to State universities encourages students to rely on surface learning at the expense of genuine understanding. Parents, anxious for their children to earn distinctions, often fail to create an environment that rewards curiosity and deep comprehension, despite their importance to long-term success. In reality, parents as a routine hire tuition masters to provide additional learning support to their children. Such tuition masters will help students to memorise answers to a given question selected by tuition masters from the past papers and do not help them to deep-learn a subject. These habits then follow students into adulthood and the workplace. Against this background, it is unsurprising that a myth-laden and superstitious Vas Kavi has gone viral: the public has been conditioned to embrace precisely such easily consumed material. When I asked several non-Buddhist friends whether they had listened to it, they said that although a notification had appeared on their smartphones, they had simply ignored it. Its circulation therefore appears to be concentrated mainly among Sri Lankan Buddhists—a troubling indication of the community’s future intellectual resilience. Once the current International Monetary Fund (IMF) program ends, Sri Lanka’s leaders will face the formidable task of moving the country beyond its present fragile stability, placing it on a sustainable growth path, and strengthening its resilience to external economic shocks. Mobilising the public behind this national effort will be exceedingly difficult if one faction cultivates superstition while another responds with equally regressive tactics. Unless this cultural decline is reversed, it could seriously endanger the country’s economic and political future Ideological enslavement and technical manipulation The struggle, therefore, is fundamentally between surface learning and deep learning. Because surface learning demands little intellectual effort, the information it conveys is often fleeting and quickly forgotten. Those seeking to bind others to an ideology understand this weakness and exploit it by repeating the same message in varied forms until an idea first absorbed through a digital shortcut becomes embedded in the public consciousness. The technique recalls the methods of relentless repetition associated with Joseph Goebbels and wartime propaganda. By repeatedly exposing the public to this Vas Kavi, its creators appear to be trying to lodge it in the nation’s collective consciousness. Yet, consistent with modern patterns of media consumption, even this feared verse has largely been absorbed at a superficial level. I asked several frequent listeners what it actually meant—whether they knew who Vajrapani was or why Sakra was believed to assume a demonic form to defend Buddhism from its supposed enemies. They could not answer. Their responses suggest that even superstition is now being consumed through the same effortless and uncritical habits that define the screen age. I recently tested this phenomenon on an acquaintance’s birthday. I created a digital poster featuring her photograph and paired it with a song carrying a deliberately unconventional message: she needed no birthday wishes because her familiar smile showed that happiness was already a constant in her life. The poster also celebrated the dedication that had enabled her to rise professionally, captured in the Latin phrase Per Aspera Ad Astra— “through hardships to the stars”. The core message was that one should stand on his own feet for success without depending on gods, spirits, demons, and lowly-born spirits to deliver the same. Within half an hour of being posted on Facebook, the image had attracted hundreds of “likes”. Yet this apparent engagement did not mean that viewers had understood its central message. The comments exposed the superficiality of their response: although the poster explicitly said that conventional birthday wishes were unnecessary, many viewers—including supposedly well-educated ones—posted routine “happy birthday” greetings or merely praised her smile. Few appeared to have read the message carefully. The episode offered a vivid demonstration of how screenagers consume content through surface learning. In a digital environment shaped by such uncritical habits, manipulators can readily fill the resulting intellectual vacuum and bind audiences to their preferred narratives. Threat to national recovery The immediate danger is that those targeted by the Vas Kavi may retaliate in kind, either by issuing a counter-curse or commissioning a Seth Kavi—a protective verse intended to shield them. Such rituals have no demonstrable physical effect: there is no evidence that a demon king named Vajrapani exists, that Sakra assumes a demonic form to defend the faith, or that supernatural forces can harm the unnamed ruler. The real danger lies instead in political factions answering superstition with superstition and drawing the country into an unproductive cycle of hostility. Such tribal confrontation could divert attention and energy from Sri Lanka’s fragile economic recovery. No nation can progress while one part of its population is persistently pitted against another. Instead of strengthening the intellectual capacities needed for creativity, invention, and innovation, Sri Lankans risk becoming passive consumers of destructive, backward-looking content. For the country, this erosion of independent thought poses a profound threat to its future sovereignty and prosperity. Once the current International Monetary Fund (IMF) program ends, Sri Lanka’s leaders will face the formidable task of moving the country beyond its present fragile stability, placing it on a sustainable growth path, and strengthening its resilience to external economic shocks. Mobilising the public behind this national effort will be exceedingly difficult if one faction cultivates superstition while another responds with equally regressive tactics. Unless this cultural decline is reversed, it could seriously endanger the country’s economic and political future. Yet the country’s intelligentsia remains conspicuously silent. Academics and professionals must speak plainly: a nation at this fragile stage of recovery cannot afford further self-inflicted damage. They should unequivocally condemn both those who originated the Vas Kavi and those responding with retaliatory verses A call to the intelligentsia and religious leaders The emerging situation carries disturbing echoes of Sri Lanka’s catastrophic economic crisis in 2022, when the country exhausted its foreign exchange reserves and could no longer import even basic necessities. The resulting queues forced citizens to sacrifice millions of productive hours—a classic deadweight loss in which individuals, the economy, and society all suffered without any corresponding gain. Yet the country’s intelligentsia remains conspicuously silent. Academics and professionals must speak plainly: a nation at this fragile stage of recovery cannot afford further self-inflicted damage. They should unequivocally condemn both those who originated the Vas Kavi and those responding with retaliatory verses. Moreover, calling upon Sri Lanka’s Head of State to grant an unconditional pardon to a person convicted of contempt of court is inconsistent with established principles of good governance. Creating such a precedent would weaken confidence in the rule of law and deter legitimate investors from entering the country. If laws appear susceptible to pressure, reputable businesses will stay away, while those seeking to exploit institutional weakness will be encouraged to invest. The result would resemble Gresham’s Law, under which bad money—debased coins—drives good money out of circulation. In the same way, investors with questionable motives could displace the credible, long-term investment Sri Lanka needs. The mainstream media likewise bears a heavy responsibility to foster deep learning rather than pursue sensationalist clicks. It must resist partisan alignment and confront the issue directly. Senior Buddhist leaders have an equally important duty—to safeguard both the integrity of the Dhamma and the welfare of the nation. If these influential institutions remain passive, the greatest burden will fall not on the elite but on Sri Lanka’s poorest and most vulnerable citizens, who will ultimately pay the price for this digital descent into superstition and tribalism. (The writer, a former Deputy Governor of the Central Bank of Sri Lanka, can be reached at [email protected] )

audit.headline: CBSL reviews lenders’ early settlement fees and parate auctions after complaints pile up
audit.summary: CBSL reviewed early settlement and parate practices in the first half of 2026 No findings or new rules have been disclosed yet The Central Bank of Sri Lanka (CBSL) carried out targeted reviews of how lenders charge borrowers for settling term loans early and how banks seize mortgaged property under parate execution, following a “significant volume of consumer complaints” in both areas, the Central Bank revealed. The thematic reviews, conducted in the first half of 2026, covered the early settlement practices of licensed banks and finance companies on term loans and the parate execution process of licensed banks. However, the Central Bank did not disclose its findings, the number of institutions examined or any corrective action, while the major policy measures it listed from July 2025 to end July 2026 include no new rules on either issue.
audit.body: CBSL reviewed early settlement and parate practices in the first half of 2026 No findings or new rules have been disclosed yet The Central Bank of Sri Lanka (CBSL) carried out targeted reviews of how lenders charge borrowers for settling term loans early and how banks seize mortgaged property under parate execution, following a “significant volume of consumer complaints” in both areas, the Central Bank revealed. The thematic reviews, conducted in the first half of 2026, covered the early settlement practices of licensed banks and finance companies on term loans and the parate execution process of licensed banks. However, the Central Bank did not disclose its findings, the number of institutions examined or any corrective action, while the major policy measures it listed from July 2025 to end July 2026 include no new rules on either issue. Officials of the Central Bank’s Financial Consumer Relations Department wrote in June that complaints relating to fees and charges increased by approximately 40 percent between 2023 and 2025, particularly over items such as processing fees, documentation charges and early settlement fees. Licensed banks accounted for 79 percent of complaints over the period and finance companies for 21 percent, meaning banks drew nearly four times as many. Complaints over high lending rates, by contrast, declined significantly. The officials pointed out that lenders “may need to strengthen disclosure practices” and “simplify fee structures”. Early settlement charges fall under the Financial Consumer Protection Regulations No. 01 of 2023, in force since February 2024, which list “requiring payment of un-accrued (future) interest/ early settlement fees on credit facilities, exceeding the levels permitted by the Central Bank, if any” as an unfair business practice. Meanwhile, parate execution allows banks to auction mortgaged property on a board resolution, without going to court, under the Recovery of Loans by Banks (Special Provisions) Act No. 4 of 1990. After the power was suspended in 2024, the government phased out relief for small and medium enterprises (SMEs) last year, ending it on June 30, 2025 for loans above Rs.50 million, September 30 for loans of Rs.25 million to Rs.50 million and December 31 for smaller loans, for borrowers who had begun talks with their banks by March 31, 2025. The first half of 2026 was thus the first period since early 2024 without any SME relief window. Banks maintain the power is rarely used, with the Sri Lanka Banks’ Association stating in July 2025 that it was applied to only about 1 percent of non-performing loans between 2019 and 2023. Borrowers are also under greater pressure, with the Central Bank raising its policy rate in May 2026 and banks’ Stage 3 loans recording slight increases at the end of both the first and second quarters of 2026, following Cyclone Ditwah, higher fuel prices and the Middle East conflict.

audit.headline: Commercial Bank named Sri Lanka’s Best Bank by Global Finance for 24th time
audit.summary: Mr Sanath Manatunge flanked by Mr Chris Giarraputo, Managing Director, Operations at Global Finance and Mr Navin Dulani, Head of APAC at Intellect, at the magazine’s annual awards event in Thailand. The Commercial Bank of Ceylon’s remarkable near two-and-a-half-decade run as Sri Lanka’s best bank was recognised on the global stage recently when Mr Sanath Manatunge, the Bank’s Managing Director/CEO accepted the Best Bank award presented to the Bank by Global Finance for the 24th time. The Global Finance Annual Awards ceremony for 2026 was held at the Dusit Thani Bangkok, coinciding with the IMF/World Bank Annual Meetings. Commercial Bank also received the Global Finance accolade for the Best Islamic Bank in Sri Lanka at the same event.

audit.headline: Dialog Axiata and IITM Pravartak forge partnership to advance research and innovation
audit.summary: Exchange of signed MOU between M. J. Shankar Jayaraman and Supun Weerasinghe Dialog Axiata PLC has entered into a strategic partnership with Indian Institute of Technology Madras (IITM) Pravartak Technologies Foundation through the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) aimed at advancing applied research and technology development in Sri Lanka. The agreement marks an important milestone in India-Sri Lanka cooperation, bringing together international expertise, and industry stakeholders to develop practical solutions to national and societal challenges. It also seeks to strengthen Sri Lanka’s research capabilities and create opportunities to translate new ideas into real-world applications. Under the agreement, Dialog will serve as the collaboration anchor and technology enabler, connecting IITM Pravartak’s research networks with Sri Lankan industry stakeholders.
audit.body: Exchange of signed MOU between M. J. Shankar Jayaraman and Supun Weerasinghe Dialog Axiata PLC has entered into a strategic partnership with Indian Institute of Technology Madras (IITM) Pravartak Technologies Foundation through the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) aimed at advancing applied research and technology development in Sri Lanka. The agreement marks an important milestone in India-Sri Lanka cooperation, bringing together international expertise, and industry stakeholders to develop practical solutions to national and societal challenges. It also seeks to strengthen Sri Lanka’s research capabilities and create opportunities to translate new ideas into real-world applications. Under the agreement, Dialog will serve as the collaboration anchor and technology enabler, connecting IITM Pravartak’s research networks with Sri Lankan industry stakeholders. The partnership will explore five key areas: innovation and incubation, applied research and university laboratories, artificial intelligence and human-centric solutions, industry skills and talent development, and international knowledge sharing. Potential areas for initial collaboration include Sinhala and Tamil conversational AI, technology-driven dengue prevention and response, and solutions to address human-elephant conflict. These will be explored through focused research initiatives and pilot projects, with opportunities for further development based on their outcomes. Commenting on the significance of the partnership, Santosh Jha, High Commissioner of India to Sri Lanka said, “India and Sri Lanka share a longstanding and multifaceted relationship, underpinned by strong historical ties and a shared commitment to progress. As our bilateral partnership continues to evolve, cooperation in technology and research presents significant opportunities to deepen engagement between our institutions and people. I welcome this initiative as another meaningful contribution to the growing partnership between our two countries.” Shankar Jayaraman, Chief Executive Officer of IITM Pravartak Technologies Foundation said, “This collaboration creates an opportunity to strengthen the connection between academic research and practical application. By working closely with Dialog, Sri Lankan universities and local stakeholders, we hope to foster an environment where researchers and students can exchange knowledge, build technical capabilities and develop solutions that respond to real-world needs. We look forward to a productive partnership that creates value for both the research community and industry.” Supun Weerasinghe, Director / Group Chief Executive of Dialog Axiata PLC said, “At Dialog, we believe the true value of technology lies in its ability to address real challenges and create meaningful opportunities for people and communities. Through this partnership, we aim to connect global expertise with Sri Lankan talent to develop solutions that can make a lasting difference. I would also like to express our sincere appreciation to His Excellency the High Commissioner and the team at the High Commission of India for their invaluable support in bringing this collaboration to fruition, as we continue our efforts to enrich and empower Sri Lankan lives and enterprises.” The partnership will adopt a phased approach, beginning with selected pilot projects to evaluate their potential before exploring opportunities to scale, ensuring that each initiative is guided by clearly defined objectives and measurable outcomes.

audit.headline: Doc990 launches SL’s 1st full-stack AI health assistant
audit.summary: From left: Digital Health Head of Business Development Thiekshana Ekanayake, Digital Health Manager Finance Madara Abeysinghe, Digital Health Manager Marketing and Growth Devindi Wanasundara, Dialog Axiata Group Chief Digital Services Officer Renuka Fernando, Digital Health Chief Executive Officer Janitth Peiris, Digital Health Head of Technology Kasun Ranasinghe, Digital Health Associate Tech Lead Amila Jayashanka and Digital Health Software Engineer Charithra Jayasinghe Introduces Suvawi: Most advanced conversational healthcare platform in Sri Lanka Doc990, Sri Lanka’s pioneering digital health solutions provider operated by Digital Health (Pvt.) Ltd — a subsidiary of Dialog Axiata PLC, Sri Lanka’s #1 connectivity provider, has officially launched Suvawi, a next generation virtual healthcare assistant designed to redefine how Sri Lankans access and navigate...
audit.body: From left: Digital Health Head of Business Development Thiekshana Ekanayake, Digital Health Manager Finance Madara Abeysinghe, Digital Health Manager Marketing and Growth Devindi Wanasundara, Dialog Axiata Group Chief Digital Services Officer Renuka Fernando, Digital Health Chief Executive Officer Janitth Peiris, Digital Health Head of Technology Kasun Ranasinghe, Digital Health Associate Tech Lead Amila Jayashanka and Digital Health Software Engineer Charithra Jayasinghe Introduces Suvawi: Most advanced conversational healthcare platform in Sri Lanka  Doc990, Sri Lanka’s pioneering digital health solutions provider operated by Digital Health (Pvt.) Ltd — a subsidiary of Dialog Axiata PLC, Sri Lanka’s #1 connectivity provider, has officially launched Suvawi, a next generation virtual healthcare assistant designed to redefine how Sri Lankans access and navigate medical care.  Seamlessly integrated into the Doc990 ecosystem, Suvawi leverages advanced conversational AI to transition the platform from a traditional booking tool into an intelligent, end-to-end digital health concierge. Unlike the standard chatbots, Suvawi solves one of the most frustrating challenges in patient care: matching immediate medical concerns with the real-world doctor availability.  The users can now simply describe their physical symptoms to the chatbot and Suvawi’s medical intelligence engine will instantly identify the exact medical specialty required.  Going a step further, the AI analyses real-time hospital schedules to recommend specific specialist channeling options tailored precisely to the user’s preferred date and geographical location. Doc990CEO Janitth Pieris said, “The launch of Suvawi marks a paradigm shift in how digital healthcare operates in Sri Lanka by eliminating the guesswork and fragmented steps of seeking medical help. With Suvawi, a patient can state what hurts, find the right specialist close to home for the exact day they are free and finalise their entire care cycle, all within a single, continuous conversation.” By integrating directly with Doc990’s extensive nationwide infrastructure, Suvawi retrieves real-time medical data to provide instantaneous, reliable guidance. The conversational assistant is now live and available to all users on the latest version of the Doc990 mobile app, paving the way for a faster, smarter and highly accessible healthcare experience across the island.

audit.headline: HNB FINANCE-Toyota Lanka expand vehicle-leasing solutions
audit.summary: From left: Toyota Lanka Managing Director and CEO Manohara Atukorala and Chairman Masaaki Kawabata followed by HNB FINANCE Managing Director and CEO Chaminda Prabhath, Chief Credit Officer Aruna Somasiri, Head of Channel Management Pathum Sampath, Head of Leasing Saman Premarathna, Head of Marketing Communications and Digital Business Madura Wijeratne and Senior Marketing Manager Ruwan Indika HNB FINANCE PLC and Toyota Lanka (Private) Limited have entered into a strategic partnership to offer competitive leasing solutions for the customers purchasing brand-new Toyota vehicles and Toyota Sure Certified Used Vehicles. The partnership was recently formalised through a memorandum of understanding (MoU), reinforcing the commitment of both parties to collaborate on this initiative.
audit.body: From left: Toyota Lanka Managing Director and CEO Manohara Atukorala and Chairman Masaaki Kawabata followed by HNB FINANCE Managing Director and CEO Chaminda Prabhath, Chief Credit Officer Aruna Somasiri, Head of Channel Management Pathum Sampath, Head of Leasing Saman Premarathna, Head of Marketing Communications and Digital Business Madura Wijeratne and Senior Marketing Manager Ruwan Indika HNB FINANCE PLC and Toyota Lanka (Private) Limited have entered into a strategic partnership to offer competitive leasing solutions for the customers purchasing brand-new Toyota vehicles and Toyota Sure Certified Used Vehicles. The partnership was recently formalised through a memorandum of understanding (MoU), reinforcing the commitment of both parties to collaborate on this initiative. Under the agreement, HNB FINANCE will provide leasing facilities for eligible Toyota customers, combining access to formal financing with a package of after-sales and ownership benefits offered by Toyota Lanka. HNB FINANCE Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer Chaminda Prabhath said, “Reliable access to vehicle finance is important not only for individual mobility but also for business activity and broader economic participation. Through this partnership with Toyota Lanka, we are looking to offer the customers competitive financing options together with the assurance of a globally recognised automotive brand and strong after-sales support.” The customers purchasing eligible Toyota vehicles under the partnership will receive free vehicle registration from Toyota Lanka, along with a comprehensive warranty covering the engine and gearbox for three years or 100,000 kilometres, whichever comes first. The Toyota forklift customers will receive a warranty of two years or 6,000 operating hours, whichever occurs first. The partnership also offers three complimentary services for Toyota vehicles and three complimentary labour services for Toyota forklifts. The MoU was exchanged in the presence of senior representatives of both companies. Toyota Lanka was represented by Chairman Masaaki Kawabata and Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer Manohara Atukorala. HNB FINANCE was represented by Managing Director and CEO Chaminda Prabhath, Deputy General Manager and Chief Credit Officer Aruna Somasiri, Assistant General Manager and Head of Channel Management Pathum Sampath, Head of Leasing Saman Premarathna, Chief Manager and Head of Marketing Communications and Digital Business Madura Wijeratne and Senior Manager Marketing Ruwan Indika.

audit.headline: JXG’s Wasanthi, 1st female recipient of CIPM Lifetime Gold
audit.summary: JXG Group Chief Human Resources Officer Wasanthi Stephen receives CIPM-Baurs Lifetime Gold Award 2026 JXG (Janashakthi Group) celebrates Group Chief Human Resources Officer Wasanthi Stephen on becoming the first female recipient of the prestigious CIPM-Baurs Lifetime Gold Award 2026, from the Chartered Institute of Personnel Management (CIPM) Sri Lanka since the award’s inception. Presented on October 14, 2026, at the opening of National Human Resource Conference (NHRC) 2026, at Monarch Imperial, the award marks a historic milestone for Sri Lanka’s human resources profession and a proud moment for JXG. The highest individual recognition in Sri Lanka’s human resource management sphere, the CIPM Sri Lanka Lifetime Gold Award celebrates individuals whose long-standing contributions have advanced the HR profession at organisational, national and international levels.
audit.body: JXG Group Chief Human Resources Officer Wasanthi Stephen receives CIPM-Baurs Lifetime Gold Award 2026 JXG (Janashakthi Group) celebrates Group Chief Human Resources Officer Wasanthi Stephen on becoming the first female recipient of the prestigious CIPM-Baurs Lifetime Gold Award 2026, from the Chartered Institute of Personnel Management (CIPM) Sri Lanka since the award’s inception.  Presented on October 14, 2026, at the opening of National Human Resource Conference (NHRC) 2026, at Monarch Imperial, the award marks a historic milestone for Sri Lanka’s human resources profession and a proud moment for JXG. The highest individual recognition in Sri Lanka’s human resource management sphere, the CIPM Sri Lanka Lifetime Gold Award celebrates individuals whose long-standing contributions have advanced the HR profession at organisational, national and international levels. It recognises professional excellence, ethical leadership, transformational impact and a sustained commitment to people and institutions. With extensive expertise spanning leadership, talent development, employee well-being, women’s advancement and the future of work, Wasanthi has made significant contributions to the evolution of HR as a strategic driver of organisational performance.  Her professional standing has also received international recognition, including the Global Recognition Award for Leadership in Human Resources in 2024. At JXG, Wasanthi plays a pivotal role in transforming people practices across the group. Her leadership has driven the establishment of an integrated shared services unit, advanced paperless HR operations and strengthened collaboration, efficiency and service delivery.  Under her leadership, group companies have earned recognition for people development, HR governance, workplace excellence and leadership, while advancing ethical decision-making and the responsible application of artificial intelligence. Throughout her career, Wasanthi has championed a people-centred approach to organisational progress, with a focus on employee well-being, professional development, women’s advancement and inclusive workplaces. Her work reflects the increasingly strategic role of HR in building organisations where people can grow, contribute and thrive.

audit.headline: Jetstar captures Australian holiday growth as SriLankan eyes Perth
audit.summary: Jetstar has captured nearly a fifth of Australia’s tourist traffic to Sri Lanka in its first full month on the Melbourne-Colombo route, absorbing the bulk of the market’s growth while SriLankan Airlines, despite adding flights, carried roughly the same number of Australian tourists, as per SLTDA data. Airlines outside SLTDA’s list of named carriers accounted for 18.78 percent of the 10,951 Australian tourists who arrived in September, up from just 0.92 percent in July. While SLTDA does not list the Qantas Group’s low-cost arm separately, the jump coincides with Australian arrivals departing from Melbourne more than doubling to 4,256 from 2,111, and those routed through Singapore and Kuala Lumpur falling 19.6 percent and 32.1 percent respectively.
audit.body: Jetstar has captured nearly a fifth of Australia’s tourist traffic to Sri Lanka in its first full month on the Melbourne-Colombo route, absorbing the bulk of the market’s growth while SriLankan Airlines, despite adding flights, carried roughly the same number of Australian tourists, as per SLTDA data. Airlines outside SLTDA’s list of named carriers accounted for 18.78 percent of the 10,951 Australian tourists who arrived in September, up from just 0.92 percent in July. While SLTDA does not list the Qantas Group’s low-cost arm separately, the jump coincides with Australian arrivals departing from Melbourne more than doubling to 4,256 from 2,111, and those routed through Singapore and Kuala Lumpur falling 19.6 percent and 32.1 percent respectively. The passengers Jetstar has won appear to have come largely from Singapore Airlines and Malaysia Airlines, whose combined share of the market fell from 40 percent in July to 28.5 percent in September, equivalent to roughly 760 fewer passengers, based on Mirror Business calculations. However, SriLankan flew an estimated 4,720 Australian tourists in September, only marginally above 4,610 in July, despite raising its Colombo-Melbourne service from seven to 10 weekly flights from 2 August.  Its share of Australian arrivals consequently slipped from 47.55 percent to 43.11 percent, well below the 55.83 percent it held in September last year, when it carried around 5,080 Australians. Australians visiting for pleasure rose by about 1,210 between July and September, accounting for nearly all of the 1,250 increase in arrivals, while those visiting friends and relatives held steady at around 3,300, based on SLTDA data.  Although SLTDA does not break this down by airline, the pattern suggests Jetstar is bringing in leisure travellers, whereas SriLankan’s Australian traffic appears anchored in diaspora visits, which made up over a third of the market before Jetstar’s launch. SriLankan itself has cited Melbourne’s large Sri Lankan community among the reasons for its success on the route. Australian arrivals rose 20.3 percent in September when compared to the same month last year, accelerating from 6.4 percent growth in July and lifting Australia above the United Kingdom to become the island’s third-largest source market for the month. As reported earlier by Mirror Business, Jetstar Executive Manager Commercial Scott Zeglin noted that the thrice-weekly flights were running over 90 percent full in each direction, though he remained cautious on adding peak-season frequencies. Jetstar’s gains come as the Sri Lanka Tourism Promotion Bureau (SLTPB) runs a Rs.1.5 billion interim digital and public relations campaign through April, with Australia leading a six-month push on Meta, TikTok and YouTube, backed by a trade roadshow across Australia and New Zealand that concluded in Perth. However, according to industry sources, SriLankan has offered very little collaboration in supporting the country’s tourism promotion. Meanwhile, SriLankan Airlines Chief Executive Officer Vipul Misra told the media last week that the national carrier is studying a direct route to Perth, citing demand identified during a recent roadshow held jointly with the Tourism Ministry. “We see there is a strong demand in Perth,” he noted, adding that aircraft would have to be sourced from outside to deploy the capacity. Misra argued that the national carrier must take on routes that private airlines would deem commercially unattractive at the outset. “Nobody would bleed their money to open that route,” he observed. A Perth service would add a third Australian gateway alongside Melbourne and Sydney, tapping travellers who currently connect via Singapore, Kuala Lumpur or the Gulf. (NF)

audit.headline: Mosvold Villa featured in National Geographic Traveller’s Indian Ocean Collection
audit.summary: A beachfront base on Sri Lanka’s south coast, run by a local team Mosvold Villa, the beachfront boutique hotel on Kabalana Beach in Ahangama, has been featured in the August 2026 Indian Ocean Collection of National Geographic Traveller (UK). The sponsored feature presents the property as a base for travellers who want to slow down, surf and get to know Sri Lanka’s south coast. Ahangama has long drawn surfers and travellers to the south coast and the villa sits right on the sand at Kabalana. Each of the 16 rooms and suites looks out over the Indian Ocean and the Founder’s Suite has its own private infinity pool. Dining focuses on Sri Lankan coastal cooking, built around seafood landed daily. It is food that belongs to the place and the kitchen treats it that way.
audit.body: A beachfront base on Sri Lanka’s south coast, run by a local team Mosvold Villa, the beachfront boutique hotel on Kabalana Beach in Ahangama, has been featured in the August 2026 Indian Ocean Collection of National Geographic Traveller (UK).  The sponsored feature presents the property as a base for travellers who want to slow down, surf and get to know Sri Lanka’s south coast. Ahangama has long drawn surfers and travellers to the south coast and the villa sits right on the sand at Kabalana. Each of the 16 rooms and suites looks out over the Indian Ocean and the Founder’s Suite has its own private infinity pool. Dining focuses on Sri Lankan coastal cooking, built around seafood landed daily. It is food that belongs to the place and the kitchen treats it that way. Mosvold’s aim is a holiday rooted in Sri Lankan culture that refreshes guests in body, mind and spirit. The service is star class and the feel is that of a private home. None of that would be possible without the people who deliver it, from the kitchen and front desk to the grounds and maintenance teams. The villa is staffed by 43 people, part of a Mosvold group team of around 185. The group recruits from the communities around its properties and across the region, extending opportunities well beyond Ahangama. For many local families, that means work close to home. Its people are what keeps the group’s hospitality personal and that remains the focus as it grows. Partnerships with vocational institutes in the Southern province give young people a route into hospitality and successful trainees are offered permanent roles. The programmes are built on practical experience, not classroom theory alone. The goal is simple: anyone who joins Mosvold should have room to grow. “At Mosvold, we are committed to recognising and empowering talent. Our people are our most valuable asset and our vision ‘Significantly You’ comes to life through the team that welcomes every guest,” said Mosvold Hotels Managing Director Nilanka Martinus. Mosvold Hotels opened its first property in Ahangama in 2012 and now operates four properties. Mosvold Villa is at 38 Welhengoda, Ahangama.

audit.headline: Over half of NBFI household borrowers in high-risk bands as Stage 2 loans nearly double
audit.summary: Some 52.4% of household borrowers at finance companies fall in high or very high risk bands, compared with 24.1% at banks Stage 2 loans at finance companies rose 92.1% in a year, while gold-backed Stage 2 loans jumped 279.2% More than half of the households borrowing from finance companies fall in the high or very high risk categories based on their Credit Information Bureau (CRIB) scores, over twice the share among bank borrowers, as early signs of stress build up in the sector’s vehicle and gold-backed loan books, as per CBSL data. As at end June 2026, 52.4 percent of household borrowers of non-bank financial institutions (NBFIs), comprising finance companies and a specialised leasing company whose registration was cancelled in June, fell within the high or very high risk categories, compared with 24.1 percent at banks.
audit.body: Some 52.4% of household borrowers at finance companies fall in high or very high risk bands, compared with 24.1% at banks Stage 2 loans at finance companies rose 92.1% in a year, while gold-backed Stage 2 loans jumped 279.2% More than half of the households borrowing from finance companies fall in the high or very high risk categories based on their Credit Information Bureau (CRIB) scores, over twice the share among bank borrowers, as early signs of stress build up in the sector’s vehicle and gold-backed loan books, as per CBSL data. As at end June 2026, 52.4 percent of household borrowers of non-bank financial institutions (NBFIs), comprising finance companies and a specialised leasing company whose registration was cancelled in June, fell within the high or very high risk categories, compared with 24.1 percent at banks. Nearly one in three, or 30.4 percent, sat in the very high risk band, more than double the 14.3 percent at banks, while only 31.6 percent were rated low or very low risk. NBFI household borrowers recorded an average CRIB score of 497.4, inside the very high risk band of 250 to 500 and 59.8 points below the bank average of 557.2, which falls in the average risk band. The overall household score improved to 538.2 from 511.6 a year earlier, although it remained in the high risk category. The Central Bank pointed out that NBFI scores had improved in recent quarters. The same divide held for businesses, with 53.9 percent of NBFI institutional borrowers in the two highest risk bands, against 21.6 percent at banks. “Nevertheless, the relatively larger share of higher risk in the NBFI sector remains an area warranting continued attention from a financial stability perspective,” the Central Bank cautioned. NBFIs are also gaining ground in household lending. Household credit grew 25.4 percent year-on-year at end June, up from 14.8 percent a year earlier, while NBFIs’ share of that lending rose to 37.5 percent from 35.5 percent. Repayment, however, improved, with loans carrying zero days in arrears rising to 67.7 percent of household exposures from 65.0 percent. Meanwhile, finance companies’ gross loans expanded 45.0 percent year-on-year, driven by vehicle-backed loans, which grew 46.3 percent, and gold-backed loans, which rose 59.8 percent. Together, the two accounted for 85.2 percent of the sector’s credit, up from 82.6 percent, a reliance the Central Bank flagged as a significant collateral concentration risk. However, the sector’s gross Stage 2 loans, which signal a significant rise in credit risk, jumped 92.1 percent, lifting the Stage 2 ratio to 15.4 percent from 11.6 percent. Stage 2 vehicle loans rose 75.5 percent, while Stage 2 gold-backed loans climbed 279.2 percent. Although the Stage 3 ratio fell to 5.1 percent from 8.3 percent, Stage 3 loans rose by Rs.23.6 billion in the second quarter alone, while Stage 3 impairment coverage slipped to 41.0 percent from 46.1 percent. The Central Bank attributed part of the Stage 2 increase to weaker repayment capacity among some borrowers following Cyclone Ditwah and the Middle East conflict. “The current uptick in Stage 2 loans reflects a potential buildup of credit risk within the sector and requires continuous monitoring and proactive risk mitigation by (finance companies),” it warned. Notably, the CRIB risk scores exclude gold-backed loans altogether, as CRIB is still incorporating pawning data and such data are not yet consistently reported by all financial institutions. This leaves out a segment that makes up 21.4 percent of finance company credit, and one in which Stage 2 loans have nearly quadrupled in a year. The Central Bank tightened loan-to-value limits on vehicle loans and introduced limits on gold-backed lending in May 2026, alongside a policy rate increase, and raised risk weights on gold-backed loans from September, measures it expects to slow credit growth in the sector in the coming quarters.

audit.headline: Pine Labs and WEBXPAY bring Indian payment experience to Sri Lanka
audit.summary: Tanya Naik Pine Labs and WEBXPAY have entered into a strategic cross-border payments partnership, the first Payment Aggregator-to-Payment Aggregator (PA-on-PA) collaboration of its kind in Sri Lanka under India’s RBI-authorised PA-CB framework. The PA-CB structure allows licensed Indian payment aggregators to partner directly with international aggregators, enabling Indian payment methods to be accepted abroad within a regulated, compliant framework. Through this partnership, WEBXPAY’s merchant network spanning hospitality, travel, retail and online commerce across Sri Lanka, can now accept UPI, UPI AutoPay, cards across major Indian issuers, net banking across 100+ banks, EMI conversions, and Credit on UPI, with T+1 settlement, embedded natively within existing integrations and available at scale from day one.
audit.body: Tanya Naik Pine Labs and WEBXPAY have entered into a strategic cross-border payments partnership, the first Payment Aggregator-to-Payment Aggregator (PA-on-PA) collaboration of its kind in Sri Lanka under India’s RBI-authorised PA-CB framework.  The PA-CB structure allows licensed Indian payment aggregators to partner directly with international aggregators, enabling Indian payment methods to be accepted abroad within a regulated, compliant framework.  Through this partnership, WEBXPAY’s merchant network spanning hospitality, travel, retail and online commerce across Sri Lanka, can now accept UPI, UPI AutoPay, cards across major Indian issuers, net banking across 100+ banks, EMI conversions, and Credit on UPI, with T+1 settlement, embedded natively within existing integrations and available at scale from day one. For Sri Lankan merchants this is a meaningful commercial unlock. Indian travellers are already walking through their doors, now they can pay the way they do at home, on rails they trust, without any changes to their existing payment infrastructure. “India’s payment stack is one of the most sophisticated in the world and Indian consumers carry that expectation with them when they travel. At Pine Labs, we believe the next frontier of cross-border commerce is making that experience portable. Sri Lanka is our first activation under the PA-CB framework, and we intend to replicate this model across Southeast Asia and every market where Indian travellers and consumers are a meaningful commercial force,” said Tanya Naik, Sr. EVP & Head of Online Business, Pine Labs. Commenting on the partnership, Thilak Piyadigama, Executive Chairman of WEBXPAY said, “India is Sri Lanka’s largest tourism market and one of our most important economic partners. Indian customers already know and trust payment methods such as UPI, cards and net banking. Bringing that familiarity into the online checkout experience of Sri Lankan merchants can remove a significant point of friction and help businesses convert more Indian demand into revenue.” “We selected Pine Labs because of the strength of its Indian payment infrastructure, breadth of payment options and ability to support a regulated cross-border model at scale. Together, we are creating a practical digital payment bridge that gives Sri Lankan businesses greater access to one of the world’s largest and most dynamic consumer markets.” The partnership establishes a scalable model through which Pine Labs and WEBXPAY can support the growth of cross-border commerce between India and Sri Lanka, with the potential for similar collaborations across other international markets.

audit.body: SLUSABC Committee  Tilak Gunawardena Eric Meyer The Sri Lanka–USA Business Council (SLUSABC) of The Ceylon Chamber of Commerce held its 10th Annual General Meeting on 14 October recently, reflecting on a decade of business engagement between Sri Lanka and the United States and setting out its priorities for the year ahead. Tilak Gunawardana, Chief Financial Officer of MAC Holdings (Pvt) Ltd, was re-elected as President for the 2026/2027 term. The AGM was attended by Eric Meyer, Ambassador of the United States of America to Sri Lanka , and Mahinda Samarasinghe together with members of the business community. Reviewing the Council’s work over the past year, Gunawardana highlighted its engagement on U.S. tariff developments, efforts to connect Sri Lankan businesses with investment opportunities through SelectUSA, and initiatives to strengthen intellectual property protection and support emerging entrepreneurs. He stressed the need for consistent policies and a predictable trade framework to help businesses plan, invest and expand. Meyer commended the Council’s efforts to foster a stronger  business environment andadvance intellectual property protections, underscoring their importance in attracting U.S. investment and expanding bilteral trade.  He pointed to opportunities to deepen commercial cooperation in technology, energy, infrastructure and logistics, while encouraging Sri Lankan businesses to explore investment opportunities in the United States, including through the upcoming SelectUSA Investment Summit. The Ambassador also emphasized the importance of transparent, predictable regulations, strong intellectual property rights, and fair competition in building investor confidence and creatinglasting economic opportunities for both countries.  For the year ahead, the Council will focus on trade policy and two-way investment, while exploring opportunities across energy, ports and logistics, technology, renewable energy and education. It also plans to widen its engagement with small and medium-sized enterprises and young entrepreneurs, helping more businesses explore opportunities in both markets. The following office-bearers were appointed for the 2026/2027 term : President - Tilak Gunawardana, , Senior Vice President - Randeewa Malalasooriya, Vice President - Tuan Farhath Armith, and Treasurer - Halin Hettigoda.

The partnership was formalised through the signing of a memorandum of understanding, marking the beginning of a collaborative effort to make property ownership more accessible through flexible financing options, personalised support and faster processing times. Under the partnership, the eligible customers purchasing property directly from Fairway Latitude can access Seylan Bank’s housing loan facilities with exclusive benefits, including repayment periods of up to 25 years and loan approvals processed within seven days.
audit.body: Seylan Bank PLC has entered into a strategic partnership with Fairway Latitude, a subsidiary of Fairway Holdings, one of Sri Lanka’s leading real estate and property development companies, to provide tailored home loan solutions to the customers purchasing luxury apartments from Fairway Latitude. Further enhancing the offering, Fairway Latitude will provide the customers with exclusive discounts on its apartments for Seylan customers. Our partnership with Fairway Latitude allows us to make that journey simpler and more accessible by combining flexible financing with personalised guidance and faster processing. We are pleased to offer the customers the financial support they need to take a confident step towards owning their dream home or property.” Fairway Holdings Chairman Virath de Alwis said, “We are delighted to partner with Seylan Bank to provide greater value and convenience to our customers. This collaboration brings together Fairway Latitude’s property solutions and Seylan Bank’s home financing expertise, giving the prospective homeowners access to attractive financing options and an exclusive offers for the Seylan customers. We believe this partnership will help make property ownership a more achievable reality for many Sri Lankans.” Seylan Home Loans are supported by dedicated home loan specialists, who offer doorstep service and free consultation from the initial inquiry through to loan disbursement. The customers can also access the facility through Seylan Bank’s islandwide branch network, where dedicated staff provide assistance with documentation and ongoing support throughout the loan process.

audit.headline: Softlogic extends warrant conversion window to November
audit.summary: Softlogic Holdings PLC has extended the payment deadline for converting its warrants into shares to 19 November, giving remaining warrant holders additional time to take part in the conglomerate’s equity raising as it continues to strengthen its capital base and pare down debt, a stock filing showed. The last date for payment, previously set for 7 October, was moved following a request to the Colombo Stock Exchange on 19 October, with the company noting that the change would not affect warrant holders who have already paid. The new shares will be deposited on or before 4 December and begin trading on 8 December. The warrants were issued at zero cost alongside Softlogic’s 2024 rights issue, which raised Rs.2.02 billion at Rs.10 a share, with subscribers receiving three warrants for every five rights shares.
audit.body: Softlogic Holdings PLC has extended the payment deadline for converting its warrants into shares to 19 November, giving remaining warrant holders additional time to take part in the conglomerate’s equity raising as it continues to strengthen its capital base and pare down debt, a stock filing showed. The last date for payment, previously set for 7 October, was moved following a request to the Colombo Stock Exchange on 19 October, with the company noting that the change would not affect warrant holders who have already paid. The new shares will be deposited on or before 4 December and begin trading on 8 December. The warrants were issued at zero cost alongside Softlogic’s 2024 rights issue, which raised Rs.2.02 billion at Rs.10 a share, with subscribers receiving three warrants for every five rights shares. Each of the roughly 121.6 million warrants is convertible into one share at Rs.10.50. As per its annual report, the company had received Rs.498 million from the conversion, with major shareholders Chairman and Managing Director Ashok Pathirage and Samena Ceylon Holdings having exercised their warrants. A further Rs.777 million is expected, lifting total proceeds to Rs.1.27 billion, earmarked for settling debt and meeting working capital needs. The fresh equity complements a debt restructuring drive under which Softlogic has signed offer letters for close to Rs.60 billion of loans, securing grace periods of six to 18 months on capital repayments, while requests covering a further Rs.15.7 billion await lender approval. Pathirage told Mirror Business last month that only a small fraction of the group’s debt remained to be restructured, with negotiations with lenders underway. Group revenue rose 24 percent to Rs.129 billion in 2025/26, while EBITDA grew 43 percent to Rs.17.8 billion and operating cash flow climbed 60 percent to Rs.14 billion. Finance costs eased 15 percent to Rs.13.7 billion, helping narrow the loss after tax by 68 percent to Rs.3.59 billion.

audit.headline: Sri Lanka needs ‘hero’ luxury resort to reset market perception: Bawa Trust chief
audit.summary: Soneva and One&Only cited as projects that reshaped global perceptions of the Maldives Calls for sharper destination branding and a rethink of setback rules in building bylaws Bawa’s essential-only design, born of a weak economy, held up as a low-cost model for resort developers By Nishel Fernando Channa Daswatte Sri Lanka needs at least one ‘hero’ luxury resort of the kind that transformed global perceptions of the Maldives, along with sharper destination branding, to capitalise on a uniqueness that is its best asset, according to Geoffrey Bawa Trust Chairperson and MICD Associates Co-Founder Channa Daswatte. In conversation with Hotelivate-Savills Chief Strategy Officer Uttam Davé, Daswatte recently pointed to Soneva in the Maldives and the One&Only brand built under Sol Kerzner as projects whose influence reached well beyond their own...
audit.body: Soneva and One&Only cited as projects that reshaped global perceptions of the Maldives Calls for sharper destination branding and a rethink of setback rules in building bylaws Bawa’s essential-only design, born of a weak economy, held up as a low-cost model for resort developers By Nishel Fernando  Channa Daswatte Sri Lanka needs at least one ‘hero’ luxury resort of the kind that transformed global perceptions of the Maldives, along with sharper destination branding, to capitalise on a uniqueness that is its best asset, according to Geoffrey Bawa Trust Chairperson and MICD Associates Co-Founder Channa Daswatte.  In conversation with Hotelivate-Savills Chief Strategy Officer Uttam Davé, Daswatte recently pointed to Soneva in the Maldives and the One&Only brand built under Sol Kerzner as projects whose influence reached well beyond their own islands.  “I think if there are some hero projects like resorts, luxury resorts, I think the way Soneva did in Maldives and the way Sol Kerzner did One&Only, it changed the perception of the market,” he observed. Soneva Fushi opened in 1995 as the Maldives’ first ‘castaway’ resort and pioneered back-to-nature luxury, while One&Only Reethi Rah, which opened in 2005, set the benchmark for the luxury resorts that followed. “Just one of those super luxury hero resorts changed the perception of the market,” Daswatte added, arguing that Sri Lanka already possesses the raw ingredients in its landscapes, people and food. “I think uniqueness is our best asset,” he remarked. Tourism earnings of US$ 3.2 billion in 2025 remained about 27 percent below the 2018 peak of US$ 4,381 million, even though arrivals last year surpassed 2018 levels. Earnings per tourist have consequently fallen from close to US$ 1,880 to roughly US$ 1,360, underlining the yield problem facing the industry. However, Daswatte did not regard regulation as a serious impediment, noting that much of Sri Lanka’s building bylaws are clear. He questioned whether setback requirements were excessive and left too little usable space, conceding that there was “definitely room for improvement there in terms of redefining the bylaws.” The larger gap, he argued, lay in how the country presents itself. “What I do see needs to be done to make the experience better is that there needs to be a little more destination branding,” he stressed. Daswatte traced the simplicity that defines Bawa’s work to the constraints of the economy in which he practiced.  “We had a really bad economy. So Bawa had the economy on his side,” he pointed out, explaining that Bawa felt no obligation to build anything beyond what was essential. Rather than ordering furniture from the latest catalogue, Bawa would design a chair himself using the simplest materials available, an approach that Daswatte noted cost practically nothing in the end. The same reliance on simple, basic and essential elements is what clients still associate with his own practice today, he added, adopted not as a stylistic choice but because it was appropriate. That thinking also shaped the Kandalama Hotel, which surprised many by carrying none of the traditional columns or decorative elements expected of an architect who was by then known, much to his dislike, as a vernacular architect. Daswatte recalled Bawa explaining to one of the directors that the whole place was scaled around looking at the horizon. Guests who spent their days amid 2,000 years of history and architecture, Bawa reasoned, should not return at night to be bombarded by yet more decoration. For Bawa, Daswatte explained, a hotel was a refuge for people arriving from completely stressed-out environments. Developers who keep guests sealed indoors, he cautioned, deny them the very place they have travelled to experience, leaving them “inside an air conditioning box looking at a view on the wall.” Good architecture, he maintained, should open up, close in and let the breeze through, so that guests experience the location they have chosen. Daswatte also warned against lifting a design element from one place and dropping it into another, insisting that context must lead. In taking Bawa’s legacy to a house he designed in Dubai, he retained ideas such as courtyards and interconnected spaces while responding to an entirely different environment and climate. Asked which principles he would embed in a resort built today, Daswatte said the core of the concept should draw on the country’s own history, while guests should always retain the option of peace and a holiday in nature. He noted that buildings Bawa designed some 50 years ago are now being restored, urging the industry to look after them. Bawa’s work has meanwhile drawn renewed international attention, with the Vitra Design Museum in Germany opening the first major retrospective of his work in two decades on 26 September, ahead of a run at M+ in Hong Kong from June 2027.

audit.body: Union Assurance PLC and Nations Trust Bank PLC (NTB) have renewed their long-standing exclusive bancassurance partnership, further strengthening an alliance that has played a pivotal role in expanding access to financial protection solutions for the customers across the country. The renewed partnership reflects the shared commitment of both organisations to delivering holistic financial solutions that seamlessly combine banking convenience with life insurance protection. Through this collaboration, the customers will continue to have convenient access to solutions designed to help safeguard their financial futures while supporting their evolving aspirations and life goals.  Over the years, the partnership has evolved into one of Sri Lanka’s leading bancassurance collaborations, underpinned by a strong focus on customer centricity, innovation and service excellence.  By combining NTB’s branch network, growing digital banking ecosystem and customer reach with Union Assurance’s expertise in life insurance, the partnership has enabled thousands of customers to access comprehensive protection, savings and investment solutions tailored to their individual needs. The renewal marks a significant milestone in the relationship between the two organisations and sets the foundation for the next phase of growth.  NTB Director and Chief Executive Officer Hemantha Gunetilleke said, “The renewal of our partnership with Union Assurance reinforces our commitment to providing the customers with comprehensive financial solutions through a trusted life insurance partner. As customer expectations continue to evolve, the need for integrated banking and protection offerings has become increasingly important. Together with Union Assurance, we look forward to further enhancing our bancassurance proposition and delivering greater value through innovative, customer-centric solutions.” Union Assurance Director and Chief Executive Officer Senath Jayatilake said, “Our partnership with NTB has been built on a shared vision of creating meaningful value for customers through seamless access to financial protection solutions. Over the years, this collaboration has consistently delivered strong outcomes by combining the strength of two trusted institutions. As we renew this partnership, we remain committed to driving innovation, expanding accessibility and helping more Sri Lankans protect what matters most while progressing confidently towards their future goals.”

audit.headline: ‘Sententia.ai’ backed by Lankan investment banker, joins NVIDIA Inception Programme
audit.summary: Sententia.ai, an early-stage legal-tech venture backed by Sri Lankan investment banker Sanjana Fernando, has been accepted into the NVIDIA for Startups Inception accelerator. The move gives the cross-border transaction structuring platform access to the chipmaker’s technical resources, AI ecosystem and global startup network, the company announced. NVIDIA’s Inception programme supports startups building AI-driven technology and does not take an equity stake in its members. Instead, it offers preferential access to NVIDIA hardware and software, technical training and exposure to its venture capital network. For a pre-commercial venture still validating its first structuring corridor, membership is a useful credential when courting design-partner law firms and institutional investors.
