It is now used to cheat in the classroom and to help faculty generate papers, but also for positive purposes, such as making PowerPoint presentations more concise and generating practice questions. I have used ChatGPT to edit and proof-read my assignments. I have also given it old assignments and asked it to generate new ones of similar difficulty. I use it to generate nested-loop practice questions similar to those I wrote from scratch during my years as a full-time lecturer at the University of Oklahoma. In industry and government, including warfare, weapons systems, and hiring, AI is taking a massive role in logistics, operations, and decision-making. Will it lead to more layoffs? Is it making people intellectually lazy? In the classroom, it is certainly making students lazy about thinking. A calculator never claimed to think for you; AI quietly does. And what happens if AI goes wrong? (By the way, calling it “Super Intelligence” is foolish, and insisting that people who say “Super Intelligence” rather than “Artificial Intelligence” are wrong; it sounds straight out of Orwellian literature when Trump says people who say AI rather than SI are enemies of the state) Warfare, strategy, and weapons are all becoming AI-dependent with less and less human judgment, so more mistakes are likely. A machine that never doubts itself should never be the last word on life and death. Can it become an addiction, like gaming or drugs? As a line in a movie put it, the more widespread AI becomes, the more Emotional Intelligence will be needed by those using it to make decisions that affect the entire human race. The more we outsource our thinking, the less we have left to outsource. Mano Ratwatte USA

audit.headline: Central Bank of the future needs to be intelligence-driven public institution, says IMF CIO
audit.summary: Emphasises technology should never make final policy calls IMF Chief Information Officer Shirin Hamid By Sanath Nanayakkare As artificial intelligence rapidly transforms global finance, forcing central banks to make strategic operational choices, IMF Chief Information Officer Shirin Hamid delivered the 76th Anniversary Oration of the Central Bank of Sri Lanka (CBSL) in Colombo on October 23, under the theme “The Intelligent Central Bank: Building Trust in the Age of AI”. Delivering the keynote address, she emphasised that the central bank of the future must evolve beyond a tech-heavy entity into an intelligence-driven public institution.
audit.body: Emphasises technology should never make final policy calls IMF Chief Information Officer Shirin Hamid By Sanath Nanayakkare As artificial intelligence rapidly transforms global finance, forcing central banks to make strategic operational choices, IMF Chief Information Officer Shirin Hamid delivered the 76th Anniversary Oration of the Central Bank of Sri Lanka (CBSL) in Colombo on October 23, under the theme “The Intelligent Central Bank: Building Trust in the Age of AI”. Delivering the keynote address, she emphasised that the central bank of the future must evolve beyond a tech-heavy entity into an intelligence-driven public institution. Expanding on this vision, she noted that the core promise of AI in central banking lies not in creating an automated efficiency engine, but in building an institutional brain – an adaptive decision-support system designed to sharpen, rather than replace, human judgment. “In the corporate world, AI is often deployed to cut costs and automate routine operations. Given that central banks manage massive datasets covering prices, payments, and credit records, automation seems like a natural step. However, relying on AI as an automated driver introduces serious risks. In public policy, speed cannot replace stability and trust. Unchecked algorithms evaluating credit risk or liquidity needs can amplify market panic, turning software errors into institutional crises,” she explained. An institutional brain, by contrast, uses data as a real-time sensory network. While traditional economic models rely on lagging quarterly indicators, AI can act as a high-resolution radar – scanning daily transaction flows and market anomalies to afford policymakers immediate situational awareness. Crucially, she stressed that technology should never make final policy calls. Key decisions on interest rates, currency management, and emergency interventions demand political sensitivity, ethics, and qualitative judgment – qualities no algorithm possesses. AI must serve as a cognitive tool while humans remain fully accountable for policy outcomes. Transforming central banks into intelligence-driven institutions requires a cultural shift, not just software upgrades. AI cannot remain confined to IT departments; central bank governors, regulators, and legal teams must learn to work alongside machine models, understanding their limits while leveraging their predictive power. Ultimately, the objective is to enhance human leadership with unprecedented clarity, ensuring central banks can navigate fast-moving financial markets while safeguarding public trust in money and markets, she concluded. audit.headline: Colombo-based diplomatic corps marks Intl Diplomat Day
audit.summary: News Published on By Share Tweet More than 150 representatives from over 21 diplomatic missions, the United Nations and Sri Lanka’s Foreign Ministry gathered in Colombo, on Saturday, to mark International Diplomat Day 2026. The event was held at the Embassy of Indonesia in Colombo and was attended by ambassadors, high commissioners, heads of diplomatic missions, members of the diplomatic community, government representatives and their families. Foreign Affairs, Foreign Employment and Tourism Minister Vijitha Herath was the Chief Guest. Dean of the Diplomatic Corps and Indonesian Ambassador to Sri Lanka Dewi Gustina Tobing paid tribute to diplomats for their dedication and sacrifices, noting that their duties often required them to work away from their home countries and families.
audit.body: News Published on By Share Tweet More than 150 representatives from over 21 diplomatic missions, the United Nations and Sri Lanka’s Foreign Ministry gathered in Colombo, on Saturday, to mark International Diplomat Day 2026. The event was held at the Embassy of Indonesia in Colombo and was attended by ambassadors, high commissioners, heads of diplomatic missions, members of the diplomatic community, government representatives and their families. Foreign Affairs, Foreign Employment and Tourism Minister Vijitha Herath was the Chief Guest. Dean of the Diplomatic Corps and Indonesian Ambassador to Sri Lanka Dewi Gustina Tobing paid tribute to diplomats for their dedication and sacrifices, noting that their duties often required them to work away from their home countries and families. She stressed the importance of international cooperation in addressing global challenges, including climate change, armed conflicts, inequality and rapid technological development. United Nations Resident Coordinator in Sri Lanka Marc-André Franche underscored the importance of the UN Charter, international law and a rules-based international order in maintaining global peace and security. Herath highlighted the importance of friendship, peace, cooperation and mutual understanding among nations, while acknowledging the contribution of diplomats and their families towards strengthening bilateral relations. The celebration featured sporting events, including mini football, badminton, volleyball, tennis, table tennis and chess, as well as traditional Sri Lankan games, karaoke and activities for children. As part of the event, the Diplomatic Corps also donated food, stationery and other essential items through the Foreign Ministry for the benefit of local communities.

audit.headline: Commercial Bank named Sri Lanka’s Best Bank by Global Finance for 24th time
audit.summary: The Commercial Bank of Ceylon’s remarkable near two-and-a-half-decade run as Sri Lanka’s best bank was recognised on the global stage recently when Sanath Manatunge, the Bank’s Managing Director/CEO accepted the Best Bank award presented to the Bank by Global Finance for the 24th time. The Global Finance Annual Awards ceremony for 2026 was held at the Dusit Thani Bangkok, coinciding with the IMF/World Bank Annual Meetings. Commercial Bank also received the Global Finance accolade for the Best Islamic Bank in Sri Lanka at the same event. Global Finance’s ‘World’s Best Banks 2026’ awards recognised top-performing banks in more than 150 countries, territories and districts across Africa, Asia-Pacific, the Caribbean, Central America, Central & Eastern Europe, Latin America, the Middle East, North America and Western Europe.

audit.headline: Communist Party opposes proposed counterterror organised crime laws
audit.summary: News Published on By Share Tweet The Communist Party of Sri Lanka (CPSL) has strongly opposed the Protection of the State from Terrorism Bill and Prevention of Organised Crimes Bill, warning that the legislation could pose a threat to democratic freedoms and fundamental rights. The CPSL has said it recognises the need to combat terrorism, organised crime and threats to public security, having itself suffered violence during both the civil conflict and the 1987-90 period. Full text of the statement: The Communist Party of Sri Lanka (CPSL) expresses its strongest opposition to the proposed Protection of the State from Terrorism Bill and the Prevention of Organised Crimes Bill, which together represent a grave threat to democracy, fundamental rights, and the freedoms guaranteed to the people of Sri Lanka.
audit.body: News Published on By Share Tweet The Communist Party of Sri Lanka (CPSL) has strongly opposed the Protection of the State from Terrorism Bill and Prevention of Organised Crimes Bill, warning that the legislation could pose a threat to democratic freedoms and fundamental rights. The CPSL has said it recognises the need to combat terrorism, organised crime and threats to public security, having itself suffered violence during both the civil conflict and the 1987-90 period. Full text of the statement: The Communist Party of Sri Lanka (CPSL) expresses its strongest opposition to the proposed Protection of the State from Terrorism Bill and the Prevention of Organised Crimes Bill, which together represent a grave threat to democracy, fundamental rights, and the freedoms guaranteed to the people of Sri Lanka. It fears that the new powers inherent in these Bills may be used to establish a dictatorial form of government over the people. The CPSL has itself been persecuted by terrorist murderers, both during the long civil conflict in the North and East of the country, and during the 1987-90 period of terror in the South. It is, therefore, fully cognisant of the need to address terrorism, organised criminal activity, and threats to public security. However, it was also banned and its leaders were jailed in 1983 by the state, which accused it falsely of being behind the racist pogrom launched by the governing party that year. So, it knows at first hand that the State should never be allowed to use laws as instruments to curtail democratic dissent, suppress social movements, or undermine the constitutional rights of citizens. The broad powers and sweeping provisions contained in these Bills, which appear to undermine and negate certain provisions of existing legislation or regulations, raise serious concerns regarding the potential for abuse and arbitrary application. Of particular worry are broad provisions which include over-criminalisation (inclusion of minor crimes which should be treated under the normal law), threats to the freedom of expression (including journalistic reporting and, potentially even having tattoos on one’s body), excessive executive power (for example arbitrarily to designate an area as forbidden) and altered conditions of detention, bail and confessions. The NPP Government has yet to prove that the existing laws and institutions are insufficient to combat terrorism and organised crime. In the absence of such proof, the proposed expansion of State powers over detention, bail conditions, confessions, and freedom of expression appears unnecessary, disproportionate, and potentially detrimental to democratic freedoms. The people of Sri Lanka have a long history of defending democratic rights through trade union struggles, student movements, peasant organisations, and popular campaigns for social justice. Legislation that creates wide powers of surveillance, detention, restriction, and criminalisation, without adequate judicial safeguards and democratic oversight, poses a danger not only to political organisations but also to workers, journalists, civil society activists, and ordinary citizens exercising their democratic rights. The CPSL is particularly concerned that vague definitions and excessive executive powers could be used to intimidate or silence legitimate criticism of government policies, social protest, industrial action, and political mobilisation. The experience of previous security legislation in Sri Lanka demonstrates the need for extreme vigilance whenever extraordinary powers are sought in the name of protecting the State or maintaining public order. The true strength of a democratic society lies not in the expansion of coercive powers but in the confidence and participation of its people. Lasting security can be achieved only through social justice, economic opportunity, respect for human rights, and due process. Measures that erode public trust and democratic accountability ultimately weaken rather than strengthen national security. The CPSL therefore calls upon the Government to withdraw these Bills and initiate a transparent and democratic process of consultation involving trade unions, legal professionals, academics, religious leaders, and representatives of civil society. Any legislation intended to address terrorism or organised crime must be fully consistent with constitutional guarantees, international human rights standards, and the principles of democratic governance. The CPSL stands firmly with all those committed to safeguarding democracy, social justice, national sovereignty, and the rights of the people. We call upon all progressive political forces, democratic organisations, trade unions, youth and student movements, and concerned citizens to unite in defence of democratic freedoms and fundamental rights. The protection of national security must never become a pretext for the erosion of civil liberties or the suppression of legitimate democratic activity.

audit.headline: Dialog Axiata and IITM Pravartak partner for Sri Lankan technological advancement
audit.summary: Driving cross-border innovation Dialog Axiata PLC has established a milestone partnership with India’s IITM Pravartak Technologies Foundation through a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU), signifying a powerful step forward in technology-driven collaboration between Sri Lanka and India. Designed to accelerate applied research, enhance national talent, and foster real-world societal solutions, this strategic enterprise bridges high-level academic research with industry infrastructure. By leveraging combined international expertise, the initiative establishes a framework for translating cutting-edge technological concepts into functional, high-impact applications across Sri Lanka.
audit.body: Driving cross-border innovation Dialog Axiata PLC has established a milestone partnership with India’s IITM Pravartak Technologies Foundation through a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU), signifying a powerful step forward in technology-driven collaboration between Sri Lanka and India. Designed to accelerate applied research, enhance national talent, and foster real-world societal solutions, this strategic enterprise bridges high-level academic research with industry infrastructure. By leveraging combined international expertise, the initiative establishes a framework for translating cutting-edge technological concepts into functional, high-impact applications across Sri Lanka. Within this framework, Dialog Axiata acts as the core technology enabler and anchor, connecting IITM Pravartak’s extensive research network with Sri Lankan enterprise leaders, academic institutions, and local communities. The collaboration focuses on five core pillars: innovation and incubation, applied research and university labs, AI-driven human-centric solutions, industry talent development, and international knowledge transfer. Initial research and pilot programs aim to tackle pressing national priorities, including the development of Sinhala and Tamil conversational artificial intelligence, tech-enabled dengue prevention systems, and innovative mitigations for human-elephant conflict. The partnership has received strong support from leadership across both nations. Santosh Jha, High Commissioner of India to Sri Lanka, highlighted the alliance as a key milestone in deepening bilateral engagement and mutual progress. Dr. Shankar Jayaraman, CEO of IITM Pravartak, emphasized the synergy created between academic research and commercial application, aiming to empower students and researchers to build localized, practical solutions. Likewise, Supun Weerasinghe, Group CEO of Dialog Axiata, underscored the company’s commitment to using technology to address real-world challenges, connecting global technical expertise with Sri Lanka’s domestic talent pool to drive sustainable growth. To ensure long-term viability and impact, the initiative will deploy a phased rollout. Beginning with targeted pilot projects, each initiative will undergo rigorous evaluation against clearly defined metrics before scaling. This measured approach ensures that every venture remains outcome-oriented, providing sustainable solutions that empower Sri Lankan communities and elevate the nation’s broader technological ecosystem.

audit.headline: Disciplining students without the cane
audit.summary: Opinion Published on By Share Tweet by Saumya Aloysius [email protected] Discipline is one of the most important qualities that students should develop during their school life. It helps them become responsible, respectful, honest and successful individuals. In Sri Lanka, schools have traditionally placed great importance on discipline, good behaviour and respect for teachers and elders. In the past, some teachers used the cane as a method of punishment to correct students who disobeyed school rules. However, education is changing, and there is increasing recognition that students can be disciplined effectively without physical punishment. The challenge today is to build a school environment in which students learn to behave well through understanding, guidance, self-control and mutual respect.
audit.body: Opinion Published on By Share Tweet by Saumya Aloysius [email protected] Discipline is one of the most important qualities that students should develop during their school life. It helps them become responsible, respectful, honest and successful individuals. In Sri Lanka, schools have traditionally placed great importance on discipline, good behaviour and respect for teachers and elders. In the past, some teachers used the cane as a method of punishment to correct students who disobeyed school rules. However, education is changing, and there is increasing recognition that students can be disciplined effectively without physical punishment. The challenge today is to build a school environment in which students learn to behave well through understanding, guidance, self-control and mutual respect. The Meaning and Importance of Discipline Discipline does not simply mean obeying orders or being afraid of punishment. True discipline means understanding the difference between right and wrong and choosing to do what is right. A disciplined student attends school regularly, arrives on time, completes homework, respects teachers and classmates, follows school rules and takes responsibility for personal actions. In Sri Lanka, schools bring together children from different social, cultural, religious and economic backgrounds. Therefore, discipline is essential for maintaining a peaceful learning environment. When students behave responsibly, teachers can teach effectively, and everyone has a fair opportunity to learn. Good discipline also prepares young people for their future responsibilities as citizens, employees, parents and community members. Why discipline without the cane is necessary Physical punishment may sometimes produce immediate obedience, but obedience based on fear does not necessarily develop good character. A student who behaves well only to avoid being beaten may not understand why the behaviour is wrong. Furthermore, physical punishment can cause physical injury, emotional distress, humiliation and a loss of trust between teachers and students. Children learn better when they feel safe, valued and respected. If a student is afraid of a teacher, the student may hesitate to ask questions, admit mistakes or seek help when facing difficulties. Such fear can negatively affect learning and personal development. Discipline without the cane does not mean allowing students to do whatever they want. Instead, it means correcting unacceptable behaviour through fair, consistent and non-violent methods. Teachers must maintain authority while treating students with dignity. Clear boundaries and appropriate consequences can help children understand that every action has a result. Role of teachers in maintaining discipline Teachers play a vital role in developing discipline among students in Sri Lanka. They should act not only as instructors but also as role models. Students often learn more from a teacher’s behaviour than from the teacher’s words. A teacher who is punctual, patient, fair and respectful encourages students to develop similar qualities. At the beginning of each school term, teachers can explain classroom rules and discuss why those rules are necessary. Students can also be encouraged to participate in creating reasonable classroom agreements. When children have a voice in setting rules, they may feel greater responsibility for following them. Teachers should correct mistakes calmly and privately whenever possible. Instead of insulting a student who disrupts a lesson, a teacher can explain the problem and give the student an opportunity to improve. Praising good behaviour, recognising effort and encouraging cooperation can also motivate students to act responsibly. Positive methods of discipline There are many effective ways to discipline students without using the cane. One method is positive reinforcement. When students demonstrate punctuality, honesty, kindness or responsibility, teachers can recognise their efforts through praise, certificates, leadership opportunities or other suitable rewards. Students who have hurt others can be guided to understand the effects of their actions, apologise sincerely and take steps to repair the harm. audit.headline: Foundation stones laid for Kelaniya temple’s centenary sacred area
audit.summary: News Published on By Share Tweet The foundation stones for the Centenary Sacred Area Garden and a new perimeter wall marking the sacred boundary of the historic Kelaniya Raja Maha Viharaya were laid on Saturday as preparations began for the centenary of the modern Kelaniya Duruthu Maha Perahera. The ceremony was held under the guidance and blessings of the temple’s Chief Incumbent, Most Venerable Kollupitiye Mahinda Sangharakkhitha Nayaka Thera, and Venerable Professor Deniyaye Pannaloka Buddharakkhitha Thera. The foundation stones were laid by businessman and entrepreneur Rayynor Silva, Dayaka Sabha Chairman Dr Saman Weerasinghe, and Basnayake Nilame Dhammika Attygalle, in the presence of members of the Maha Sangha, the Dayaka Sabha, devotees and well-wishers.
audit.body: News Published on By Share Tweet The foundation stones for the Centenary Sacred Area Garden and a new perimeter wall marking the sacred boundary of the historic Kelaniya Raja Maha Viharaya were laid on Saturday as preparations began for the centenary of the modern Kelaniya Duruthu Maha Perahera. The ceremony was held under the guidance and blessings of the temple’s Chief Incumbent, Most Venerable Kollupitiye Mahinda Sangharakkhitha Nayaka Thera, and Venerable Professor Deniyaye Pannaloka Buddharakkhitha Thera. The foundation stones were laid by businessman and entrepreneur Rayynor Silva, Dayaka Sabha Chairman Dr Saman Weerasinghe, and Basnayake Nilame Dhammika Attygalle, in the presence of members of the Maha Sangha, the Dayaka Sabha, devotees and well-wishers. The proceedings began with the observance of the Five Precepts, followed by an introduction to the project and the foundation stone-laying ceremony. Videos on the centenary of the Duruthu Maha Perahera and the proposed Sacred Area Garden were also screened. The project, led by the Dayaka Sabha, will involve rebuilding, modernising and securing the temple’s boundary and surrounding gardens, using modern technology, sustainable materials and contemporary construction methods. The project is also intended to create a safe and serene environment for families and children in Kelaniya who live around and help protect the temple. Kelaniya is traditionally regarded as the sacred site visited by the Buddha during his third visit to Sri Lanka, following an invitation from Naga King Maniakkhika. The Duruthu Maha Perahera, which had ceased during the period following the ancient kings, was revived in 1927 through the efforts of Don Walter Wijewardene, son of Helena Wijewardene. The 100th Kelaniya Duruthu Maha Perahera is scheduled to be held on January 21, 2027.

audit.headline: Future Life Investments marks its 10th anniversary at Employee Convention
audit.summary: Future Life Investments, which marks a decade of operations in Sri Lanka’s microfinance sector, recently held its employee convention to recognise outstanding performers during the first two quarters of the 2026/27 financial year. Attended by more than 900 employees, the event celebrated exceptional performance with a range of rewards, including awards, certificates, overseas trips and new motor vehicles. The convention, held under the leadership of the company’s senior management, recognised achievements at both individual and branch levels. Selected members of the ‘FLI Eagles’ were also honoured for their outstanding performance. The initiative underscored the company’s commitment to recognising employee dedication, efficiency and contribution towards achieving organisational goals.

audit.headline: HLAB Fund launches LKR 3bn initiative to scale Sri Lankan startups
audit.summary: In a major boost to the domestic entrepreneurial ecosystem, startup incubator Hatch, the Lankan Angel Network (LAN), and venture capital firm BOV Capital have launched HLAB—a collective LKR 3 billion fund designed to help early and growth-stage Sri Lankan companies scale regionally. Unveiled at the finale of the First Capital Startup Nation initiative organized by Hatch, the fund addresses a critical structural gap in the country’s business landscape: expanding access to long-term growth capital for local founders attempting to transition from early-stage proof of concept to sustainable, market-ready enterprises. Adding institutional backing to the private sector coalition, First Capital Holdings PLC has committed LKR 300 million as the fund’s anchor limited partner, representing 10 percent of the total fund size.

audit.headline: Historic Kithulgala Rest House reimagined under EKHO banner
audit.summary: The iconic Kithulgala Rest House, a landmark destination in Sri Lanka’s hospitality history along the banks of the Kelani River, has entered a new phase of operation following its transformation into EKHO Kithulgala. The transition marks the seventh property to join the EKHO Hotels & Resorts portfolio, following the recent revitalization of the former Belihuloya Rest House into EKHO Belihuloya. Together, the two redevelopments reflect a broader effort to restore and modernize Sri Lanka’s network of classic public rest houses, balancing historical preservation with upgraded amenities for contemporary travelers. The property features 20 refreshed guest rooms divided between Garden View and River View options, along with structural enhancements to its common spaces designed to retain the rest house’s traditional architecture and familiar nostalgia.
audit.body: The iconic Kithulgala Rest House, a landmark destination in Sri Lanka’s hospitality history along the banks of the Kelani River, has entered a new phase of operation following its transformation into EKHO Kithulgala. The transition marks the seventh property to join the EKHO Hotels & Resorts portfolio, following the recent revitalization of the former Belihuloya Rest House into EKHO Belihuloya. Together, the two redevelopments reflect a broader effort to restore and modernize Sri Lanka’s network of classic public rest houses, balancing historical preservation with upgraded amenities for contemporary travelers. The property features 20 refreshed guest rooms divided between Garden View and River View options, along with structural enhancements to its common spaces designed to retain the rest house’s traditional architecture and familiar nostalgia. Set within Sri Lanka’s wet zone rainforest corridor, the property has long served as a key base camp for naturalists, birdwatchers, and outdoor enthusiasts exploring the adjacent Makandawa Forest Reserve, a prime habitat for endemic avian species. In addition to nature tourism, the site retains a distinct operational advantage for adventure travel: the primary white-water rafting run down the Kelani River terminates directly at the property’s shoreline, allowing rafters to disembark straight onto the hotel grounds. The surrounding area also carries enduring historic interest through its connection to David Lean’s 1957 Oscar-winning epic The Bridge on the River Kwai, which was filmed along this stretch of the Kelani River and continues to draw cinema history enthusiasts.

audit.headline: Indian High Commissioner meets Lalkantha
audit.summary: News Published on By … ships declare ‘state of emergency’ by Shamindra Ferdinando Forty Iranian sailors from Iranian oil tankers stranded outside Sri Lanka’s territorial waters have been repatriated. Foreign Minister Vijitha Herath confirmed the evacuation of the Iranian sailors by the Navy and their repatriation to Iran on Sunday. Responding to The Island query, Minister Herath said that the government had acted following a request from Iran. Sri Lanka intervened amidst accusations that refusal to provide assistance to vessels was contrary to international laws. About 21 Iranian vessels are believed to be stranded off Sri Lanka’s southern coast for several months due to the ongoing US blockade on Iranian ports. The crew members included Indians and Bangladeshis. The Island learns that humanitarian intervention had been made with the understanding of the US.

A spokesperson for the Embassy of the Islamic Republic of Iran, in Colombo, told The Island : “These individuals were brought ashore and taken to hospital for medical treatment due to health issues, following the declaration of a state of emergency by the vessels, in accordance with the obligations arising under the relevant international conventions concerning the rescue of persons aboard ships.” News Published on By SJB and Opposition Leader Sajith Premadasa has sought international support to oppose the government’s proposed security laws. Premadasa convened a consultation with representatives of diplomatic missions and international organisations at the Office of the Leader of the Opposition, Colombo 7, on Sunday, to underscore serious concerns relating to proposed security legislation, constitutional safeguards and democratic accountability. The discussion focused on the Protection of the State from Terrorism Bill and the Prevention of Organised Crimes Bill. Former MP M. A. Sumanthiran, together with participating serving and former Members of Parliament, also expressed serious concerns about the proposed legislation and its potential implications for fundamental rights and the rule of law. Premadasa underlined the responsibility of the parliamentary Opposition to scrutinise government legislation, protect independent institutions and ensure that executive power remains subject to the Constitution. He reaffirmed that decisive action against terrorism and serious organised crime must be accompanied by effective judicial oversight and respect for civil liberties. Particular attention was drawn to the Human Rights Commission of Sri Lanka’s (HRCSL) official statement of 21 October, 2026, on the Prevention of Organised Crime Bill. The Commission assessed the proposed Bill as “wholly incompatible” with the fundamental-rights chapter of the Constitution and Sri Lanka’s international human-rights obligations, and described it as potentially more draconian than the Prevention of Terrorism Act of 1979. These are the HRCSL’s assessments, not findings by a court. The Commission identified concerns about the admissibility of confessions made to senior police officers, detention ordered through the executive, the extensive definition of “serious crime”, criteria such as clothing, tattoos or association when assessing alleged criminal-group membership, and provisions that restrict judicial discretion over remand and bail. Crucially, the HRCSL recommended that the Prevention of Organised Crime Bill be withdrawn and substantially revised to comply with constitutional and international human-rights standards. In observations, dated 1 October, 2026, on the Ministry-published draft terrorism Bill, the HRCSL separately urged the Government to narrow the proposed definition of terrorism, subject detention orders to judicial oversight, preserve meaningful judicial authority to grant bail, guarantee prompt access to legal counsel and ensure the independence of the proposed review mechanism. It also reiterated its view that terrorism offences should be addressed under general criminal law. The Bar Association of Sri Lanka (BASL), in its statement of 21 October, called for withdrawal of the organised crime Bill and withdrawal or amendment of the terrorism Bill in its present form. It also sought publication of the expert committee report and recorded dissent relating to the terrorism Bill, raising concerns over departures from the committee-approved draft. Premadasa emphasised the need for a transparent legislative response: publication of relevant expert recommendations; clear and proportionate definitions of offences; meaningful judicial discretion over detention, remand and bail; protection against coerced confessions and arbitrary surveillance; and consultation with the BASL, HRCSL and other relevant stakeholders before legislation with such far-reaching implications proceeds. He stressed that these safeguards are not privileges of politicians or activists. They protect ordinary citizens, young people, families, businesses and all others who may come into contact with the criminal justice system. The Opposition’s position is that national security and the rule of law must reinforce, not undermine, one another. The consultation provided an opportunity to share independently documented concerns with diplomatic and international representatives. Premadasa reaffirmed Sri Lanka’s sovereignty and the primary responsibility of Parliament, the judiciary and national institutions to resolve domestic legal questions, while emphasising constructive dialogue rather than external intervention or partisan endorsement. The Opposition Leader reiterated his commitment to constructive parliamentary engagement on effective security legislation that protects the public from serious crime while upholding constitutional democracy, judicial independence and individual liberty. News Published on By The Supreme Court has declared null and void a presidential pardon granted by President Ranil Wickremesinghe to a man sentenced to 29 months in prison for failing to pay Rs. 1.74 million in maintenance arrears. In a judgment delivered last Friday (23), a three-judge bench held that the remission granted to Mohamed Ameen Mohamed Naseem, under a general amnesty in September 2024, violated his former wife’s fundamental right to equality and equal protection of the law guaranteed under Article 12(1) of the Constitution. The judgment was delivered by Justice Janak De Silva, with Justices Dr. Sobhitha Rajakaruna and Sampath K.B. Wijeratne agreeing. The case was filed by Naseem’s former wife, Ahamend Jaleel Farmilla Begum, challenging his release after he served less than two months of the 29-month sentence. Naseem had been imprisoned in July 2024 for failing to comply with a maintenance order issued by the Quazi Court. He was released on September 12, 2024, under a general amnesty granted to mark Prisoners’ Day. The Supreme Court found that Naseem had been given preferential treatment after his imprisonment was recorded as being for non-payment of a fine, while another prisoner, imprisoned over similar maintenance arrears, had received only a one-week reduction in his sentence. The Court held that the difference in the wording of the two prisoners’ commitment warrants did not justify the unequal treatment. Accordingly, the Court ruled that former President Wickremesinghe, the Secretary to the Ministry of Justice and the Commissioner General of Prisons, had violated the petitioner’s fundamental rights. The Court declared the remission granted to Naseem null and void, thereby restoring the legal effect of his original sentence. In a significant observation, the Court said Naseem, having been released while his sentence remained legally valid, was now a “fugitive from justice” and should surrender immediately to law enforcement authorities. The Court further held that the original warrant issued by the Negombo Magistrate’s Court remained valid and provided sufficient authority for prison officials to detain Naseem and enforce the sentence. However, it said no further order from the Supreme Court was necessary to enforce the sentence, as the Magistrate’s Court already had the authority to take the necessary steps. The judgment also clarified that the President was not precluded from granting a fresh remission to Naseem, provided it was done in accordance with the law and after considering all relevant circumstances. The ruling was delivered in Fundamental Rights Application No. 319/2024.

audit.headline: Insecurity haunts affluent Europe
audit.summary: Editorial Published on By Share Tweet Monday 26th October, 2026 Parts of Europe are in turmoil. In several European countries, protests against high cost of living, housing unaffordability, welfare cuts and deteriorating public services have escalated into riots, arson, looting and violent clashes between police and protesters. Police have used force to disperse protesters in France, Italy, Belgium and Albania. Videos of unruly mobs looting shops and police crackdowns have gone viral. Out of sheer desperation to stem the rising wave of protests, these European nations are apparently doing exactly the opposite of what they urge the developing countries to do in similar situations. Causes of public unrest in Europe are not limited to the soaring cost of living and serious policy disputes.
audit.body: Editorial Published on By Share Tweet Monday 26th October, 2026 Parts of Europe are in turmoil. In several European countries, protests against high cost of living, housing unaffordability, welfare cuts and deteriorating public services have escalated into riots, arson, looting and violent clashes between police and protesters. Police have used force to disperse protesters in France, Italy, Belgium and Albania. Videos of unruly mobs looting shops and police crackdowns have gone viral. Out of sheer desperation to stem the rising wave of protests, these European nations are apparently doing exactly the opposite of what they urge the developing countries to do in similar situations. Causes of public unrest in Europe are not limited to the soaring cost of living and serious policy disputes. Agitations have stemmed from a host of issues, mainly economic insecurity, falling standard of living, social inequality, misplaced public spending priorities and lack of political accountability. Welfare cuts and austerity measures have aggravated the situation. Media reports, quoting the French Interior Ministry, yesterday said about 410,000 people had protested on Saturday, but trade unions placed the number at 800,000. About 70,000 police personnel were deployed to break up demonstrations, with several cities facing various restrictions. However, the police were far outnumbered, and protests turned violent, triggering another wave of arson attacks and looting. Police excesses are jet fuel for protests although they may seem to work initially. It is feared that protests and riots could engulf more countries in Europe, as they tend to have a cross-border domino effect, as we saw during the Arab Spring protests and the waves of agitations in this part of the world during the past several years. Most European nations are experiencing economic grievances, youth unrest and distrust of political leadership, and they run the risk of facing trouble. The danger is not confined to Europe, according to observers. There is the possibility of protests in Europe inspiring agitations in the US mostly due to domestic issues the Trump administration has failed to address. One may recall that in 2011, Occupy Wall Street (OWS) protests spread in the US against widespread economic inequality and corporate greed. Grievances that gave rise to the OWS protest movement remain, and the Trump government is testing the patience of the public. Meanwhile, Europe is a major destination for migrants from the Global South, seeking better economic opportunities. History shows that economic insecurity in developed countries severely strains relations between sections of native-born populations and immigrant communities, especially where housing, public services and employment are under pressure. A similar situation prevails elsewhere. The latest Canadian government research, published in 2026, shows that public attitudes have become less favourable towards immigration, following a sharp shift in 2023 and 2024. There is evidence of a disturbing rise in anti-Indian sentiments in New Zealand. Several causes of this hostility have been identified, and they include high immigration levels, economic insecurity, the cost of living, political rhetoric, misinformation, cultural identity, racial prejudice and wide publicity for isolated incidents. Some European countries are no strangers to violence associated with immigration tension. France and the UK are among them. Economic pressures are behind rising anti-immigrant hostility in Germany, where years of weak growth, industrial job losses, housing pressures and concerns about public expenditure have intensified insecurity among sections of the population. Far-right groups are capitalising on these anxieties and concerns. It is imperative that rulers of the countries, particularly in the Global South, where youth unrest, economic hardships, distrust of governments and accountability issues are far worse than in Europe, redouble their efforts to eliminate the factors driving unrest. Overreliance on the police and the judiciary to break up protests is counterproductive. Parts of Europe are in turmoil. audit.headline: It’s demagoguery, not democracy
audit.summary: Features Published on By Share Tweet This Curse of Partisan Politics in Sri Lanka – II The revival of our country’s economy starts here by Brigadier Ranjan de Silva [email protected] The latest curse: How partisan politics used the Gnanasara case forgetting Buddhism and the country. audit.body: Features Published on By Share Tweet This Curse of Partisan Politics in Sri Lanka – II The revival of our country’s economy starts here by Brigadier Ranjan de Silva [email protected] The latest curse: How partisan politics used the Gnanasara case forgetting Buddhism and the country. If you want to see 78 years of partisan politics in one case, look at the case of Venerable Galagoda Aththe Gnanasara. It is not a story about Buddhism. It is a story about how every political camp has used the saffron robe to achieve its own partisan goal, with no care for the good name of Buddhism or the common good of all Sri Lankans. FIRST – WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENED – THE FACTS On January 25, 2016, at Homagama Magistrate’s Court, during a hearing into the disappearance of journalist Prageeth Eknaligoda, Ven. Gnanasara disrupted court proceedings, addressed the court without permission, and intimidated participants. On August 8, 2018, the court of appeal found him guilty on four counts of contempt of court and sentenced him to 19 years rigorous imprisonment to run concurrently — an effective term of six years. On May 23, 2019, President Maithripala Sirisena granted him a full presidential pardon. He had served less than nine months. On September 10, 2026, the Supreme Court, in a landmark ruling, declared that pardon “arbitrary and invalid” and null and void. The bench held that executive clemency must be reasoned and cannot undermine judicial authority. On October 3, 2026, after weeks of evading arrest, Ven. Gnanasara was arrested at Thiniyawala Aranya in Kalutara by the Colombo Crimes Division. On October 5, the Court of Appeal ordered the Commissioner General of Prisons to enforce the remaining period of his six-year sentence. There is a separate 9-month sentence for insulting Islam, upheld by the Colombo High Court in October 2026, now under appeal to the Supreme Court. These are court records, not political opinions. SECOND – HOW EACH PARTY USED THEM Party One: The pardon as votes. The 2019 pardon was granted days before a presidential election cycle. President Sirisena, who had fallen out with his own prime minister, was courting the Sinhala-Buddhist nationalist vote bank. Pardoning the General Secretary of Bodhu Bala Sena was not a legal act — the supreme court has now said it was arbitrary — it was a partisan calculation. Party Two: The appointment as legitimacy In 2020, President Gotabaya Rajapaksa appointed the same monk — then a convicted contenmer out on a contested pardon — to head a Presidential Task Force on legal reforms to implement the one country one law concept. For that administration, the appointment signaled a hardline nationalist credential. What does protection mean when you appoint a figure convicted of contempt of court to reform law itself? Party Three: The prosecution as politics Now, the current revival of enforcement is also being used by partisan interests on the other side. Some groups who were silent when courts were disrupted in 2016 are now the loudest defenders of rule of law in 2026; not because they care for judicial independence, but because the monk’s imprisonment embarrasses their opponents. Justice becomes a weapon, not a principle. In all three acts, Buddhism is the loser. THIRD – THE DAMAGE TO BUDDHISM’S GOOD NAME Buddhism in Sri Lanka has survived 2,300 years because of its moral authority, not by state power. Buddhism is the one moral doctrine that spread across the world without the aid of the gun. We Buddhists in Sri Lanka sullied that reputation. The Dhammapada says: “Hatred is never appeased by hatred; by non-hatred alone is hatred appeased.” When partisan politics drapes itself in the saffron robe to justify intimidation in a courtroom, or to justify a pardon that the supreme court later calls unlawful, or to justify appointing a contemner to a law reform panel — the public sees politics failing Buddhism. FOURTH. THE DAMAGE TO THE COMMON GOOD When we make one monk a symbol of Sinhala pride – a convicted one at that -or a symbol of Sinhala extremism, we avoid the real conversation: How do we rebuild trust after 30 years of war and post-war religious riots? How do we ensure that the law protects Sandya Eknaligoda — the wife of a disappeared journalist — as much as it protects a powerful monk and hold the scales of justice even? The Supreme Court’s September 10 ruling is important not because it punishes Gnanasara Thera. It is important because it restores a principle: In a democracy, no president can arbitrarily erase a court order to please a vote bank. That principle protects every citizen. FIFTH- ENDING THE CURSE My first article argued that 78 years of partisan politics put party before country. The Gnanasara case is the latest proof. What should putting country first look like here? 1. Let the law run its course without political rallies outside the Presidential Secretariat or public parks. 2. Let the Buddhist leadership, not party headquarters, speak for Buddhism. 3. Let us stop using court judgments as election slogans. On October 5, 2026 the court of appeal did its duty. Now we must do ours — to defend both the rule of law and the good name of Buddhism from those who would exploit both for personal gain; because if we cannot separate the saffron from party colours, we will lose both. The country’s economy will suffer most of all. Eradicating poverty will remain a forlorn hope. Singapore rose from third world to first in my lifetime. Sadly, our leaders led our country in the opposite direction to become an international basket case with their partisan politics and demagoguery.

audit.headline: JXG’s Wasanthi Stephen makes history as first female recipient of CIPM Sri Lanka Lifetime Gold Award
audit.summary: JXG (Janashakthi Group) proudly celebrates Wasanthi Stephen, Group Chief Human Resources Officer, on becoming the first female recipient of the prestigious CIPM-Baurs Lifetime Gold Award 2026 from the Chartered Institute of Personnel Management (CIPM) Sri Lanka since the award’s inception. Presented on 14 October 2026, at the opening of the National Human Resource Conference (NHRC) 2026 at Monarch Imperial, Kotte, the award marks a historic milestone for Sri Lanka’s Human Resources profession and a proud moment for JXG. The highest individual recognition in Sri Lanka’s Human Resource Management sphere, the CIPM Sri Lanka Lifetime Gold Award celebrates individuals whose long-standing contributions have advanced the HR profession at organisational, national, and international levels.
audit.body: JXG (Janashakthi Group) proudly celebrates Wasanthi Stephen, Group Chief Human Resources Officer, on becoming the first female recipient of the prestigious CIPM-Baurs Lifetime Gold Award 2026 from the Chartered Institute of Personnel Management (CIPM) Sri Lanka since the award’s inception. Presented on 14 October 2026, at the opening of the National Human Resource Conference (NHRC) 2026 at Monarch Imperial, Kotte, the award marks a historic milestone for Sri Lanka’s Human Resources profession and a proud moment for JXG. The highest individual recognition in Sri Lanka’s Human Resource Management sphere, the CIPM Sri Lanka Lifetime Gold Award celebrates individuals whose long-standing contributions have advanced the HR profession at organisational, national, and international levels. It recognises professional excellence, ethical leadership, transformational impact, and a sustained commitment to people and institutions. With extensive expertise spanning leadership, talent development, employee wellbeing, women’s advancement, and the future of work, Wasanthi has made significant contributions to the evolution of HR as a strategic driver of organisational performance. Her professional standing has also received international recognition, including the Global Recognition Award for Leadership in Human Resources in 2024.

audit.headline: Lakdhanavi clinches five major Asian engineering awards
audit.summary: ‘A national benchmark beyond a corporate recognition’ Lakdhanavi Limited, a subsidiary of the LTL Group, achieved significant regional recognition by winning five major honors at the Asian Power Awards and Asian Water Awards 2026, held in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. This impressive performance highlights Sri Lanka’s engineering capabilities in power generation, technological innovation, industrial water management, and corporate responsibility on an Asian regional stage. The core driver of Lakdhanavi’s success was its 300MW Yugadanavi Combined Cycle Power Plant, an essential component of Sri Lanka’s energy infrastructure since its commissioning in 2010. At the Asian Power Awards, Lakdhanavi was named Independent Power Producer of the Year.
audit.body: ‘A national benchmark beyond a corporate recognition’ Lakdhanavi Limited, a subsidiary of the LTL Group, achieved significant regional recognition by winning five major honors at the Asian Power Awards and Asian Water Awards 2026, held in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. This impressive performance highlights Sri Lanka’s engineering capabilities in power generation, technological innovation, industrial water management, and corporate responsibility on an Asian regional stage. The core driver of Lakdhanavi’s success was its 300MW Yugadanavi Combined Cycle Power Plant, an essential component of Sri Lanka’s energy infrastructure since its commissioning in 2010. At the Asian Power Awards, Lakdhanavi was named Independent Power Producer of the Year. Yugadanavi secured the Innovative Power Technology of the Year award for developing an engineering solution to heat inlet gas turbine fuel (HFO) based on viscosity—demonstrating how in-house continuous improvement can solve complex operational challenges in legacy infrastructure. The plant also received the ESG Program of the Year award for its environmental, social, and governance initiatives. Beyond power generation, Yugadanavi demonstrated excellence in sustainable resource management by taking home two accolades at the Asian Water Awards. Its seawater treatment facility earned the Water Technology Excellence Award (Industrial), while its sustainability efforts received the Water Reuse and Recycling Project of the Year award. These recognitions underscore that modern power infrastructure relies heavily on advanced supportive functions like industrial water treatment and recycling. Overall, the achievements of Lakdhanavi and the LTL Group reflect their end-to-end expertise across the infrastructure ecosystem – spanning design, construction, commissioning, operations, and maintenance – both domestically and in global markets. Ultimately, these awards represent more than a commercial victory; they serve as a point of national pride, celebrating the skill, dedication, and technical competence of Sri Lankan engineers and technical professionals.

audit.headline: Lanka records lowest hunger score in South Asia
audit.summary: News Published on By Share Tweet Lanka has recorded the lowest hunger score among South Asian countries with available data, according to the 2026 Global Hunger Index (GHI), marking a significant improvement in the country’s hunger situation over the past two decades. Sri Lanka scored 10.2, placing it 53rd among 122 countries assessed in the index, released on October 14. Nepal recorded the second-lowest score in South Asia at 14.5, followed by Bangladesh at 19.2, India at 24.1, Pakistan at 25.5 and Afghanistan at 28.6. No scores were assigned to Bhutan and the Maldives due to insufficient data. Sri Lanka’s GHI score has improved considerably, from 22.1 in 2000 to 19.9 in 2006, 20.8 in 2012, 11.4 in 2018 and 10.2 in 2026. However, the country remains in the “moderate” hunger category, indicating that food security and nutrition challenges continue to persist.
audit.body: News Published on By Share Tweet Lanka has recorded the lowest hunger score among South Asian countries with available data, according to the 2026 Global Hunger Index (GHI), marking a significant improvement in the country’s hunger situation over the past two decades. Sri Lanka scored 10.2, placing it 53rd among 122 countries assessed in the index, released on October 14. Nepal recorded the second-lowest score in South Asia at 14.5, followed by Bangladesh at 19.2, India at 24.1, Pakistan at 25.5 and Afghanistan at 28.6. No scores were assigned to Bhutan and the Maldives due to insufficient data. Sri Lanka’s GHI score has improved considerably, from 22.1 in 2000 to 19.9 in 2006, 20.8 in 2012, 11.4 in 2018 and 10.2 in 2026. However, the country remains in the “moderate” hunger category, indicating that food security and nutrition challenges continue to persist. The report said 4.9% of Sri Lanka’s population is undernourished, while 10.1% of children, under five, are stunted, and 9.3% suffer from wasting. The under-five mortality rate is 0.6%. The GHI measures hunger based on four indicators — undernourishment, child stunting, child wasting and child mortality — with lower scores indicating less severe hunger. Globally, the 2026 index warned that hunger has begun to rise again after nearly two decades of progress, with conflict, climate shocks and economic crises identified as key drivers.

audit.headline: Lanka rushes 27 Iranian sailors ashore for treatment
audit.summary: News Published on By Share Tweet Sri Lanka provided humanitarian assistance to 27 Iranian sailors brought ashore after they fell ill aboard vessels outside the country’s territorial waters, in accordance with international maritime law and recognised humanitarian principles, Addressing the media, Deputy Health Minister Hansaka Wijemuni said Sri Lanka’s response was guided by its international obligations and that humanitarian assistance would be provided, irrespective of nationality, religion or country of origin. The 27 crew members were brought ashore on Friday after falling ill aboard Iranian crude oil tankers, anchored off Sri Lanka’s southern coast, according to the Southern Province Senior Deputy Inspector General’s Office.
audit.body: News Published on By Share Tweet Sri Lanka provided humanitarian assistance to 27 Iranian sailors brought ashore after they fell ill aboard vessels outside the country’s territorial waters, in accordance with international maritime law and recognised humanitarian principles, Addressing the media, Deputy Health Minister Hansaka Wijemuni said Sri Lanka’s response was guided by its international obligations and that humanitarian assistance would be provided, irrespective of nationality, religion or country of origin. The 27 crew members were brought ashore on Friday after falling ill aboard Iranian crude oil tankers, anchored off Sri Lanka’s southern coast, according to the Southern Province Senior Deputy Inspector General’s Office. The evacuation was carried out following intervention by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, with the Sri Lanka Navy deploying two craft to transport the affected personnel to Galle Port. The crew members were subsequently transferred to a private hospital in Colombo for treatment. Wijemuni also referred to an earlier incident involving the Iranian naval vessel IRIS Dena off the Sri Lankan coast, saying local emergency teams had provided medical treatment to injured personnel and assisted survivors. Arrangements had also been made to repatriate the bodies of those killed to Iran, he said. The Deputy Minister said strict adherence to established international procedures would help Sri Lanka meet its humanitarian obligations while avoiding unnecessary diplomatic complications. He said Sri Lanka would continue to act transparently and in accordance with international maritime conventions when responding to similar incidents.

audit.headline: Lula holds off far right with victory in Brazil presidential election
audit.summary: Foreign News Published on By Share Tweet Leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has defeated right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro in Brazil’s contentious presidential race, pulling off a remarkable comeback after a first-round loss that galvanised the country’s political right. Around 9:13pm Brasilia time (00:13 GMT), Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court called the race for Lula, who had earned 51 percent of the vote. More than 51.49 million ballots were cast for the incumbent. Bolsonaro, meanwhile, netted 48.68 percent of the vote, or 48.8 million ballots. Just over 2.6 million votes separated the two candidates. With his victory, Lula has made history. No other politician in modern Brazilian history has lost the first round of a presidential election, only to win the second round.
audit.body: Foreign News Published on By Share Tweet Leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has defeated right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro in Brazil’s contentious presidential race, pulling off a remarkable comeback after a first-round loss that galvanised the country’s political right. Around 9:13pm Brasilia time (00:13 GMT), Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court called the race for Lula, who had earned 51 percent of the vote. More than 51.49 million ballots were cast for the incumbent. Bolsonaro, meanwhile, netted 48.68 percent of the vote, or 48.8 million ballots. Just over 2.6 million votes separated the two candidates. With his victory, Lula has made history. No other politician in modern Brazilian history has lost the first round of a presidential election, only to win the second round. Still, the vote process was marred by allegations of voter suppression, after reports emerged that public transportation in some areas had been suspended. Lula’s allies accused Bolsonaro’s supporters of reducing the transportation in a bid to dampen the president’s working-class base. Heavy rains, meanwhile, affected southern areas considered to be Bolsonaro strongholds. The campaigns of both Lula and Bolsonaro ultimately petitioned the Supreme Court for a voting extension. Polls across the country were kept open two hours later than expected, until 7pm Brasilia time (22:00 GMT). Sunday’s victory means that Lula will retain the presidency of the largest country in Latin America, denying a crucial victory to the region’s right wing. In recent years, right-wing leaders have swept presidential races in nearby countries like Peru, Colombia, Argentina, Bolivia and Ecuador. Many have ridden a wave of anti-incumbent energy and have enjoyed support from United States President Donald Trump, who returned to office in January 2025. (Aljazeera)

audit.headline: Nirosh De Silva elected president of JASTECA
audit.summary: Nirosh De Silva has been elected President of the Japan Sri Lanka Technical and Cultural Association (JASTECA) for the 2026–2028 term, following his election at the association’s 40th Annual General Meeting on August 21, 2026. Established in 1984, JASTECA promotes bilateral relations, Japanese management philosophies—such as Kaizen, 5S, and Lean Management—and professional development through training partnerships with the Association for Overseas Technical Cooperation and Sustainable Partnerships (AOTS). Under De Silva’s leadership, the incoming administration aims to drive digital transformation, environmental, social, and governance (ESG) practices, and sustainable business development while bridging traditional management models with modern innovation.
audit.body: Nirosh De Silva has been elected President of the Japan Sri Lanka Technical and Cultural Association (JASTECA) for the 2026–2028 term, following his election at the association’s 40th Annual General Meeting on August 21, 2026. Established in 1984, JASTECA promotes bilateral relations, Japanese management philosophies—such as Kaizen, 5S, and Lean Management—and professional development through training partnerships with the Association for Overseas Technical Cooperation and Sustainable Partnerships (AOTS). Under De Silva’s leadership, the incoming administration aims to drive digital transformation, environmental, social, and governance (ESG) practices, and sustainable business development while bridging traditional management models with modern innovation. Key priorities for the new term include expanding professional opportunities for AOTS alumni, engaging young professionals, and strengthening institutional collaborations with key Japanese partners like the Embassy of Japan, JICA, and JETRO. Furthermore, JASTECA will continue its National Awards programme to recognize organizational excellence in 5S, Kaizen, and corporate social responsibility, ultimately supporting a more productive, globally competitive Sri Lankan economy.

audit.headline: Over 22 kilos of heroin, ‘ICE’ seized in two raids
audit.summary: News Published on By Share Tweet by Norman Palihawadane Police have seized over 21 kilos of heroin and more than one kilo of crystal methamphetamine (‘ICE’) in two separate raids in Katana-Giriulla and Thalangama. The Police Narcotics Bureau (PNB) arrested a suspect with 21.7 kilos of heroin during a raid in the Katana-Giriulla area yesterday. Police said the raid was carried out, based on information uncovered during the interrogation of two suspects, previously arrested over drug-related offences. A subsequent examination conducted with the assistance of Police Narcotics Bureau (PNB) experts confirmed that the consignment contained more than 239 kilos of ‘ICE’ or crystal methamphetamine, and over 321 kilos of heroin. The seized narcotics and the dinghy are to be handed over to the PNB for further investigations and legal action. Police Headquarters sources said almost all the major narcotics consignments detected in recent times had allegedly been linked to ‘Dehi Bale’, who is believed to have been transporting drugs to several locations along the southern coastal belt. A separate investigation is also under way into several senior police officers suspected of colluding with ‘Dehi Bale’ in operating his drug network in the southern coastal region, the sources said. According to investigators, ‘Dehi Bale’ is currently operating his drug network from Georgia after fleeing Dubai, following the arrest of his younger brother, Patabendige Thushan Nethsara, alias ‘Kalu Malli’, by Dubai authorities. ‘Kalu Malli’, 25, described by police as an organised criminal and drug trafficker, was arrested in Dubai, in September 2026, on the basis of a Red Notice issued through Interpol and information provided by the State Intelligence Service. The Interpol Red Notice had reportedly been issued in connection with murder cases in the Southern Province. ‘Kalu Malli’ remains in Dubai police custody and is expected to be deported to Sri Lanka. The two brothers had previously been identified by the PNB as suspects allegedly responsible for bringing large quantities of narcotics into Sri Lanka. On October 21, 2025, Colombo Chief Magistrate Asanka S. Bodaragama ordered police to immediately arrest ‘Dehi Bale’ and ‘Kalu Malli’, who were reported to be hiding overseas while operating drug rackets in Sri Lanka. The Magistrate ordered that the suspects be arrested and produced before court and also imposed travel bans on them. The PNB had informed court that investigations had revealed that the two suspects, both residents of Devinuwara, were allegedly responsible for bringing the narcotics consignments into the country. Five fishermen arrested in connection with a drug seizure were also produced before court by PNB officers and ordered to be remanded. The latest seizure is also being viewed against the backdrop of several major drug detections, allegedly linked to the ‘Dehi Bale’ network. On October 14, 2025, the Navy seized more than 839 kilos of ‘ICE’, heroin and hashish found in packages floating in the southern seas. Five fishing trawlers, allegedly belonging to ‘Dehi Bale,’ were seized on November 26, 2025, by the Illegal Assets Investigations Division of the CID. The trawlers, valued at approximately Rs.200 million, were seized while anchored at the Dikwella Fisheries Harbour. Police also seized a house built on a 15.8-perch land in Devinuwara, estimated to be worth around Rs.230 million, which was allegedly owned by the wife and family of ‘Dehi Bale’. Meanwhile, police are investigating a shooting reported near the Dewundara Devalaya, in Matara, on July 22, 2026, which is suspected to have been linked to a dispute between two organised criminal figures. Investigators suspect that the shooting was carried out by a group, allegedly linked to ‘Dehi Bale’. audit.headline: Police warn of dating app scams
audit.summary: News Published on By Share Tweet Police have warned the public to exercise caution when forming relationships with strangers through dating apps. This warning follows a rise in financial scams involving fraudulent mobile apps. Police have warned that such applications, which may appear to be legitimate, could contain malicious files capable of compromising mobile phones and stealing online banking details. Once installed, the malicious applications could allow scammers to obtain usernames and passwords when victims conduct online transactions, enabling them to gain access to financial accounts and fraudulently withdraw money. Police said methods used in financial scams, through social media and messaging platforms, were rapidly evolving, with criminals increasingly exploiting promises of love and companionship to gain access to victims’ financial information.

This warning follows a rise in financial scams involving fraudulent mobile apps. Police have warned that such applications, which may appear to be legitimate, could contain malicious files capable of compromising mobile phones and stealing online banking details. Once installed, the malicious applications could allow scammers to obtain usernames and passwords when victims conduct online transactions, enabling them to gain access to financial accounts and fraudulently withdraw money. Police said methods used in financial scams, through social media and messaging platforms, were rapidly evolving, with criminals increasingly exploiting promises of love and companionship to gain access to victims’ financial information. The public has been advised not to install applications from unknown sources or disclose banking details, passwords, one-time passwords (OTPs) or other personal information to strangers. Police also urged people not to share personal photographs or videos with unknown individuals and stressed the need for caution when interacting with strangers online.

audit.headline: Port City Colombo and University of Moratuwa Sign Framework Agreement
audit.summary: Linking Urban Development with Talent Development CHEC Port City Colombo (Pvt) Ltd. and the Department of Town and Country Planning of the University of Moratuwa have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to strengthen collaboration between academia and industry in urban development, urban informatics, research, innovation and talent development. Signed on 29 September 2026 at the University of Moratuwa, the agreement will create opportunities for students and academics to engage more closely with the development of Port City Colombo and its planning and development process. A key focus of the partnership will be student development. The agreement provides for structured internships, industry exposure, academic projects and skills development, with opportunities for longer-term engagement through initiatives such as career fairs involving Port City Colombo-registered entities.

Signed on 29 September 2026 at the University of Moratuwa, the agreement will create opportunities for students and academics to engage more closely with the development of Port City Colombo and its planning and development process. A key focus of the partnership will be student development. The agreement provides for structured internships, industry exposure, academic projects and skills development, with opportunities for longer-term engagement through initiatives such as career fairs involving Port City Colombo-registered entities. “As a master developer, we see value in working closely with universities because urban development is not something that happens in isolation. We see this as a partnership where both sides have something to gain. Students and academics gain closer access to a major urban development and the practical aspects that come with it, while Port City Colombo gets the benefit of working with people who are researching and thinking about the future of cities. That kind of exchange is something we want to develop further with the University of Moratuwa across all disciplines, as we build Port City Colombo as a platform to further expose Sri Lankan talent to the world,” said Mr Xiong Hongfeng, Managing Director, CHEC Port City Colombo (Pvt) Ltd. audit.headline: Protests against killing of Kavantissa
audit.summary: News Published on By Share Tweet By S.K. Samaranayake Two protests were held in Kandy yesterday (25) condemning the killing of tusker Kavantissa and the continued killing and mistreatment of wild elephants. One protest was organised by the Central Environmental Conservation Alliance, near the George E. de Silva Park, while the other was held along Lake Round, in front of the Wahalkada of the Sri Dalada Maligawa. The latter was jointly organised by social media activists and environmental groups. Protesters, at both demonstrations, called for strict legal action against those responsible for the killing of Kavantissa. They also urged the authorities to take immediate and effective measures to end the killing and mistreatment of wild elephants and ensure their protection.

audit.headline: SL faces toxic fallout from unregulated battery recycling, CEJ warns
audit.summary: News Published on By Share Tweet By Ifham Nizam More than 5,000 metric tonnes of sulphuric acid could be entering Sri Lanka’s environment each year through improper lead-acid battery recycling, while more than 2,000 lead-smelting operations, reportedly operate across the country without adequate environmental safeguards, the Centre for Environmental Justice (CEJ) has warned. The organisation said the scale of the industry raised urgent concerns over the uncontrolled disposal of hazardous acid, lead, cadmium and arsenic, exposing workers, nearby communities and the wider environment to potentially serious health risks. It called for immediate regulatory action, systematic collection and treatment of battery waste, and stronger monitoring of both registered and unregistered facilities.
audit.body: News Published on By Share Tweet By Ifham Nizam More than 5,000 metric tonnes of sulphuric acid could be entering Sri Lanka’s environment each year through improper lead-acid battery recycling, while more than 2,000 lead-smelting operations, reportedly operate across the country without adequate environmental safeguards, the Centre for Environmental Justice (CEJ) has warned. The organisation said the scale of the industry raised urgent concerns over the uncontrolled disposal of hazardous acid, lead, cadmium and arsenic, exposing workers, nearby communities and the wider environment to potentially serious health risks. It called for immediate regulatory action, systematic collection and treatment of battery waste, and stronger monitoring of both registered and unregistered facilities. According to the CEJ, waste generated during battery recycling, including discarded slag and residual acid, can contain lead, cadmium and arsenic, posing risks to human health and the environment if not handled and disposed of safely. The organisation has called for stricter enforcement of existing environmental laws, effective monitoring of battery recycling facilities and a formal system for collecting, treating and recycling the sulphuric acid and other hazardous waste generated by the industry. The concerns were highlighted during activities organised in Sri Lanka from October 18 to 24 to mark the global lead poisoning prevention awareness week, under the theme “From Detection to Prevention”. The international campaign, coordinated by the International Pollutants Elimination Network (IPEN) and its member organisations, seeks to protect people, particularly children, from lead exposure and its potentially irreversible health consequences. The CEJ said its activities in Sri Lanka included awareness programmes on electronic waste and lead-related hazards for schoolchildren and waste-handling workers attached to the Kolonnawa Municipal Council. Information leaflets explaining common routes of lead exposure were also distributed, alongside a digital campaign to raise public awareness. A further online discussion, led by CEJ Chairman Hemantha Withanage, focused on the environmental challenges associated with lead-acid battery recycling in Sri Lanka. Alda Dubey of India’s Toxics Link and Sudesh Nandasiri of Ceylon Waste Management (Pvt) Ltd., also delivered presentations. The CEJ identified the handling and disposal of sulphuric acid as a major concern in the country’s battery recycling industry. It said more than 5,000 metric tonnes of the acid were estimated to be released into the environment annually without proper management. The organisation also expressed concern that environmental requirements and licensing procedures were not adequately addressing the disposal of battery acid and toxic residues generated during recycling. It called for the establishment of a systematic collection and treatment mechanism for hazardous waste, together with stronger regulatory oversight of both registered and unregistered operations. The reported presence of more than 2,000 lead-smelting facilities, including unregistered operations, underscores the need for authorities to establish the actual scale of the industry and determine whether the facilities comply with environmental and occupational safety standards. Lead exposure is a major public-health concern because no level of exposure is considered safe. Children are particularly vulnerable, as lead can interfere with brain development and cause lasting damage to their cognitive and neurological functions. Exposure can also affect adults, contributing to cardiovascular and kidney problems. The CEJ stressed that preventing lead poisoning requires coordinated action by regulatory authorities, industry operators, waste-management companies and the public. The problem also extends beyond battery recycling. Lead may enter the environment through poorly managed industrial waste and electronic waste, while unsafe handling practices can expose workers and nearby communities to contamination. The organisation has called for stronger public awareness, improved waste-management practices and effective implementation of environmental laws to prevent hazardous substances from contaminating soil and other environmental resources. The warning comes as international efforts intensify to eliminate lead from paints and reduce exposure through better regulation of hazardous chemicals and products. IPEN and its member organisations have also been advocating a complete ban on lead in paint and stronger controls on the international trade in hazardous chemicals under the Rotterdam Convention framework. The CEJ said protecting children and the environment from lead poisoning required a concerted effort by all stakeholders, with prevention, effective regulation and responsible waste management taking priority over remedial action after contamination has occurred.
