audit.headline: Sri Lanka managing the tide amid global commodity volatility, CBSL data shows
audit.summary: Sri Lanka’s economic recovery continues to encounter a complex global landscape, successfully balancing domestic stabilisation against mounting external pressures and commodity volatility. As latest data from the Central Bank of Sri Lanka illustrates, the nation’s economic machinery is holding a resilient course even as international headwinds test its buffers. Global commodity markets have introduced renewed friction, most notably through sharp movements in energy prices. Amid supply concerns stemming from ongoing geopolitical tensions in the Middle East, crude oil prices trended upward during October 2026, with Brent crude touching a five-month high. For an import-dependent economy, such volatility directly impacts external trade accounts.
audit.body: Sri Lanka’s economic recovery continues to encounter a complex global landscape, successfully balancing domestic stabilisation against mounting external pressures and commodity volatility. As latest data from the Central Bank of Sri Lanka illustrates, the nation’s economic machinery is holding a resilient course even as international headwinds test its buffers. Global commodity markets have introduced renewed friction, most notably through sharp movements in energy prices. Amid supply concerns stemming from ongoing geopolitical tensions in the Middle East, crude oil prices trended upward during October 2026, with Brent crude touching a five-month high. For an import-dependent economy, such volatility directly impacts external trade accounts. During the first eight months of 2026, total imports expanded by 24.1 per cent to reach $16,557.1 million, outpacing export growth and widening the trade deficit. Consequently, the year-to-date depreciation of the Sri Lankan rupee against the US dollar was recorded at 6.6 per cent by late October. Yet, the economy’s shock-absorption capacity has noticeably strengthened. External resilience is being powerfully reinforced by robust worker remittances, which surged by 18.1 per cent year-on-year to reach $6,865.4 million between January and September 2026. This steady inflow of foreign exchange, coupled with tourism earnings climbing to $2,245.2 million over the same period, provides a vital cushion against imported inflation and currency fluctuations. Furthermore, gross official reserves stood at a solid $6,851 million at the end of September 2026, underpinning fundamental monetary stability. Domestically, this external resilience is mirrored by cautious macroeconomic management. Headline inflation, as measured by the National Consumer Price Index (NCPI), held steady at 8.1 per cent year-on-year in September, while monetary policy maintained a balanced stance with market liquidity remaining in a comfortable surplus. Private sector credit expansion of 24.5 per cent year-on-year by August indicates that domestic economic activity remains engaged despite credit-cost adjustments. Ultimately, while external commodity volatility will remain a persistent challenge, Sri Lanka’s robust foreign buffers and disciplined policy framework demonstrate an economy increasingly equipped to weather global storms while protecting its hard-won macro stability.

audit.headline: Sunshine Healthcare expands into digital healthcare with strategic investment in Doc990
audit.summary: Sunshine Healthcare Lanka Limited (SHL), a subsidiary of Sunshine Holdings PLC (CSE: SUN), has acquired a minority stake of 22% in Digital Health Private Limited (DHPL), the company behind Doc990. The investment marks a significant step in Sunshine’s continued expansion across the healthcare value chain, extending its presence into the rapidly evolving digital healthcare space. Operated by DHPL, a subsidiary of Dialog Axiata PLC, Doc990 connects patients, doctors, healthcare providers and corporates through mobile, web and call-based channels. As one of Sri Lanka’s leading integrated digital healthcare platforms, Doc990 facilitates doctor appointments, digital consultations, payments and other healthcare services, helping patients access care with greater convenience.

As one of Sri Lanka’s leading integrated digital healthcare platforms, Doc990 facilitates doctor appointments, digital consultations, payments and other healthcare services, helping patients access care with greater convenience. The investment represents a natural progression in Sunshine Healthcare’s growth strategy, complementing its established capabilities across pharmaceutical manufacturing, research and development, medical devices, pharmaceutical distribution and retail pharmacy operations. By entering the digital healthcare segment, Sunshine is further strengthening its presence across multiple healthcare verticals while establishing a more direct connection with patients. Partnerships have played a central role in Sunshine’s expansion across these healthcare segments. Its pharmaceutical agency business has been built on longstanding relationships with international principals, some spanning over four decades. In 2020, Sunshine combined its healthcare operations with those of Akbar Brothers, strengthening its pharmaceutical manufacturing capabilities and establishing a fully integrated healthcare business.

audit.headline: ‘All-inclusive Constitution’: Harini’s statement in CNN interview draws criticism
audit.summary: News Published on By Share Tweet By Shamindra Ferdinando Former SLPP MP Gevindu Cumaratunga says the government should explain what Prime Minister Dr. Harini Amarasuriya has really meant by the all-inclusive new Constitution. The civil society activist said that the government owed an explanation as to how it intended to address the root causes of the war that was brought to a successful conclusion in May 2009. Cumaratunga said so when The Island sought his response to PM Amarasuriya declaration, in an interview with Richard Quest, on CNN. Responding to queries pertaining to constitutional reforms, PM Amarasuriya, while declaring serious flaws in the country’s supreme law, made reference to the 22 Amendments enacted over the years. The Premier emphasised that though the war ended, a new Constitution was needed to deal with the root causes that led to conflict.

Cumaratunga said so when The Island sought his response to PM Amarasuriya declaration, in an interview with Richard Quest, on CNN. Responding to queries pertaining to constitutional reforms, PM Amarasuriya, while declaring serious flaws in the country’s supreme law, made reference to the 22 Amendments enacted over the years. The Premier emphasised that though the war ended, a new Constitution was needed to deal with the root causes that led to conflict. The country couldn’t move forward unless these issues were addressed, she said, while stressing the importance of transparency and accountability in the process. Cumaratunga said that he, too, recognised the need for a new Constitution but the issue at hand is the direction of the proposed Constitution and its objectives. The ex-parliamentarian said in the run-up to Eelam War IV, in August 2006, different governments addressed concerns not only of Tamil-speaking political parties but terrorist groups as well. Cumaratunga said that Tamil was made an official language by the implementation of the 13th Amendment to the Constitution in 1987. English was constitutionally recognised as the link language by the 16th Amendment to the Constitution in 1988, the former MP said. Cumaratunga said that at the behest of India, Sri Lanka implemented a Provincial Council system, in line with the Indo-Lanka Accord, signed on 29 July, 1987, but fighting erupted just 10 weeks after the tripartite consensus. The interviewer could be unaware of the situation on the ground at that time but the Premier couldn’t be ignorant of the devastating repercussions of the 16th Amendment that deprived the Sinhala community the constitutional right to use Sinhala language in the northern and eastern administrative districts, Cumaratunga said. Responding to another query, Cumaratunga said that the powers that be several years ago quietly stopped issuing cut off marks pertaining to the Year 5 Scholarship examination conducted in the Jaffna, Kilinochchi, Mannar and Batticaloa districts while Tamil speaking students didn’t experience that unfortunate situation in any part of the country. Cumaratunga said that obviously the CNN interviewer hadn’t been aware that the JVP joined hands with the UNP, TNA and the SLMC in a despicable plan to put off Provincial Council polls indefinitely during the Yahapalana administration. Those who now represented the main Opposition Samagi Jana Balawegaya (SJB) backed that project as all of them feared the emergence of the SLPP as the winner at most councils, Cumaratunga said. The ex-MP said that over 6.9 mn people exercised their franchise for Gotabaya Rajapaksa to bring in a new Constitution that reflected the post-war situation on the ground. Recalling an assurance given by Vijitha Herath, in the run up to the 2024 September presidential election, that the country’s unitary status wouldn’t be harmed, police and land power granted in the 1th Amendment to the Constitution wouldn’t be fully implemented and in terms of Article 9 of the Constitution (found in Chapter II) Buddhism would continue to receive the foremost place and that the State has a duty to protect and foster the Buddha Sasana. Cumaratunga recalled the failed Yahapalana bid, in consultation with Geneva, to introduce a new Constitution during the 2015-2019 period, and President Gotabaya Rajapaksa’s effort a few years later. Premier Amarasuriya, during a short interview with Quest, responded to the ongoing West Asia war between US-Israel combine and Iran and its fallout, particularly the impact on Sri Lanka and the NPP having to work with the IMF after having relentlessly attacked the lending agency. Dr. Amarasuriya humbly admitted that they didn’t have any other option but to remain committed to the agreement Sri Lanka entered into with the IMF in 2023. audit.headline: 12 children injured in train-bus collision
audit.summary: 26 Oct 2026 | BY Dhanushka Dharmapriya Twelve children were injured when a train collided with a bus at a railway crossing in Koggala, within the Habaraduwa Police Division, yesterday (25), with nine receiving treatment at Karapitiya Teaching Hospital, according to the Police Media Division. When contacted by The Daily Morning , the Division stated three of the injured children had since been discharged from Hospital, while the remaining nine were receiving treatment. The train, travelling from Beliatta to Maradana, struck the rear of the bus. Initial investigations found that the bus was carrying 41 children, 14 tuition teachers and six parents from Kottawa. The group was returning from a visit to the Martin Wickramasinghe Folk Museum in Koggala, and the children were aged 14 and 15.
audit.body: 26 Oct 2026 | BY Dhanushka Dharmapriya Twelve children were injured when a train collided with a bus at a railway crossing in Koggala, within the Habaraduwa Police Division, yesterday (25), with nine receiving treatment at Karapitiya Teaching Hospital, according to the Police Media Division. When contacted by The Daily Morning , the Division stated three of the injured children had since been discharged from Hospital, while the remaining nine were receiving treatment. The train, travelling from Beliatta to Maradana, struck the rear of the bus. Initial investigations found that the bus was carrying 41 children, 14 tuition teachers and six parents from Kottawa. The group was returning from a visit to the Martin Wickramasinghe Folk Museum in Koggala, and the children were aged 14 and 15. Police stated the bus driver and conductor have been arrested, and Habaraduwa Police were conducting further investigation. The crossing had no protective gate, but was equipped with an electronic light and bell system to warn road users of approaching trains. Karapitiya Hospital Deputy Director General Dr. Priyantha Atapattu said injured children had been admitted to the hospital. "One child, aged around 14, has suffered internal bleeding and undergone emergency surgery. Another is in a relatively serious but not critical condition. Based on the examinations completed at the time, the other children are not in critical condition, he said. Sri Lanka Railway Station Masters’ Association General Secretary Kasun Chamara Jayasekara told The Daily Morning that the crossing near the Museum was among more than 400 unprotected railway crossings in the country. Attempts to reach Railway General Manager Ravindra Padmapriya for comment on what action would be taken regarding these crossings were unsuccessful.

audit.headline: 16 spill gates of Rajanganaya Reservoir to be opened; residents of low-lying areas cautioned
audit.summary: 26 Oct 2026 | By Staff Writer The Irrigation Department says 16 spill gates of the Rajanganaya Reservoir are to be opened to release more than 15,000 cubic feet of water per second into the Kala Oya. The measure is to be taken to control the volume of water flowing into the reservoir as of 12 noon today (26). The department stated that the number of spill gates opened may change depending on rainfall in the reservoir’s catchment areas and the volume of water flowing into the reservoir. Accordingly, residents living in the low-lying areas of the Rajanganaya Reservoir and in areas surrounding the Kala Oya basin have been advised to remain vigilant about changes in water levels and follow notices issued by the Irrigation Department and disaster management authorities. Meanwhile, four spill gates of the Tabbowa Reservoir, located in the Mee Oya basin, have also been opened by one foot each.

audit.headline: 2026 Asian Para Games: Janani and Pradeep deliver gold for SL
audit.summary: Sri Lanka secured two gold medals at the 2026 Asian Para Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, Friday (23), with athletes Janani Dhananjana Wickramasinghe and Pradeep Somasiri producing sterling performances in their respective events. Janani Dhananjana Wickramasinghe grabbed gold in the women’s long jump (T47) event, setting a new Games record with a jump of 5.52 metres. Her record-breaking performance added another gold medal to Sri Lanka’s tally at the Games. Meanwhile, Pradeep Somasiri secured the gold medal in the Men’s 1,500m (T46) event after an outstanding performance against strong competition from other Asian athletes. Somasiri maintained a competitive performance from the beginning of the race to finish in first place. India secured the silver medal in the event, while the Philippines clinched the bronze medal.

audit.headline: 40 Iranian sailors brought ashore at Galle
audit.summary: Around 40 Iranian sailors aboard commercial vessels about 24 nautical miles off Sri Lanka’s coast have been brought ashore through the Galle Port in a humanitarian operation, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said yesterday (25). The Ministry said the operation followed urgent requests for assistance over the sailors’ health. The Iranian Embassy in Colombo organised the operation and made the necessary arrangements. After receiving medical treatment, the sailors left for Iran, the Ministry said.

audit.headline: AFC Prez praises tremendous progress of SL Football
audit.summary: The Asian Football Confederation (AFC) President Shaik Salman bin Ebrahim Al Khalifa, met Football Federation of Sri Lanka (FFSL) President Jaswar Umar on the sidelines of the AFC Extraordinary Congress in Tokyo, Japan last week. During the meeting, the AFC President praised the recent progress of the Sri Lanka national football team, highlighting its significant rise in the FIFA Men’s World Rankings as a reflection of the country’s growing potential and ambitions in regional football. Umar expressed his sincere gratitude to the AFC leadership for its continued support and commitment to the development of football in Sri Lanka, especially for granting two new high-quality football pitches to strengthen the nation’s football infrastructure.
audit.body: The Asian Football Confederation (AFC) President Shaik Salman bin Ebrahim Al Khalifa, met Football Federation of Sri Lanka (FFSL) President Jaswar Umar on the sidelines of the AFC Extraordinary Congress in Tokyo, Japan last week. During the meeting, the AFC President praised the recent progress of the Sri Lanka national football team, highlighting its significant rise in the FIFA Men’s World Rankings as a reflection of the country’s growing potential and ambitions in regional football. Umar expressed his sincere gratitude to the AFC leadership for its continued support and commitment to the development of football in Sri Lanka, especially for granting two new high-quality football pitches to strengthen the nation’s football infrastructure. In addition to financial grants, the AFC continues to provide vital infrastructural and technical assistance to Sri Lanka, supporting the development of the sport at both grassroots and elite levels. Sri Lankan football has undergone a significant transformation over the last two years under the stewardship and strategic vision of Jaswar Umar. This progress is increasingly evident via the national team’s improved international performances, its stunning rise in the FIFA Men’s World Rankings, and the continued development of domestic competitions and football infrastructure. The recognition from the AFC head further reinforces Sri Lanka’s growing momentum and reflects the importance of sustained international partnerships, strategic investment and effective leadership in building a stronger and more competitive footballing nation. Sri Lanka Football is moving forward-with renewed ambition, stronger foundations and a clear vision for the future.

audit.headline: Audit report on electric vehicles: EV surge leaves a battery time bomb
audit.summary: 26 Oct 2026 | By Buddhika Samaraweera 100,000 EVs on the road No tracking system or local recycling plant CEA’s battery guideline still not gazetted Only two charging operators certified 16 years after law took effect Sri Lanka’s electric vehicle (EV) fleet has grown from about 30,000 in September 2025 to more than 100,000 by June 2026, but the country still has no system to track, collect or recycle used EV batteries, the Auditor General (AG) has found. The findings are in the AG’s Environmental Audit Report on Electric Vehicle Usage, Post-Usage Management and Environmental Impact Assessment in Sri Lanka (Report No. ENV/2025/03). The report was released on 22 September 2026 and covers 2020 to 2025. EV registrations rose from 340 in 2020 to 12,519 in 2024. Of the 30,426 EVs registered by September 2025, 84 per cent were motorcycles.
audit.body: 26 Oct 2026 | By Buddhika Samaraweera 100,000 EVs on the road No tracking system or local recycling plant CEA’s battery guideline still not gazetted Only two charging operators certified 16 years after law took effect Sri Lanka’s electric vehicle (EV) fleet has grown from about 30,000 in September 2025 to more than 100,000 by June 2026, but the country still has no system to track, collect or recycle used EV batteries, the Auditor General (AG) has found. The findings are in the AG’s Environmental Audit Report on Electric Vehicle Usage, Post-Usage Management and Environmental Impact Assessment in Sri Lanka (Report No. ENV/2025/03). The report was released on 22 September 2026 and covers 2020 to 2025. EV registrations rose from 340 in 2020 to 12,519 in 2024. Of the 30,426 EVs registered by September 2025, 84 per cent were motorcycles. EVs still make up only a small share of the country’s more than nine million vehicles. The audit said this growth has outpaced the rules for dealing with used batteries. They are classed as scheduled waste and handled by 14 e-waste collectors licensed by the Central Environmental Authority (CEA). However, the CEA’s guideline on used lithium-ion batteries has not been gazetted, and there is no national tracking system. There is also no separate Harmonized System (HS) code for EV batteries, making imports hard to trace. The Department of Motor Traffic does not record battery replacement or disposal. With no local recycling plant, used batteries are either stored informally or exported at high cost. Auditors found batteries stored in the open during a site visit. For now, most owners keep their old batteries for solar or home power storage, so large volumes of waste have yet to appear. The National Environmental (Amendment) Act No. 15 of 2026 provides for an Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) system that would make importers and producers responsible for used batteries. The regulations to implement it are not yet in place. A USD 9.65 million project to promote EVs, funded by the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) and the Global Environment Facility (GEF), has also not become operational, despite approval in September 2022. The audit blamed its transfer between ministries, delays in finalising the cooperation agreement and the lack of a monitoring framework. Sri Lanka has no approved National Transport Policy, which the report said has fragmented EV initiatives. The Public Utilities Commission of Sri Lanka (PUCSL) has had the power to regulate charge point operators since 2009 but began certifying them only in March 2025. Only two had been certified by that August. Inspections in Colombo found some charging stations not working and several lacking safety signs or certification labels. On emissions, the report cited research showing that electric motorcycles cut carbon dioxide emissions by about 66 per cent and electric three-wheelers by about 64 per cent. But these gains are limited by the country’s reliance on thermal power. Renewables supplied 53.5 per cent of electricity in 2024, against a target of 70 per cent by 2030. There is also no national system to measure emission reductions from EVs. In a survey of 190 EV users, 40 per cent found charging inconvenient, and only 27 per cent were aware of government EV policies or incentives. The AG made 13 recommendations. These include: a national database to track every EV battery from import to disposal gazetting the CEA’s battery guideline a PUCSL register of charging stations and a tariff framework a programme to electrify motorcycles and three-wheelers a single system to measure EV emission reductions a national e-mobility framework with clear roles, targets and timelines 200 e-buses stuck after bond fraud A Cabinet-approved plan to bring 200 electric buses into public transport has stalled after the only bid received was found to be backed by a fraudulent performance bond, the AG’s report said. Under the plan, approved in 2023, the Ministry of Transport was to procure the buses for the Sri Lanka Transport Board (SLTB). They were to run mainly in the Colombo Metropolitan Region and the Gampaha District, cutting fuel imports and air pollution. Ten bidders bought the tender documents, but only one submitted a proposal. It was disqualified over the bond, and the procurement was terminated on 20 July 2024. As of 27 October 2025, no action had been taken to restart it. The audit blamed weak procurement governance, inadequate due diligence and the lack of a contingency plan. It also cited poor coordination between the ministry, the Treasury and the SLTB.

The showroom was ceremonially declared open by Mr. Vijitha Bandara, Director and Chief Executive Officer of Browns EV. Located at No. 401, Kumarathunga Mawatha, Pamburana, the new 80-perch facility expands access to BAW and Wuling EVs across the Southern Province, delivering an all-in-one experience from vehicle displays and test drives to expert financing guidance and reliable after-sales support. Commenting on the new milestone, Mr. Vijitha Bandara, Director and Chief Executive Officer of Browns EV said “Our ambition with Browns EV is to build more than a portfolio of electric vehicles. The BAW E7 secured over 2,000 pre-orders ahead of launch, while the company surpassed 1,500 EV deliveries by early 2026. Since then, Browns EV has expanded its BAW and Wuling portfolio to include models such as the BAW E7 Pro, BAW M8, Wuling Eksion, Wuling Darion and Wuling Mitra. By September 2026, the company had handed over more than 3,000 vehicles, including over 2,250 BAW vehicles, reflecting its rapid growth and the increasing adoption of electric mobility in Sri Lanka. Browns EV continues to strengthen Sri Lanka’s EV ecosystem through financing, insurance, after-sales services and charging infrastructure, including its partnership with TELD for island-wide charging facilities. Its “Drive to Own” initiative further supported EV accessibility. The company is also expanding its footprint with showrooms planned in Kurunegala and Kirulapona, alongside continued product diversification. The opening of the Matara showroom marks another step in Browns EV’s nationawide expansion, bringing its growing BAW and Wuling portfolio closer to customers in the Southern Province while supporting Sri Lanka’s transition towards sustainable transportation. Newly opened Browns EV Showroom in Matara Mr. Vijitha Bandara, Director and Chief Executive Officer of Browns EV

audit.headline: Disaster Alert: 12 dead, over 10,000 affected
audit.summary: 26 Oct 2026 | BY Dhanushka Dharmapriya and Buddhika Samaraweera Heavy showers of over 100 mm expected in coming days Twelve people have died, 25 have been injured and one is missing after floods, heavy rain, landslides and strong winds affected 10,311 people from 2,826 families between 18 September and 26 October, with more heavy rain forecast. During the period, 28 houses were completely damaged and 1,807 partially damaged, along with six small and medium-sized enterprises and 23 critical infrastructure facilities. Three safety centres are sheltering 67 people from 23 families. The affected areas cover 206 Divisional Secretariat Divisions in 22 districts: Matale, Kandy, Nuwara Eliya, Matara, Hambantota, Galle, Ampara, Batticaloa, Trincomalee, Anuradhapura, Colombo, Gampaha, Kalutara, Kegalle, Ratnapura, Puttalam, Kurunegala, Vavuniya, Mannar, Mullaitivu, Jaffna and Kilinochchi.
audit.body: 26 Oct 2026 | BY Dhanushka Dharmapriya and Buddhika Samaraweera Heavy showers of over 100 mm expected in coming days Twelve people have died, 25 have been injured and one is missing after floods, heavy rain, landslides and strong winds affected 10,311 people from 2,826 families between 18 September and 26 October, with more heavy rain forecast. During the period, 28 houses were completely damaged and 1,807 partially damaged, along with six small and medium-sized enterprises and 23 critical infrastructure facilities. Three safety centres are sheltering 67 people from 23 families. The affected areas cover 206 Divisional Secretariat Divisions in 22 districts: Matale, Kandy, Nuwara Eliya, Matara, Hambantota, Galle, Ampara, Batticaloa, Trincomalee, Anuradhapura, Colombo, Gampaha, Kalutara, Kegalle, Ratnapura, Puttalam, Kurunegala, Vavuniya, Mannar, Mullaitivu, Jaffna and Kilinochchi. In a forecast issued at 4 p.m. yesterday (25), the Department of Meteorology said a depression over the Bay of Bengal had intensified into a deep depression. It is very likely to become a cyclonic storm by this morning (26) and a severe cyclonic storm over the west-central Bay of Bengal by tomorrow (27) morning. Although the system is not expected to directly affect Sri Lanka, its associated wind flow is likely to increase rainfall in the south-western parts of the island in the coming days. Showers or thundershowers are forecast in the Northern, Western, Sabaragamuwa, Southern, North-Western and Central Provinces and the Anuradhapura District, with falls above 100 mm possible in places. Showers are also expected in the Uva Province and the Ampara and Batticaloa Districts after 1 p.m. Winds of 40–50 kmph are expected at times over the western slopes of the Central Hills, the Northern, North-Central and North-Western Provinces, and the Trincomalee and Hambantota Districts. The public has been advised to take precautions against strong winds and lightning. The Natural Hazards Early Warning Centre has advised naval and fishing communities not to venture into the deep seas of the Bay of Bengal between 10°N–20°N and 80°E–95°E until further notice. Those already there have been told to move to safer locations. The National Building Research Institute (NBRI) said several landslide-prone areas could become active with heavy rain. NBRI Senior Scientist Wasantha Senadheera told The Daily Morning that rainfall in these areas had dropped in recent days. “If the rainfall thresholds for these areas are exceeded, we will immediately issue warnings,” he said. Disaster Management Centre Media Spokesperson Pradeep Kodippili said that although no direct impact was expected beyond heavy rain, pre-disaster warning systems were being activated in all 25 districts. Teams and equipment, including boats, are ready in disaster-prone areas.

audit.headline: Energy crisis: SL to accelerate renewable energy transition
audit.summary: Sri Lanka may exceed its 70% renewable electricity target by 2030, as soaring fossil fuel import costs intensify pressure to shift towards cleaner energy sources, said Minister of Energy Anura Karunathilaka, speaking to French news agency AFP . “There are some wake-up calls...pushing us to move more to renewable energy,” the Minister said, adding that maximising renewable energy generation would be a key government policy priority in the coming years, as reported by the agency. Sri Lanka, which depends entirely on imports to meet its oil and gas requirements, has been severely affected by rising energy costs following the US-Israeli war with Iran and disruptions to shipping through the strategically important Strait of Hormuz.
audit.body: Sri Lanka may exceed its 70% renewable electricity target by 2030, as soaring fossil fuel import costs intensify pressure to shift towards cleaner energy sources, said Minister of Energy Anura Karunathilaka, speaking to French news agency AFP . “There are some wake-up calls...pushing us to move more to renewable energy,” the Minister said, adding that maximising renewable energy generation would be a key government policy priority in the coming years, as reported by the agency. Sri Lanka, which depends entirely on imports to meet its oil and gas requirements, has been severely affected by rising energy costs following the US-Israeli war with Iran and disruptions to shipping through the strategically important Strait of Hormuz. Higher fuel, gas and electricity prices, along with rationing and rising inflation, have placed additional pressure on an economy still recovering from its worst-ever economic crisis in 2022. According to the Energy Ministry, the Government has at times spent up to 30% of its foreign exchange reserves in a single month to finance fossil fuel imports, highlighting the economic burden of the country’s dependence on imported energy. Sri Lanka’s existing energy policy targets generating 70% of its electricity from renewable sources by 2030, compared with approximately 60% currently. Hydropower accounts for about 40% of the country’s electricity generation. “We will probably have to go beyond 70%,” Karunathilaka said. He added that the Government planned to strengthen the national transmission network by adding five major transmission lines from 2027 to improve the capacity and stability of the electricity grid. The rapid growth of rooftop solar installations has also created challenges, with electricity generation sometimes exceeding demand during daylight hours. A six-hour islandwide blackout earlier this month followed a disruption to the national grid, with excess solar power generation cited as a possible contributing factor. The Minister said certain solar power plants sometimes had to be temporarily curtailed to maintain grid stability, stressing that such measures did not indicate a lack of government support for solar energy. The Government aims to increase solar power generation capacity to nearly 4,400 megawatts by 2029, representing a 388% increase from 2024 levels, according to the Minister. The Government is also considering changes to the pricing arrangements governing privately generated solar electricity. Under the existing system described by the Minister, some solar producers can supply excess electricity to the grid during the day and withdraw an equivalent amount at night without an additional energy charge under applicable arrangements. Minister Karunathilaka said the system had become financially unsustainable because electricity supplied during daylight hours, when demand is often lower, could be used to offset consumption at night, when generation costs are higher. “The additional cost is borne by the State,” he said, adding that the Government intended to propose a new financial model that would be fair to both solar producers and electricity consumers. Expanding battery storage is another priority, as the Government seeks to manage fluctuations in renewable generation and improve the reliability of electricity supplies. Despite the challenges, the Government remains committed to reducing dependence on imported fossil fuels over the longer term. Karunathilaka acknowledged that the country’s existing electricity system, investment levels and infrastructure were not yet sufficient to replace coal and naphtha completely. However, he expressed confidence that Sri Lanka could significantly reduce its reliance on these fuels over the next 10 to 15 years. The Government ultimately aims to achieve a renewable energy share of 90% to 95%, a target that would require substantial investment in generation, transmission infrastructure and energy storage. The transition is expected to remain a key element of Sri Lanka’s efforts to reduce exposure to global fuel price volatility, strengthen energy security, and support a more sustainable electricity sector.

audit.headline: False statements: Court orders removal of statements targeting LOLC
audit.summary: The Magistrate’s Court of Colombo has issued a conditional court order directing the removal of online access to specific URLs containing false and misleading statements circulating about LOLC Holdings PLC and its business activities, through a conditional directive issued last week (23), unless cause is shown to the contrary. The judicial action was instituted by LOLC Holdings PLC on 16 October 2026 under Section 24 of the Online Safety Act No. 09 of 2024. The company sought legal relief against the continued dissemination of false and misleading online publications that constitute prohibited statements under Sri Lankan law. The legal proceedings name key regulatory and tech entities as respondents, including: Internet service providers (ISPs) operating in Sri Lanka; Telecommunications Regulatory Commission of Sri Lanka (TRCSL); Meta Platforms, Inc and Instagram LLC.

The company sought legal relief against the continued dissemination of false and misleading online publications that constitute prohibited statements under Sri Lankan law. audit.headline: For once, just listen
audit.summary: 26 Oct 2026 | BY SAVITHRI RODRIGO Around 80 million people worldwide stutter, about one in every 100, that is about one per cent of the world’s population. It is also estimated that one in 20 children will go through a phase of it. Yet, most of us have never learned how to listen. To mark the International Stuttering Awareness Day which was marked last week, ‘ Kaleidoscope ’ discussed the challenges faced by those who stutter with Padeniya. audit.body: 26 Oct 2026 | BY SAVITHRI RODRIGO Around 80 million people worldwide stutter, about one in every 100, that is about one per cent of the world’s population. It is also estimated that one in 20 children will go through a phase of it. Yet, most of us have never learned how to listen. Visura Padeniya is an artist, actor, and writer with the Stages Theatre Group which is currently staging a play titled ‘ Katawaha’ , to highlight stuttering. Padeniya himself stammers and hopes to one day contribute to the field of speech and dysfluency. To mark the International Stuttering Awareness Day which was marked last week, ‘ Kaleidoscope ’ discussed the challenges faced by those who stutter with Padeniya. Following are excerpts from the interview : When you think about stammering, at the onset, you know straightaway what stammering is. When you see a person making a more pronounced effort to get their words out, that’s when you can pinpoint it as stammering. But, I want to make a distinction between what it means to stammer and what it means to be discombobulated. John C. Harrison, who has written about stammering, wrote a book called Redefining Stuttering: What the struggle to speak is really about and he made this unique contrast where he says that when you’re discombobulated, nervous or not as confident, people might also stumble over their words. But stammering, in particular, doesn’t depend on the context. It’s just that I’ve a block, and it comes at very unexpected moments. What’s the biggest myth about stammering that you’d like to dispel? Most myths about stammering predominantly stem from attributing it to cognition because people assume that it’s something in your mind. They assume that you also stammer in your mind. My mind is completely clear. It’s also assumed that the person’s speaking too fast and that their thoughts are moving too quickly. Those are some myths that have come about. For someone who has never experienced stammering, what actually happens in the moment of that block in your mind and body? Our actors who are portraying the boy who stammers actually articulate it quite well. People often think that because they can see the stammer happen on the face, it’s something to do with the mouth. But the block is actually felt across your body. Normally, if I experience it, I experience my gut freezing, and it’s just that effort to get your words out. Then you can see a struggle come about in your mouth. It’s more pronounced. Then you are already committed to what you’re trying to say. But because you’re so blocked, your eyes might shut. At that moment, you’re not actually thinking of much. You are just thinking; how do I get this word out somehow? How does stammering actually shape information in your life, whether it’s in restaurants, schools, phone calls, or even job interviews? There is no shape, because we don’t have a proper structure for someone who stammers to be accommodated when approaching an interview. There’s no proper structure or accord, or even communication happening on that front. So, it comes about every time you speak. It’s something that always operates in the back of your mind, and it’s something that we get more accustomed to as we grow up and mature. When it comes to language, is there anything that happens differently in English, Sinhala, or Tamil? As long as you are comfortable with your language, it’s not the language itself. If I'm more comfortable speaking in English, then the chance of stammering in English is less. But that’s mainly based on how comfortable you’re. If I’ve had more bad experiences while speaking in Sinhala, then I’m more likely to stammer in Sinhala. What’s your experience been like? Are people impatient? How does a listener respond to someone who stutters? I think that it varies, honestly, based on how they conduct a conversation. Particularly among my peers and generation, there’s a bit of impatience, insofar as we don’t have that great an attention span. At times, the conversation just moves fast. You feel as if you’re lagging behind while everyone’s talking. But, on the flip side, we’ve come to a point where there’s an effort to be a bit more accommodating. People are willing to wait and hear out what the person has to say. I think that I can credit that conscious effort. You are a good example of how, when people go into acting, singing, or music, stammering just doesn’t happen. What does that tell us about stammering and how does that happen? Even in this interview itself, the blocks that I experience are far less pronounced. I think that there’s an effect of being on stage and putting on a performance. It also partly comes from being depersonalised from your voice. The normal communication that I would have with you in this interview might not be the same as this. When I’m trying to sing a song or act as a character, I put on an accent. The way that I see it is that it’s not me making the conscious effort to communicate. There’s a particular pattern in singing, a pattern in an accent. Even in this interview, as I’m speaking, there’s a pattern that goes on in my mind, which isn’t there in a regular conversation particularly. I think that that’s where conversation becomes a bit trickier for people who stammer. Did you stammer from the time that you were an infant or when you started talking, or did it come later? For me, I only remember my stammer since Grade Five. My mum did tell me that I did have it. But, in a classroom, if a teacher asked a question, I would say, ‘Miss, Miss…’ I was just excited in those moments. Over time, at least the way that I see it, when I became more conscious of my stammer and felt worse about it, when I was made to feel shame about it, I think that it became more pronounced. What I understand about stammering is that it’s a very double-edged sword. In this instance, because I need to show my stammer, it doesn’t come about as strongly. But let’s say that I try to hide it. The more that I try to hide it, the more strongly it comes about, because it’s the block that you feel inside your own body. If a child is stammering, what should teachers and parents know? What should they do? Disclaimer: I’m not a professional. If you find early-onset disfluencies in a child, the earlier that you attend to it, the better. You’re able to make sure that the child doesn’t feel ashamed of speaking in a particular way. You can also develop cultivated practices at a critical age, when the child can develop better structures to cope with it. I think that that’s very crucial for children at a young age. For teachers, though, especially in Government curricula, they need to have a sense of empathy. Personally, for me, a huge contributor to the shame that I feel as a person who stammers comes from my experience with teachers. One example would be our Grade 5 classroom. We would put the entire Grade, around 700 kids, into one hall. This teacher would come and hold a mic and address the crowd. One time she said, ‘I’m going to talk to you about lying because if a child lies, they’ll stammer.’ My teacher would also say, ‘You’ve to learn to speak properly.’ There’s a time when I’d stammer on a word, and the teacher would point it out, just to make me aware of the fact that I stammered. If I’m less aware of it, and if an environment can be made conducive to me feeling less aware of it, I think that it’d be helpful. What does support look like here? I was going through speech therapy support structures before I sat down with you, and I came across a study conducted in 2023. It said that, for every 100,000 people in Sri Lanka, there are only 0.4 speech pathologists. In terms of retaining qualified speech professionals, especially at the grassroots level and in rural areas, it’s a wider policy issue. I don’t think that it’s the best, but, with the resources that we have, we’re trying our best. My personal experience with speech therapy is that you go into an enclosed room and the therapist takes sentences and breaks them down, asking you to break them into syllables. They say, ‘Okay, within one minute, you’ll be reading 100 syllables.’ In that controlled environment, I’ve no problem speaking at any speed. But how does it address real speaking situations? How can it be applied to other contexts? How do I feel about my stammer? How do I cope with it? I don’t think that that conversation has come through as strongly in speech therapy. I think that it’s mainly focused on trying to align a particular pattern of speech, as opposed to the emotions and everything surrounding it. We know that teachers need more awareness and training, that’s for sure. What do you think employers need to make a workplace more inclusive? For employers, if you start from the beginning, in the interview process itself, there needs to be a conversation. That’s what we try to do with this play and campaign as well. This’s a very silent community because people are made to feel shame, and you might not come across many people who stammer because they’re made to feel ashamed of it. When you come across someone, it’s a new thing for you. Firstly, they need to start the conversation and ask, ‘If a person who stammers comes to our interview, how do we accommodate them? How do we reassure them?’ Even in the workplace, how do we assess their competency? Our speech is our main way of showing who we are. There is a huge restriction when you stammer, because there’s a speed and a way in which you want to communicate your ideas. People aren’t made to feel as if they can communicate what they want to in a workspace. I think that that conversation needs to start. Looking ahead, what would a more understanding Sri Lanka look like 10 years from now? I think that we need more third spaces for vulnerable communities. This goes across the board. I advocate for people who stammer, and they need spaces where they can share their experiences and talk about their struggles. There’s no proper third space. As a person who stammers, I wanted to meet other people who stammer in Sri Lanka and talk about what it’s like. I think that those spaces exist to some extent in the West. If we could also bring those concepts here, it’d be really helpful. Not only for closure, but also to make sure that there’s a community that can speak for its needs and wants. What is your message to someone who stammers and someone who doesn’t? To all people who stammer: we are most often a silent community. It’s up to us to make sure that we’re heard and that we put ourselves out there in some capacity. For fluent speakers out there, I’ll just give you my campaign slogan: ‘For once, just listen.’ The writer is the host, director, and co-producer of the weekly digital programme ‘Kaleidoscope with Savithri Rodrigo’ which can be viewed on YouTube, Facebook, Instagram and LinkedIn. She has over three decades of experience in print, electronic, and social media The views and opinions expressed in this column are those of the interviewee, and do not necessarily reflect those of this publication

audit.headline: GMOA warns of possible rise in dengue cases amid rainy weather
audit.summary: 26 Oct 2026 | By Staff Writer The Government Medical Officers’ Association (GMOA) has warned that dengue cases could rise again amid prevailing rainy weather conditions. Speaking at a press conference today (26), Dr. Chamil Wijesinghe of the association stressed the need to take preventive measures to curb a potential resurgence of dengue. Noting that intermittent rainfall has been experienced since the beginning of this month, he said the prevailing conditions could lead to an increase in dengue cases. He added that entomological data had also indicated a rise in mosquito and mosquito larval densities. Dr. Wijesinghe emphasised the importance of cleaning homes, workplaces and other premises, stating that such measures are essential for the long-term control and eradication of dengue.

Speaking at a press conference today (26), Dr. Chamil Wijesinghe of the association stressed the need to take preventive measures to curb a potential resurgence of dengue. Noting that intermittent rainfall has been experienced since the beginning of this month, he said the prevailing conditions could lead to an increase in dengue cases. He added that entomological data had also indicated a rise in mosquito and mosquito larval densities. Dr. Wijesinghe emphasised the importance of cleaning homes, workplaces and other premises, stating that such measures are essential for the long-term control and eradication of dengue. He further noted that the commencement of the North-East monsoon during October and November could contribute to a rapid increase in dengue cases, particularly in the Eastern, Northern and North Central provinces, which are affected by the monsoon. “Given the prevailing weather conditions, the likelihood of an increase in dengue cases is higher than usual. We repeatedly emphasise that when dengue cases rise, we should not focus solely on the number of patients or deaths. Instead, we should dedicate even a day or two to cleaning our homes and workplaces. We must work towards the long-term control and eradication of dengue,” he added.

audit.headline: Hospitals face colostomy bag shortage
audit.summary: 26 Oct 2026 | BY Dilanthi Jayamanne Questions have been raised over the availability of colostomy bags in Sri Lanka after social media posts claimed that the National Hospital of Galle (Karapitiya) had sought public donations to buy them. One post claimed patients were spending around Rs 20,000 a month on the bags. Speaking to The Daily Morning yesterday (25), National Hospital of Galle Deputy Director General Dr Priyantha Atapattu said colostomy bags were not available in hospitals across the country. He said two companies had submitted offers for local procurement, one quoting around Rs 9,000 per bag and the other around Rs 3,000. As the lower-priced bags had not been used in Sri Lanka before, the Technical Evaluation Committee decided to obtain 50 for testing before going ahead with the rest of the purchase, he said.
audit.body: 26 Oct 2026 | BY Dilanthi Jayamanne Questions have been raised over the availability of colostomy bags in Sri Lanka after social media posts claimed that the National Hospital of Galle (Karapitiya) had sought public donations to buy them. One post claimed patients were spending around Rs 20,000 a month on the bags. Speaking to The Daily Morning yesterday (25), National Hospital of Galle Deputy Director General Dr Priyantha Atapattu said colostomy bags were not available in hospitals across the country. He said two companies had submitted offers for local procurement, one quoting around Rs 9,000 per bag and the other around Rs 3,000. As the lower-priced bags had not been used in Sri Lanka before, the Technical Evaluation Committee decided to obtain 50 for testing before going ahead with the rest of the purchase, he said. “We obtained 50 colostomy bags through a local purchase because they were not available in the country. We are currently using these bags and have not encountered any problems with them,” Dr Atapattu said. He added that the first batch of colostomy bags purchased this year had failed quality tests and had been withdrawn from use, and that no further purchases had been made since. Meanwhile, informed sources said a tender to procure colostomy bags was under way at the Medical Supplies Division (MSD). Attempts by The Daily Morning to contact the MSD Deputy Director General for comment were unsuccessful.

audit.headline: Human Elephant Conflict: Tri-forces to gather information on tuskers
audit.summary: 26 Oct 2026 | BY Dilanthi Jayamanne Drones and local residents expected to assist monitoring The tri-forces will mainly be responsible for gathering information on the country’s tuskers under the proposed national programme to improve elephant protection and reduce human-elephant conflict, Army Spokesperson Major General Waruna Gamage said. Speaking to The Daily Morning yesterday (25), he said the information would help authorities monitor the elephants’ locations and check on their safety. “Our main role will largely be to gather information. There are around 13 tuskers in Sri Lanka, if I am not mistaken. We will gather information about them, including where they are and whether they are safe.” Technology, including drones, could be used to collect information, he said, adding that details would also be obtained from people living in areas where the elephants were found.
audit.body: 26 Oct 2026 | BY Dilanthi Jayamanne Drones and local residents expected to assist monitoring The tri-forces will mainly be responsible for gathering information on the country’s tuskers under the proposed national programme to improve elephant protection and reduce human-elephant conflict, Army Spokesperson Major General Waruna Gamage said. Speaking to The Daily Morning yesterday (25), he said the information would help authorities monitor the elephants’ locations and check on their safety. “Our main role will largely be to gather information. There are around 13 tuskers in Sri Lanka, if I am not mistaken. We will gather information about them, including where they are and whether they are safe.” Technology, including drones, could be used to collect information, he said, adding that details would also be obtained from people living in areas where the elephants were found. Responding to further questions, Major General Gamage said the initial stage of the programme had already begun. However, he said it was not possible to identify a specific district where the work had started because tuskers moved between different areas. The programme would be carried out in coordination with the Department of Wildlife Conservation, which would identify the areas where the elephants were located, he added. The initiative is being developed under a concept proposed by Defence Ministry Secretary, retired Air Vice Marshal Sampath Thuyacontha. The decision was taken at a meeting held at the Ministry of Environment on 23 October under the chairmanship of Environment Minister Dr Dhammika Patabendi. A special operations centre has been proposed at Army Headquarters to improve coordination and information-sharing among the tri-forces, the Department of Wildlife Conservation, veterinary specialists and other relevant institutions. The programme is expected to focus on preventing the killing of wild elephants and other wildlife crimes, improving surveillance and intelligence-sharing, and supporting joint operations in areas where human-elephant conflict is frequent. The proposal also includes specialised training for military personnel involved in elephant protection and closer cooperation between the armed forces and wildlife officials.

audit.headline: Kotmale Reservoir nears spill level amid heavy rain, Warning issued to downstream residents
audit.summary: 26 Oct 2026 | By Staff Writer An advance warning has been issued regarding the possible opening of spill gates at the Gamini Dissanayake Reservoir in Kotmale amid prevailing adverse weather conditions. The reservoir’s water level currently stands at 696.96 metres above mean sea level (MSL), with its storage capacity at 78.71 per cent. According to the notice, the reservoir has a remaining storage capacity of 36.381 million cubic metres (MCM) before reaching its maximum operating water level of 703.00 metres MSL. With adverse weather conditions continuing, the reservoir could reach spill level depending on the rate of water inflow. Residents living downstream along the Kotmale Oya, including Nugawela, Riverside and Mawathura, have been urged to remain highly vigilant.

audit.headline: Making space for wildlife in every garden
audit.summary: 26 Oct 2026 | By Apsara Rodrigo A garden can be more than a collection of flowering plants and neatly arranged pots. It can also become a home for insects, spiders, birds, frogs and other small creatures that play an important role in the natural world. However, many people overlook this possibility when they design and maintain their gardens. Concern about mosquitoes, dengue and unwanted insects often leads them to remove potential habitats or use chemicals to eliminate creatures they consider pests. Naturalist Channa Ekanayake believes that gardens can be managed differently. By making small changes to the way people arrange plants, reuse materials and maintain water containers, it is possible to create spaces that support wildlife without neglecting practical concerns such as mosquito control.
audit.body: 26 Oct 2026 | By Apsara Rodrigo A garden can be more than a collection of flowering plants and neatly arranged pots. It can also become a home for insects, spiders, birds, frogs and other small creatures that play an important role in the natural world. However, many people overlook this possibility when they design and maintain their gardens. Concern about mosquitoes, dengue and unwanted insects often leads them to remove potential habitats or use chemicals to eliminate creatures they consider pests. Naturalist Channa Ekanayake believes that gardens can be managed differently. By making small changes to the way people arrange plants, reuse materials and maintain water containers, it is possible to create spaces that support wildlife without neglecting practical concerns such as mosquito control. He made these observations at a lecture held by the Sri Lanka Natural History Society on the 20th of October at the Colombo University Faculty of Science. The event encouraged people to look beyond the appearance of their gardens and consider the life they can sustain. Pots, branches and other everyday materials can provide shelter for creatures that might otherwise struggle to find suitable places to live. Even a small garden can contribute to local biodiversity when it offers food, shelter and safe places for wildlife to complete its life cycles. Ekanayake also challenges the assumption that every insect is harmful. Rather than indiscriminately killing insects, he encourages people to understand their roles in the environment and find ways to coexist with them. His message is simple: a garden should not only be a space for people to enjoy, but also a place where other living things can thrive. Gardens can provide valuable habitats for creatures that people rarely notice. According to Ekanayake, ordinary garden materials can be reused to create spaces where insects and other small animals can shelter and reproduce. The spaces inside pots can offer dark, dry and sheltered conditions for insects, spiders, ants and other creatures. Moths can also use suitable places to shelter while their caterpillars complete their development. “These small habitats may not always be visible to the people maintaining a garden but they can support different stages of an animal's life cycle,” Ekanayake said. Ekanayake's approach encourages gardeners to consider how their choices affect the creatures living around them. Instead of removing every object that appears untidy, they can look at whether it provides useful shelter for wildlife. One of the common concerns about wildlife-friendly gardening is the risk of dengue. People may worry that keeping pots or other containers in their gardens will encourage mosquitoes to breed. Ekanayake addresses this concern by explaining the mosquito life cycle. Mosquitoes pass through several stages before becoming adults, beginning with eggs that hatch into larvae. The larvae subsequently develop into pupae before emerging as adult mosquitoes. He explains that the process takes time, making regular maintenance important. “Gardeners who use water containers should check them frequently, remove standing water where necessary and refresh the water regularly,” he said. According to Ekanayake, changing the water every three to four days can help manage the risk associated with these containers. His wider point is that people do not necessarily have to abandon wildlife-friendly gardening because they are concerned about dengue. Instead, they can take practical precautions while continuing to provide habitats for other creatures. “However, water management should form part of a broader mosquito-control routine, particularly in areas where dengue is prevalent,” he said. People often divide insects into two categories: useful creatures and pests that should be eliminated. Ekanayake challenges this approach, arguing that indiscriminate killing can harm creatures that have important roles in the environment. “Insects contribute to natural processes, including pollination and the food chains that sustain other animals,” he said. “Spiders also help control populations of smaller creatures.” Using toxic chemicals against every insect, regardless of its role, can therefore have consequences beyond the immediate garden. Ekanayake encourages people to learn about the creatures around them rather than automatically treating them as threats. Understanding their behaviour can help gardeners decide which problems genuinely require intervention and which creatures can safely be left alone. This approach does not mean ignoring genuine risks. Instead, it calls for a more considered response that protects people while avoiding unnecessary harm to wildlife. For Ekanayake, a garden should be a place where different forms of life can coexist. Birds, frogs, insects and other creatures are part of the natural environment, and gardens can provide them with opportunities to find shelter and survive. He points to the contrast between people expressing affection for nature and the way they sometimes manage their own surroundings. While many people say they love wildlife, their gardens may offer little space for it to live. Creating a wildlife-friendly garden does not necessarily require a large property or expensive equipment. Small changes, such as retaining suitable shelters, choosing plants that support local wildlife and reducing unnecessary chemical use, can make a difference.

audit.headline: Medium Term Revenue Strategy: Tax weaknesses to be in focus
audit.summary: 26 Oct 2026 | By Nethmi Rajawasam Sri Lanka can expect to see greater focus on addressing weaknesses in broadening its tax base and increasing tax compliance within the Medium Term Revenue Strategy (MTRS), which is to include the consultative input of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), IMF Resident Representative to Sri Lanka Martha Tesfaye Woldemicheal said in a recently published (24) exclusive webinar held by CT Smith last month. “These two points: broadening the tax base and addressing compliance and so on, are best addressed also in a holistic manner in the development of a Medium-Term Revenue Strategy (MTRS) and this is something very important that we are discussing with the authorities and also providing support on,” she said.
audit.body: 26 Oct 2026 | By Nethmi Rajawasam Sri Lanka can expect to see greater focus on addressing weaknesses in broadening its tax base and increasing tax compliance within the Medium Term Revenue Strategy (MTRS), which is to include the consultative input of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), IMF Resident Representative to Sri Lanka Martha Tesfaye Woldemicheal said in a recently published (24) exclusive webinar held by CT Smith last month. “These two points: broadening the tax base and addressing compliance and so on, are best addressed also in a holistic manner in the development of a Medium-Term Revenue Strategy (MTRS) and this is something very important that we are discussing with the authorities and also providing support on,” she said. The need for Sri Lanka to develop a Medium-Term Revenue Strategy (MTRS) was underscored in the end-of-mission statement of the Seventh EFF review in September. Stressing on the importance of sustaining Sri Lanka’s revenue target achievements under the Extended Fund Facility (EFF), Woldemicheal said that the significance of the achievements would be naught unless they were to be upheld in the long term. “The country has achieved marco-stability – now the focus is on growth. While thinking about growth, it is also important to safeguard this macro-economic stability, it’s not a given. What does Sri Lanka need to be able to respond to shocks, or absorb shocks? It all boils down to rebuilding fiscal buffers – that’s through maintaining the fiscal discipline we have seen so far. That’s exactly what enabled the Government to respond very quickly when Ditwah hit. They were able to approve a supplementary budget,” Woldemicheal said. With Fitch Ratings’ long-term issuer default rating upgrade of Sri Lanka from ‘CCC+’ to ‘B-’ with a stable outlook, the international credit ratings agency also noted Sri Lanka’s fiscal position as a key reason for the upgrade. Further, the agency noted that while continued improvements in public debt ratios and foreign exchange reserves could support a future upgrade, weaker fiscal discipline or renewed external liquidity pressures could lead to negative rating action. “It’s very important to acknowledge the very good performance the country has been showing on the fiscal targets. Tax revenue, the primary balance – all these key fiscal targets are performing really well and I agree that going forward, the focus should also be on broadening the tax base and also strengthening compliance, which is an area where we still see weaknesses,” Woldemicheal said. Referring to the EFF Fifth and Sixth review statements published by the IMF, Woldemicheal said that the IMF’s tax diagnostics are to also feed the upcoming MTRS. “If you look at our latest published document, the authorities commit under the EFF arrangement to conduct a tax diagnostics just to take stock of the tax system. And then the outcome of this exercise will feed into the development of a medium-term revenue strategy.” Woldemicheal explained that the purpose of the MTRS is to anchor revenue reforms in the medium-term, which includes identifying relevant policy or administrative reforms that need to be implemented to ensure that the revenue mobilisation effort is sustained. “It’s very important to acknowledge that the fiscal support that the Government was able to extend in 2026 was made possible by the overperformance from last year and there’s still this commitment to return to the original target starting from 2027,” she said. Sri Lankan academics have raised that though Sri Lanka’s tax policy adjustments made in the recent past under the EFF programme have reaped major fiscal gains and enabled target outperformance, the lack of parallel institutional reforms, particularly on tax administration strengthening, fail to ensure long-term sustainability of gains.

audit.headline: Officials from Mecca pact countries to meet Iranian officials in Tehran today
audit.summary: 26 Oct 2026 | by Staff Writer Top officials from Mecca Pact countries Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan are to meet Iran's leaders in Tehran on Monday in their first high-level contact since the kingdom became a pressure point in the wider Iran conflict. Saudi Arabia will be represented by Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, Pakistan by army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir, and Turkey by intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin, Saudi and Iranian officials said. The talks come as attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis have spiralled over recent weeks and rhetoric between Washington and Tehran has grown more heated. Both countries have also drawn up plans to restart the wider war, possibly after the US midterm elections on November 3.
audit.body: 26 Oct 2026 | by Staff Writer Top officials from Mecca Pact countries Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan are to meet Iran's leaders in Tehran on Monday in their first high-level contact since the kingdom became a pressure point in the wider Iran conflict. Saudi Arabia will be represented by Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, Pakistan by army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir, and Turkey by intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin, Saudi and Iranian officials said. The talks come as attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis have spiralled over recent weeks and rhetoric between Washington and Tehran has grown more heated. Both countries have also drawn up plans to restart the wider war, possibly after the US midterm elections on November 3. Monday's planned talks would be the first high-level contact between Iran and all members of the three-nation bloc since Saudi Arabia was drawn deeper into the conflict. Under the Mecca ⁠Joint Defence Agreement signed in August, an armed attack on one member is considered an attack on all. Qatari mediators met Iranian officials in Tehran on Sunday in a push to de-escalate regional tensions, Reuters reported. Qatar has, for months, played a key mediating role between Tehran and Washington. A senior Iranian official said the meeting was initiated by Pakistan, during Munir's visit to Tehran last week, as he met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and other senior officials. During the visit, Iranian officials told him there would be no talks with Washington until Tehran's demands were met, according to Iranian media. Earlier mediation efforts involving both Pakistan and Qatar helped produce an interim peace agreement in June, but the deal quickly unravelled as fighting between Iran and the United States resumed weeks later. The deputy secretary of Iran's top security body, Ali Baqeri-Kani, told state TV that Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid, Pakistan's Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin would visit Tehran for consultations with Iran’s Supreme National Security Council on regional security. Saudi Deputy Minister for Public Diplomacy Rayed Krimly said the meeting is part of ongoing efforts by the Mecca Pact countries to de-escalate the ⁠current crisis, promote diplomatic solutions, and support mediation efforts led by Qatar and Pakistan."The visit also underscores the pivotal role of the Mecca Pact states in fostering regional security and stability, and their commitment to working with all nations in the region toward achieving this goal," Krimly posted on X. Pakistan's military media wing and Turkey's Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Saudi Arabia intercepted another wave of missiles and drones on Sunday as fighting with the Houthis continued unabated. Ministers from the Mecca Pact countries held an emergency meeting in Riyadh earlier this month and agreed to ensure the "rapid deployment" of ⁠military forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia. The Houthi attacks have become an increasingly destabilising element in the US-Israeli offensive against Iran, turning US ally Saudi Arabia into a pressure point in the wider war. Tensions between Washington and Tehran have sharpened in recent days. President Donald Trump said on Friday the US may carry out another military operation against Iran and Iran's leaders have said that a renewed US military campaign would be ⁠met with a stronger response than before. Iranian security officials have told Reuters that Tehran has drawn up detailed plans to hit Gulf undersea cables if the United States and Israel attack again. A US intelligence memo this week warned that Iranian plots against American personnel had reached "advanced stages". The war, now nearly eight months old, has weighed on President Donald Trump's approval ratings ahead ⁠of the midterms. The Mecca agreement's first article says the parties shall use "all necessary means" to eliminate threats to one another's territorial integrity, sovereignty or internationally recognised borders, according to a text seen by Reuters. Efforts by Turkey’s parliament to ratify the agreement began last week and are still underway, while Pakistan approved the pact last week.

audit.headline: PHP security: Govt institutions directed to fix critical vulnerabilities
audit.summary: The Ministry of Digital Economy has directed government institutions across Sri Lanka to urgently address critical security vulnerabilities identified in PHP software, warning that the flaws could expose systems to unauthorised access, data theft and service disruptions. According to a statement issued by Sri Lanka CERT, the Ministry issued a circular on 23 October 2026, identifying the vulnerabilities as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and calling for immediate corrective action. The directive covers ministries, provincial councils, commissions, government departments, corporations, statutory bodies and government-owned companies. Under the instructions, institutions must identify all PHP-based systems and web applications and verify the software versions currently in use.
audit.body: The Ministry of Digital Economy has directed government institutions across Sri Lanka to urgently address critical security vulnerabilities identified in PHP software, warning that the flaws could expose systems to unauthorised access, data theft and service disruptions. According to a statement issued by Sri Lanka CERT, the Ministry issued a circular on 23 October 2026, identifying the vulnerabilities as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and calling for immediate corrective action. The directive covers ministries, provincial councils, commissions, government departments, corporations, statutory bodies and government-owned companies. Under the instructions, institutions must identify all PHP-based systems and web applications and verify the software versions currently in use. Affected systems must be updated promptly using the relevant security patches and following the official guidance available at www.php.net. Institutions have also been instructed to review system logs for suspicious activity and investigate any unusual incidents. Systems that cannot be updated immediately should have their internet access restricted or be disconnected from the internet where necessary to minimise potential risks. Meanwhile, GovTech Sri Lanka, which operates under the Ministry of Digital Economy, has developed a vulnerability detection tool to help identify PHP-related security weaknesses in websites. The tool is available at www.govtech.lk/cvesecure, and technical personnel responsible for government websites have been encouraged to use it to check for potential vulnerabilities. The Ministry has further instructed relevant officials to facilitate the use of the tool and coordinate with Sri Lanka CERT to obtain technical assistance where required. Government institutions have been urged to treat the matter as a priority and implement the necessary security measures without delay to protect digital infrastructure, safeguard information assets and minimise the risk of cyber incidents, the Ministry of Digital Economy added.

audit.body: Internal affairs units have been set up in State institutions to receive public complaints about wrongdoing and unfair treatment by officials, President’s Secretary Dr Nandika Sanath Kumanayake said. He was speaking at a recent programme at Temple Trees to brief District Secretaries, Divisional Secretaries and district planning directors on the next steps of the Praja Shakthi National Programme. Recalling the public protests during the economic crisis, Dr Kumanayake said public servants had faced criticism alongside corrupt politicians. However, the public had no means of seeking action against officials. “The people had the opportunity at the last election to send corrupt politicians home and bring a new force to power. But they cannot transfer or send public officials home. There is no system for that. When people go to a State institution to get something done and face wrongdoing, injustice or unfair treatment, there must be a place where they can report it. That is why we established internal affairs units in State institutions,” he said. He said some public servants did not clearly understand corruption, which he described as officials using the authority entrusted to them for personal gain. “If action is not taken against these practices at the beginning, and if people at the top behave in this way, it becomes the normal way of doing things,” he said. Dr Kumanayake said corruption had discouraged investors and led to unnecessary projects being implemented at the expense of essential ones. He said it had also contributed to the country’s debt burden, the foreign exchange shortage that hit fuel imports, higher taxes and rising poverty. He added that corruption had spread into the private sector and that Sri Lanka had fallen to one of the lowest positions internationally in preventing it. He said people had previously been reluctant to report wrongdoing because they feared for their safety and did not know where to turn. “Eventually, these issues erupt somewhere. The public protests were one such occasion,” he said. He urged the public to use the new units. “Report the wrongdoing and injustice you experience to these units. We will intervene,” he said. He also called on officials to strengthen coordination in implementing development programmes, including Praja Shakthi, and to act with integrity and efficiency.
