audit.body: 26 Oct 2026 | By Sindy Fernando Sri Lanka is considering setting up provincial-level ‘Packaging Clinics’ to help local industries improve product packaging, add value to their products, and tap into new markets, Minister of Industries and Entrepreneurship Development Sunil Handunnetti said at LankaPak 2026 on Friday (23). Handunnetti said: “We can launch the ‘Packaging Clinic’ initiative at the provincial level, starting within our industrial estates, as the IDB already possesses such industrial estates,” referring to the proposal by Sri Lanka Institute of Packaging (SLIP) President Nishan Perera, to help local industries to improve product packaging. “Packaging is often not given much consideration, as local manufacturers tend to concentrate solely on their production and are reluctant to incur the additional costs involved. However, effective use of packaging can create a significant market potential, even within Sri Lanka, while helping local industries,” he said. Handunnetti also highlighted the potential for Sri Lanka’s packaging industry to expand into international markets, particularly in South Asia and the wider Asia-Pacific region. “If the packaging industry truly grasps the art of this transformation, there is significant scope for growth for the sector across several countries in the South Asian and Asia-Pacific regions, where untapped potential exists well beyond the borders of Sri Lanka,” he said. Handunnetti added: “High-quality packaging, a robust packaging industry, is an absolute necessity at every stage. This means that ‘packaging’ cannot exist as a single, static moment. The packaging that exists today will change tomorrow, due to shifts in people, technological advancements, the integration of AI, changes in human mindsets and desires, and fluctuations in purchasing power.” “In my view, the global marketplace today is truly defined by change,” he said. Handunnetti also highlighted the importance of transport infrastructure in moving goods from industrial zones to ports and airports. “By 2030, we anticipate a nationwide network of expressways and new industrial zones will be established, enabling the transport of goods from anywhere in the country to ports within just two to three hours,” he said. “Our objective is to ensure that our goods reach various ports, not limited to the Colombo Port, but also the ports of Trincomalee and Kankesanthurai, as well as airports, as quickly as possible,” he added.

audit.headline: SLC awards certificates to 51 Level 5 umpires
audit.summary: Sri Lanka Cricket (SLC) awarded certificates to 51 newly qualified umpires who passed the Level 5 examination, the entry-level qualification for umpiring in Sri Lanka. This was stated by the SLC in a media release. The group comprised 47 males and four female umpires, who will now have the opportunity to officiate at District and Provincial tournaments organised by Sri Lanka Cricket. Their addition forms part of Sri Lanka Cricket’s ongoing efforts to ensure an adequate number of match officials are available to officiate at School, District, Provincial level competitions. The newly qualified umpires have entered a development pathway that offers opportunities to progress towards international umpiring, based on their commitment and performance. Beginning at Level 5, umpires can advance through Levels 4, 3 and 2 before progressing to First-Class status.

audit.headline: Several houses damaged by strong winds in Chilaw
audit.summary: 26 Oct 2026 | by Staff Writer Strong winds that swept through Samidugama, Iranawila in Chilaw last night (25) have damaged several houses. The strong winds reportedly struck the area at around 11:00 p.m., causing the roofs of several houses to be blown off and trees to fall. As a result of the roof damage, rainwater has seeped into the affected homes, causing considerable hardship for residents. Meanwhile, the sea off the coast of the affected area has reportedly become extremely rough. Moreover, over the past 24 hours, heavy rainfall has been reported across many parts of the island, with the highest rainfall recorded in the Karandipowal area of the Puttalam District, the Department of Meteorology said. According to the department, Karandipowal received 195.7 mm of rainfall.

audit.summary: 26 Oct 2026 | BY Staff Writer Shadab Khan scored his maiden One-Day International century to guide Pakistan to a thrilling one-wicket victory over England in Lahore on Sunday(25). Chasing 242, Pakistan recovered from 154 for nine, with Shadab remaining unbeaten on 113 off 96 balls. Gampaha recorded the highest number at 22,053, followed by Colombo with 20,384, Kandy with 8,378 and Kalutara with 6,592. A total of 4,377 cases were reported during the first 25 days of October.

audit.headline: Sustainable solutions to emotive issues
audit.summary: 26 Oct 2026 | BY DR JEHAN PERERA The Government appears set to overcome the first major challenge to one of its foundational principles, but at a cost. It has had to face down demands from sections of the Buddhist clergy and Opposition parties to release the General Secretary of the nationalist Sinhala grouping, the Bodu Bala Sena, Ven. Galagoda Aththe Gnanasara Thera from his prison sentence for contempt of court. The Government had to face a protest march organised by Buddhist monks and the Opposition parties. audit.body: 26 Oct 2026 | BY DR JEHAN PERERA The Government appears set to overcome the first major challenge to one of its foundational principles, but at a cost. It has had to face down demands from sections of the Buddhist clergy and Opposition parties to release the General Secretary of the nationalist Sinhala grouping, the Bodu Bala Sena, Ven. Galagoda Aththe Gnanasara Thera from his prison sentence for contempt of court. The Government had to face a protest march organised by Buddhist monks and the Opposition parties. Its supporters organised an even bigger march to support the Government’s position. It is notable that the general population did not get involved in either march in any substantial number. The issue has now become a test of whether the Government will uphold its commitment to apply the law equally, irrespective of a person’s position or status, even when doing so brings it into conflict with powerful nationalist and religious sentiments. The case has a specific legal history. Ven. Gnanasara was sentenced to six years of imprisonment by the Court of Appeal in 2018 for contempt of court in a case involving former military personnel where he disrupted the proceedings. The Supreme Court (SC) rejected his appeal in 2018. Former President Maithripala Yapa Sirisena subsequently granted him a Presidential pardon in 2019. Last month (September), the SC invalidated that pardon. The initial demand by Buddhist monks and their lay supporters was that Ven. Gnanasara should be permitted to wear his Buddhist robes when appearing in public before courts. The Government has indicated its willingness to examine the procedures governing the treatment of Buddhist monks in prison, in consultation with the relevant religious authorities. However, the initial demand has now been escalated into a demand for a Presidential pardon. One of the central promises of the National People’s Power (NPP) during its Election campaign two years ago was to apply the law equally to all. This commitment has shaped the Government’s approach to allegations of corruption and criminality involving individuals who previously wielded political power. The NPP Government was swept into power on a tidal wave of antipathy towards those in previous Governments who were perceived to have abused their positions for private gain. The economic collapse that Sri Lanka experienced in 2022, and the hardships endured across society, remain vivid in the public memory. The past two years have seen the Government pursuing those accused of corruption and other offences. Several high-ranking members of previous Governments have faced arrest and legal proceedings and been sentenced to jail. The ability of Opposition parties to mobilise widespread resistance against proceedings involving their leaders has been limited, as much of the general population continues to favour accountability for past financial crimes. However, the case of Ven. Gnanasara is different. It does not concern allegations of financial corruption, but the relationship between religious authority, the courts and the law of the land. This is where the distinction between respecting religious traditions and upholding the law becomes crucial. There is a sense among sections of the general population that Buddhist monks should not be treated on a par with others and that requiring Ven. Gnanasara to appear in court without his robes was unjust and contrary to the national ethos. Such sentiments reflect the special place that Buddhism occupies in Sri Lanka’s history and society. Sinhala Buddhist nationalism has been a potent political force throughout the country’s history, drawing on a heritage that extends back more than two millennia. The question is whether respect for Buddhism needs to also entail the exemption of individual monks from the ordinary requirements of the law and thereby treat them differently. Intellect and rationality may say one thing, emotion and sentiment another. The challenge would be to accommodate legitimate religious concerns through rational and lawful procedures without allowing the religious status to become a source of legal privilege. The Government has been amenable to addressing the issue of monastic robes, but has so far resisted the demand to release Ven. Gnanasara through a new pardon. President Anura Kumara Dissanayake and Government members have insisted that the Government would not bend the law to accommodate any individual. They have taken the position that any shortcomings in existing rules should be addressed by changing the rules through proper procedures, rather than by making an exception for a particular individual. If the Government holds its position, it will demonstrate that its commitment to the rule of law extends even to constituencies that have historically enjoyed considerable political influence. The Government’s approach is important not only for the country’s democratic institutions but also for its economic future. Sri Lanka is seeking to recover from its economic collapse and establish the foundations for sustained growth. The International Monetary Fund’s (IMF) analysis of Sri Lanka’s governance weaknesses have repeatedly emphasised the economic costs of corruption and institutional deficiencies. Its 2024 analysis of governance and growth concluded that comprehensive and coherent reforms could bring significant macroeconomic benefits. The IMF’s last year’s (2025) assessment also highlighted the importance of sustained governance reforms in unlocking the country’s growth potential. Investors, both domestic and foreign, need confidence that public institutions function according to predictable rules, that contracts and property rights are protected, and that political connections or social status will not determine how the law is applied. Sri Lanka has long sought the leap towards prosperity that has proved elusive under successive Governments. Economic reform alone will not achieve it. The connection between the rule of law and economic prosperity is direct. Businesses are more likely to invest when they can expect disputes to be resolved fairly, public resources to be managed transparently and regulatory decisions to be made on rational grounds. No country can achieve a durable economic take-off if its institutions are perceived to operate according to political favour, inherited privilege or communal pressure. Sri Lanka cannot afford to return to a political culture in which powerful interests are shielded from accountability while ordinary citizens bear the costs. Changing a political culture that has evolved over the decades if not centuries is a difficult undertaking, particularly in a country where political leaders have long relied on religious and communal identities to consolidate their support. It requires not only firmness but also sensitivity, dialogue and a willingness to reform laws and institutions where genuine deficiencies exist. The present controversy offers an opportunity to demonstrate that these objectives need not be in conflict. The Government can respect the Buddhist clergy’s concerns about the treatment of monks in prison while not conceding an exemption from a judicial sentence. It can recognise the importance of Buddhism to the country while maintaining that no religious or political authority stands above the law. The question is whether national traditions and the ethos are interpreted in ways that strengthen justice, responsibility and social harmony, or invoked to defend privileges that undermine them. The country needs a transformation in public expectations from privilege to accountability, from communal claims to equal citizenship, and from personal discretion to institutions governed by the law. This requires negotiation and discussion with the people including the religious clergy. The Government’s handling of the case involving Ven. Gnanasara is therefore about more than one monk or one sentence. This particular case will determine whether the Government can build a system in which no Government, religious authority or politically influential individuals can place themselves beyond the law. A sustainable solution will ultimately require public acceptance and support. The writer is the Executive Director of the National Peace Council The views and opinions expressed in this column are those of the writer, and do not necessarily reflect those of this publication

audit.body: 26 Oct 2026 | BY JATILA KARAWITA Ex-captain says took leaf out of Brook’s book Credits Avishka and Pavan’s maturity and class Notes victory will be tonic for SL cricket Ex-Sri Lanka white-ball captain Dasun Shanaka says that the team had always believed chasing down a daunting target of 429 to win their run-laden Bank Alfalah ODI Tri-Series match against England on Thursday (22) by 2-wickets, was within their abilities. He made this remark speaking to emcee Zainab Abbas of the host broadcaster, during the post-match review by the television commentary team, on what proved to be a record-shattering One-Day International (ODI) at the Rawalpindi Cricket Stadium. “It was an incredible run chase from where we were a couple of nights before,” Shanaka said. “It was very important to cross over the line and chasing 400 plus is never easy. Really happy about the way each individual performed.” Asked as to when Sri Lanka had believed it was chasable when faced with a humongous total mid-innings, the former skipper put it down to pre-match team talk and a new-found belief. He identified them as factors which had turned a seemingly insurmountable target to one which they managed to overcome with a delivery to spare. “See there was a lot of team talk before the games happened and one thing which stands out is Gary (Kirsten). He is very clear about how we must play.” The all-rounder said that if England captain Harry Brook could bat the way he did in producing a double century (116-ball 202) to propel his team to what seemed to be a match-winning score at the half way stage, there was no reason for Sri Lanka to not take a leaf out of his book and get across the line. “To be honest Brooksy played one of the knocks, credit to him and we really enjoyed it being the opposition team. But at the same time what we thought was, if they (England) could do that, why couldn't our team do that. That was the discussion.” Shanaka recalled to the format after more than two years, remarked that in a chase as steep as the one which they faced on Thursday, it was crucial to start well, and noted that they had got there despite skipper Kusal Mendis perishing for a duck via a runout without facing a delivery. He credited centurion Pavan Rathnayake (130) and opener Avishka Fernando (97) for underlining their maturity and class during the now-emphatic chase, and praised Janith Liyanage-with an unbeaten 61 off 27 balls, for finishing things off for the Lankans. “He (Liyanage) hasn’t finished off that many games in that way, and it was a wonderful knock to see as well,” observed Shanaka, who himself dazzled his way to a 50-ball 97 inclusive of eight maximums and six fours, to keep the Lankan reply afloat after being promoted in the order. When questioned by commentator Roshan Abeysinghe as to how his team had psychologically managed to be in the game when faced with an uphill challenge, the former captain put it down to being in a now or never situation, having lost the triangular series opener to hosts Pakistan two days earlier by 37-runs. “See, for us it was now or never. If we had lost tonight then we would have been out of the competition. It was the mindset of the players. To be honest, I think Janith (Liyanage) had spoken to the coach and captain, of myself going higher in the order. So, I think it was the right decision to make in this game and it was the turning point.” He added that he had felt the target was within his team’s reach during the 166-run third-wicket partnership between Fernando and Rathnayake, and emphasised that his mindset was to time the ball well while rotating the strike, when striding out to bat. Pressed as to what the surreal result would do to cricket here, Shanaka observed that it was important to turn tables on a strong ODI team as England, and maintained that there were still match-winners sitting out as well as more talented players back home. “There are a few players who are absent as well. I feel that this win could boost Sri Lankan cricket, for the players and to everyone that see that we can do this, so keep believing that is the thing we need to ask.”

audit.headline: Tourism: Arrivals surpass 1.8 m in 2026
audit.summary: Sri Lanka recorded over 1.8 million tourists arrivals so far this year, according to latest data released by the Sri Lanka Tourism Development Authority (SLTDA). According to the latest figures, a total of 1,813,484 tourists arrived in the country between 1 January and 22 October, while SLTDA reported that 119,805 tourists arrived in Sri Lanka between 1 October and 22 October. India topped as the leading source of tourist arrivals this year, with a total of 482,944 Indian nationals visiting Sri Lanka, followed by the United Kingdom (UK) with 169,405 arrivals, China 120,980 arrivals and Germany 102,920 arrivals, SLTDA stated. India also recorded the highest number of tourist arrivals during the first 22 days of October, with 45,530 visiting the country, according to SLTDA.

audit.headline: Un admission: Govt mulls cut in humanities intake
audit.summary: 26 Oct 2026 | BY Dhanushka Dharmapriya The Government is considering curtailing student intake for humanities courses at universities, as part of proposed revisions to degree programmes aimed at improving graduate employability. Deputy Minister of Dr Madhura Senevirathna told The Daily Morning that the Ministry was considering several approaches to address the mismatch between university education and the skills required in the job market. “We need to revise the courses to align them with our National Development Goals and improve employability. But this alone will not solve the problem,” he said. He said new policies were being developed for engineering, agriculture and medical education, given their importance to the country’s future development. He added that Sri Lanka would need more technicians, technologists and engineering designers in the coming years.
audit.body: 26 Oct 2026 | BY Dhanushka Dharmapriya The Government is considering curtailing student intake for humanities courses at universities, as part of proposed revisions to degree programmes aimed at improving graduate employability. Deputy Minister of Dr Madhura Senevirathna told The Daily Morning that the Ministry was considering several approaches to address the mismatch between university education and the skills required in the job market. “We need to revise the courses to align them with our National Development Goals and improve employability. But this alone will not solve the problem,” he said. He said new policies were being developed for engineering, agriculture and medical education, given their importance to the country’s future development. He added that Sri Lanka would need more technicians, technologists and engineering designers in the coming years. “In agriculture, we are looking at a wider range of roles, including farming and research. A system is also being developed to improve communication with farmers and help increase agricultural productivity,” he said. Dr Senevirathna said Sri Lanka had one of the highest proportions of humanities students relative to those in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) fields. “The high number of humanities graduates facing difficulties finding employment has prompted us to consider changes to university admissions and course content. On the one hand, we will be looking at curtailing the high number of humanities intakes, while on the other hand, we will examine how humanities courses can be made more employable,” he said. The Deputy Minister’s remarks come amid concerns raised by local academics, activists and international organisations, including the International Monetary Fund (IMF), over the gap between university education and the skills sought by employers.

audit.headline: Why Police warnings keep falling on deaf ears
audit.summary: The Police Media Division has once again urged the public to be wary of strangers who come calling through dating applications and social media. Its latest warning, issued on Saturday (24), describes a now familiar pattern. A fraudster poses as a would-be friend, lover or even prospective spouse, spends days or weeks winning the victim's trust, and then persuades him or her to install an application presented as a dating platform. In reality, that application is malicious software, often an Android package file, which opens the door to the victim's phone, passwords and, ultimately, bank account. There is nothing wrong with the advice. Indeed, it is sensible, clear and timely. However, it is hardly new.
audit.body: The Police Media Division has once again urged the public to be wary of strangers who come calling through dating applications and social media. Its latest warning, issued on Saturday (24), describes a now familiar pattern. A fraudster poses as a would-be friend, lover or even prospective spouse, spends days or weeks winning the victim's trust, and then persuades him or her to install an application presented as a dating platform. In reality, that application is malicious software, often an Android package file, which opens the door to the victim's phone, passwords and, ultimately, bank account. There is nothing wrong with the advice. Indeed, it is sensible, clear and timely. However, it is hardly new. The Police, the Central Bank and the commercial banks have issued similar warnings for years, whether about lottery messages, fake parcel deliveries, investment schemes promising impossible returns or callers pretending to be bank officials. Yet the complaints keep coming and the losses keep mounting. The more uncomfortable question, therefore, is not what the public should do, since that is already well known, but why so many people continue to ignore what they have been told. Part of the answer lies in the nature of the trap itself. These scams do not target the intellect; they target the heart. A lonely widower, a young man working far from home or a spouse starved of attention does not greet a warm message with the caution he or she would apply to a stranger asking for a loan. The fraudster knows this, and so takes time to build what feels like a genuine bond before making the first request. By the time the link arrives, the victim is no longer dealing with a stranger, at least in his or her own mind. Moreover, shame works in the criminal's favour. Many victims, particularly those lured by promises of sexual services or illicit companionship, are reluctant to report what has happened, because doing so means admitting how they were caught. Consequently, the true scale of the problem is almost certainly larger than the complaints suggest, and the lessons that might have been learnt from each case are never shared. There is also a deeper problem, and it is one of literacy. Sri Lanka has moved rapidly to smartphones, mobile banking and digital payments, but public understanding of these tools has not kept pace. A great many users cannot tell a genuine app store from a file forwarded on WhatsApp, nor do they understand why a one-time password must never leave their hands. Financial literacy is similarly thin, and those who do not grasp how money moves between accounts are easy prey for anyone who speaks with confidence. Warnings alone, therefore, will not solve the problem. A press release reaches those who already follow the news; it rarely reaches those most at risk. What is needed is a sustained national effort to raise digital and financial literacy, much as earlier campaigns improved public awareness of health and road safety. The school curriculum is an obvious starting point, since today's students will be tomorrow's account holders, if they are not already. Banks and telecommunications companies, which have profited handsomely from the digital shift, must also shoulder more of the burden. They could send regular, plain-language alerts in Sinhala, Tamil and English, hold back unusual transactions for verification, and make it far easier for customers to freeze an account at the first sign of trouble. Grama Niladharis, religious institutions, community organisations and the media have a role to play too, particularly in reaching older citizens and those in rural areas. At the same time, the law must be seen to work. When fraudsters are traced, prosecuted and punished, and when those cases are publicised, the deterrent value is considerable. Victims, for their part, should be able to come forward without fear of ridicule. Ultimately, however, no campaign can replace personal vigilance. A stranger who asks for money, a password or the installation of an unknown application is not a friend, whatever he or she may claim. If the public can be taught to pause, question and verify, these criminals will find this country a far less profitable hunting ground.

audit.headline: Wimalasurendra Reservoir begins to spill following heavy rains
audit.summary: 26 Oct 2026 | by Staff Writer The Wimalasurendra Reservoir began spilling today (26) following heavy rainfall reported in the Norton Bridge area since morning. Accordingly, water levels in the Kehelgamu Oya, which flows into the Kelani River, as well as in the Kelani River itself, have risen, authorities noted. In view of the rising water levels, authorities have urged residents in low-lying areas along the rivers and in surrounding areas to exercise heightened vigilance over the next several hours.
